articles.title: "It's Just About Being with My Friends": Children's Perspectives on the Use, Risks and Benefits of Virtual Worlds Platforms
articles.authors: Cláudia Silva; Miguel Barreda-Angeles
articles.abstract: Despite the central role that virtual worlds based on user-generated content, such as Roblox, play in the digital lives of children and adolescents, research incorporating their first-hand experiences and perspectives of these platforms remains limited. Roblox is one of the world's largest virtual world platforms, used predominantly by children and adolescents, with most users estimated to be under the age of 16. Grounded in a children's rights perspective, this study adopts an arts-based qualitative approach that combines cognitive mapping through drawing with follow-up interviews to explore what children's and adolescents' perceptions of Roblox reveal about its risks and benefits. To address this aim, we engaged 29 children aged 10–16 in partnership with an international school in Italy. Our analysis identifies three key findings with theoretical and regulatory implications. First, rather than simply as a game, participants perceive and use Roblox primarily as a social platform where they play and communicate with friends, form new relationships, and maintain long-distance connections. Related to that, participants also perceive Roblox as operating in ways that resemble social media platforms.  Second, these social dynamics are closely intertwined with risks, including exposure to scams, toxic interactions, grooming, online dating practices, and monetisation pressures. Third, participants routinely migrate to platforms such as Discord and WhatsApp for communication, circumventing Roblox's age-based restrictions and complicating platform-specific safeguarding efforts. These findings highlight the need for adaptive safeguarding strategies and contribute to theoretical discussions of the increasingly blurred boundaries between digital games and social media and children’s online safety.

articles.title: Who Speaks When the Chatbot Answers? Generative AI as Institutional Speech
articles.authors: Bibhor Acharya; Sandesh Gupta; Himani Moktan
articles.abstract: When a branded chatbot answers a customer, the reply is often taken as the institution speaking. This paper treats that uptake as a media and communication problem rather than as a model-accuracy problem alone. Using Erving Goffman’s account of footing—the gap between who animates an utterance and who stands as its principal—and Austin and Searle’s account of commitments as speech acts, we read the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal decision in Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149) as a public episode of institutional speech gone wrong. A website chatbot told Jake Moffatt that a bereavement fare could be claimed retroactively within ninety days; a different page on the same site, and later human staff, denied that path. Air Canada argued it should not be held liable for the chatbot; the tribunal disagreed and ordered damages. The case lets us follow authorization, utterance, uptake, contested repair, and the failed attempt to split the animator from the principal. While systematic reviews of AI disadvantages map privacy, displacement, and bias at a macroeconomic scale, they leave open this micro-communicative surface where an institution’s name is attached to a fluent reply. We argue that handoff to a named human is part of the speech act when commitment is at stake, not an optional engineering fallback.

articles.title: The Architecture of the Unreal: Translating Kandinsky’s "Inner Necessity" into a Cinematic Framework
articles.authors: Amirhossein Amini
articles.abstract: Modern narrative cinema frequently traps itself in a materialist cage, caught between the mechanical reproduction of mundane reality and the hollow calculation of digital spectacle. This paper resurrects Wassily Kandinsky’s 1911 philosophy of "inner necessity" (Kandinsky, 1977) and translates it into a structural framework for Unreal Cinema. Rather than accepting the "unreal" as a generic aesthetic, this theory demands reality-breaking. By establishing an exacting Subtraction Test, the methodology explicitly dismisses commercial franchise spectacle—where the impossible serves merely as digital decoration over a fundamentally materialist core—to isolate films whose dramatic engines strictly require impossibility. The paper constructs a comprehensive taxonomy divided into four categories of materialist escape: Autonomous Reality, The Impossible Intrusion, Historical Subversion, and The Subjective Fracture. Utilising a diverse roster of directors—including Guillermo del Toro, Peter Jackson, Hayao Miyazaki, Darren Aronofsky, Satoshi Kon, and Tomm Moore—as core case studies, the framework establishes a hierarchical gradient to map the remaining cinematic landscape. This gradient rigorously separates true structural rebellion from ambitious edge cases, such as expressionist exaggeration or rationalised psychological tethers. By expanding Kandinsky’s vision to the cinematic medium, this paper argues that true cinematic art demands the creativity and courage to project an internal reality, actively refusing to merely recapture the world as it is. Cinema reaches its highest generative threshold only when it requires the architectural invention to abandon the pre-existing scaffolding of the physical world. To achieve the profound spiritual weight Kandinsky demanded on the canvas, filmmakers must systematically shatter the physical laws of the baseline universe.

articles.title: Moving Beyond Statistical Significance: How to Improve the Reporting and Interpretation of Medical Research
articles.authors: Alessandro Rovetta; Mohammed Ali Mansournia; Pavlos Msaouel; Winston Lin; Steven Stovitz; Alessandro Vitale; Anna Chiara Frigo; Richard Riley; Sander Greenland
articles.abstract: Many methodologists have warned against interpreting statistical estimates through dichotomous labels such as “significant” and “non-significant.” Yet, articles in medical journals still rely heavily on P-value thresholds and confidence interval boundaries to guide inference and communication of research findings. Here, Rovetta and colleagues discuss how such a focus on statistical “significance” obscures clinical relevance and uncertainty, whilst distorting evidence appraisals. Rather, they suggest P-values and confidence intervals should be interpreted as continuous measures of compatibility between data and hypotheses, which also reflect choices about how data are collected, modeled, and analyzed.

articles.title: From ban to boundaries: how 100 high-impact journals regulate AI-generated images after the 2026 policy shift
articles.authors: Shirley Yang
articles.abstract: Generative AI can draw explanatory figures and can also fabricate research images. We asked how the 100 highest-impact journals regulate AI-generated images and how those rules changed in a year. On 30 September 2026 we captured each journal’s author instructions and the publisher policies they cite. We retrieved archived versions from September–October 2025 and coded rules for five image types. At baseline, 79 journals belonged to publishers that prohibited AI-generated images. Between May and August 2026, Taylor & Francis, Elsevier and Springer Nature replaced these bans with rules that depend on image type. By September 2026, 55 journals explicitly permitted AI-generated explanatory illustrations and 58 permitted AI-assisted data visualisations, usually with disclosure or reproducibility conditions. For 89 journals, AI-created or AI-altered primary research images were prohibited; no journal permitted them. Rules for graphical abstracts and covers varied most. The Science journals, The Lancet family and JAMA Psychiatry still restricted illustrative uses. Twenty-seven journals gave instructions that contradicted or lagged behind their publisher’s current policy, including 20 of 31 Springer Nature journals. Authors need to check journal-level instructions, and publishers need to align them.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Prevalence and Persistence of Data Implicated in Article Retractions
articles_hidden.authors: Ashvin Narayan; A.J. Million; John T Kubale
articles_hidden.abstract: Sharing study data has become a regular aspect of the research process, often required by journals, funding agencies, and other stakeholders to facilitate study replication and collaboration among researchers. However, while post-publication remedies—retractions, corrections, and expressions of concern—have long been used to flag ethical issues in scientific literature, their application to corresponding data is inconsistent, potentially contributing to the spread of dis- and misinformation. A lack of standardized corrective mechanisms to address problematic data hinders the identification of problematic datasets, researcher assessments of their impact, and associated determinations of data reliability. Using the Inter-University Consortium for Social and Political Research (ICPSR) and its catalog of social-scientific data as a case study, we seek to identify problematic datasets and establish workflows for evaluating the reliability of archived data. In this paper, we identify ICPSR datasets associated with publications requiring post-publication remedies. We examine editorial notices of post-publication remedies and data documentation to identify errors and/or ethical concerns affecting ICPSR datasets. Our work highlights how inconsistent documentation and communication about post-publication remedies inhibit the use of traditional corrective publishing mechanisms extended to the research data space. This work also seeks to identify resources and practices that may better facilitate processes of data re-evaluation and remediation, helping to mitigate the downstream impacts of data-related issues on scientific research.

articles.title: One Gender Axis, Two Vocabularies: How People Conceptualize Gendered Speaking and Singing Voices
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Gender-affirming voice care is organized around speech, yet many people also want to change how they sing. Whether the two rest on one concept of vocal gender is unknown. Participants (N = 2,536) described what makes a speaking voice and a singing voice sound feminine and masculine, rated their current and ideal voices in each modality, and named people whose speaking and singing voices they would like to have. I embedded the descriptions with a sentence encoder and analyzed them, together with word frequencies, in exploratory analyses. The feminine–masculine direction in speaking descriptions was nearly identical to the direction in singing descriptions (cosine = .967), and a classifier trained on one modality separated the other with almost no loss (area under the curve = .960 and .979). The shared direction was carried by register, softness, and depth words; singing descriptions added range, notes, and power, and speaking descriptions added softness, roughness, and monotony. Individuals’ own contrasts aligned only modestly across modalities (mean cosine = .362). Wanting a more feminine speaking voice predicted choosing a female singer but not a more acoustically feminine singer within gender category. Vocal gender appears to be a shared, category-level abstraction expressed in modality-specific vocabulary.

articles.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to estimate how common alcohol references and alcohol-related brand references are among influencers on Instagram
articles.authors: Jack Delmenico; Dan Anderson-Luxford; Emmanuel Kuntsche; Jingda Du; Zhen Du; Megan Cook; Charlotte Jonhston; Paula O'Brien; Simone Pettigrew; Benjamin Riordan
articles.abstract:
Background: Young people spend hours on social media every day, where following influencers is the norm. Influencers post frequently about alcohol and alcohol brands and there has been a rise in influencer marketing. However, prevalence estimates rely on manual analyses of only a small number of posts. We used a large language model (LLM) to estimate at scale how often top Australian Instagram influencers reference alcohol and alcohol brands, and whether this varies by influencer type.
Methods: We identified 988 of the most-followed Australian Instagram influencers and retrieved all 667,531 of their posts that were visible to all users, including those under 18 (i.e., not age gated). An LLM classified whether each post referenced alcohol and these were screened manually to record brand references. Influencers were coded into 14 types (e.g., athletes, actors).
Results: Most influencers (87.45%) referenced alcohol and 47.10% referenced an alcohol brand in at least one post. Overall, 20,448 posts (3.06%) referenced alcohol and 2,869 (0.43%) a brand (14% of alcohol-related posts). Food influencers posted the most alcohol and brand-related content, while athletes posted the least alcohol-related content but had the highest proportion referencing a brand.
Conclusions: Influencer alcohol-related and alcohol-related brand content is pervasive on Instagram and reaches audiences of every age, including those under 18 who should not see alcohol advertising.
So what: Given the link between exposure and use, health promotion should aim policies and strategies at reducing alcohol-related content, particularly branded content that likely reflects influencer marketing.

articles.title: From Named Voice to Measured Sound: A Recording-to-Representation Pipeline and a Leakage-Safe Protocol for Repeated-Stimulus Designs
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: People routinely name a singer they would ideally sound like. Turning that named exemplar into a measurable acoustic target, and asking whether a person’s verbal concept of a gendered voice predicts the sound they select, requires a reproducible bridge from catalog metadata to validated vocal acoustics and an evaluation protocol that cannot be satisfied by memorizing which artists appear in training. I describe both. A recording-to-representation pipeline (exemplar resolution, preview retrieval, vocal-stem isolation, eGeMAPS and singing-specific feature extraction, and artist-mean aggregation with reliability filtering) yielded acoustic profiles for 113 artists from 1,690 tracks, linked to 1,546 of 2,536 participants. In a discovery, confirmation, and hold-out design specified in a dated analysis plan, the desired direction of vocal change predicted the acoustic gender profile of the chosen singer, but its generalization to artists never seen in training did not meet the plan-specified criterion once a leakage step was corrected (retention 67.2%, 95% CI [.23, .88]), whereas participants’ specific verbal descriptions added no acoustic information beyond gender category and popularity (a bounded null). A contrastive two-tower model, retrained under a corrected protocol, also recovered no structure beyond that category. I provide the protocol in reusable form: blocking by the repeating stimulus, a retention ratio that diagnoses memorization, a chance-corrected retrieval metric, a leakage audit, and a runnable worked example.

articles.title: Unconscious Archetypal Selection Bias in Professional Ice Hockey: A Multivariate Positional Analysis of Astrological Ephemeris Data and the Relative Age Effect
articles.authors: David R. Juillet; Jorge M. Rodrigues; Joanne V. Longtin
articles.abstract: This study investigates whether unconscious scouting bias exists in National Hockey League (NHL) talent acquisition, driven by psychological and behavioral archetypes. Analyzing a dataset of 777 players across all 32 NHL rosters, the research quantifies standard physical maturity biases, such as the Relative Age Effect (RAE), against independent lunar variables (Sign, Element, Modality) mapped to emotional typologies. Utilizing exact binomial tests, Cohen’s h effect sizes, and Savage-Dickey Bayes Factors (B10), 4,864 distinct positional configurations were evaluated. Results indicate no archetypal solar advantage capable of overcoming the RAE physical penalty. However, when evaluating independent lunar placements across specific positional subgroups (e.g., Centers, Left Wings, Right Wings, Defensemen), extreme localized scouting biases emerge. Front offices consistently filter players through highly distinct, positional psychological profiles, with 13 franchises exhibiting three or more concurrent statistical anomalies, indicating that human evaluation networks unconsciously draft for specific behavioral mechanics.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: The samplr package: A tool for modeling human cognition with sampling algorithms
articles.authors: Lucas Castillo; Yun-Xiao Li; Adam N Sanborn
articles.abstract:
Many models of cognition have sampling as a central component. These have been used to explain human performance across a wide range of tasks, involving perception, probability reasoning, and choice. 
One family of these models takes inspiration from sampling approaches developed in statistics, either by adjusting samples with prior beliefs or by implementing a sampling algorithm that overcomes the difficulty of independent samples at the expense of autocorrelation. 
While these models have been successful in modeling human behavior, their adoption has been slowed by the technical difficulties in applying them. 
Here, we introduce the samplr package, which includes a variety of these algorithms and cognitive models built upon them. We show how models in this package can match qualitative patterns found in human data, and walk readers through an example of how to compare these models quantitatively to human data. This tool aims to make these methods accessible to many more researchers.

articles.title: Cultural and Personality Predictors of Attitudes Toward AI Chatbots: A Systematic Literature  Review
articles.authors: Michelle Ming Ertl; Katherine Moore
articles.abstract:
As AI chatbots are becoming increasingly relevant in our daily life, understanding what shapes
people’s attitudes toward them is becoming more important. This systematic literature review
brings together the findings of 34 articles (from across multiple countries) to examine how
personality traits and one’s cultural background predict attitudes towards AI chatbots. The
review suggests that culture works as a primary filter that sets a person’s starting position when
they encounter AI. Western users tend to approach chatbots with more skepticism and stronger
privacy concerns, while on the other hand East Asian users show higher comfort with social AI
interaction. Within each of these cultural settings, individual personality traits fine-tune these
responses, but which trait matters most changes depending on the culture. Agreeableness
drives trust in Western samples, while Conscientiousness drives trust in Arab ones. Technology
specific variables like Personal Innovativeness in Information Technology (PIIT) and AI
configuration anxiety turned out to be stronger predictors than broad personality traits overall.
The review also identifies a persistent global gender gap in AI adaptation that operates
differently depending on cultural setting. Limitations include the overrepresentation of young
university educated participants in existing research, the Western bias present in both study
samples and AI training data, and the ongoing confusion between physical robot findings and
text-based chatbot research. The paper concludes that effective chatbot design and AI policy
require culturally adapted approaches rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

articles.title: Affect and Words: An Instrument for the Quantitative Analysis of Emotional Vocabulary in Open-ended Responses.
articles.authors: Nigel Manchini; Óliver Jiménez; Natalia Sylvia Ramos Díaz; Daniel Trias
articles.abstract: In a context where emotions play a central role in discussions on psychology and education, the availability of various techniques and resources to assess emotional experience becomes essential. Quantitative language analysis provides a window to emotional experiences, rarely used in Spanish-speaking contexts. This study develops and cross-culturally validates an annotated dictionary of explicit emotional vocabulary, a tool for analyzing affective variables from texts and open-ended responses. A systematic protocol and expert judgment were used to select and annotate 1,041 lexical families (3,051 lemmas and 18,934 words), and pre-recorded hypotheses about the validity of the instrument were tested. Participants, adolescents from Uruguay (n = 1,208, 59% female, age M = 14.4) and Spain (n = 596, 41% female, age M = 15.7), completed Subjective Well-Being (SWB) scales and wrote about their emotional experiences in an open-ended response. The dictionary showed convergence with other instruments and acceptable inter-rater reliability. When applied to open-ended responses, it captured a substantial proportion of the words written by participants and showed significant correlations with SWB in both the Uruguayan and Spanish samples. These results suggest that quantitative analysis of open-ended responses allows the exploration of well-being, and that this freely available instrument is a valid resource for doing so, serving as a complement to quantitative and qualitative approaches for research or intervention purposes.

articles.title: Two sides of the same coin in memory: Speech and its accompanying gesture are remembered together
articles.authors: Yang Liu; Tilo Kircher; Luyao Chen; Yifei He; Benjamin Straube
articles.abstract: When a speaker gestures, speech and gesture form one multimodal event. Memory research mostly asks how gestures help people remember speech, not how the gesture is remembered or how the two relate. Participants watched videos of an actor speaking sentences with a related gesture or none (Experiment 1, N = 20), or a related or unrelated gesture (Experiment 2, N = 43). They recognized written sentences and, for each called old, judged whether a gesture had been present (Experiment 1) or related (Experiment 2), with confidence ratings. Recognition was better after related than unrelated gestures, but not better after related gestures than none. Gesture judgments were above chance and more accurate for confidently recognized sentences; for these, participants also tended to report non-matching gestures as matching (Experiment 2). Gesture reports thus appear partly retrieved with the sentence and partly inferred from it: memory for speech and gesture is closely coupled.

articles.title: “Puzzling, Yet So Refreshing”: Experiencing the Value of Neurodiversity Within an Inclusive Choir
articles.authors: Nicolas Petit; Géraldine Dessertenne; Fanny Aprile; Lucie Jurek
articles.abstract: The social challenges encountered by autistic people are increasingly understood as a double empathy problem: a mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic individuals, rather than an autistic deficit. This paradigm highlights a need for inclusive spaces that foster mutual understanding, yet this remains challenging, especially in the French sociocultural context which is less familiar with the social model of disability developed in the anglophone world. As this model stresses that the majority largely shapes the social environment, finding ways to influence the general population’s attitudes toward autism is critical. Choral singing offers a promising medium to do so and facilitate cross-neurotype dynamics, as it is thought to have evolved as a biological mechanism to foster social bonding. Accordingly, this qualitative study explored how 12 general population choristers experienced a 6-month neurodiverse choir shared with 8 autistic adolescents and 3 autism specialists. We used a two-stage qualitative design, first capturing individual experiences through an open-ended online questionnaire, and subsequently deepening our analysis through a discussion with a community stakeholder panel. The findings revealed an intrinsically demanding experience, especially emotionally and cognitively, counterbalanced by important benefits, as it was also described as joyful and powerful, encouraging personal growth among the choristers and a shift in their perceptions of autism. These findings support the neurodiversity paradigm and suggest that choral singing may offer a promising double empathy solution, facilitating intergroup contact to reduce prejudice and thereby remove social barriers to the inclusion of autistic voices.

articles.title: When the brain can change: effects of neuroplasticity education on beliefs about brain-based mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery. We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs. Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control. The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2. The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall. The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders. In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance. These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.

articles.title: Coming of Age in Polarized Times: Affective Polarization Across Adolescence
articles.authors: Jakob Kasper; Gijs Schumacher; Lysanne te Brinke; Eveline Crone; Bert N. Bakker
articles.abstract: Concerns about affective polarization among young people have grown in political, media, and academic debate. Yet, despite adolescence being a crucial period of identity formation and young people’s central role in shaping the future of democratic societies, little is known about when affective polarization emerges, and how it varies across adolescence and political environments. Drawing on survey data from adolescents (N = 7,031; ages 11–25) and adults (N = 9,997; ages > 25) in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Austria, Poland, and Greece, we examine within-adolescence age differences in affective polarization, adolescent-adult differences, and temporal variation in affective polarization levels around a major political event. We find that affective polarization is already visible by early adolescence and differs remarkably little across adolescent age groups, challenging the expectation that affective polarization increases sharply around the transition to the legal voting age. Comparisons with adults in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and Austria show that adolescents are consistently less affectively polarized than adults. Further, our longitudinal panel evidence from the Netherlands suggests that adolescent affective polarization varies with the broader political environment, increasing around the 2023 parliamentary election and declining thereafter. This illustrates that adolescent affective polarization is not fixed but varies with political dynamics, highlighting adolescence as an important period for educational efforts that foster democratic engagement and constructive political disagreement.

articles.title: Measuring musicality at home: Preliminary validation of the Music@Home questionnaires in a Greek population
articles.authors: Katerina Drakoulaki; Christina Anagnostopoulou; Angeliki Triantafyllaki; Orianna Bairaktari; Aikaterini Nina Polytimou
articles.abstract: Music@Home was developed in the United Kingdom as a systematic instrument for the assessment of informal musical interactions in the home environments of children under the age of 5. It has been successfully adapted and validated in German, and widely used in research with typically developing children, children with neurodevelopmental disabilities, and adults reporting their early music exposure retrospectively. In the present study, we adapted and conducted a preliminary validation of the Music@Home Infant and Preschool questionnaires for a Greek-speaking population. A total of 238 Greek-speaking primary caregivers completed either version, along with measures of cognitive stimulation at home and child language and communication development. Both Greek questionnaires demonstrated acceptable to good confirmatory fit, strong internal reliability, and evidence for divergent validity, with test-retest reliability established for the Preschool version, indicating that musical engagement represents a distinct aspect of the home environment rather than general cognitive stimulation. Exploratory analyses revealed modest positive associations between Infant scores and parent-reported language outcomes, consistent with previous research linking early musical experiences and language development. These findings provide initial evidence that the Greek Music@Home is a psychometrically sound tool for assessing the home musical environment in Greek-speaking populations and highlight the value of cross-cultural adaptations for research on music cognition, language, and broader developmental outcomes.

articles.title: Ostensive affective feedback and the emergence of the capacity to negotiate communicative content: the psychology of establishing agreement.
articles.authors: Wouter Wolf
articles.abstract: Inferring agreement, that is, inferring that mental content is mutually considered to be sufficiently aligned for the purposes of an interaction, is crucial for many facets of human sociality. Importantly, humans are highly skilled at facilitating such inferences through communication. Yet even within communicative interactions, agreement might fail for interpretive reasons (uncertainty or misunderstanding) or alignment reasons (disagreement). Solving either of these problems often requires iterative communicative interactions during which the content of mental states is negotiated until misunderstandings are repaired and/or disagreements are resolved through compromise. But what social cognitive mechanisms allowed humans’ successful negotiation capacities to emerge, even when conventionalized negotiation and communication systems were not available? Here, I argue that humans developed the capacity to directly negotiate the content of communication by understanding the interactive intent underlying ostension in a previously underappreciated way: To infer a lack of agreement in communicative interactions, a key piece of evidence lies in how the other reacts to one’s communicative act. However, this reaction is often ambiguous. I argue that ostension helps facilitate interpreting such reactions, not only through assumptions of mutual relevance, but in large part due to pragmatic tension that arises from ostensive non-affirmative affective feedback. This tension forces individuals to isolate content as a separate dimension of communicative acts that can be evaluated and negotiated. This facilitates the resolution of interpretive problems through boundary-setting and disagreement through compromise. As such, ostensive feedback has likely played a major role in the emergence of human sociality.

articles.title: Made in the Culture, Not the Voice: Lyrical Camp, Production Texture, and the Queer Anthemization of Popular Songs
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Why do some popular songs become queer anthems while others, including many by openly queer artists, do not? We tested musical affordance and historical contingency accounts in a purposive corpus of 100 songs (69 artists) designed to dissociate queer authorship, explicit queer lyrical content, and community adoption. Adoption was measured as an evidence-coded anthemization score from URL-verified documentation of Pride, drag, ballroom, club, activist, and queer-media use. Anthemization was unrelated to whether artists were publicly queer (rs = −.02) and only weakly related to explicit queer lyrics (rs = .22). Among 16 language-model-coded lyrical themes, camp potential predicted anthemization after family-wise correction and controls for era, genre, authorship, and explicit content (partial r = .40, n = 55). The association replicated with masked lyrics, among songs the coding model could not identify, with a second coding model, and with two independent outcome coders (partial r = .45–.54, n = 46), although it was not robust when the model's own anthem judgements were also partialled out. Full-mix acoustic descriptors related to formant energy and voicing predicted anthemization (|rs| = .38–.43, family-wise p < .05) but vanished when computed on Demucs-separated vocal stems (n = 80), locating the acoustic signal in production texture rather than the singer's voice; spectral brightness was confounded by genre and era. Outcome reliability was moderate (weighted κ = .57). The results support reception-centred accounts of musical queerness. They implicate lyrical camp and production as affordances for queer adoption, not a characteristic queer voice.

articles.title: The impact of professional development programs on K–12 teachers’ AI literacy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: YING MA; Chloe Gordon; Tingting Li; Ziwen Teuber; Theresa Dicke; Taren Sanders; Michael Noetel; Rebecca J Collie; Kewen Liao; Chengliang Wang
articles.abstract: Teachers' artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is an increasingly important focus of professional development (PD). This systematic review synthesized evidence from 62 empirical studies (61 records), including 36 studies eligible for effect-size estimation, involving pre-service and in-service teachers. Most programs emphasized AI-related knowledge and skills, with less systematic attention to attitudinal and ethical dimensions. Common design features included temporal flexibility (e.g., synchronous and asynchronous learning), role diversification (e.g., co-designers and collaborators), and contextual orientation (e.g., task- and project-based learning). The primary combined-design multilevel meta-analysis after influence diagnostics, based on 212 effect sizes from 34 studies, indicated a significant positive average effect across knowledge, skills, and attitudes/values (g = 0.76, 95% CI [0.50, 1.02], p < .001). Substantial heterogeneity indicated considerable variation across programs and contexts. Although possible small-study effects and publication selection may have inflated the magnitude of the primary pooled estimate, Bayesian selection-model analyses continued to support a positive average effect. No statistically significant moderation was detected by career stage, school level, intervention-duration category, research design, outcome measurement type, or gender composition. These findings provide an important quantitative benchmark for the emerging evidence base and indicate that AI literacy PD can support multiple dimensions of teachers' AI literacy.

articles.title: Multi-party simulations with human participants and role-based LLM conversational agents: A design framework and validity evidence for organizational research
articles.authors: Yuki Nozaki; Naho Fujisawa; Yoshinobu Kano
articles.abstract: Dynamic organizational phenomena often unfold through ongoing communication among multiple interdependent actors, yet studying them involves trade-offs among realism, controllability, and scalability. We propose a methodological framework for using role-based conversational agents powered by large language models (LLMs) as multi-party interaction partners in organizational research. It specifies how to create standardized but contingent interaction environments through scenario design, persona prompts, interaction protocols, and iterative testing. In a preregistered illustrative study of leadership communication, we analyzed 394 employees’ text-based simulations powered by GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5 Flash, or Claude Sonnet 4.6. Across models, participants perceived the agents as anthropomorphic and animate, and as acting consistently with their assigned backgrounds, personalities, and linguistic styles. Behavioral coding corroborated and extended these perceptions, with deviations from assigned persona prompts in 2.59% of utterances. Participants’ utterances also yielded codable indicators of theoretically relevant behavior, in this case leadership communication. These findings provide initial validity evidence that multi-party LLM-agent simulations can create plausible interaction environments, deliver persona-consistent stimuli, and elicit behaviorally analyzable responses. We also offer practical guidelines on model selection, replicability, and ethics.

articles.title: Echoes of Thought: Task Complexity, Inner Speech Analogs, and Prompt Design Shape LLMs' Response
articles.authors: Franziska Usée; Daniel Schad
articles.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across a wide range of tasks, yet
the mechanisms behind theirresponse behaviorremain poorlyunderstood. Drawing on insights from
cognitive science and the computational framework of model-free and model-based reinforcement
learning (RL), we examined conditions under which GPT-3.5 and four open-weight LLMs can exhibit
behavioral signatures of model-based RL in the two-step task, a well-established paradigm for
studying human learning and decision-making. Across nine simulation studies, we varied the task
complexity and prompt design to examine conditions under which previously reported model-based
RL signatures could be replicated. We found that GPT-3.5 showed model-based RL signatures in
simplifiedtasksettings,butthattheseeffectsdisappearedunderde-simplifiedtaskversions.Crucially,
model-based reasoning signatures could be re-established when incorporating an inner speech-
analog prompt, requiring the LLM agent to reflect on previous trials and anticipate consequences of
future actions. For the open-weight LLMs tested, diminished signatures of model-based reasoning
evolved under both de-simplified and facilitative task conditions. Our fine-grained analyses of
behavioral learning dynamics highlight the role of structured reflective and anticipatory linguistic
processes in enabling complex response patterns in LLMs and reveal both similarities and differences
to human decision-making patterns.

articles.title: Adaptive Memory and Metacognition in Older Adulthood: A Path Towards Successful Aging
articles.authors: Ashley Chen; Kara Hoover; Emma Kandel; Alan Castel
articles.abstract: Aging is characterized by normative changes in memory and a continued capacity for goal-directed learning and adaptation. Consequently, the maintenance and preservation of cognitive abilities that enable responsible remembering (e.g., selectivity, schematic support) and build resilience may equip older adults with the skills needed to navigate memory challenges in a technologically-advanced world. Research demonstrates that older adults can effectively monitor and self-regulate their behaviors under high task demands, modify encoding strategies to compensate for memory declines, and draw upon prior knowledge and expertise to reinforce learning. Regularly engaging in leisure activities (e.g., creative hobbies, curiosity-driven exploration, educational classes about aging and cognition) may also enhance neuroplasticity, lower dementia risk, and promote positive self-perceptions of aging. Overall, leveraging older adults’ metacognitive abilities and enhanced motivation through targeted interventions may offer a promising approach to promoting successful aging among an increasingly growing aging population.

articles.title: The Male Evaluator Penalty: How Participant Sex and Relationship Context Shape the Perceived Credibility of Male Sexual Violence Victims
articles.authors: Martina Giorgio; Robyn Mooney
articles.abstract: Male victims of female-perpetrated “forced-to-penetrate” sexual violence experience significant psychological harm and stigma shaped by traditional gender scripts. However, research is scant regarding how such victims are perceived by others. This study investigated how participant sex (male vs. female), perpetrator-victim relationship context (intimate partners vs. strangers), and male rape myth acceptance affect the perceived credibility of male sexual violence victims. Using an experimental vignette design, 300 participants (50.3% male, aged 18-35) living in the Netherlands were asked to read a description of a female-perpetrated sexual assault and complete self-report measures of perceived victim credibility and male rape myth acceptance. Results of a moderated multiple regression analysis indicated that higher myth acceptance universally predicted lower credibility ratings for the male victim. Furthermore, male evaluators displayed significantly higher myth acceptance and rated the victim as less credible overall than female evaluators. Crucially, male victims assaulted by an intimate partner were perceived as significantly less credible than those assaulted by a stranger, but this penalty was applied exclusively by male evaluators. These results highlight the urgent need for targeted education for legal professionals and gender-inclusive legal reforms to ensure equitable justice for male victims of female-perpetrated sexual violence.

articles.title: Dyadic Theory of Mind profile shapes verbal cooperation and the trajectory of non-verbal cooperation
articles.authors: Roksana Markiewicz; Ali Mazaheri; Katrien Segaert
articles.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is thought to support cooperation, yet it is studied as a property of individuals, even though cooperation is achieved by two people together. We examined whether cooperation depends on the ToM profile of a dyad: the pair's average ToM and the mismatch (absolute difference) between partners. Unacquainted pairs completed two cooperation tasks. In a verbal task, each partner held information needed to solve a shared problem, and partners had to talk to combine it. In a non-verbal task, partners synchronised button presses without communicating, adjusting their timing based on feedback. ToM was assessed using the Movie for the Assessment of Social Cognition (MASC; Dziobek et al., 2006); fluid intelligence was controlled. Across both paradigms, we found converging evidence that cooperative performance was shaped by the interaction between partners’ ToM abilities, beyond individual ToM ability in isolation. In the verbal task (N=171 pairs), larger ToM mismatches were associated with poorer cooperative performance in pairs with relatively low average ToM, whereas higher average ToM attenuated this detrimental mismatch effect. In the non-verbal task (N=175 pairs), the same pattern emerged only over time: pairs with large ToM mismatches and relatively low average ToM improved their synchrony more slowly, so that their disadvantage was most pronounced late in the task, when cooperation depends more on anticipating the partner’s adjustments. Taken together, our findings suggest that ToM operates not only as an individual socio-cognitive capacity but also as a dyadic resource that shapes how partners establish shared representations in cooperative settings.

articles.title: Aligning how we measure and support social media addiction with young people's lived experience
articles.authors: Lukas J. Gunschera; Jamil Adjallah; ioanna fokas; Gabriel Mackie; Jo Hickman Dunne; Alice Roe; Jade Davies; Camilla Nord; Margarita Panayiotou; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Social media use is widely conceptualised as a potential addiction. However, the instruments used to index it are reformulations of criteria developed for established addictions, presuming pathology rather than establishing it. We inverted the direction of inference, integrating lived experience from adolescents who feel addicted to social media and experienced substantial life impairment as a consequence. We conducted eight in-person workshops with 44 adolescents (contributors) to discuss experiences constituting social media addiction, their perceived harms, and how those experiencing it could best be supported. We examined correspondence between lived experiences and features of established addictions, such as conflict (interpersonal struggles and loss of self-control), salience (preoccupation with social media), and tolerance (needing more to get the same effect). Discussions of how, by whom, and through what means adolescents could be supported were analysed using framework analysis. Correspondence between lived experience and the prevailing addiction model was partial and asymmetric. Of 121 experiences, 58.7% described conflict or salience, none described tolerance, and few described withdrawal (2.5%) or relapse (7.4%). A fifth (20.7%) fell outside the model. Effects on sleep, attention, mental health, and time displacement were ranked as most harmful, while impaired control and social comparison ranked lower. Discussions of support revealed a strong sense of individual responsibility, alongside agreement that platform redesign, provision of alternative activities, and shifts in social norms would be most effective. Clinical addiction intervention was rarely raised, despite frequent use of medical addiction language and analogies. These results raise questions about current addiction models and the assumption of pathology applied to social media use. Future work should move beyond these frameworks and ground conceptualisation and measurement in lived experience rather than predefined notions of disorder.

articles.title: Do People Think ChatGPT Is Conscious? Evidence from a Large Polish Sample
articles.authors: Hubert Plisiecki
articles.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT are increasingly treated by the public as if they
possess subjective experience, with multiple studies probing the popular opinion on the matter. The
present study provides the first large-scale measurement of this phenomenon in Poland. A
nationally distributed online survey panel (N = 1,736) rated ChatGPT’s capacity for conscious
experience on a 1–100 scale. "Most respondents (74%) attributed ChatGPT at least minimal
consciousness on the continuous rating scale, closely mirroring prior U.S. findings; because this
figure is sensitive to question format, however, we conservatively estimate that more than 10% of
respondents would affirm ChatGPT's status as an experiencer under a stricter, categorical framing.
Small exploratory associations suggested that older and more highly educated participants were
slightly more skeptical, whereas right-leaning respondents attributed slightly more consciousness.
A multivariate regression confirmed that these associations were not simply artifacts of
confounding among demographic variables, though together they explained less than 3% of the
variance in consciousness attributions. These effects, though modest, indicate theoretically relevant
variation. Interpreting these results through Epley’s three-factor anthropomorphism model, the
work argues that limited mechanistic understanding of LLMs, highly human-like behavior, and
unmet social needs likely contribute to widespread phenomenal consciousness attribution. Given
ethical concerns about over-trust, parasocial attachment, and responsibility misperception, these
beliefs matter for AI deployment and governance. Our findings highlight the need for evidence-
based educational strategies that improve public understanding of how LLMs work while allowing
beneficial use of the technology

articles.title: Morphological analysis when morphemes are hard to detect: evidence from infixation and reduplication
articles.authors: Dave Kenneth Tayao Cayado; Kathleen Rastle
articles.abstract: There is substantial psycholinguistic evidence that skilled reading involves morphological analysis, whereby morphologically complex words like teacher are recognised via constituent morphemes {teach}+{-er}. The ability to recognise morphemes is vital as it allows readers to interpret both familiar and unfamiliar words. However, over 50% of the evidence for this claim comes from studies of suffixation in English, where morphemes typically have a relatively consistent surface form across exemplars (clean in cleaner, cleanliness; -ed in walked, jumped). It remains unclear whether morphological analysis is also robust when morphemes lack a consistent surface form. Using the morpheme interference paradigm in Tagalog, we test whether infixes and reduplicants are detected during prelexical processing. Infixes are inserted within a stem and therefore reduce the consistency of its surface realisation (e.g., tawag → t-in-awag ‘called’), while reduplicants involve partial or full copying of a stem and therefore lack a consistent surface realisation (e.g., tawag and lundag become tatawag ‘will call’ and lulundag ‘will jump’, where ta- and lu- are instances of the same reduplicant morpheme). We found robust morpheme interference effects in both accuracy and RTs. Specifically, nonwords with morphological structure induced significantly lower accuracy and longer RTs than nonwords without. Our findings show skilled readers’ acquired sensitivity to these sophisticated morphological structures and motivate refinements to theories of morpheme learning.

articles.title: Retro-cue Characteristics and Visual Masking Differentially Influence Voluntary and Involuntary Attention
articles.authors: Germán A. Cipriani; Carlos González-García; Elisa Martín-Arévalo; Juan Lupiáñez; Fabiano Botta
articles.abstract: This study examined whether voluntary and involuntary retrospective attention prioritize competing working memory (WM) representations involving low-level perceptual features and high-level semantic categories. In external attention, interactions between attentional voluntariness and representational level have been reported, with voluntary and involuntary attention differentially modulating high- and low-level content. In contrast, previous WM studies using either central or peripheral retro-cues found no such interaction. We therefore tested whether increasing retro-cue predictivity and using fully non-predictive cues would reveal this dissociation. We also investigated whether late visual masking promotes retrospective attention by protecting WM representations from visual interference. Across four experiments (n=140), retro-cue reliability (Experiments 1a–1b) and late visual masking (Experiments 2a–2b) were manipulated using peripheral and central retro-cues. Reaction times and accuracy were modeled using hierarchical drift-diffusion modeling. Voluntariness did not differentially modulate competing perceptual and semantic WM contents. Furthermore, four novel findings emerged: (1) voluntary attentional benefits on WM representational quality were enabled by increasing the reliability of central retro-cues and operated through protection from visual interference; (2) reducing retro-cue predictivity from low to non-predictive had little effect on involuntary attention elicited by peripheral retro-cues, whereas evidence for central retro-cues remained ambiguous; (3) eliminating late visual masking generally did not reduce voluntary attentional deployment; and (4) for peripheral retro-cues, masking selectively altered involuntary attentional benefits across representational quality and retrieval processes in opposite directions, while increasing the difference between voluntary and involuntary attentional deployment. Together, these findings indicate that retro-cue type, reliability, and visual masking differentially influence voluntary and involuntary selection in WM without altering their relative effects on competing perceptual and semantic representations.

articles.title: Naar een nieuwe generatie gedragsinzichten voor beleid: Denk na over hoe mensen kunnen en willen meedoen in de samenleving
articles.authors: Denise De Ridder; Lotte Frederike van Dillen; Marleen Gillebaart; Inge Merkelbach; Lars Tummers; Beate Volker; John de Wit
articles.abstract: In de afgelopen jaren zijn grote stappen gezet om beleid effectiever te maken door beter rekening te houden met wanneer en waarom mensen bereid en in staat zijn om hun gedrag te veranderen. Nu is het tijd om te bedenken wat belangrijke opgaves zijn voor de toekomst van gedragsinzichten voor beleid. Wij zien vier belangrijke kwesties: (1) Baseer beleid op het inzicht dat mensen in beginsel zonder hulp van buitenaf in staat zijn om verstandige keuze te maken; (2) Integreer interventies gericht op individuen in structurele of systemische maatregelen die mensen helpen hun gedrag te veranderen; (3) Richt interventies op intermediaire actoren en sociale netwerken die een rol spelen bij de implementatie van gedragsinterventies; en (4) Gebruik falende interventies als diagnostisch instrument om beleidsmaatregelen aan te passen. Mede op basis van een opiniepeiling onder Nederlandse beleidsmakers/gedragskundigen, gaan we in deze sessie in debat met de deelnemers over innovatie in gedrag en beleid met als doel hen te inspireren. We bespreken de relevantie van deze speerpunten, en hoe de wetenschap de praktijk hierin het beste kan ondersteunen.

articles.title: Can You Read Me Through the Screen? Only Extraversion Shows Distinctive Personality Accuracy in Face-to-Face and Videoconferencing Interactions
articles.authors: Valentina Andreeva; Maxim Likhanov; Elina Tsigeman
articles.abstract: Existing theories yield competing predictions regarding personality perception accuracy in face-to-face versus videoconferencing. While cue-reduction frameworks suggest videoconferencing deceases accuracy, social presence perspectives argue decreased constraints facilitate self-expression, leaving the impact of videoconferencing unresolved. This study examined personality perception accuracy following face-to-face and videoconferencing interactions. Previously unacquainted participants (N = 168; 40 videoconferencing and 44 face-to-face dyads) engaged in 40-minute interaction. Pre- and post-interaction Big Five self- and partner-ratings were analyzed via the Social Accuracy Model, partitioning accuracy into distinctive and normative components and controlling for assumed similarity. Results demonstrated that videoconferencing neither impaired nor enhanced distinctive personality accuracy relative to face-to-face. Trait-level analyses revealed only extraversion exhibited significant distinctive accuracy across both formats. These findings indicate perceptual accuracy is driven less by communication modality and more by diagnostic behavioral cues and trait observability.

articles.title: Measuring Multimodal Social Skills in the Digital Age: Development and Validation of a Questionnaire
articles.authors: Aike Horstmann
articles.abstract: As inherently social beings, humans possess specialized communicative capacities, that are essential for fostering social connection and supporting both personal and collective well-being. In an increasingly technology-driven social landscape, a psychometrically sound instrument is crucial for assessing these evolving social skills, identifying individuals experiencing interpersonal difficulties, and evaluating targeted interventions over time. This paper reports the development and validation of the Multimodal Social Skills Questionnaire (MSSQ), an instrument designed to assess social skills across diverse interaction modalities, including both online and offline environments. Multimodal social skills comprise six core dimensions: Assertiveness, Receptivity, Flexibility, Authenticity, Appreciativeness, and Resilience. Across two studies, the aim was to establish the scale’s factor structure, reliability, and construct validity. In Study One (N = 322) an initial pool of 120 items was subjected to exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and iterative item reduction, resulting in a preliminary six-factor solution. In Study Two (N = 260), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the refined six-factor structure. Construct validity was supported by expected patterns of convergent and discriminant correlations with established measures. Across both studies, the MSSQ showed strong internal consistency. Overall, the findings support the MSSQ as a reliable and valid instrument for assessing multimodal social skills in the evolving digital age.

articles.title: Constraints on kinship semantics reflect cognition over cultural practice
articles.authors: Maisy Hallam; Simon Kirby; Fiona Jordan; Kenny Smith
articles.abstract:
Languages encode similar semantic features in their kinship terminologies, the set of words denoting family members, but different languages seem to prioritise different distinctions. Is any configuration of kinship semantics possible, or are there commonalities across languages in which distinctions are encoded? We use computational methods to identify clear cross-linguistic tendencies in how six semantic features are encoded in kinship terms. Across 1242 languages, all encode information on Generation, while other features like Gender or Seniority are less consistently encoded. Importantly, the features are encoded in a predictable order of importance.  We find that this tendency mirrors participants' behaviour in a linguistic categorisation experiment, suggesting kinship semantics reflect cognitive biases active at the level of the individual. 
Additionally, despite claims that kin terms are a straightforward reflection of social practice, we find varying evidence for this; kin term semantics systematically correspond with patterns of descent, but not marriage norms.

articles.title: Slips of Action in Everyday Life: Capturing Habitual Smartphone Checking with a Decoy App Paradigm
articles.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Jonas Dano; Michael J. Moustaka; Lukas J. Gunschera; Sanne de Wit
articles.abstract: The study of habit has long faced a trade-off between experimental control and ecological validity. We translated a core laboratory test of habit to daily life: whether people continue responding despite knowing it no longer produces its outcome. For one week, participants (N = 74) replaced a frequently used social media app with a nonfunctional decoy icon. The original app was either removed (Detox) or relocated (Switch). Taps on the decoy were recorded as action slips. Nearly all participants slipped (97%), with mean daily slips dropping from 9.76 on the first day to 1.08 on the last across both groups. Slips correlated with baseline app openings (rs = .61) and self-reported automaticity (rs = .40), but not with motivation to reduce usage, problematic use, perceived control, or well-being (|rs| ≤ .09). Decoy slips thus capture a key behavioural signature of habit and reveal how strong app-checking habits can be.

articles.title: Loneliness is reflected in the sub-second temporal dynamics of the resting brain: an EEG microstate study
articles.authors: Kentaro Ono
articles.abstract: Loneliness, a subjective state of perceived social isolation characterized by chronic social hypervigilance, is a profound risk factor for physical and mental health conditions. While functional neuroimaging studies link loneliness to altered salience network connectivity, the sub-second temporal dynamics of the resting lonely brain remain unexplored. We investigated the relationship between trait loneliness and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) microstates. Sixty-one healthy young adults completed the UCLA Loneliness Scale and Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) and underwent 3-minute resting-state EEG recording. A criterion-based five-class microstate solution identified a topography corresponding to the canonical Class C/E, associated with both self-referential and salience-related processing. Higher loneliness scores were significantly associated with reduced Class C/E occurrence, which remained significant after controlling for depressive symptoms, age, and sex. Exploratory source localization revealed that lonelier individuals showed reduced current density in the middle cingulate cortex (MCC). These findings suggest that chronic social hypervigilance suppresses the spontaneous mobilization of the salience network at rest, with reduced MCC engagement reflecting a dispositional attenuation consistent with chronic relational threat.

articles.title: Seeing good and bad for what they are: Preverbal infants discern valence in geometric-agent interactions
articles.authors: Yaying (Tiffany) Bai; Hiromichi Hagihara; Yasuhiro Kanakogi
articles.abstract: Animated shapes have informed much of what is known about early sociomoral cognition, but concerns have been raised about this approach and the interpretations based on it. In particular, whether infants perceive interactions between geometric agents as socially and affectively meaningful has received little direct attention, despite being a prerequisite for moral evaluations. Two preregistered experiments conducted between 2025 and 2026 addressed this gap in infants aged 6.5 to 10.5 months (N = 92; 43 girls), recruited from middle-socioeconomic-status families living in urban and suburban areas of [city name], Japan (all Japanese or other East Asian). In Experiment 1 (n = 28; 13 girls), infants preferentially attended to agent-directed, relative to perceptually matched object-directed, caressing (prosocial) and hitting (antisocial), which indicates sensitivity to social structure. In Experiment 2 (n = 64; 30 girls), infants attended more when caressing and hitting were preceded by affectively congruent rather than incongruent music (i.e., prosocial-positive, antisocial-negative), suggesting that they attributed corresponding valence to these interactions. The results substantiate the use of geometric-agent paradigms and provide evidence that foundational evaluations of good and bad emerge within the first year of life, extending prior findings beyond simple approach-avoidance responses to prosociality and antisociality.

articles.title: Biased processing of multiple outcomes in human reinforcement learning: evidence from computational modeling and eye-tracking
articles.authors: Henri Vandendriessche; Gruson Charlotte; Antonios Nasioulas; Camille Straboni; Maël Lebreton; Stefano Palminteri
articles.abstract: In many circumstances, choices result in multiple simultaneous outcomes, all of which should be integrated to optimally update reward expectation. Yet, to date, empirical investigations of reinforcement learning have mostly focused on situations where choices deliver only one outcome at a time. To understand how humans learn from multiple outcomes, we designed a new reinforcement learning task, where the selection of an option resulted in two outcomes drawn from the same underlying distribution over potential gains and losses, even if ultimately only one of the two counted for the final payoff. Behavioral results show that the two - equally informative- outcomes are considered, yet asymmetrically as function of their valence. This behavioral observation is backed up by computational analyses showing that, on top of previously documented asymmetric update, multiple outcome integration is biased, such as it overweighs rewards over punishments. Behavioral and computational results were paralleled by eye-tracking analysis showing that attention deployment is biased by outcome valence and relevance. The main results were confirmed in a second experiment featuring complete feedback information. Overall, our findings suggest that, when options deliver multiple discordant outcomes, losses tend to be neglected compared to gains.

articles.title: Embodied mirroring increases interpersonal synchrony of movement and social connection established in subsequent conversations
articles.authors: Yasemin Abra; Christine Falter-Wagner; Irene Sophia Plank
articles.abstract: Interpersonal synchrony, the alignment of behaviours between individuals, is thought to facilitate social connection and rapport. However, less is known about whether synchrony can be intentionally fostered and whether its effects extend beyond the context in which it is established. We examined whether participation in the Mirror Game, a fundamental exercise from theatre where two players nonverbally imitate each other’s movements, influences subsequent interactions between previously unacquainted strangers. Using recordings of facial expressions, gaze patterns, and movement, we captured multi-modal conversational dynamics during a conversation. In line with our preregistered hypothesis, dyads who played the Mirror Game before conversing exhibited greater interpersonal synchrony of movement than those who performed a non-social movement exercise, suggesting a carry-over effect of instructed to emerging interpersonal synchrony. Furthermore, playing the Mirror Game prior to the conversation also increased positive social connection and rapport. However, increased interpersonal synchrony of movement on the level of the dyad did not account for these social benefits, challenging straightforward accounts linking synchrony to social connection. By contrast, exploratory analyses further revealed that behavioural patterns capturing interpersonal adaptation at the individual level predicted participants’ positive social experiences and feelings of connection emerging in the conversation. Together, these findings demonstrate that a brief shared embodied activity can shape the quality of a subsequent interaction and provide new insight into the processes through which positive social connections emerge between strangers.

articles.title: Expertise Shapes the Multidimensional Perception of Stories
articles.authors: Qingzhi Ruby Zeng; Derek Lilienthal; Coraline Rinn Iordan; Aaron Steven White; Elise A. Piazza
articles.abstract: Storytelling is a primary means of human connection and creative expression, but it is unclear how mechanisms of story perception may vary across people with differing expertise. Here, we examined how expertise in creative storytelling shapes ratings of five dimensions of story quality (creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, cohesiveness), as well as how these ratings are influenced by four linguistic feature categories (language productivity, lexical predictability, semantic similarity, and lexical composition). Online storytellers (N=18) improvised six spoken stories each (for a total of 108 stories). The transcript of each story was rated by both novices (N=10-31) and creative writing/storytelling experts (N=15) on the five story dimensions and analyzed using the four linguistic feature categories above. Overall, experts and novices provided similar average ratings, and their rating spaces both showed two distinct underlying principal components–essentially, creativity and cohesiveness–which were, in turn, predicted by distinct linguistic features. However, experts perceived the five dimensions as more differentiated, and their ratings were less driven by linguistic features than novices’. These findings indicate that experts’ judgments are more nuanced but also may rely less on fine-grained structural features of narratives, highlighting the importance of capturing individual differences and multidimensionality in story perception.

articles.title: Everyday use of AI for emotion regulation depends on the person and the situation
articles.authors: Simon M. Li; Junkang Averi Lin; Shufang Sun; Shanshan Xu; Bin Yu; Mark S. Chen
articles.abstract: Young adults increasingly use AI to seek support and manage their feelings. Understanding when and where they use AI for emotion regulation (ER) and its effectiveness can provide evidence needed for research, practice, and policy. In a 13-day ecological momentary assessment study, 3,048 Chinese university students reported emotional situations, ER strategies, and affect four times daily. AI use for confiding, advice, or emotional support was reported on 2.0% of 134,275 prompts and by 17.3% of participants at least once. In person-level logistic regression, use was concentrated among students with greater lifetime AI use (OR up to 3.12); in multilevel logistic regression, it was more likely during digital, academic, and interpersonal situations (OR 1.22-2.56). AI use did not predict next-prompt affect overall, but was followed by lower positive affect when neither stressors nor positive events had occurred, weakening as more events co-occurred. AI has entered everyday ER as a context-dependent resource.

articles.title: The Genesis of Grievance: Examining the Formation of Grievances and their Impact Upon Violent Extremist Outcomes
articles.authors: Bettina Rottweiler; Paul Gill
articles.abstract: The causal role of grievances, personal and political, is commonly attributed to the development of violent extremist outcomes. However, our conceptual and empirical understandings of how grievances develop and why only a minority with grievances go on to become radicalised remain underdeveloped. This paper uses structural equation modelling to examine the effects of perceived victimhood, personal grievances, and anger rumination on attitudes and intentions to engage in violent extremism via revenge motivation and reduced self-control capacity. We further analyse the protective effects of trait forgiveness on anger rumination and revenge motivation as well as self-control. The findings demonstrate that the experience of personal grievances mediates the effects of individuals’ tendency for interpersonal victimhood on anger rumination. The findings further highlight the mediating effects of revenge motivation and low-self-control on individuals’ attitudes and intentions to engage in extremist violence. We also demonstrate the indirect protective effects of trait forgiveness on support for and intentions to engage in extremist violence via its negative relationship with anger rumination, revenge motivation and low self-control. Our findings have important practical implications. Anger rumination may serve as a warning sign that an individuals’ perceived victimhood and personal grievances are translating into an increased vulnerability and potential escalation towards engagement in violent extremism, and thus may be a crucial point of intervention. During this rumination phase, there may be opportunities to intervene in the case by sign-posting critical information or warning signs about the consequences of going further than simply ruminating. Collectively, this suggests ways to inform programmatic approaches to prevent and counter violent extremism, while suggesting future avenues for joint risk assessment and management efforts tackling violent extremism.

articles.title: Bounding Causal Effects in Pretest-Posttest Designs with a Control Group
articles.authors: Muwon Kwon; Peter M. Steiner
articles.abstract: With data from a pretest-posttest design with a nonequivalent control group, researchers have two main options for identifying the causal impact of a treatment: covariate adjustment (CA) or difference-in-differences (DID). Each strategy rests on strong assumptions: the adjustment criterion (unconfoundedness) for CA and the common trend assumption for DID. In practice, neither of these assumptions is typically fully satisfied, resulting in biased effect estimates. To address uncertainty about potential assumption violations, we propose reliability-based bounds for the average treatment effect (ATE) that rely on a linear structural causal model and the reliability of the outcome's pretest measure with respect to an unobserved confounder. Unlike existing bracketing approaches, the reliability-based bounds do not require the stationarity assumption and remain valid even when the pretest and posttest measures are on different scales. Using simulated data, we demonstrate that the proposed bounds outperform existing methods by covering the true ATE even when stationarity is violated, while often producing narrower bounds when stationarity holds. The bounds also remain informative under moderate violations of linearity and the single-unobserved-confounder assumption. An empirical example illustrates how the bounds are established based on subject-matter knowledge and that they tend to cover the benchmark effect estimate from a corresponding randomized experiment.

articles.title: Does Parent-Rated Neurocognitive Functioning of Children with ADHD Moderate the Effects of Different Behavioral Parent Training Techniques?  A Randomized Controlled Microtrial
articles.authors: Dominique Petra Amadee Doffer; Barbara van den Hoofdakker; Tycho Dekkers; Rianne Hornstra; Marjolein Luman; Saskia van der Oord
articles.abstract: The effectiveness of behavioral parent training (BPT) techniques for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may vary across individuals. Using a microtrial, we studied whether parent-ratings of child “hot” and “cool” executive functions moderated effects of stimulus-control (antecedent-based) versus contingency-management (consequent-based) techniques on child behavioral difficulties. Parents of 92 children with ADHD were randomly assigned to antecedent-based training, consequent-based training or waitlist. Results indicated that consequent-based techniques were particularly effective for children with lower arousal regulation and higher reward responsivity, while antecedent-based techniques were most effective for children with lower sensitivity to aversive stimuli. Possible explanations for these findings are discussed.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: Digital Reflections of Social (Dis)connectedness: A Snapchat Data Donations Study
articles.authors: J. Loes Pouwels; Milou Tilstra; Lara Vreeswijk; Nienke Prot; Michelle Alexandra Pingel
articles.abstract: By linking self-reported psychosocial experiences to actual Snapchat interactions, the present study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of how social experiences are reflected in digital contexts. Specifically, the study investigates how adolescents’ experiences of friendship closeness, peer belongingness, loneliness, and social exclusion are related to adolescents’ online interactions with friends by combining real-time experience sampling methodology (ESM) with objective social media data from Snapchat. Participants were 123 adolescents (M age = 13.33 years; SD = 1.10; 58.50% girls). Adolescents with higher disconnectedness (i.e., greater loneliness and social inclusion) had more unanswered friendship requests and spent relatively more time on messaging. After controlling for multiple testing, social (dis)connectedness was not associated with the actual number of sent or viewed messages in the past two months, the number of friendships, Snapscore, or Snapchat AI usage. These findings do not provide clear evidence for either the social enhancement hypothesis or compensation hypothesis.
