articles.title: Displacement and Compensation: How Online and In-Person Interactions Relate to Adolescents’ Social and Emotional Connectedness
articles.authors: J. Loes Pouwels; Marlies Maes; Daan Hulsmans; Maaike Verhagen
articles.abstract: By proposing that superficial online interactions displace deeper, in-person connections, displacement theory has given rise to widespread societal concerns about adolescents' use of social media. However, previous research only showed limited evidence for the displacement theory. Therefore, this study aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of how both online and in-person interactions shape adolescents' sense of connectedness. A total of 335 adolescents in Grades 7-9 participated in a 4-week Experience Sampling Methodology study. Three times a day, they reported on their in person and online interactions with friends and peer groups, as well as the quantity and quality of these interactions and their perceived connectedness to their friends and peer groups. Multilevel analyses will be used to examine how the occurrence of in-person and online contact, as well as the quantity and quality of these interactions, are related to adolescents’ social and emotional connectedness.

articles.title: The other side of social dance for mental health: What needs to be addressed before it can be offered to vulnerable populations?
articles.authors: Brennan Delattre
articles.abstract: A growing body of research suggests that social dance can be good for mental health, especially for individuals with depression, anxiety, and loneliness. However, less work has been conducted investigating for whom and in what circumstances social dance is beneficial, what safety considerations should be in place, and who might not yet be included in social dance spaces. In light of ongoing research investigating whether salsa dancing should be offered as an option to patients seeking care for depression and anxiety through the United Kingdom’s National Health Service (NHS) Talking Therapies as a social prescribing initiative and on a larger scale, and given the growing interest in social dance as a mental health solution more broadly, this Perspective piece highlights key issues that need to be addressed in community-based social dance spaces before social dance can be offered safely and equitably for vulnerable populations through public healthcare prescribing channels.

articles.title: Beyond Standardized Affirmation: Transgender and Nonbinary Youths’ Experiences and Recommendations for Flexible Crisis Care
articles.authors: Juan Pablo Zapata; Alyssa N Gorkin; Aileen Kangavary; Amanda Smock
articles.abstract: Suicide rates are particularly high among transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) youth. Although gender-affirming care is increasingly incorporated into crisis services, little is known about how its delivery across crisis-care touchpoints may support or undermine safety and affirmation. This study used a youth-centered, iterative, qualitative design to examine practices shaping TGD youths’ experiences of gender-affirming care across crisis encounters. The study included 12 TGD youth aged 13–17 years (M = 16.3), all of whom reported suicidal-related thoughts and behaviors within the past month. Participants completed 22 semi-structured interviews across two iterative waves. Wave 1 explored experiences across crisis-care touchpoints and informed prototypes of gender-affirming practices, which participants reviewed and refined in Wave 2. Data underwent two-phase inductive-deductive analysis, with Wave 1 interviews coded to identify themes, and Wave 2 interviews coded to examine responses to emerging findings and practices. Across in-person acute care and virtual touchpoints, three themes described a mismatch between crisis response and gender affirmation: (1) standardized gender-affirming practiced could feel scripted; (2) agency and control over disclosure and decisions about care, shaped whether encounters felt affirming; and (3) direct and indirect experiences shaped trust and future use of crisis-care resources. A fourth theme focused on proposed improvements to gender-affirming care; across waves, participants favored approaches that adapted affirmation to individual identities, knowledge, and preferences rather than applying standardized practices uniformly. Findings highlight the need for crisis care that addresses immediate safety while tailoring gender-affirming practices to youths’ identities, knowledge, preferences, and disclosure control.

articles.title: The Not So Illusory Truth Effect: Source Credibility and the Effect of Repetition on Belief
articles.authors: Reed Orchinik; David Gertler Rand; Rahul Bhui
articles.abstract: The illusory truth effect, in which repetition increases belief, is often seen as a cognitive bias. Here, we argue that it may reflect a rational adaptation to generally high-quality information environments. A formal model shows that increasing belief in repeated statements improves accuracy when a source usually tells the truth but sometimes errs. The model captures previous findings and, unlike existing accounts, predicts that repetition should do little to increase belief when the source is not credible. In a large (N = 4,947) preregistered experiment with a quota-matched U.S. sample, the effect was substantially smaller when headlines appeared in a mostly false rather than mostly true newsfeed. In a second preregistered experiment (N = 2,484), repetition increased partisans' belief only in claims from the 2024 U.S. presidential candidate they trusted. Repeated misinformation may therefore be most persuasive when it comes from sources people trust.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of adolescent neuroticism on short-form video overuse: A comment on Liu and Wu (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Liu and Wu, we reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking adolescent neuroticism to short-form video overuse (SVO). We demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported neuroticism, depression, anxiety, and SVO are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Is GenAI Helpful for Writing? A Re-Analysis Using Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA)
articles.authors: Shawn Hemelstrand
articles.abstract: A recent meta-analysis showed that genAI has a strong impact on writing. The current analysis instead shows that the effects are negligible after correcting for heterogeneity and publication bias.

articles.title: To replicate or not to replicate? My nine failures to publish a successful replication
articles.authors: Sharon Gilaie-Dotan
articles.abstract: Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) proposed disclosure-based practices — a priori power analyses, full reporting of conditions and exclusions, results reported with and without exclusions applied — as a remedy for the replication crisis. Following these practices explicitly, our lab attempted to publish an online replication and extension of our earlier PNAS findings on image size and memory, expecting that doing so would make publication straightforward. It did not. The manuscript was rejected nine times over 2.5 years, largely on the grounds that a transparent, successful replication lacked sufficient theoretical novelty to warrant publication on its own; it was accepted only after this framing was substantially minimized in favor of additional analyses and an alternative theoretical framework. Here, I reflect on this experience and raise open questions about whether the field's evaluation of replications has kept pace with its stated commitment to them.

articles.title: The Meta-Awareness – Equanimity Framework of Self for Psychiatry: Phenomenological Insights from Psychosis and Mindfulness
articles.authors: Saampras Ganesan; Antoine Lutz; Andrew Zalesky; Vanessa Cropley; Barnaby Nelson
articles.abstract: Psychiatric disorders remain a major global health challenge, yet research does not adequately incorporate first-person lived experience. A central component of lived experience is the sense of self, which is often profoundly altered in psychiatric conditions and can serve as a prognostic phenomenological marker, particularly in psychosis. In psychiatry, the most minimal form of self, i.e., the basic-self, is conventionally conceptualized as an enduring, individuated subjectivity defined by perspectival ownership and a clear boundary between self and world. Conversely, some contemplative frameworks, including mindfulness and certain non-dual perspectives, view the basic-self as a dynamic, conditioned process, such that experience need not be fundamentally structured by a self–world distinction or a fixed perspective. Drawing on phenomenological evidence from published first-person reports, we argue that the contemplative view can illuminate previously unexplored mechanisms underlying basic-self disturbances in psychosis-spectrum disorders. We formalize this view in a testable meta-awareness - equanimity (MA–E) framework of self that maps key phenomenological overlaps and distinctions across mindfulness, psychosis, and psychedelic experiences. Finally, we outline future research directions for validating and operationalizing the MA–E framework with implications for intervention design in psychosis.

articles.title: On Color and Emotion: What Can Vision Science Learn from the Rorschach?
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract: For a century, clinicians have recorded how people use color when they interpret inkblots, rank colored cards, or draw. They believed that how a person handles color reveals how that person handles feeling. Vision science has rarely read this literature, and the most complete modern review of color and emotion research excluded it. This paper introduces the projective color literature to vision scientists in plain language. Three conclusions follow. First, the tradition’s central belief, that chromatic color stirs emotion directly, was tested from the 1940s onward and largely failed. Second, narrower findings survived. The degree to which a person lets color lead over form in an ambiguous image is modestly related to several independently assessed clinical, behavioral, and biological outcomes. Some indices that set color in balance with other responses, such as coping versus overload, are also supported. What these scores measure is disputed. Third, the findings concern how color is weighted against form, which vision science already studies, yet only one study has linked that weighting to an object-recognition task, and none has used calibrated stimuli. I then read both literatures through a constructivist model of color in which the percept and the wider event it belongs to determine each other reciprocally. On this reading, the question is not only whether color influences emotion but also whether emotion influences color. The projective tradition raised the second question. Modern color-emotion science has mostly set it aside. Five studies are proposed that would join the two fields.

articles.title: Form Theory: The Conceptual Architecture of Human Thought
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Human thought takes place in a world that is uncertain and constantly changing. Yet the character of human thought is often quite different. People routinely simplify complex realities and hold their beliefs with a certainty and rigidity the world itself rarely warrants. The present paper develops Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure according to which these recurring tendencies are surface signatures of a common underlying format. Form Theory proposes that each concept contains a central form: a default structure that encodes a compressed subset of the concept’s information, gives that information default influence within cognition, and activates strong default beliefs about the encoded information. On Form Theory, distortion is one natural consequence of this structure. Yet the same structure also yields benefits for cognition. By encoding selected information in a stable, certainty-generating, domain-neutral format, the central form makes rapid, complex thought possible, supports conceptual and linguistic creativity, helps establish an internal sense of identity, and provides stable conceptual structure for the frameworks through which people organize their mental worlds. Form Theory therefore characterizes the conceptual architecture of human thought as a default conceptual structure whose signatures recur throughout cognition, with both benefits and costs for cognition and for human life.

articles.title: The multidimensional structure of perceptual and aesthetic evaluation: Independent features, interacting feature values, and perceptual unity
articles.authors: Eline Van Geert; Nori Jacoby
articles.abstract: Subjective appearance and aesthetic appreciation are inherently multidimensional, arising from the combined influence of a variety of visual features such as color, shape, and size. Yet, how multiple feature dimensions jointly shape perceptual and aesthetic evaluations remains poorly understood. Most previous studies either employ multidimensional stimuli without precise parametric control or use parametrically controlled stimuli that vary along only one dimension, limiting our understanding of the multidimensional structure underlying subjective evaluations. To address this challenge, we combined two methodological advances: the Order & Complexity Toolbox for Aesthetics (Van Geert et al., 2023), which enables the generation of parametrically controlled multidimensional stimuli, and Gibbs Sampling with People (Harrison et al., 2020), which efficiently characterizes subjective evaluations in high-dimensional stimulus spaces. Our stimuli consisted of visual displays containing multiple elements that varied in color, shape, and size and were arranged according to different organizational structures. Across nine experiments involving more than 1,000 participants and over 125,000 evaluations, we estimated multidimensional probability distributions underlying perceptual evaluations of order and complexity and aesthetic evaluations of pleasure and interest. Three main findings emerged. First, evaluations depended on both absolute feature values and relative differences between elements for each feature dimension, indicating that observers are sensitive not only to the characteristics of individual elements but also to the relations among them. Second, the influence of these relative differences depended on the overall perceptual organization of the display. Preferences for simplicity — operationalized as small differences in feature values between elements — varied systematically across evaluation criteria and with the degree of perceptual unity within the display. Third, despite these contextual effects, different visual features (color, shape, and size) conributed largely independently to the evaluations, suggesting that their influences on subjective evaluations are relatively separable. Together, these findings provide a multidimensional account of how visual features and their relations jointly shape perceptual and aesthetic evaluations.

articles.title: Changes in Single People’s Attachment Models and Co-Development with Life Satisfaction
articles.authors: Michael Dominik Krämer; R. Chris Fraley; Laura Buchinger; Julia Stern; Omri Gillath; William J. Chopik; Geoff MacDonald; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: Attachment security (i.e., low levels of attachment anxiety and avoidance) is important for both partnered and long-term single people’s well-being. However, research gaps limit knowledge to what extent attachment processes generalize to single people. Research has often not distinguished global and relationship-specific attachment; most studies of single people were cross-sectional; and little is known about attachment change and its co-development with well-being. The present study examined selection into long-term singlehood, change in relationship-specific attachment, and co-development with life satisfaction. We used longitudinal data spanning 30 months (N = 3,542; 39,492 assessments; 82% women; M_age = 34.54) and compared consistently single, consistently partnered, and intermittently partnered people. Baseline global, romantic, and friend-specific avoidance, but not anxiety, prospectively predicted remaining single. Compared to consistently partnered people, consistently single people showed higher global and romantic attachment insecurity, and both groups decreased mostly in parallel. However, single people increased slightly more adaptively in some of the non-romantic attachment models. Intermittently partnered people were similar in romantic attachment at baseline to single people but became more secure over time. Across most attachment models, people who increased in attachment security also increased in life satisfaction. This co-development was similar between groups, except that decreasing romantic avoidance was less closely tied to increasing life satisfaction among single people. Together, persistent differences in global and romantic attachment may reflect selection into relationship status rather than distinct development. In addition, similar attachment–well-being links across groups indicate that attachment operates in similar ways in both partnered and long-term single people.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: The Other-Race Effect in Implicit Memory for Face Combinations
articles.authors: Yoko Higuchi; Kiwako Shimada
articles.abstract: Other-race faces are remembered less accurately than own-race faces, a robust phenomenon known as the other-race effect or cross-race effect. However, most evidence for the other-race effect comes from tasks that require explicit encoding or recognition of individual face identities, leaving unclear whether the effect is confined to explicit memory demands. Here, we report evidence for an other-race effect not only in explicit memory, but also in implicit memory for repeated face combinations. In Experiment 1, Japanese participants intentionally encoded Asian and Caucasian faces and later performed an explicit recognition task; recognition sensitivity was higher for own-race Asian faces than for other-race Caucasian faces. In Experiment 2, Japanese participants performed an implicit memory task in which repeated face combinations were presented without awareness of the repetitions; implicit memory for repeated face combinations developed more reliably for own-race Asian faces than for other-race Caucasian faces. Taken together, these results suggest that the cognitive difficulties associated with other-race faces should be understood not only as a problem of explicit face memory, but also as a problem of implicit memory formed through repeated face exposure in everyday life.

articles.title: Facial evidence matters less for stereotype-consistent judgments: Weaker formidability-aggression associations in Black vs. White faces
articles.authors: Kirstan Brodie; Brandon Cohen; Youngki Hong
articles.abstract: Facial characteristics are reliably associated with social judgments, but these relationships may depend on whether a judgment is consistent with stereotypes of the target’s social group. Across four studies with adult participants, we tested this possibility using perceived aggression and threat in Black and White faces. Perceived dominance (Study 1, N=117) and physical strength (Study 2, N=626) predicted aggression judgments less strongly for Black than White faces. Dominance also predicted perceived threat less strongly for Black than White faces after controlling for several threat-related covariates (Study 3, N=380). Furthermore, machine learning analyses found less overlap in dominance- and threat-predictive facial information for Black faces. Finally, face morphing that matched featural variation across race while manipulating apparent race showed a weaker dominance-aggression relationship for Black-appearing faces (Study 4, N=467). Together, these findings are consistent with the possibility that facial evidence has reduced influence on judgments of stereotype-consistent traits.

articles.title: Characterizing deaf and hard-of-hearing language experiences as arousal-regulation processes
articles.authors: Christina Kim; Laurel Aichler; Onudeah Nicolarakis; Shilpa Hanumantha Lacy; Rachel Sortino; Rachel Pizzie
articles.abstract: Empirical language research with deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) groups often includes proficiency, age of acquisition, or language background measures but excludes people’s socioemotional context. Measuring socioemotional context depends on characterizing the socioemotional experiences associated with DHH language development and use. We used the biopsychosocial model of arousal regulation as a theoretical lens to explore 11 qualitative interviews with DHH participants. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we developed three characteristic themes: 1) Deafness is not a monolith, 2) Name it to tame it – Language Anxiety, and 3) Positive roots for resilient shoots. These themes show that DHH language experiences are heterogeneous, that negative experiences can represent language anxiety, and that positive experiences modulate arousal regulation. Our study highlights new socioemotional considerations for language processing research like how emotions influence language use, how motivations support language skills, and how communication strategies impact social interactions within DHH communities.

articles.title: Growing Beyond Traits: A Skill-Based Approach to Volitional Personality Change
articles.authors: Christopher J. Soto; Christopher Napolitano; Madison Nicole Sewell; Heejun Roy Yoon; Tommaso Feraco; Nathan W. Hudson; Brent Roberts
articles.abstract: Recent research suggests that individuals can intentionally change their personality traits. This article proposes a complementary, skill-based approach to volitional change, arguing that social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills—defined as learned capabilities rather than dispositional tendencies—represent more direct and intuitive targets for intentional development. We introduce the Cumulative Practice Model (CPM), a framework that integrates principles from the personality development, clinical intervention, managerial coaching, and cognitive science literatures. This model proposes that the volitional development of SEB skills can occur most effectively through a repeating cycle of motivation, instruction, opportunity, practice, feedback, and skill change. We then review preliminary evidence supporting this model. This evidence indicates that individuals generally find developing SEB skills to be more desirable and feasible than changing personality traits. It further shows that skills exhibit plasticity across the lifespan, with both normative age trends and individual-level changes linked to relevant life experiences. Crucially, it suggests that interventions centered on deliberate practice can facilitate SEB skill development, and that gains in these skills are linked with positive life outcomes including academics, occupational interests, social relationships, health, and well-being. Thus, the Cumulative Practice Model offers a promising framework for individuals who wish to improve their SEB skills, practitioners who wish to facilitate skill development and growth, and researchers who wish to better understand the antecedents, process, conditions, and outcomes of volitional change. This skill-based approach to volitional change also highlights open questions and promising directions for future research.

articles.title: Dawdling at Dusk: Affect and Bedtime Procrastination
articles.authors: Yijun Lin; Erin Corwin Westgate
articles.abstract: Why don’t people go to bed on time? Most research on bedtime procrastination has focused on individual differences (e.g., self-regulation, chronotype), potentially conflating between-person patterns with within-person processes. To address this, we examined whether affective valence and arousal predict bedtime procrastination within people, between people, or both. In Study 1, we replicated cross-sectional associations between negative affect and bedtime procrastination in a Chinese community sample. In Studies 2–3, we attempted to manipulate valence and arousal in separate week-long diary experiments; the manipulations produced limited shifts in affect and did not significantly change bedtime procrastination. Across both diary studies, however, analyses of self-reported affect revealed a consistent pattern: people who generally felt less positive were more likely to procrastinate, whereas evening-to-evening fluctuations in affect did not predict whether they procrastinated on a given night. Exploratory analyses in Study 2 suggested that this between-person association was partly indirect through feeling less able to go to bed. Taken together, these findings suggest that whether people put off going to bed may be more closely tied to how they typically feel than to how they feel on a given evening, highlighting the importance of separating between-person and within-person levels.

articles.title: Profiles in aesthetic engagement: A new survey and a snapshot of behavior in the United States
articles.authors: Eileen R. Cardillo; Hannah Meghan Merseal; Raphael Englander; Anjan Chatterjee
articles.abstract: The measurement of art engagement, typically relies on narrow views of engagement, emphasizing attendance at fine arts institutions. Such approaches underestimate the variety of aesthetic participation and likely underrepresent groups who experience barriers to access or engage with aesthetics outside traditional art venues. The rise of digital modes of participation further challenges the adequacy of conventional assessments. To address these gaps, we developed the Assessment of Aesthetic Participation, a new survey that builds on the strengths of nationally administered National Endowment of the Arts surveys, and captures a broader spectrum of aesthetic behaviors, including everyday aesthetic activities, religious and heritage embedded practices, and digitally mediated engagement. To establish its utility for experimental research, we validated the Assessment of Aesthetic Participation against commonly used measures in empirical aesthetics—the Revised Aesthetic Fluency Scale and the Aesthetic Responsiveness Assessment. Results from a nationally representative U.S. sample (N=1501) replicate previously observed demographic trends related to age and education, while suggesting a more complex pattern for race and gender. An exploratory latent profile analysis suggested five distinct styles of engagement, differentiated by frequency and preferred activities: low participation by the Disengaged, intermediate but distinguishable patterns of the Spectator, the Fan, and the Enthusiast, and the highly engaged Aesthete. The Assessment of Aesthetic Participation offers a flexible, inclusive tool that addresses limits in existing measures of arts engagement, bridges the measurement needs of population-level and experimental researchers, and can advance future research on the benefits of aesthetic experiences.

articles.title: Towards the Social Microstructure of Human Movement as a Topic of Psychological Inquiry
articles.authors: Mark Jaime
articles.abstract: Human action unfolds through movement, and how that movement is organized can itself reveal psychological information about the person producing it. I use social microstructure to refer specifically to patterned organization within unfolding movement that bears systematically on socially relevant characteristics or processes of the person producing it. The purpose of this paper is to develop social microstructure as a perspective for expanding the psychological questions we ask through the examination of movement. Doing so means treating social microstructure as a topic of inquiry and asking what psychological questions become possible when the organization within movement is related systematically to the person producing it. Advances in computer vision, machine learning, and related computational methods now make increasingly rich representations of unfolding human movement available for such analysis. I pursue several questions opened by this perspective, including how different representations derived from recorded movement preserve psychologically relevant organization, how social microstructure may change across development, and what organization within self-generated and socially relevant movement might contribute to our understanding of the self and social functioning. Across these directions is a common question: what can be learned about the person from variation within the unfolding of an action itself?

articles.authors: Christopher J. Soto; Christopher Napolitano; Madison Nicole Sewell; Heejun Roy Yoon; Tommaso Feraco; Nathan W. Hudson; Brent Roberts

articles.title: ‘Clean Air for Everyone (CLAIRE): Ventilatie en luchtreiniging voor pandemische paraatheid’
articles.authors: Stefanie H Meeuwis; Amy Louise de Bruijn; Marloes Duijzings; Jennifer Mareen Becker; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen
articles.abstract: Onderzoek toont aan dat luchtkwaliteit in binnenruimtes vaak ondermaats is. Dit kan leiden tot gezondheidsrisico's, zoals verergerde luchtwegproblematiek en een groter risico op infectieziekten. Luchtbehandelingstechnieken, waaronder ventilatie en (mobiele) luchtreinigers, zijn potentieel effectieve methoden om deze gezondheidsrisico's terug te dringen, maar het is niet duidelijk of stakeholders de inzet ervan aanvaardbaar en haalbaar achten. Dit rapport omvat de bevindingen uit een interviewstudie en een focusgroepen studie. Binnen deze onderzoeken zijn stakeholders uit basisscholen en ouderenzorg (beleidsmakers en gebruikers) geïnterviewd en gevraagd of zij bereid zijn ventilatie en luchtreiniging in te zetten en onder welke omstandigheden. Thema’s die een rol spelen bij de aanvaardbaarheid en haalbaarheid van de inzet van deze technieken worden in het rapport beschreven en geëvalueerd.

articles.title: Perceived error climate in elementary school classrooms: A multidimensional perspective
articles.authors: Jana Spear; Donna Bryce; Cara-Sophie Enste; Robert Grassinger; Markus Dresel
articles.abstract: The error climate in the classroom captures the extent to which errors are positively perceived and treated as constructive learning opportunities by teachers and students. It has been conceptualized as comprising eight subdimensions organized under a single second-order factor among secondary school students (Steuer et al., 2013). However, this structure has not yet been investigated in younger students. Consequently, we examined the error climate’s structure in elementary school classrooms while additionally proposing a novel and more differentiated second-order structure distinguishing between emotional and instructional support following errors. Among 2,628 elementary school students from 187 classrooms across two domains (maths and German), multilevel multigroup confirmatory factor analyses at the individual and classroom level were conducted. Results revealed a multifaceted error climate perception already in elementary school, with eight subdimensions loading onto the two proposed second-order factors. These, in turn, were also positively related to students’ individual adaptive reactions to errors.

articles.title: Gaze semantics: A scoping review of how gaze conveys and constrains meaning in social contexts
articles.authors: Nikol Figalová; Anne Böckler; Lynn Huestegge
articles.abstract: Humans rely on gaze to encode information and signal to others. Gaze may indicate where someone is attending, but its contribution extends beyond spatial orientation. Evidence is scattered across different research traditions. This scoping review synthesises 361 publications on gaze as a meaningful social cue. Gaze semantics describes the systematic contribution of gaze to conveying and constraining social meaning. A cross-domain synthesis identified four recurrent operations: gaze orients by making objects, people, or locations socially relevant; addresses by positioning people as recipients or interaction partners; qualifies by modifying how other cues are interpreted; and coordinates by organising participation and unfolding action. These functional contributions can co-occur within a single gaze event. Gaze interpretation is inferential, shaped by five categories of contextual factors: signal properties; interactional availability; multimodal and sequential embedding; cultural, social and activity frame; and gazer and observer states and interactional history. We propose a Gazer-Observer Model of Gaze Understanding that integrates these findings to describe the dynamic relation between gaze production and interpretation. The same gaze pattern may support different interpretations across situations yet allow a relatively specific interpretation within a particular encounter. Gaze can therefore systematically affect social interpretation while remaining semantically underdetermined to varying degrees.

articles.title: Effort discounting of environmental and personal outcomes in a consequential decision-making task
articles.authors: Shiwei Yang; Ruth Krebs
articles.abstract: Effort investment is an important barrier that keeps individuals from engaging in pro-environmental behaviors and previous studies revealed that expected cognitive effort can reduce motivation for pro-environmental goals. The current study sought to investigate whether effort changes the shape of the cost-benefit analysis, and in particular whether it leads to stronger discounting of outcome value. The study employed a within-subjects experimental design through an online study (N = 400) using the Work for Environmental Protection Task (WEPT) featuring both pro-environmental and personal outcomes. We assessed participants' binary choice to accept or decline specific trial of a number identification task based on expected effort-reward-outcome combinations. Questionnaires were added to explore inter-individual characteristics. Overall, participants preferred trials with higher reward magnitude, lower effort requirements, and those benefiting them personally. Moreover, pro-environmental outcomes featured more pronounced effort discounting, or in other words, a weaker shielding of effort effects by outcome magnitude. Together, this provides experimental evidence for a general inferiority of pro-environmental outcomes (replicating previous data) and reveals a skewed costs-benefit analysis that prioritizes effort costs over outcome magnitude.

articles.title: Strengths and Weaknesses: Early word learning skills and profiles of vocabulary development
articles.authors: Laia Fibla; John P Spencer; Larissa K. Samuelson
articles.abstract: Early vocabulary development predicts later cognitive functioning and school success. We sought to examine how processing differences across several skills that contribute to early word learning relate to variability in children’s vocabulary development. Building on recent direct measures of early vocabulary and language learning processes, we collected data from 166 children between 15- to 27-months in a single eyetracking task measuring lexical speed of processing, comprehension, novelty bias, word mapping and new word retention. We found clear differences in responding across the different measures and robust patterns of developmental change. Children’s comprehension grew over development, and across word classes they showed clearly distinct looking patterns, reflecting fundamental differences in word type processing and more efficient noun recognition compared to adjectives and verbs. Speed of processing and online comprehension showed strong relationships with concurrent vocabulary, similar to previous reports. Children also showed a strong improvement in referent selection over development, but as found in previous literature, they did not show evidence of retaining new word-object mappings formed on earlier trials of the task. Data driven classification found two robust clusters of children. One group showed faster speed of lexical processing, better comprehension and were better at linking new nouns to novel objects. Numerically, this group had the highest parent-reported concurrent productive vocabulary scores. Data are discussed in relation to similar work in the literature, what concurrent measurement of multiple word learning processes reveals about the system of multiple processes supporting early vocabulary development, and children’s individual trajectories of word learning.

articles.title: Problematic Internet Use and Anxiety in Adolescents: A Scoping Review of Mechanisms and Contextual Influences
articles.authors: Cleo Albertus; Freda Scheffler; Sibeko; Dan J. Stein; Christine Lochner; Nynke A. Groenewold
articles.abstract: Problematic internet use (PIU) and anxiety are prevalent, co-occurring difficulties during adolescence, yet their shared psychological mechanisms remain insufficiently mapped. This scoping review investigated evidence on the PIU-anxiety relationship in adolescents aged 13-18 years, following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, EBSCOhost, and Web of Science were searched from January 2014 to December 2025, supplemented by hand-searching of reference lists. Ninety-six studies from 20 countries were included. Across all modalities, PIU was associated with elevated anxiety. Longitudinal studies indicated suggestive but not definitive bidirectional associations with symptoms of anxiety. Avoidance-based coping and cognitive-emotional dysregulation emerged as primary mechanism clusters, with emotion dysregulation as a central transdiagnostic process. Co-occurring internalising phenomena including depressive symptoms and loneliness were included where they provided relevant context for interpreting the association between PIU and anxiety in adolescents. Family functioning, social support, and environmental stressors moderated associations. These findings indicate that PIU and anxiety should be assessed concurrently. Interventions may benefit from targeting shared transdiagnostic mechanisms, particularly emotion dysregulation, while taking family and environmental contexts into account.

articles.title: Return-to-office (RTO) is multidimensional: Attendance level and trajectory predict different employee outcomes
articles.authors: Yingyue Luan; Yeun Joon Kim; Pengzhao Lyu; Soo Min Toh
articles.abstract: Organizations increasingly require employees to return to the office, yet evidence on the consequences of return-to-office (RTO) policies remains limited and typically treats RTO as a binary change. We propose a multidimensional perspective of RTO that distinguishes attendance-level— the proportion of time employees spend in the office over a given period—from attendance-trajectory—changes in attendance over time. Analyzing 13,956 employee-month observations from badge-swipe records for 1,163 employees whose attendance remained stable or increased at a multinational financial services organization over 12 months, we examined how these two dimensions related to ten subsequent outcomes: job performance, stress and burnout, three perceptions of organizational culture, and four forms of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and utilization. Attendance-level and attendance-trajectory showed distinct patterns of association across outcome domains. For job performance, overall attendance-level was unrelated to subsequent performance; instead, a faster increase in attendance predicted lower performance. Well-being showed the opposite pattern: higher overall and initial attendance-level predicted greater stress and burnout, while trajectory was unrelated to either outcome. Culture perceptions and AI adoption showed more complex patterns involving both dimensions, with higher or increasing attendance generally linked to more positive culture perceptions and deeper AI engagement, though the relevant dimension differed by outcome. These findings indicate that attendance-level and attendance-trajectory are not interchangeable and carry benefits in some domains while imposing costs in others. RTO policies should be designed and evaluated according to both how much and how quickly attendance increases, rather than being assumed uniformly beneficial or harmful.

articles.title: Parental ethnic-racial socialization in Europe: A scoping review
articles.authors: Ymke de Bruijn; Jana Vietze
articles.abstract: Objectives: Children in Europe grow up in societies with high ethnic-racial diversity. It is therefore imperative to understand how they learn about ethnicity and race (ethnic-racial socialization). Knowledge on parental ethnic-racial socialization, however, is very heavily based on U.S. research, and sociohistorical and -political differences limit generalizability. Therefore, the aim of the present study is to create an overview and synthesis of research on parental ethnic-racial socialization in the European context. Methods: A preregistered scoping review was conducted following the PRIMSA-ScR guidelines. Three electronic databases (PsychInfo, ERIC, Web of Science) were searched for papers published up and till 2024. After two rounds of screening, 32 out of 1431 papers were deemed eligible and included for data extraction and synthesis. Results: The findings display an overrepresentation of Northern/Western European countries, families of immigrant or minoritized backgrounds and quantitative research on adolescence. Cultural socialization by families or immigrant or minoritized backgrounds has received the most attention. Qualitative study results furthermore describe how parental ethnic-racial socialization is shaped by developmental timing, reactive and reciprocal processes, intersecting identities, and selective engagement with cultural “others. Conclusions: The findings of this scoping review underscore both the promise and current limitations of research on parental ethnic-racial socialization in Europe. To further this research agenda, we need more systematic inclusion of underrepresented populations, greater investments in qualitative and mixed-methods designs, openness to diverse and self-identified ingroup boundaries and identity meanings, and the development of conceptualizations and measures that reflect Europe’s distinctive sociohistorical trajectories, demographic diversity, and linguistic practices.

articles.title: Epistemic Stances in Humanoid Robot Evaluation: Evidence from the Frankenstein Syndrome Questionnaire and Morph-Based Perceptual Judgements
articles.authors: Ilaria Maria Antonietta Benzi; Francesca Ciardo
articles.abstract: Humanoid robots occupy an ambiguous position between social partners and artefacts, and people differ markedly in how they evaluate them. Research on individual differences in human–robot interaction has focused on personality, anthropomorphic tendencies and technology acceptance, leaving largely unexamined the processes by which people decide whether an artificial agent can be treated as a credible source of social information. The present study introduces epistemic stances, as conceptualised within the mentalizing tradition, to this literature. Seventy adults completed the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire, along with measures of generalized attitudes toward robots (Frankenstein Syndrome Questionnaire, Negative Attitudes toward Robots Scale, Robotic Social Attributes Scale), and a morph-based task in which robot faces varying in human likeness were rated for likeability, eeriness and human likeness. Epistemic stances were selectively associated with generalized social evaluations: Epistemic Trust predicted higher Robot Anxiety and lower attributed Warmth, whereas Credulity predicted higher attributed Warmth, with no associations for perceived Competence. At the stimulus level, morph condition strongly shaped all three judgements, whereas epistemic stances added little. Rather than a failure to extend person-level effects, this dissociation follows from the claim that epistemic stances operate on socially communicated information rather than on perceptual appraisal. Epistemic functioning may therefore shape the social meaning attributed to artificial agents, offering a testable framework for the design of robot communication.

articles.title: Psychiatric Overdiagnosis as Diagnostic Stretching in Response to Clinical Need
articles.authors: Awais Aftab
articles.abstract: I define psychiatric “overdiagnosis” as the observation that there has been a rapid rise in the rate of mental health diagnoses in recent decades, combined with the suspicion that a substantial proportion of these diagnoses are illegitimate or unwarranted. I propose that a major and under-recognized contributor to both the rise and the suspicion is diagnostic stretching: the application of a specified diagnostic category to a presentation that does not meet its official criteria but is accompanied by clinically significant distress or impairment, to make that presentation legible to the institutions that organize care. Since the 1990s, specified categories such as major depressive disorder, ADHD, bipolar disorder, and autism have been stretched in clinical practice to cover patients who have the relevant symptoms and clinically significant distress or impairment but whose presentations are subthreshold or phenomenologically adjacent. Increased awareness of mental health problems has lowered the help-seeking threshold, so that the population that comes to clinical attention is converging on the population that meets a burden threshold independent of help-seeking. Stretching is a response to genuine clinical need interacting with official classifications that are too narrow, not too broad. The overdiagnosis backlash correctly perceives a mismatch between official criteria and diagnostic practice but misidentifies its source, reading as laxity what is better understood as unmet need routed through official categories that are not adequate to the task.

articles.title: Making Sense of Sensory Differences: Identifying Sensory Processing Phenotypes and Their Relationship to Social and Executive Functioning in Neurotypical Children.
articles.authors: Adrianna M Molenaar; Natalia Van Esch; Nichole Scheerer
articles.abstract: Sensory processing varies substantially across individuals, yet research on distinct sensory phenotypes has focused primarily on neurodivergent populations. We examined whether comparable sensory phenotypes could be identified in 200 children aged 4-12 years with no known neurodevelopmental or psychiatric diagnoses, and whether phenotype membership was associated with executive functioning, social competence, mental health, alexithymia, and neurodivergent traits. K-means clustering of parent-reported sensory processing identified four sensory phenotypes: Sensory Adaptive, Generalized Sensory Differences, Under-responsive/Filtering Differences, and Sensory Sensitive. Children in the Sensory Adaptive group showed fewer executive functioning difficulties than children in all other groups and higher social competence than those in the Generalized Sensory Differences and Sensory Sensitive groups. In contrast, phenotypes did not differ significantly in autistic or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder traits, alexithymia, anxiety, or depression. These findings demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in sensory processing among children without diagnosed conditions and suggest that sensory phenotypes may be meaningfully related to everyday cognitive and social functioning. Future transdiagnostic work should directly examine the extent to which these phenotypes are shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children.

articles.title: An inverted U-shape association between mind health and generative AI-use frequency
articles.authors: Jerzy Bala; Tara Thiagarajan
articles.abstract: Generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude have rapidly become part of how we work and live, yet there is little systematic understanding of what they do to the human mind. Here we use a global Internet-enabled sample of 176,198 adults aged 18+, collected in 2025-2026, to examine how frequency and type of generative AI use relate to mind health. Respondents completed a 47-item assessment of emotional, social, cognitive, and physical capacities and problems, aggregated into an overall mind health score, the MHQ, alongside questions on AI use, lifestyle, and life context. Mind health rises with low to moderate GenAI use and then falls sharply with daily use, an inverted U most pronounced among adults aged 18-34. The pattern holds for both cognitive and emotional purposes, although those using GenAI for emotional support or companionship have markedly lower MHQ at every frequency, reflecting higher levels of suicidal thoughts, confused or slow thinking, hallucinations and other problems linked to psychosis. These associations are cross-sectional and cannot be considered causal, but they persist after adjustment for education, trauma, exercise, nature exposure, and sleep. As GenAI becomes part of daily life, these results suggest a downward trajectory of collective global mind health.

articles.title: Peer Transmission of Mental Health Information Increases ADHD Self-Diagnosis
articles.authors: Tanay Katiyar; George Gillett; Adam Hunt; Amanda M Ferguson; Alessia Pascale; Alberto Acerbi; Nikhil Chaudhary; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Increased sharing of mental health information online has intensified public concern that social media may amplify mental health self-diagnosis rates. While much work has examined the types of mental health information available online, little attention is paid to the mechanisms governing how this information is created and consumed. Taking a cultural evolutionary perspective, we posit that social media facilitates peer-to-peer transmission of psychiatric information in novel formats and provides new motivations to transmit such information; this alters the information people see and their reactions to it. We investigate this through an adapted transmission chain paradigm where participants sequentially modify and transmit Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) explanations amongst each other, allowing us to examine how self-diagnostic tendencies evolve during this process. Across four studies, we find that such transmission increases participants’ tendency to diagnose themselves, and another individual with subclinical traits, with ADHD. Participants’ tendency to recommend this other individual to seek professional help also increases. Transmission format (i.e. generating an example list versus narrative summary) and motivation (i.e. making an explanation for maximising likes versus accuracy) moderate some effects. These results indicate that peer-to-peer transmission may play a key role in determining psychiatric diagnostic trends and shaping the public understanding of mental health.

articles.title: Multimodal Dynamics in Learning and Explaining Abstract and Concrete Concepts: A Triadic Interactive Task with Families
articles.authors: Chiara De Livio; Claudia Mazzuca; Francesca Bellagamba; Alessandro Gennaro; Giuliana Mazzoni; Silvia Mazzoni; Julian Zubek; Anna M. Borghi
articles.abstract: Studies have shown that learning abstract concepts (e.g., freedom compared to table) may be particularly challenging. To address concept learning, most studies use paradigms involving a single participant, such as lexical decision, match to sample, induction, and rating tasks. Here, we use an interactive task involving three family members—mother, father, and a 5-year-old child—and examine how concepts differing in abstractness are explained by the parents, either individually or together, and how the child learns and employs them. We investigate multimodal dynamics in interaction, studying gestures, movements of bodily parts, and movement coordination among interactors, in an effort to capture different embodied signatures characterizing concepts differing in abstractness. Results reveal that people gesture differently with abstract and concrete concepts, but in both cases tend to instantiate the conceptual referent, either metaphorically or iconically. Subtle differences in head movements and social touch suggest that people struggle more to understand the meanings of abstract concepts than concrete ones. Finally, with abstract concepts, coordination episodes are longer. Overall, the results provide support for the view that, with abstract concepts, people use more communicative signals and tend to converge more than with concrete concepts.

articles.title: Object Details Persist in Visual Working Memory Regardless of Category Sufficiency for Search
articles.authors: Ryan Williams; Joseph M. Saito; Keisuke Fukuda; Susanne Ferber
articles.abstract: When searching for objects in complex environments, performance often improves with more specific target representations. Yet, sometimes a more general representation may be preferable. For example, when repeatedly searching for unique exemplars from the same object category, a shared category-based representation could help alleviate the cognitive burden of constantly encoding and maintaining new exemplar representations. We therefore examined whether the format of target representations used for search is sensitive to the sustained preservation of object-category membership. Across two experiments, observers searched consecutively for images of real-world objects from the same basic-level category. We recorded contralateral delay activity (CDA), an electrophysiological marker of visual working memory (VWM) maintenance, to assess whether the encoding of object-specific details diminished across category repetitions in favor of more generalized representations. In Experiment 1, we manipulated whether object-category membership alone sufficiently differentiated each unique target from nontargets in the search array. In Experiment 2, we preserved category sufficiency but allowed the targets to additionally repeat at the level of the exemplar to examine how repeatedly searching for the same object differs from repeatedly searching for the same kind of object. We found that while fewer object-specific details were maintained in VWM when category membership was sufficient, the amount of detail only diminished across repetitions of the exact same object. Moreover, observers exhibited sensitivity to the sustained preservation of the target category in the form of perceptual and semantic expectancy violations following category switches, as indexed by N2pc and N400 ERP components. Together, we show that, even though the sustained preservation of a target object category does not continuously reduce the encoding of object-specific details, categorical information is nonetheless represented in parallel. We speculate that object-specific representations principally serve attentional guidance, while categorical representations benefit target-match decisions.

articles.title: The structure and degree of social connection is associated with the structure and idiosyncrasy of emotion perception
articles.authors: David Dodell-Feder; Tamar Galvin; Tara Augenstein
articles.abstract: Social connection is associated with broad aspects of social cognition. Here, we probe the nature of this association in two studies (Ns=305, 759) with college-aged samples in which we measured different aspects of social (dis)connection (e.g., loneliness) and performance on a measure of emotion perception. We find that intersubject differences in social connection mirrored intersubject differences in emotion perception, suggesting a shared fingerprint between the experience of one’s social relationships and the perception of emotion information. Further, greater levels of social disconnection were associated with greater idiosyncrasy in emotion perception, which was largely driven by task inaccuracy. This finding suggests that social disconnection may distort internal models of affective states in a way that pulls individuals from a canonical understanding of how emotions are expressed in faces. Although findings were specific to Study 2, these results provide important context to how social connection relates to emotion perception and highlights emotion perception as a potential intervention target for social disconnection.

articles.title: Growing Up With Conversational AI: A Developmental Framework for Adolescent Agency Over Conversational AI Use
articles.authors: shanting chen; Mary Kate Koch; Renkai Ma; Cindy Liu; Natalie C. Ebner
articles.abstract: Conversational generative AI has rapidly reached majority adoption among U.S. adolescents. These systems now provide advice, emotional support, academic assistance, simulated social interaction, and opportunities for identity exploration at a critical phase in development when mental health needs are rising and capacities for self-regulation, autonomy, and social competence are still developing. Scholars and clinicians have raised urgent questions about what these systems do to adolescents, and early findings point to both benefits and risks. In this article, we ask what adolescents do with AI and introduce the concept of adolescent agency over conversational AI use: the degree to which adolescents purposefully direct, critically evaluate, and set limits on their engagement with conversational AI. Existing constructs such as AI literacy and AI self-efficacy describe what young people know or believe about AI and the risks associated with its use, but they do not capture how adolescents exercise agency across areas of their lives. We identify nine processes that arise at the intersection of conversational AI’s features and key developmental tasks during the period of adolescence, which we label AI-ERA: autonomy, identity, emotion regulation, relationships, and achievement. We distinguish this agency from existing constructs, including agentic engagement with AI and AI overreliance, and then propose how it is shaped by adolescents’ developing capacities, adult scaffolding, and peer influence. We conclude with implications for families, schools, clinicians, and researchers, as well as considerations regarding the design, regulation, and ethics of AI systems.

articles.title: People With Lower Well-Being Show Longer and Less Stable Smartphone Use: A Large-Scale Analysis of 12 Datasets
articles.authors: Anna M Langener; Philip Chow; Aurelio Fernández; Nicholas C. Jacobson; Martien Kas; Anne Milek; Rüdiger Pryss; Theda Radtke; Ramona Schoedel; David de Segovia Vicente
articles.abstract: Debate over whether smartphone use relates to poorer well-being is limited by self-reports, small single-country samples, and a focus on average use. We harmonized objective app-use from 12 studies  (2,945 participants; 37,229 person-days; 851,865 person-hours) across five countries to examine associations of well-being with smartphone use and its variability. Additionally, we examined variations in smartphone use across age, gender identity, and time-of-day and day-of-week. Daily, participants averaged 3.27 hours of use (SD = 2.28), accessed 15.9 apps (SD = 6.16), and were unstable (40.6% of the total variation accounted for by within-person changes). Poorer well-being was associated with longer, more variable use; a depressive symptom increase of 10% of the scale range corresponded to 7 additional minutes of daily use and 7.5% higher within-person variance. Overall, younger persons and women used their phones more frequently, and higher wellbeing was related to consistently lower smartphone usage.

articles.title: Enrichment of weak free associations in the aging mental lexicon and the limits of methodological inference
articles.authors: Dasol Jeong; Thomas Hills
articles.abstract: Older adults’ lexical networks often appear sparser than those of younger adults, a pattern typically interpreted as evidence of cognitive decline. The enrichment model instead proposes that lifelong experience creates richer lexical representations in which associative strength is distributed across more weak connections. Across two stimulation studies, we examine this model and the limits of methodological inference when studying free association networks. Study 1 reproduced empirical aging data, showed that lifelong learning enriched networks with age, leading to more distributed free associations that appear as an enrichment of weak associations with age. Study 2 demonstrated that these patterns depended on participant sample size and lexicon size. In particular, increasing the number of participants reduced or reversed apparent age-related sparsity by revealing weak and infrequently observed associations. This also follows the logic of ecological studies that call for increased sampling when rare species may be undersampled. Overall, these findings suggest that aging enriches and redistributes associative strength across a broader lexical network and that observed sparsity may reflect methodological limitations rather than a genuine loss of lexical connectivity.

articles.title: Triangulating Careless Responding: Quantitative Models Meet Qualitative Insights on Response Processes
articles.authors: Malin Müller; Dominique Maciejewski; Leonie Schorrlepp; Tanja Lischetzke; Leonie V. D. E. Vogelsmeier
articles.abstract:
Detecting careless responding in experience sampling methodology (ESM) is essential for ensuring data quality. Although quantitative detection methods are increasingly available, their low alignment raises questions about what they capture. Evaluation is constrained by the lack of ground truth in real-world data, while simulations require assumptions about the form of careless responding. This methodological catch-22 leaves disagreements among methods unresolved. We demonstrate how qualitative information about response processes (i.e., cognitive processes involved in rating items) can triangulate quantitative classifications and provide insight into what different methods capture. Using 4,175 measurement occasions from 41 participants in a 28-day ESM study, we compared a measurement-model-based mixture model using five emotion items and an indicator-based mixture model using four careless responding indices within a mixture continuous-time latent Markov framework. The models classified 35% and 15% of occasions as careless, respectively, with moderate overlap (Jaccard similarity = .37). Across models, careless occasions had more coded response processes and longer descriptions than attentive occasions. A qualitative analysis of 350 occasions showed how inductively derived classifications and response behavior codes provide complementary information about convergence and divergence between quantitative approaches. Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential value of triangulation for understanding what careless responding detection methods capture.
Keywords: experience sampling methodology, careless responding, response processes, qualitative triangulation, latent Markov model

articles.title: How AI chatbots shape political attitudes when they are not prompted to persuade
articles.authors: Sayeh Yousefi; Jens Koed Madsen
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots to find information, including information about politicians and political issues. Given evidence that Large Language Models (LLMs) have high persuasive capacities, this has raised concerns about their potential to have undue influence on political attitudes. However, most existing research on AI persuasion explicitly prompts the LLM to persuade the user, which is not representative of how people typically engage with LLMs. Whether undirected political conversations with LLMs shift political attitudes, and whether personalisation amplifies any such effect, remains unclear. We address these questions across two studies. First, in a quota-matched survey of UK adults (N = 2,137), we find that political use of AI is already widespread and its outputs are generally perceived as being politically neutral. Second, in a pre-registered randomised controlled trial (N = 2,081), participants conversed with an LLM about either a politician or political issue, with the LLM not being prompted to persuade. We find that conversations about politicians increased favourability toward them, while conversations about policies modestly reduced support. Conversation personalisation did not amplify these effects. Our findings show that AI chatbots are already a meaningful source of political information in the UK, and that undirected chatbot conversations can influence political attitudes.

articles.title: Battling Bots and Combating Fraud in Digitally Mediated Social Science Research: A Typological Toolbox of Countermeasures
articles.authors: Bradley E. Cox; Yilun Jiang; Brett Ranon Nachman; Karly Ball Isaacson
articles.abstract: As social science researchers increasingly use online mechanisms to recruit participants and collect data, they must also defend against the growing threat of fraudulent submissions from autonomous bots and bad-faith human respondents. This paper describes such threats and outlines conditions that make some studies particularly vulnerable. It also provides explicit guidance for researchers by introducing a typology of 30 protective countermeasures designed to deter, prevent, track, and detect fraudulent responses.

articles.title: Mesmer’s error: Beliefs reverse the rubber hand illusion (a Registered Report)
articles.authors: Peter Lush; Zoltan Dienes
articles.abstract: In the rubber hand illusion (RHI), participants report ownership of a fake hand which is stroked in synchrony with their own concealed hand, with lower ownership ratings for asynchronous stroking. This effect has been historically attributed to multisensory integration. However, such a pattern of results is consistent with experimental demand characteristics, and an alternative theory proposes that the RHI is an effect of phenomenological control (the trait ability to change experience to satisfy goals). To date, support for a phenomenological control theory of the RHI has been limited to correlational evidence. Here we conduct a pre-registered causal test of the relative contribution of these two proposed mechanisms in RHI effects. 25 high phenomenological control participants (top 15%) were tested in an RHI procedure and the classic effects of greater response for synchrony than asynchrony were replicated. The procedure was then repeated following imaginative suggestions for a reversal of the classic effect (i.e. greater synchrony than asynchrony effects). Ratings of ownership and proprioceptive drift were modulated by suggestion. Effects for ownership and drift were reversed. Exploratory analysis showed the same pattern of results for referred touch ratings. Participant beliefs arising from demand characteristics dominated over multisensory mechanisms in RHI ownership of a fake hand and proprioceptive drift. Multisensory synchrony was not necessary to produce the classic effects, falsifying the theory that the illusion requires multisensory integration. Claims of an illusion beyond that attributable to demand characteristics and phenomenological control require experimental evidence from controlled experiments.

articles.title: Early caregiving adversities and parental context effects on adolescents’ momentary emotion differentiation
articles.authors: Lior Abramson; Anna Vannucci; Camila Vicioso; Daniela Juarez; Erin Joyce; Andrea Fields; Erica Niemiec; Lisa Gibson; Niall Bolger; Nim Tottenham
articles.abstract: Emotion differentiation—the ability to identify specific experienced emotions—associates with psychological health. Although theorized to develop through caregiving experiences, contextual effects on emotion differentiation in developmental populations have rarely been investigated, particularly among youth who have experienced disruptions in early caregiving. Here, we examined how adolescents’ momentary emotion differentiation varies across socioemotional contexts and whether these patterns differ following exposure to severe caregiving-related early adversities. Adolescents aged 10–17 with or without caregiving-related early adversities (N=81; mean age=13.49, SD = 1.97; 53% male/47% female, 9%-Asian American, 28%-black, 34%-white, 28%-other) completed 7-day ecological momentary assessment (4–5 surveys/day), reporting emotions and social contexts. At the trait level, there were no significant group differences in emotion differentiation. At the momentary level, negative momentary emotion differentiation decreased following negative parent-related contexts compared to other contexts. However, the momentary emotions’ standard deviation indicated also differentiated phasic intensification of a few negative emotions. Importantly, exposure to caregiving-related early adversities attenuated these contextual effects, L.Ratio(3) = 9.178 - 11.263. These findings provide initial evidence linking severe caregiving-related early adversities to affective dynamic processes and raise the hypothesis that early caregiving disruptions mitigate momentary parental modulation effects on emotion differentiation.

articles.title: Beyond Turing Equivalence:  The Human Premium in Human–AI Interaction
articles.authors: Ophelia Deroy
articles.abstract: Asking whether we can know whether a given text or output is coming from a machine or a human, which was at the core of the Turing test, is being progressively retired. This opens a new and no less interesting question: what happens when we know? This paper reviews evidence that when humans encounter exactly the same content, presented here as coming from a human and there from an AI, they do not behave similarly. The evidence across different kinds of interaction, advice giving, compliance, reciprocal interaction, and preferential choice, is that humans respect other humans more than they respect machines. This difference is often described as a 'machine penalty' where we distrust machines or lack familiarity with them, and predicted to decrease as AI becomes more prevalent. The paper offers a different interpretation, showing that we treat humans better for good reasons, including utility calculations, and that this human premium is likely to stay.

articles.title: Profiling the Chinese Participants in Psychological Science: Non-WEIRD but Not Representative
articles.authors: Lei Yue; Zhangweiwei; Chunxiao Wang; Xi-Nian Zuo; Hu Chuan-Peng
articles.abstract: Psychological science aims at understanding the human mind and behavior, but it primarily relies on participants from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic regions, i.e., the WEIRD problem. This lack of diversity and representativeness of participants compromises the generalizability of psychological science. To address this issue, large-scale international collaborative projects have been initiated, and more data have been collected from non-WEIRD regions. However, it is unknown whether participants from non-WEIRD regions can represent their local population. In this preregistered report, we depicted the demographic profile of Chinese participants reported in 1, 000 empirical studies (n = 554, 794) published in five mainstream Chinese psychological journals and in 27 large-scale international collaborative projects (n = 29, 006, accounting for 2.12% of all participants). We found that age and sex were the most reported demographic variables, and other aspects of participants were less reported. The available demographic information revealed that Chinese participants were not representative of the population: most were young, well-educated, and resided in East China. Also, Chinese participants in large-scale international collaborative projects are less representative than those from Chinese journals in terms of geographical distributions. The demographic profile of Chinese participants in psychology is similar to their counterparts in many other countries and regions, suggesting the globalization of young and highly educated participants in psychological science. Together, our findings indicate that problems of representativeness are deeply entrenched in global psychological science and require coordinated cross-sector efforts.

articles.title: Pleasurable beliefs and hedonic belief-based utility
articles.authors: Stephen Gadsby
articles.abstract: Humans are consistently biased towards pleasurable beliefs, for example, that we are better than average regarding desirable traits and that our futures will be brighter than statistically plausible. According to an influential theory within psychology, neuroscience, and behavioural economics, we are biased towards these (and other) pleasurable beliefs because they maximise hedonic belief-utility. I challenge this theory and suggest alternative explanations for pleasurable beliefs and the psychological processes that produce them. According to the view I present, such beliefs stem from processes that have little to do with maximising belief-utility.

articles.title: Self-Defeating Utilitarianism:  Laypeople Think that Aiming to Maximize Societal Welfare Will Backfire
articles.authors: Jonathan Zev Berman; Stefan Schubert; Lucius Caviola
articles.abstract: Utilitarianism holds that morally right actions are those that maximize aggregate welfare. One might therefore expect a society that adopts utilitarianism as its guiding moral code to flourish. However, across five preregistered studies (plus one preregistered supplemental study; total N = 2,626), we find that laypeople view utilitarianism as being self-defeating. Participants expect a society that adopts a welfare-maximizing moral code to contain less happiness and more suffering than a society that adopts a moral code based on fixed rules or duties. While individuals endorse welfare maximization as a societal aim and believe that promoting moderate versions of utilitarianism’s implications—especially greater impartiality and personal self-sacrifice—would advance this aim, they view utilitarianism as promoting these implications to an extreme and ultimately self-defeating degree. This yields a fundamental paradox in lay moral reasoning: the moral philosophy explicitly designed to maximize welfare is expected to fail to do so at scale.

articles.title: AI or Human Support for Suicide Prevention?  Examining Help-Seeking Intention in Suicidal Crisis
articles.authors: Daisuke Nakamura; Hajime Sueki; Jiro Ito
articles.abstract:
This preprint has now been published in the peer-reviewed journal Suicide Policy Research. Please read and cite the published version:

Nakamura, D., Sueki, H., & Ito, J. (2026). AI or human support for suicide prevention? Examining help-seeking intention in suicidal crisis. Suicide Policy Research, 5(1), 1–12.

The published article is freely available at:
https://jscp.or.jp/assets/img/SPR_5-1_1_Nakamura.pdf


Background:
Chat-based crisis support is a common strategy for suicide prevention, and artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have the potential to improve the low response rates to such support. Although AI chatbots are technically feasible for crisis support, it remains unclear whether individuals experiencing suicidal ideation intend to use them.

Aims:
To examine the intentions of adults with depressive symptoms experiencing suicidal ideation to use chat-based crisis support (human vs AI) and explore how these intentions relate to their background characteristics.

Methods:
A cross-sectional web-based survey was performed, recruiting participants aged 18–69 with a Kessler-6 score ≥13 from an internet research company’s database in Japan. Participants completed a questionnaire assessing their intention to use chat-based crisis support when feeling suicidal, sociodemographic factors, and suicide-related characteristics. Subsequently, participants were categorized into four groups: (1) those intending to use both human and AI-based chats, (2) AI chat only, (3) human chat only, and (4) neither. We calculated the proportions of each group and used the chi-square, Kruskal–Wallis, and Fisher’s exact tests to compare group differences.

Results:
Overall, 1,024 participants completed the survey, and we determined that 19.5% intended to use AI chat support and 21.3% intended to use human chat. The proportions of participants who intended to use both human- and AI-based chat, AI chat only, human chat only, and neither option were 15.6 %, 3.9 %, 5.7 %, and 74.8 %, respectively.
