Significant differences were observed in gender (p = 0.028), history of crisis support use (p <0.001), and current issues (financial problems [p = 0.002)] and sexuality-related concerns (p = 0.006) across the groups.

Conclusion:
In this web-based survey, approximately 20% of individuals with depressive symptoms feeling suicidal were willing to seek help, even if it was provided by AI.

articles.title: Development and Preliminary Psychometric Validation of the Guna-Based Social Media Consumption Questionnaire: Associations with Social Networking Addiction and Nomophobia
articles.authors: Divyansh Pandey; Arnav Bhavsar; Alok Bajpai
articles.abstract:
Objective: This study aimed to develop and conduct preliminary psychometric validation of the Guna-Based Social Media Consumption Questionnaire (G-SMCQ) and examine its associations with social networking addiction (SNA) and nomophobia (NMP) using the Triguna framework from Indian psychology.
Method: Participants were 106 Indian undergraduate students (86 males, 20 females; aged 16–20 years, M = 18.05, SD = 0.72). A cross-sectional design evaluated the preliminary psychometric properties of the G-SMCQ and its relationships with the Social Networking Addiction Scale and the Nomophobia Questionnaire.
Results: MCA provided some preliminary evidence that the G-SMCQ response patterns were characterised by a multidimensional structure. Mean scores for the three Gunas indicated that Sattvic consumption was 9.86 (SD = 4.24), Rajasic consumption was 5.97 (SD = 3.66), and Tamasic consumption was 1.17 (SD = 1.75). Internal consistency reliability coefficients for the three Gunas were reported to be .840, .776, and .697, respectively. The relationship between Sattvic consumption and social networking addiction and nomophobia was negative (SNA: ρ = −.530, p < .001; NMP: ρ = −.295, p = .002), while Rajasic consumption was positively correlated to both constructs (SNA: ρ = .463, p < .001; NMP: ρ = .284, p = .003). However, Tamasic consumption was correlated to SNA (ρ = .270, p = .005) only, but not with nomophobia (ρ = .157, p = .109).
Conclusion: The results provided some preliminary psychometric evidence that suggests the potential of the G-SMCQ as a culturally-grounded measure of the Triguna-based social media consumption patterns.
Keywords: Social Media Consumption; Social Networking Addiction; Nomophobia;
Triguna Theory; Digital behavior

articles.title: When do intentions predict action? The temporal dynamics of the intention–action gap
articles.authors: Peiyuan Zhang; Luisa Leonelli; Yijun Lin; Wei Ji Ma
articles.abstract: Procrastination is defined as voluntarily delaying an intended course of action, yet the gap between intention and action is rarely measured directly, and little is known about how it unfolds over time. We gave 127 adults seven days to complete 180 units of a self-paced online reading task and recorded the timestamp of every completed unit. Before the task began, 67 of them reported how many units they intended to complete on each of the seven days, so that intended and actual work were expressed in the same units on the same days. Among those who finished, work was concentrated 0.59 days later than intended, although the day people finished did not differ from the day they had planned. The gap widened through Day 4, stopped growing on Day 5, and narrowed over the final two days. Intentions predicted when people started but not when they finished, and their influence faded after the first half of the task. Trait procrastination showed the opposite pattern, predicting actual but not intended work and shaping the timing of work throughout the task, most strongly in the middle.

articles.title: Explicit affective inferences enhance behavioral sensitivity to naturalistic expressions
articles.authors: Doron Atias; Maria Gendron
articles.abstract: Emotion theories highlight the fundamental function of emotional expressions in regulating social behavior. Yet, this basic premise relies mostly on studies using posed expressions that may fail to capture the diversity of real-life emotional signals and invite explicit affective inferences due to their salient symbolic nature. Across three studies (N=1,529), we tested how naturalistic emotional expressions differentially shape affective judgments and prosocial behavior. Participants watched videos of distressed individuals expressing typical crying, atypical crying, typical laughter, or no vocalization, and either inferred the targets’ affect (Study 1) or donated real money to help them from a provided budget (Study 2). Perceivers were sensitive to the vocal crying variation when explicitly inferring affect, but not when making donation decisions. Importantly, when perceivers explicitly inferred affect before donating (Study 3), they donated nearly 40% more and showed increased sensitivity to vocal cue variation. These findings suggest that inferring other people’s affect when making behavioral decisions is not routine and can facilitate helping behavior and the sensitivity to others’ emotional signals. This also highlight the important role of explicit inferential processes in linking real-life emotional expressions to prosocial behavior in everyday life.

articles.title: Dynamic Semantic–Prosodic Integration in Emotional Speech Perception: From Channel Dominance to Precision-Weighted Predictive Coding
articles.authors: Yi Lin; Yang Zhang
articles.abstract: Emotional speech is an important carrier of affective information in spoken communication. Its perception depends on the joint processing of emotional semantics and prosody, yet the relative contribution of these two information sources varies across individuals and contexts. However, a unified account is still lacking of why their processing weights change and how the brain dynamically adjusts them according to the reliability of incoming information. This review synthesizes evidence on emotional semantics and prosody, from relatively independent processing to interactive integration, and argues that their relationship is best understood in terms of dynamic weight allocation. On this basis, we propose a Precision-Weighted Predictive Coding Model (PW-PC), which integrates Bayesian inference, cue precision, and prediction error within a unified framework. The model assumes that semantic and prosodic information are continuously reweighted according to current evidence and its estimated precision, while incorporating sensory reliability, experience-based expectations, contextual diagnosticity, and reweighting flexibility. This framework shifts the focus of emotional speech research from identifying which channel dominates to explaining when, why, and how the brain dynamically reallocates weight across multiple affective information sources, thereby providing a unified theoretical perspective linking behavioral performance, neural dynamics, and computational mechanisms.

articles.title: Functional Neuroanatomy of Sign Language Production: An ALE Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Lydia Wiernik; Angela D. Friederici; Karen Emmorey; Patrick C. Trettenbrein
articles.abstract: Sign languages are natural languages expressed by a distinct set of linguistic articulators: the hands, face, and body. Several neuroimaging studies of the neural substrates underlying sign production have observed the recruitment of brain regions previously identified as being involved in speech production, despite the difference in production channels. However, no prior work has provided a statistical synthesis of this available literature. Here, we report a pre-registered meta-analysis of the published positron emission tomography (PET) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) literature on sign language production (N experiments = 15, N participants = 168). Combining an Activation Likelihood Estimation (ALE) approach with jackknife re-sampling to validate the robustness of our findings, we identify four clusters consistently associated with the production of single signs across studies in the literature located in (1) left inferior frontal gyrus including BA 45 and extending into (2) left anterior insula, (3) the left superior frontal gyrus, and (4) the medial and right cerebellum. Meta-analytic connectivity modelling using data from a large-scale database of neuroimaging studies confirmed that the IFG, insula, and SFG clusters observed for sign language production are also recruited for spoken language production and comprehension. Moreover, our results also highlight the importance of the cerebellum during sign production and indicate modality-dependent convergence patterns in cerebellar subregions. In sum, our findings complement prior work on sign language comprehension and spoken language production, suggesting substantial overlap in the neural substrates of language processing and production-related mechanisms between sign and spoken language.

articles.title: Modality-Independent Core Brain Network for Language as Proved by Sign Language
articles.authors: Patrick C. Trettenbrein; Nina-Kristin Meister; Ksenija Slivac; Thomas A. Finkbeiner; Markus Steinbach; Angela D. Friederici; Emiliano Zaccarella
articles.abstract:
The human brain has the capacity to automatically compute the grammatical relations of
words in sentences, be they spoken or written. This species-specific ability for syntax lies at
the core of our capacity for language and is primarily subserved by a left-hemispheric fronto-
temporal network consisting of the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (pIFG), as well as the
posterior middle temporal gyrus and superior temporal sulcus (pMTG/STS). To date, it
remains unclear whether this core network for syntactic processing identified for spoken and
written language in hearing people also holds for the processing of the grammatical structure
of a natural sign language in deaf people. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, a
sign language paradigm that systematically varied the presence of syntactic and lexical-
semantic information, and meta-analytically defined functional regions-of-interests derived
from a large dataset of syntactic processing in hearing non-signers, we demonstrate that deaf
native signers of German Sign Language (DGS) also recruit left pIFG and pMTG/STS for
computing grammatical relations in sign language—indicating the universality of the core
language network. These findings suggest that the human brain evolved a dedicated neural
network for processing the grammatical structure of natural languages independent of
language modality, which flexibly interacts with different externalization systems depending
on the modality of language use.

articles.title: Repetition increases belief more for trivia statements than news headlines
articles.authors: Raunak M Pillai; Steven Yang; Qiwenjing Jiang; Lisa Fazio
articles.abstract: Repetition increases belief in true and false statements. This “illusory truth effect,” has been documented across dozens of experiments using materials ranging from trivia statements to claims about consumer products to political news. Further, current theories of the effect focus on low-level psychological cues like processing fluency that arise spontaneously and that should affect judgements of truth uniformly for all such types of statements. In contrast to this picture, we find that the size of the illusory truth effect varies for different types of statements, with larger effects occurring when people see banal trivia statements as opposed to political or viral, health-related news headlines. We report six studies (total N = 1,749 US MTurkers) demonstrating this effect or testing potential explanations. We find that these differences appear to be driven by the overall context of the type of statements participants encounter rather than features of each individual statement. These findings speak to the malleable nature of the link between repetition and belief, with repetition being more a more impactful contributor to beliefs in contexts where people are saying some kinds of statements (e.g., trivia statements) than others (e.g., political or health-related news).

articles.title: Making Sense of Sensory Differences: Identifying Sensory Processing Phenotypes and Their Relationship to Social and Executive Functioning in Neurotypical Children.
articles.authors: Adrianna M Molenaar; Natalia Van Esch; Nichole Scheerer
articles.abstract: Sensory processing varies substantially across individuals, yet research on distinct sensory phenotypes has focused primarily on neurodivergent populations. We examined whether comparable sensory phenotypes could be identified in 200 children aged 4-12 years with no known neurodevelopmental or psychiatric diagnoses, and whether phenotype membership was associated with executive functioning, social competence, mental health, alexithymia, and neurodivergent traits. K-means clustering of parent-reported sensory processing identified four sensory phenotypes: Sensory Adaptive, Generalized Sensory Differences, Under-responsive/Filtering Differences, and Sensory Sensitive. Children in the Sensory Adaptive group showed fewer executive functioning difficulties than children in all other groups and higher social competence than those in the Generalized Sensory Differences and Sensory Sensitive groups. In contrast, phenotypes did not differ significantly in autistic or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder traits, alexithymia, anxiety, or depression. These findings demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in sensory processing among children without diagnosed conditions and suggest that sensory phenotypes may be meaningfully related to everyday cognitive and social functioning. Future transdiagnostic work should directly examine the extent to which these phenotypes are shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children.

articles.title: No evidence of phonosymbolic effects in Polish echoic reduplications with sr-
articles.authors: Antonio Benítez-Burraco; Mingshan Xu; Monika Lisowska
articles.abstract: Expressives (i.e. linguistic items used for conveying emotions) can be phonosymbolic in nature or culturally-motivated. In Polish, echoic reduplicated sequences with the formant sr- are frequently used to convey contempt. We conducted an online survey to determine whether sr- is universally associated with this emotion. We tested speakers of Polish, but also of 2 other Indo-European languages (English and Spanish), and 3 non-Indo-European languages (Hungarian, Turkish and Indonesian). Findings suggest that only Polish speakers associate sr- with contempt, but less than expected. This suggests that this association does not result from any phonosymbolic effect or is typical of Indo-European languages generally. But is confined instead to Polish language, seemingly because sr- is the onset of one derogatory term in this language (srać). Still, the effect is stronger when concerning real words compared to pseudowords.

articles.title: Why do preschoolers struggle with the 3-cups-task? Further evidence for cognitive asymmetries in representing what and where uncertainty
articles.authors: Marlene M. Meyer; Marina Proft; Hannes Rakoczy
articles.abstract: Prior research on modal thought has yielded conflicting findings regarding children’s ability to represent mutually exclusive possibilities. While some studies suggest that even infants and non-human animals understand possibilities to some degree, older children struggle in experimental paradigms that require them to consider multiple alternatives. In the 3-cups-task, for instance, they fail to systematically prefer a certain reward (in A) over two uncertain options (in B or C). This has been taken as evidence for that children below age 4 lack genuinely modal representations of possibility. However, recent metacognitive research suggests that already three-year-old children can recognize epistemic uncertainty about possible, mutually exclusive object identities (X or Y). So, why do 3-year-olds metacognitively acknowledge their ignorance in some contexts, but obviously fail to do so in trying to solve the 3-cups task? We addressed this question in three preregistered experiments (N = 278 three-year-old children) in which we investigated whether details of the task pragmatics, question format or the contents of the uncertainty judgments pose specific performance factors in the 3-cups-task. There was no clear evidence that task pragmatics or question format per se explain these difficulties. But there was strong evidence that the content of the uncertainty judgments matters: Children found it much more difficult to represent uncertainty where an object is (in cups B or C) than to represent uncertainty which of two objects (X or Y) was in a given box. These results converge with other recent findings to suggest a fundamental where/what asymmetry in children’s early modal reasoning and raise crucial questions about the robustness of early modal competence.

articles.title: Real-Time Associations Between Emotional Responses to Social Media and Mood Differ By Adolescent: Implications For Risk and Resilience
articles.authors: Melissa J Dreier; Jennifer Susan Silk; Evan Kleiman; Jessica L. Hamilton
articles.abstract: Adolescents differ in their vulnerability to social media’s mental health effects. Some may experience stronger links between emotional reactions to social media (ERSM) and mood, increasing risk for subsequent mental health problems. In the current study, 131 adolescents (ages 14–17) completed baseline assessments and eight weeks of ecological momentary assessment (3x/day). A dynamic structural equation model tested group-level and person-specific relationships between negative ERSM and depressed mood, controlling for prior mood. Adolescents showed substantial heterogeneity in ERSM-mood relationships. Stronger coupling was associated with baseline depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and nonsuicidal self-injury, but not suicide attempts. Throughout the study, stronger coupling was associated with higher depressed mood, suicidal thoughts, and mood volatility. It was not associated with the frequency or intensity of negative ERSM or in-person experiences or emotion regulation strategies. Taken together, adolescents whose mood is more strongly tied to ERSM may be at heightened risk for mental health problems.

articles.title: What beliefs are most debunkable?
articles.authors: Esther Boissin; Thomas H Costello; David Gertler Rand; Gordon Pennycook
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can persuade people to revise their beliefs, but it is unclear which beliefs are most "debunkable," and why. Across three pooled studies, participants (N = 3,341 online U.S. adults) discussed a self-reported conspiracy or other epistemically suspect belief with GPT-4, instructed to debunk it using facts and evidence. An LLM classified each belief by content domain (i.e., conspiratorial, paranormal/supernatural, pseudoscience, political, religious, other) and evidential status, from strong counterevidence to supported by evidence. Confidence decreased in every domain, but belief updating tracked evidential status rather than domain: reductions were substantial wherever the belief was open to counterevidence — strong, weak, or uninvestigated — and small for non-falsifiable and supported beliefs. Domain no longer predicted change once evidential status was accounted for, and the counterevidence the LLM deployed partially mediated the gradient. AI debunking appears most effective for falsifiable beliefs resting on weak evidence.

articles.title: Comparing the efficacy of virtual reality and flat screen delivery of breath control training for anxiety management
articles.authors: Grace Yat Sum Leung; Naresh Subramaniam; Benjamin Cook; Lucie Daniel-Watanabe; Johanna Finnemann; Toby Woolley; Craig Powell; Sergey Sitnikov; Paul Fletcher
articles.abstract: Game-based biofeedback offers a promising approach for learning and practising breath control techniques to manage anxiety and stress. Traditionally known as a response-modulation emotion regulation strategy, biofeedback operates through a closed-loop system that measures and feeds back real-time physiological information for users to monitor and subsequently manage their bodily responses. Few studies, however, have directly compared breath control training integrated with game-based biofeedback across two-dimensional flat screen display and three-dimensional immersive environment. It remains unclear whether differences in realism and immersiveness might influence the efficacy of breath control training. The present study investigated training effectiveness and user evaluation of a novel biofeedback-based breath control game among forty-five healthy adolescents. The breath control training was delivered in both virtual reality (VR) and flat screen modalities in a randomised and counterbalanced order using a within-subject study design. Consistent with hypotheses, the biofeedback game significantly improved both subjective and physiological (standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN) and heart rate) markers of anxiety. While the two modalities indicated comparable intervention efficacy, the VR biofeedback game contributed added benefits in increasing SDNN, a physiological indicator of stress that reflects overall autonomic nervous system activity, as well as facilitating greater levels of interest and enjoyment, as indicated by ratings of intrinsic motivation to engage in the self-regulation training. These findings suggest that VR-based breath control training may enhance engagement and specific physiological responses, with implications for the design, development and evaluation of VR games for improving anxiety and stress.

articles.title: Redundancy Protects Human Collaborations from Failure
articles.authors: Elizabeth Mieczkowski; Rachit Dubey; Natalia Vélez; Thomas L. Griffiths
articles.abstract: In the name of efficiency, organizations and governments around the world are increasingly trimming redundancy---personnel or overlapping capabilities beyond what routine operations require. Drawing on distributed computing and cognitive science, we challenge this view. Using queueing simulations and a preregistered multiplayer experiment (N = 832 in 187 teams of 3–6), we show that redundancy improves performance through two distinct routes. Adding collaborators to a team improves resilience, with larger teams completing more tasks when members became temporarily unable to contribute. Giving team members overlapping capabilities also improved efficiency, with teams in which collaborators could perform multiple roles completing substantially more work. These findings suggest that efforts to improve short-term efficiency by reducing redundancy may come at a cost, quietly eroding a team’s capacity to withstand unexpected failures.

articles.title: Longitudinal, Reciprocal Associations Between Social Self-Evaluation and Depressive Symptoms Across the Second Decade of Life
articles.authors: Victoria Guazzelli Williamson; Samantha Chavez; John Coleman Flournoy; Nicholas B. Allen; Jennifer H Pfeifer
articles.abstract: Background: A key developmental task in adolescence is social self-concept development. Adolescence is also a period of heightened risk for internalizing psychopathology, particularly depression. While prior research has found links between self-processing and depression, social self-concept remains understudied and the causal direction of these associations remains unclear. Methods: Data come from a longitudinal study of adolescent girls (N = 172, aged 10-13 at baseline, ~18-month inter-wave intervals). Results: We show that negative social self-evaluation and depressive symptoms display longitudinal, reciprocal associations across four waves of data spanning early to late adolescence. Additionally, while self-negativity increased over time, self-positivity did not change, and both aspects of self-perception were independently associated with depressive symptoms. Conclusions: These findings suggest that social self-evaluation and depressive symptoms mutually influence each other across adolescence, and that negative social self-evaluation may be a useful intervention target for preventing and treating depressive psychopathology among adolescents.

articles.title: Multiple neural signatures of serial order access in verbal working memory
articles.authors: Giulia Cristoforetti; Yangwen Xu; Simone Viganò; Jean Philippe van Dijck; Roberto Bottini; Wim Fias
articles.abstract: Serial order working memory allows information to be maintained as structured sequences, yet the neural formats supporting access to serial position remain unclear. Behavioral evidence suggests that temporal order can be recoded into spatial representations, but serial order may also rely on representations that generalize beyond the spatial configuration of encoding. Here, participants memorized digit sequences presented either left-to-right or right-to-left, thereby reversing the mapping between ordinal position and external space while keeping retrieval cues centrally presented during fMRI. Behaviorally, spatial coding during retrieval was modulated by encoding direction. Multivoxel pattern analysis revealed direction-specific decoding in lateral parietal cortex: left inferior parietal cortex encoded serial position after left-to-right encoding, whereas right inferior parietal cortex did so after right-to-left encoding. In contrast, cross-direction decoding revealed direction-invariant effects in left supramarginal and precentral regions, suggesting serial-position information that generalized across spatial layouts. Finally, univariate parametric modulation revealed activity scaling with serial position in bilateral posterior parietal cortex, left anterior hippocampus, and action-control regions. Together, these findings indicate that serial order access in working memory relies on multiple neural signatures, including spatially context-dependent representations, direction-invariant ordinal codes, and graded process-related activity.

articles.title: Nonverbal Cognition is Associated with Discourse Production in Persons with Aphasia: Evidence from Expository and Picture Description Tasks
articles.authors: Hana Kim; Manaswita Dutta
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Spoken discourse analysis has gained empirical and clinical attention, yet current practice predominantly relies on picture-based tasks which may not fully capture the language impairments experienced by persons with aphasia (PWA) in more complex contexts. Expository discourse, though more cognitively demanding and structurally complex, remains under-researched in aphasia despite its ecological relevance. This study aimed to (1) compare nonverbal cognitive abilities in PWA and neurologically healthy adults (NHA); (2) examine the effects of discourse task by comparing expository and picture description performance in PWA; and (3) investigate associations between nonverbal cognitive abilities and discourse outcomes. 
Method: Participants (PWA = 24; NHA = 13) completed nonverbal cognitive tasks that assess processing speed, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. They also completed expository discourse tasks (expressing opinions on the healthcare system and homeschooling). Discourse samples were analyzed using six variables (MATTR, Percent CIU, Verbs per utterance, syntactic complexity, local and global coherence) selected to represent linguistic, propositional, and macrostructural domains in discourse.
Results: Significant group differences were found in cognitive flexibility task accuracy, and response times on tasks measuring cognitive flexibility and processing speed. In expository discourse, PWA performed worse than NHA across the linguistic, propositional, and macrostructural domains. Notably, task comparisons revealed that expository discourse elicited greater performance in syntactic complexity but poorer coherence than the picture description task in PWA. Cognitive influences on discourse differed by tasks and groups: in PWA, cognitive flexibility generally showed strong associations with all discourse domains across both tasks, with fewer correlations for the picture description task. Also, the pattern of associations varied across cognitive tasks and discourse measures for the picture description task. No significant associations were observed among controls. 
Conclusion: Findings highlight the unique interplay between cognitive and linguistic skills in the expository task. This finding supports the potential use of expository discourse in aphasia assessment.

articles.title: Cognitive constraints govern collective outcomes in strategic network formation
articles.authors: Hicham DAHMOU; Frédéric Moisan; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Social networks are built through local decisions, yet the value of a connection depends on paths that individuals cannot fully observe. How such bounded information shapes collective efficiency remains unclear. Here we develop a computational model in which agents revise links using a limited view of the network, an expectation about connections beyond that view, and stochastic choice. Starting from an inefficient empty network, the model reaches near-efficient structures within an intermediate regime: agents must value unseen opportunities enough to initiate connectivity, but not so strongly that continued linking prevents the removal of redundant ties. This favorable regime narrows as groups grow, although broader visibility partly restores it and agent heterogeneity preserves its qualitative form. Earlier action or link receipt is associated with eventual hub status, while stable agent-level decision parameters are associated with persistent payoff ranks across repeated networks. Introducing one agent that forms links without considering payoffs reduces welfare in small groups but increases it in larger groups, while concentrating costs on the builder. These results identify a scale-dependent balance between exploration, local representation and value-sensitive pruning through which bounded individual decisions can generate collective efficiency and structural inequality.

articles.title: Noun memory advantage drives sentence internal primacy and recency at clause boundaries
articles.authors: Sebastián Mancha; Ellen Lau
articles.abstract: Classic research in psychology has shown that comprehenders in recall tasks ‘chunk’ word lists in order to facilitate later retrieval. Here we ask how chunking mechanisms apply in grammatically structured sentence stimuli. How do comprehenders make use of this grammatical structure to guide chunking of a sentence’s component words in memory? In previous studies of multi-clause sentence recall, many researchers have argued that chunking is clause-based, as evidenced by scalloped serial accuracy curves in which primacy and recency effects are observed within each clause. Here we suggest that these previous findings may have been driven by the correlation of sentence boundaries with nouns, a lexical class known to demonstrate an independent accuracy advantage in recall. Using immediate serial recall of naturalistic biclausal English sentences and manipulating noun placement, we find evidence that nouns indeed confer a large accuracy boost at the internal clause boundary that can explain prior results. We discuss the difficulty of applying serial position logic to highly structured representations such as those that underlie sentence forms.

articles.title: Comprehenders’ Error Correction Mechanisms are Finely Calibrated to Language Production Statistics
articles.authors: Peng Qian; Roger Philip Levy
articles.abstract: An essential feature of human communication is robustness to errors: even when speakers and writers make mistakes, listeners and readers can usually determine the intended meaning. A leading hypothesis is that comprehenders achieve robust error correction by internally deploying a "noisy-channel" model of the language production process. Crucially, to best achieve error robustness, a comprehender's noisy-channel model should be finely calibrated to the environmental statistics of language production, incorporating not only prior expectations about communicative intents but also structure-sensitive likelihoods of different types of speaker error. This environmentally-calibrated noisy-channel hypothesis has been difficult to test, because the rates of most types of language production errors are hard to estimate. Here we test this hypothesis by experimentally investigating comprehenders' interpretations of subject-verb agreement errors, for which context-contingent language production error rates are feasible to estimate. In a novel free-form error correction task,  participants edited sentences with subject-verb agreement mismatches to indicate what they think was intended. Bayesian analysis of the resulting data shows that comprehenders' interpretations reflect both item-specific prior expectations and structure-sensitive error likelihoods that closely correspond to error rates in language production. These results provide quantitative evidence that humans closely track prior statistics over linguistic forms and deploy a noisy-channel model finely calibrated to statistics of the linguistic environment to achieve robust language understanding.

articles.title: What is it like for matter to matter?
articles.authors: David Vandenheever
articles.abstract: Consciousness research often asks where, when, or under what conditions neural processing becomes conscious. Here I introduce the Distributed Architecture of Valenced Evaluation (DAVE), which starts from a different premise. Nervous systems continuously represent states in terms of what those states imply for the organism, and these evaluations are physically instantiated in dispositions that bias bodily, attentional, predictive, and action systems. DAVE proposes that, where such organism-relative evaluation is embedded in the embodied dynamics through which a represented state can alter the organism, its evaluative character is already minimally phenomenal. Each such evaluative event constitutes a micro-quale: not a miniature conscious subject or an independently experienced percept, but a local phenomenal contribution to the experience of the organism. Recurrent interaction among many micro-qualia forms the richly differentiated, context-sensitive, and apparently unified phenomenal tapestry familiar in human experience. Attention, task demands, working memory, and self-representation selectively amplify, stabilize, and organize parts of this tapestry, producing increasingly integrated, accessible, and self-related forms of experience. Because introspection presents the integrated tapestry rather than its constituent evaluative events, phenomenal character may appear to be an additional property beyond the physical organization that constitutes it. This conception of phenomenal character makes the explanatory gap seem inevitable. DAVE does not solve the hard problem by discovering a mechanism that converts nonphenomenal processing into phenomenality; it attempts to dissolve the need for such a conversion by identifying minimal phenomenal character with organism-relative evaluative disposition itself.

articles.title: Green Against the Machine: Natural Environment Exposure Attenuates Subjective and Physiological Responses to Technostress Across Levels of Agency
articles.authors: Simone Di Plinio; Claudia Greco; David Perpetuini; Massimo De Acetis; Miriam D'Ignazio; Arcangelo Merla; Daniela Cardone; Sjoerd Ebisch
articles.abstract: Urban living often limits routine contact with nature, while digital technologies have become deeply embedded in everyday life and cognition. Yet technological malfunctions, intrusions, and diminished user agency can elicit technostress, raising the question of whether exposure to natural environments can buffer its effects. This study examined whether exposure to a natural (green) environment, compared with a built urban (gray) environment, attenuates psychophysiological responses to technostress. Fifty-two healthy adults were assigned to either a green (garden-like) or gray (built urban) environment. Before and after two outdoor walking sessions in the assigned environment, participants completed a word-selection task manipulating technology-induced stress and sense of agency. High-resolution infrared thermal imaging was used as a contact-free method to monitor facial temperature dynamics, providing indirect indices of peripheral autonomic regulation during task performance, while heart rate variability (HRV) was monitored as an index of cardiac autonomic activity during task performance. High technostress reduced task accuracy and increased perceived stress. Under the condition combining high technostress and reduced agency, perceived stress decreased following green, but not gray, exposure. Facial thermal responses, particularly in the nose-tip and perioral regions, also differed between the green and gray groups under stressful task conditions, indicating that environmental exposure modulated peripheral physiological responses associated with technostress. No effects were observed for HRV. After gray, but not green, environmental exposure, an increase in self-report agency measures under high technostress was accompanied by an increase in perioral temperature, indicating a relationship between subjective experience and peripheral activation. These findings suggest that even brief exposures to natural green environments may reduce vulnerability to technostress by attenuating subjective stress and modulating peripheral physiological responses. The results contribute to the growing literature on restorative environments, human–technology interaction, and psychophysiological resilience.

articles.title: Eye Movements Reflect Listening Effort and Visualizable Speech
articles.authors: Geneva Mariotti; Bjorn Herrmann; Jennifer D. Ryan
articles.abstract: Eye movements can index the recruitment of cognitive resources. During listening, increased effort is associated with reduced eye movements. However, eye movements also support mental imagery, suggesting that reduced eye movements during effortful listening may reflect the difficulty of creating mental images to support speech comprehension. Here, we examined how speech content and listening difficulty interact to shape eye movements during listening and later recall. Young adults listened to, and subsequently recalled, descriptions for which rich, visual details were (i.e., concrete descriptions) or were not (i.e., abstract described) spoken in different levels of background noise (easy vs hard) while eye movements were recorded. During listening, fixation rate, saccade amplitude, and gaze dispersion decreased under difficult listening conditions and for concrete descriptions. Gaze dispersion timecourses tracked spatial-relational words, but not other relational content, in concrete descriptions. During recall, eye movements were lower for concrete descriptions, particularly when encoded under hard listening conditions. Notably, gaze dispersion peaked before the recall of spatial-relational details, especially in participants with higher recall accuracy. Together, these findings suggest that listening effort shapes eye movements, while visualizable speech content elicits distinct patterns in which eye movements may be co-opted to represent imagined space and support memory accuracy.

articles.title: Temporal associations between short-form video use and affective dynamics: A 14-day ecological momentary assessment among Chinese university students
articles.authors: Yu Gu; Wen Zheng; Johannes Thrul
articles.abstract: Short-form video use is associated with poor emotional well-being, yet its short-term temporal relationship with affect in daily life remains unclear. We conducted a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study to examine bidirectional associations between reported short-form video use (SV) and affective states, seperate within-person fluctuations from between-person differences, and assess whether the daily SV use rate was associated with affective inertia and innovation variability. A total of 134 Chinese university students contributed 17,514 valid EMA responses, yielding 14,899 complete same-day lag-1 transitions. Using Bayesian dynamic structural equation modeling, we identified several associations at the momentary timescale: 1) SV use during the preceding survey interval was associated with lower positive affect at the subsequent assessment; 2) SV use and above-zero negative affect intensity were positively associated in both directions, whereas no credible association was observed between SV use and the all-zero negative affect state. At the daily timescale: 1) Daily SV use rate was not associated with mean levels of either positive or negative affect; 2) Higher daily SV use was associated with weaker inertia in both positive affect and above-zero negative affect, as well as lower innovation variability in positive affect. In conclusion, our findings highlight the dynamic associations between SV use and affect across multiple timescales. These findings motivate further research using objective use logs and designs capable of supporting causal inference.

articles.title: Parsing structured semantic knowledge from arbitrary text with GenAI
articles.authors: A.T. Lopes Rego; Joshua Snell; Martijn Meeter
articles.abstract: Frame Semantics offers a compelling framework for representing meaning as structured conceptual scenarios (frames). FrameNet operationalizes this theory as a lexical resource linking words to frames and their conceptual roles (frame elements, FEs). However, applying Frame Semantics to arbitrary text has historically required either laborious manual annotation or complex, task-specific classification pipelines that presuppose known targets and/or frames. Here we present an open-source method that leverages Generative AI (GenAI) to automatically parse semantic frames and their FEs from any input text, without requiring pre-specification of frames or target spans, or task-specific model training. The tool combines a retrieval step, in which candidate frames are identified via embedding-based semantic similarity, with a selection step, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) is prompted, using zero- or few-shot examples, to determine which frames are evoked, which spans trigger them, and which spans fill their FEs, returning a structured, machine-readable output. We detail installation, execution, and output interpretation, and provide a built-in evaluation module supporting exact, semantic, and graph-based matching against FrameNet's human-annotated data. This freely available tool lowers the barrier to frame-semantic analysis for researchers across linguistics, who wish to explore structured semantic content in naturalistic text, including in relation to behavioral and neural measures of language comprehension.

articles.title: Short-term Cultural Evolution in Response to COVID-19:  Integrating Quantitative Analysis with AI-Assisted Thematic Analysis
articles.authors: Aiya Wang; Patricia M. Greenfield
articles.abstract: Using Greenfield’s Theory of Social Change, Cultural Evolution, and Human Development as a framework, we examine psychological, cultural, and behavioral shifts in China during the first 70 days of COVID-19. We focus on three levels—mortality salience at the psychological level, collectivism at the cultural level, and subsistence activities at behavioral level. Our big-data sample consists of over 200,000 social media posts. Quantitatively, we found a significant increase in mentions of mortality salience, collectivism, and subsistence activities, consistent with prior results established in the U.S., Mexico, Indonesia, and Japan, suggesting a universal response to existential threat. Qualitatively, AI-assisted thematic analysis, an innovation of the present study, identified the most frequent recurring themes across three levels, which complemented the quantitative analysis by providing in-depth insight into the COVID experience. A methodological strength was to compare expert human coder to AI coding, establishing both the reliability and validity of AI coding.

articles.title: Embodied mirroring increases interpersonal synchrony of movement and social connection established in subsequent conversations
articles.authors: Yasemin Abra; Christine Falter-Wagner; Irene Sophia Plank
articles.abstract: Interpersonal synchrony, the alignment of behaviours between individuals, is thought to facilitate social connection and rapport. However, less is known about whether synchrony can be intentionally fostered and whether its effects extend beyond the context in which it is established. We examined whether participation in the Mirror Game, a fundamental exercise from theatre where two players nonverbally imitate each other’s movements, influences subsequent interactions between previously unacquainted strangers. Using recordings of facial expressions, gaze patterns, and movement, we captured multi-modal conversational dynamics during a conversation. In line with our preregistered hypothesis, dyads who played the Mirror Game before conversing exhibited greater interpersonal synchrony of movement than those who performed a non-social movement exercise, suggesting a carry-over effect of instructed to emerging interpersonal synchrony. Furthermore, playing the Mirror Game prior to the conversation also increased positive social connection and rapport. However, increased interpersonal synchrony of movement on the level of the dyad did not account for these social benefits, challenging straightforward accounts linking synchrony to social connection. By contrast, exploratory analyses further revealed that behavioural patterns capturing interpersonal adaptation at the individual level predicted participants’ positive social experiences and feelings of connection emerging in the conversation. Together, these findings demonstrate that a brief shared embodied activity can shape the quality of a subsequent interaction and provide new insight into the processes through which positive social connections emerge between strangers.

articles_hidden.title: Where, Not How Far: Gender-Diverse Pronoun Use and the Ideal Singing Voice
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett
articles_hidden.abstract: Many transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people want their voices to change, but how pronoun use, a public expression of gender that only partly overlaps with identity labels, relates to the voice people want is unknown. In an online survey (N = 2,536), participants placed their current and ideal singing voices on a 5-point masculine–feminine scale. In exploratory analyses, participants who used they/them pronouns, alone or with she or he (n = 130), wanted larger changes than binary-pronoun users (n = 2,272; d = 0.84, 95% CI [0.66, 1.02]). The difference was robust to age and sex assigned at birth and was attenuated but still present after adjustment for gender identity and recruitment cohort. Among TGD participants, however, the two pronoun groups wanted changes of similar size (d = 0.11 [−0.16, 0.37]), so the full-sample contrast largely reflected comparison with cisgender binary-pronoun users. Pronoun use instead distinguished the destination of change: among TGD participants, 48.1% of gender-diverse pronoun users placed their ideal at the gender-neutral midpoint, compared with 18.3% of binary-pronoun users, whose ideals more often lay at a masculine or feminine pole. A moderation pattern in which singing-related gender incongruence strengthened the link between desired change and the acoustics of a chosen model singer did not replicate in a held-out test set and is not supported. Pronoun use appears to index where, more than how far, people want their singing voices to go; vocal goals and the scales that measure them should accommodate gender-neutral targets.

articles_hidden.title: Willpower or Choice? A Within-Country, Cross-Linguistic Comparison of Free Will Judgments
articles_hidden.authors: Alison Oliver; Paulius Rimkevičius; Renato Cesar Cardoso; Marcel Brass; Uri Maoz
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the language we speak influence how we think about free will? Previous work has often compared free will judgments across linguistic and cultural groups without isolating language from broader cultural differences. More recent work has found cross-cultural variation, but these designs could not determine whether language itself contributed to that variation. Here we report two exploratory studies in which language was varied while culture was held relatively constant. In Study 1, monolingual English- and French-speaking Canadians rated comics depicting choice and willpower on whether they represent free will. The English phrase free will makes will, and so willpower, salient; the French phrase libre arbitre makes choice salient (as in “to arbitrate”). If language shapes the concept, English-speakers should associate free will relatively more with willpower, and French-speakers relatively more with choice. They did not: the two groups showed almost exactly the same preference for choice, and equivalence testing rules out anythingbeyond a small difference. Study 2 asked why choice comics were favored. Participants rated thesame comics on choice, willpower, doing what one wants, and absence of constraints. Across thenine comics, free will judgments closely tracked ratings of doing what one wants and of choice, but tracked absence of constraints less closely. Free will might therefore be associated most closely with choice and doing what one wants.

articles_hidden.title: Wrong Note, Wrong Time: Age and Musicianship-Related Influences on Rhythmic and Melodic Timing
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett; Sarah Anne Sauvé; Andrea Rita Halpern; Benjamin Zendel
articles_hidden.abstract: Musical expectancy theory posits that listeners anticipate both the pitch that will occur and when it will occur; however, the interaction between these dimensions across age and expertise is less understood. In this study, 175 adults (ages 18–82; musicians and non-musicians) rated the final note of short monophonic melodies on its melodic and temporal fit. Endings were systematically manipulated in terms of pitch (tonal, chromatic, or atonal) and timing deviations. Results showed a strong effect of melodic expectancy: pitch deviations substantially reduced goodness-of-fit ratings, whereas timing shifts had comparatively weak effects. Musicians gave lower ratings overall, indicating heightened sensitivity to expectancy violations, whereas non-musicians were more lenient. Although age alone did not predict ratings, an age × musician interaction emerged: older musicians diverged most strongly from older non-musician peers, suggesting that expertise sharpens expectancy sensitivity across the lifespan. These findings demonstrate that pitch dominates expectancy judgments, while also revealing how aging and musicianship jointly influence the perception of musical errors—an area that remains underexplored in music cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Color cues, developmental coupling, and the limits of the late-sighted model: A commentary on Vogelsang et al. (2024)
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract:
Vogelsang et al. (2024) report in Science that congenitally blind individuals who gain sight late in life rely disproportionately on color cues for object recognition, unlike normally sighted controls. They propose that this pattern reflects the adaptive value of neonatal color immaturity: because typical infants experience a period of degraded chromatic input, they develop object representations grounded in luminance rather than color.
The theoretical account, however, rests on an incomplete engagement with the developmental literature. Decades of research indicate that color and luminance sensitivity are developmentally coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity: the same front-end bottleneck that degrades chromatic input in neonates simultaneously degrades luminance and spatial processing. If this coupling is real, there is no luminance-first window, because the bottleneck lifts for both dimensions together. The account's central premise is therefore undermined not by arguing independence, but by showing that color and luminance do not develop in the sequence the account requires.
I further identify methodological concerns: a small and unusual sample, a fixed order confound in the primary behavioral task, a computational model implementing a binary switch rather than the gradual chromatic cascade of normal development, and a color sensitivity test using non-equiluminant stimuli, leaving open the possibility that luminance rather than chromatic contrast sensitivity drove performance.
Together, these issues require qualification of the conclusions of Vogelsang et al. and reconciliation of the proposed account with classical findings in infant visual development. This broader question remains important, but the answer is unlikely to hinge on color alone.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on Clinical Risk Judgement: An Example from Alcohol Use Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Charles M. Bolton; Kiwon Song; Katelyn A. Wasson; Clintin P Davis-Stober; Konstantina Sokratous
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being explored for medical risk assessment, yet performance on standardized benchmarks does not necessarily establish clinical competency. The present study evaluated whether LLM-generated Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) risk judgments aligned with epidemiological evidence and remained consistent as clinical and demographic context changed. Three LLMs—GPT-5.5, LLaMA-2-70B, and MEDITRON-70B—completed four pairwise-comparison experiments involving DSM-5 AUD criteria, demographic characteristics, criteria paired with demographic characteristics, and narrative clinical vignettes. LLM-implied rankings were compared with epidemiological benchmarks derived from the National Epidemiological Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions, Wave Three (NESARC-III). Our results show that none of the LLMs reproduced the implied severity ordering of the AUD criteria. Demographic cues consistently influenced AUD risk judgments, although the direction and magnitude of these effects varied across LLMs, demographic attributes, and clinical contexts. Demographic rankings also showed only partial stability as contextual information changed. LLMs differed substantially in decisiveness, with GPT-5.5 assigning substantially higher probability to selected responses than LLaMA-2-70B or MEDITRON-70B. These findings demonstrate a gap in current LLM risk-assessment capabilities and highlight the importance of evaluating the direction, magnitude, stability, and certainty of LLM judgments alongside accuracy.

articles_hidden.title: Subjective and Behavioral Difficulties in Social Contexts: Unique and Interacting Effects on Social Dysfunction Transdiagnostically
articles_hidden.authors: Kathryn Kemp; Carly A Lasagna; Scott D. Blain; Cynthia Z. Burton; Costanza Colombi; Aubrey M Moe; Ivy Fei Tso
articles_hidden.abstract: Prior research indicates that social functioning is impacted by both social engagement and subjective experience regarding social interactions. The goal of this study was to examine the extent to which each component, as well as their interaction, contributes to social dysfunction in a combined nonclinical and transdiagnostic psychiatric sample. A sample of young adults (n=193) spanning the social dysfunction spectrum completed measures that capture different forms of psychopathology relevant to social dysfunction, from which two dimensions – Subjective Psychosocial Difficulties (SPD) and Observed Social Difficulties (OSD) – were extracted using Principal Components Analysis. Participants additionally completed a variety of clinician-rated and self-reported social functioning measures that were aggregated into one overall social functioning score. Hierarchical regression was used to examine the unique contribution of SPD and OSD and their interaction on overall social functioning. SPD and OSD explained unique variance (Δr2=61.0%), indicating that elevated SPD and OSD levels predicted worse social functioning. The SPD-by-OSD interaction was positive and explained significant additional amounts of variance (Δr2=1.9%), indicating a less-than-additive effect on social dysfunction. The findings suggest that examining observable social behaviors and subjective psychosocial experience simultaneously is important for understanding social functional outcomes in clinical populations.

articles_hidden.title: Interval-Dependent Effects of Action and Choice Availability on Temporal Binding
articles_hidden.authors: Lauren Claire Fong; Silvia Seghezzi; Paul Michael Garrett; Mia Nightingale; Philip L. Smith; Robert Hester; Daniel Feuerriegel
articles_hidden.abstract: Temporal binding research proposes that voluntary actions compress perceived time between actions and their outcomes, reflecting an implicit sense of agency. However, it remains unclear whether such effects are stable across action--outcome interval durations and whether they depend on the degree of decisional freedom, such as the availability of choice options. Here, we investigated whether action generation (action vs. no action) and choice availability (one vs. two options) influence interval estimation across multiple action-outcome intervals using a yoked action-baseline design. Across two experiments, action-baseline differences consistent with temporal binding were observed only at the shortest interval (300 ms), where action trials produced relatively shorter interval estimates than matched baseline trials. However, these differences did not generalise to longer intervals and reversed in direction at longer intervals in one experiment. Across the full interval range, baseline estimates shifted more steeply with interval duration than action estimates, producing a crossover pattern in which shorter intervals were overestimated and longer intervals underestimated across conditions. We did not find evidence that choice availability, operationalised as one versus two options, modulated interval estimates in either experiment. These findings suggest that action-related differences in interval estimation are temporally constrained and may arise from an interaction between action-related processes and general perceptual biases in temporal estimation, including regression toward the mean. More broadly, the results show that apparent temporal binding effects in interval-estimation tasks can depend strongly on where tested intervals fall within the broader interval range, highlighting the importance of accounting for interval-dependent estimation biases when interpreting temporal binding effects in interval estimation tasks as proxy measure of the sense of agency.

articles_hidden.title: A Transcultural, Digital, and Global Perspective: Beyond Family Risk Environments in Adolescent Alcohol Use Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Carlos Fernando Pantoja-Muñoz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and Aims: high-resource Western models restrict adolescent alcohol use disorders (AUD) to static micro-environmental or behavioral variables. This study aims to refute conventional linear predictive frameworks and validate the Global Multidimensional Paradigm against contemporary restrictive models.
Design and Setting: A systematic methodology based on the PRISMA statement was employed to contrast transnational linear parameters against structural evidence derived from an epidemiological screening across 21 Latin American countries.
Participants and Measurements: a pre-pandemic (2015–2020) screening of 16,921 epidemiological records was conducted, extracting data from 18 included studies to consolidate a total aggregated sample of 5,253 adolescents. Transnational profiles from the World Bank and WHO (cellular toxicity, acute intoxication, and immunosuppression) were analyzed alongside macro-structural variables.
Findings: comparative analysis demonstrates that traditional Anglo-Saxon models fail by omitting global macro-structural forces highlighted by the Lancet Commission. The proposed paradigm reveals that alcohol use disorders are determined by a three-dimensional interaction intersecting the micro-family environment with 21st-century digital dynamics (algorithmic marketing on TikTok and Instagram, e-commerce, and systemic violence), validating Krieger’s eco-social theory of embodiment (2024).
Conclusions: by displacing linear biomedical approaches, this study establishes that adolescent alcohol use disorders constitute the literal biological embodiment of macro-structural inequalities, offering an indispensable new conceptual standard for international epidemiology. 

Keywords: adolescence, alcohol use disorders, multidimensional model, biological embodiment, digital networks.

articles_hidden.title: Event segmentation aligns emotional learning and episodic memory
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick Laing; Josh Cisler; Joseph E. Dunsmoor
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotion prioritizes not only what was significant, but when it was significant. When temporal structure is insufficient to bind emotional relevance to distinct episodes, emotional experiences can lead to overgeneralization and source confusion. Here, we tested whether event boundaries serve as a control mechanism that allows emotional prioritization in memory to reset and re-bind as relevance changes over time. Participants completed a preregistered two-day Pavlovian category-conditioning in which category-shock associations reversed across multiple learning phases. In one group, each reversal phase was preceded by a brief but explicit event boundary signaling an associative transition; in the other group, reversals occurred continuously without an explicit boundary. Episodic recognition memory for trial-unique conditioned stimuli, tested 24-hours later, showed selective enhancement for threat-predictive items in the segmentation group—most prominently during early and final learning epochs—whereas continuous encoding produced flatter, less selective memory profiles that failed to fully track changing emotional contingencies. Individual differences in learning dynamics during encoding predicted selective episodic memory at 24hrs, with event segmentation shifting this learning-memory coupling to the most recent threat reversal rather than the earliest one. Overall, event boundaries promoted tighter alignment between episodic memory and emotional relevance at the time of experience. These findings suggest that event segmentation supports adaptive memory prioritization by binding emotional significance to what is most relevant in the moment.

articles_hidden.title: Domain-Specific or Domain-General? An Examination of Patterns of Mathematics Performance Across Achievement Groups
articles_hidden.authors: Hillary Mastarciyan; Michael Slipenkyj; Lien Peters; Alyssa Counsell; H Moriah Sokolowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Many children experience persistent difficulties in mathematics throughout elementary school. However, relatively little is known about whether patterns of mathematical performance differ in children whose low achievement is specific to mathematics compared to those whose low achievement extends across academic domains and to typically achieving children. Curriculum-based educational assessments, which evaluate multiple aspects of mathematics achievement, provide a unique opportunity to compare patterns of performance across mathematics domains in population-based samples. The present study examined whether children with low mathematics achievement, low general achievement and typical achievement exhibit distinct patterns of performance across five mathematics curriculum strands in Grades 3 and 6. Data were drawn from three cohorts of children who completed a province-wide math assessment in Canada, yielding a population-based sample of 2,968 elementary school students who were identified as belonging to one of three achievement groups. Analyses compared patterns of strand-level mathematics performance across the three achievement groups in Grades 3 and 6. Children with low math and low general achievement demonstrated strikingly similar patterns of performance across strands, which differed from those of typically achieving children. These findings provide new evidence that children with low mathematics achievement and low general achievement share similar patterns of curriculum-based mathematics performance, informing theories of domain-specific and domain-general academic achievement.

articles_hidden.title: Engaging residents in district heating retrofit:  A qualitative evaluation of a mine water heat network project in the United Kingdom
articles_hidden.authors: Michael A. Smith; Faye Doughty; Danielle Goldring; Helen Simmons
articles_hidden.abstract: The expansion of district heat networks (DHNs) is central to achieving net zero heating targets, yet social acceptance remains a major barrier to large-scale domestic retrofit. Although resident engagement is widely recognised as critical to addressing these barriers, there is little empirical evidence evaluating how engagement strategies operate during live retrofit projects. This study addresses this gap through a qualitative evaluation of the resident support and engagement approach employed during the connection of 16 existing low-rise homes to a mine water DHN in the United Kingdom. Data were collected from 18 stakeholders, including residents, local authority officers and construction contractors. The findings demonstrate that effective engagement extends beyond the provision of information. Social acceptance was strengthened through opportunities to build trusting relationships, meaningful resident involvement in decision-making, early engagement, and adaptations that responded to residents' accessibility needs. Participants also highlighted the importance of organisational coordination, accessible communication materials, clear points of contact, and the use of trusted community networks and lived experience to enhance the credibility of project information. These findings suggest that successful DHN retrofit depends not only on technical delivery but also on engagement processes that foster trust, agency and equitable participation. The present study provides the first qualitative evaluation of resident engagement during a live mine water DHN retrofit project and offers practical recommendations for engaging residents during the design and delivery of future DHN projects.

articles_hidden.title: Testing Alternative Approaches to Manipulation of Environmental Self-Identity: Behavior Recall, Anchoring, and Category-Range Manipulations
articles_hidden.authors: Jan Urban; Štěpán Bahník; Markéta Braun Kohlová
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental self-identity, defined as the extent to which an individual sees themselves as an environmentally friendly person, has become an important concept in environmental psychology. One of the reasons for the prominence of environmental self-identity is that it has been proposed as one of the causal factors of pro-environmental behavior. Experimental studies of environmental self-identity have relied on a recall manipulation that alters the frequency scales on which people report their past pro- and anti-environmental behaviors, thus making past pro- or anti-environmental behaviors more salient. In the current study, we tested two additional alternative approaches to experimental manipulation of environmental self-identity. These rely on two powerful strategies of changing the perception of one’s past behavior, namely anchoring manipulation and category-range manipulation. We conducted a high-power web-based study (N = 4,139) to assess and compare the efficacy of the behavioral-recall manipulation and the two alternative approaches of manipulating environmental self-identity and affecting pro-environmental intention. We found substantial evidence that the three manipulations altered people's self-reports of their past pro-environmental behavior, but this did not change environmental self-identity. Evidence also favored no effect on environmental intention for the recall and anchoring manipulations, whereas evidence for the category-range manipulation was inconclusive. Other manipulations of environmental self-identity that do not rely on self-perception theory are needed for experimental research on environmental self-identity. Practical interventions are unlikely to influence pro-environmental behavior merely by highlighting or changing people's records of their past behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociable neural oscillations track subjective value under risk and ambiguity
articles_hidden.authors: Shuting Mei; Leyou Deng; Gökhan Aydogan; Christian Carl Ruff; Ya Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: How the brain values uncertain prospects and translates them into choices is a central question in decision neuroscience. Current accounts propose that decisions under risk and ambiguity share a valuation process that integrates outcome with probability information, with ambiguity additionally requiring evaluation of the uncertainty about the probabilities themselves. Here we used computational modeling to estimate trial-wise subjective value and tested whether it was tracked by shared or distinct neural dynamics under risk and ambiguity. Participants accepted or rejected risky and ambiguous monetary gambles while we recorded neural activity using electroencephalography (Experiment 1) and magnetoencephalography (Experiment 2). Across both experiments, alpha-band (9–14 Hz) activity localized to the precuneus and superior parietal cortex tracked subjective value under both risk and ambiguity. By contrast, delta-band (1–3 Hz) activity localized to the ventromedial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices tracked subjective value only under ambiguity. These findings reveal dissociable neural signatures for the two forms of uncertainty and suggest that the brain resolves ambiguity by combining a shared valuation process indexed by alpha activity with an additional process indexed by delta activity that may reflect the motivational salience of options with ambiguous outcome probabilities.

articles_hidden.title: ‘The difference between us is that I am an optimist and you are a pessimist.’ An autoethnographic study on suppression of critical scholarship
articles_hidden.authors: P. Matthijs Bal; Mehmet A. Orhan; Yvonne van Rossenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Critical scholarship constitutes an important part of business and management research, including related fields such as work psychology. However, critical work is also often met with resistance from colleagues and gatekeepers within the discipline. Yet, there is little insight into how this resistance manifests in daily academic practice. This autoethnographic study by multiple critical scholars in work and organizational psychology analyzed 34 events whereby their critical work was suppressed and silenced. Thematic analysis of the events revealed ten different mechanisms through which critical work is suppressed, which could be ordered within four sequential stages of suppression: closing space, discrediting work, discrediting research(-ers), and disciplinary control. Jointly, these stages represent an escalating process of how alternative perspectives, including critical work, are suppressed and silenced in hegemonic fields. The paper contributes to existing critical scholarship by being the first to empirically elucidate how and through which strategies critical work is silenced. The study has important implications not only for the development of critical perspectives within scientific fields, but also for academia more widely, as political and societal forces that undermine academic freedom call for a better understanding of how critical work is suppressed, and how it could be nurtured for a more dignified, equal, and democratic society.

articles_hidden.title: The Impasse Model: A Clinical Formulation Framework for Understanding Psychological Impasse and Restoring Movement
articles_hidden.authors: Clare Layhe
articles_hidden.abstract:
Psychological impasse is defined here as a state in which change, resolution or 
movement is experienced as necessary or desired, yet no sufficiently viable route can currently 
be perceived, accessed or enacted. The Impasse Model arose from collaborative clinical 
formulations in which people were often highly mobilised rather than passive. They had 
explained, repaired, problem-solved, pursued reassurance, withdrawn or protected themselves, 
yet their available field of action had progressively narrowed. Relational difficulty and 
mismatches in communication or understanding were recurrent, though not universal, pathways. 
The model identifies impasse as a clinically useful warning point before higher-cost coping or 
protective responses become necessary. Formulation then proceeds in two directions: backwards, 
to understand how viable movement became restricted and forwards, to identify the smallest 
change capable of reopening it. Existing literatures on entrapment, action crisis, psychological 
inflexibility, hopelessness, decisional conflict, uncertainty and systemic constraint overlap 
substantially with this territory. The proposed contribution is therefore not a new universal 
mechanism but a clinically organised formulation framework whose distinctiveness and utility 
are open to empirical test.
Keywords: psychological impasse, formulation, entrapment, trauma, dissociation, anxiety, 
systemic formulation, EMDR, therapeutic intervention

articles_hidden.title: Charting the ontogeny of mnemonic processes in childhood: the COMIC dataset
articles_hidden.authors: Tydings McClary; Elisa Buchberger; Ann-Kathrin Joechner; Ulman Lindenberger; Chi T. Ngo; Markus Werkle-Bergner
articles_hidden.abstract: The human memory system balances two complementary functions: generalization, which involves extracting regularities across experiences, and specificity, which involves retaining the unique details of individual events. Understanding how this balance develops can benefit from a neurocomputational perspective in which three core computations, pattern categorization, pattern separation, and pattern completion, differentially support generalization and memory specificity. Guided by this framework, we present a dataset from 180 children aged 4–8 years who completed four age-appropriate memory tasks that provide behavioral indices of these computations. Children additionally completed three standardized intelligence subtests. Alongside the dataset, we describe a semi-automated data-cleaning pipeline designed for developmental behavioral data, which can serve as a template for identifying and resolving common data-quality issues in studies with young children. In sum, this dataset provides a resource for investigating the development of memory computations supporting adaptive functioning across early and middle childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Induced sad mood biases responses to sad and neutral faces under low visibility: behavioral and ERP evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Xueqiao Li; Elisa Vuoriainen; Elina Kangas; Piia Astikainen
articles_hidden.abstract: Facial expression recognition is shaped by both stimulus properties and the perceiver’s affective state. Research on emotional face processing under backward masking has largely focused on threatening expressions, and few studies have examined how an observer's mood influences recognition of non-threatening facial expressions under limited visibility. The present study investigated how experimentally induced sad versus neutral mood modulates behavioral and neural responses to sad and neutral facial expressions under low (10 ms) and high visibility (200 ms) backward masking conditions. Participants underwent sad and neutral mood induction on separate days and performed a facial expression categorization task while electroencephalography was recorded. Behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) analyses included 25 and 20 participants, respectively. Behaviorally, a mood effect on response criterion was observed in the low visibility condition: the criterion was lower in sad than neutral mood, reflecting a reduced tendency to categorize faces as neutral. Discrimination sensitivity was higher under high than low visibility but was not significantly affected by mood. Facial expressions modulated N170, P2, and P3 amplitudes under high visibility, and N170 and P2 under low visibility. P2 amplitude in the low visibility condition showed an interaction effect between mood and facial expression. In neutral mood, sad faces elicited larger P2 amplitudes than neutral faces, whereas in sad mood, the relation was the opposite. These findings highlight the influence of the observer’s affective state on behavioral and neural responses to facial expressions under limited visibility, extending previous findings beyond threat-related expressions to sadness.

articles_hidden.title: Noradrenergic influences on human thought
articles_hidden.authors: Claire O'Callaghan
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuromodulators help balance the trade-off between flexibility and stability that is needed for adaptive cognition and behaviour. Among the neuromodulators, the noradrenergic system plays a key role in balancing this trade-off: it helps shape whether we pursue a given behaviour or task, versus shifting our behaviour to pursue an alternate strategy. Put differently, the noradrenergic system drives the balance between a stable versus flexible engagement with the world around us. How might this capacity relate to human thought? In this chapter, we review the functional and organisational principles of the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic system, and consider how it might modulate different aspects of human thought. Highlighting examples from attention, belief-updating, spontaneous thought and stress. Together, revealing how the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic system helps shape the balance of flexibility and stability in human thought.

articles_hidden.title: CARTE: An LLM-based automated tool for semantic clustering and switching identification in associative verbal fluency
articles_hidden.authors: Lucie Vigreux; Victor Altmayer; Mathias Benedek; Thomas Hills; Yoed Kenett; Emmanuelle Volle
articles_hidden.abstract:
Semantic Verbal fluency is a core component of neuropsychological assessment,
valued for its clinical sensitivity and ease of administration. Yet, its full potential is rarely
fully exploited: performance is typically reduced to a total word count, overlooking the rich
dynamics of semantic foraging, such as clustering (exploitation within a semantic category)
and switching (exploration across categories). Although these dynamics are central to models
of memory search, they require laborious manual coding, limiting their large-scale analysis
and use for scoring. Automated alternatives exist, but none can identify which specific
category each response belongs to, and their agreement with manual scoring remains only
moderate.
Here, we introduce CARTE (Category Attribution and Response Transitions
Evaluation), an automated scoring method that identifies semantic categories and detects
