clustering/switching transitions in responses to the Polysemous Fluency Task (PolyFT).
Because PolyFT is an associative verbal fluency task relying on polysemous cue-words,
semantic categories map naturally onto distinct cue-meanings, making them easier to identify
- a process we automate in CARTE by means of a large language model. Analyzing responses
from 90 French-speaking participants across 35 polysemous cues, we show that CARTE
outperforms existing automated methods in matching human raters. Crucially, CARTE’s
performance is independent of sample size: once classified, a word is permanently indexed in
a cumulative semantic database, ensuring computational efficiency, reproducibility, and
scalability across studies. By bridging cognitive richness and methodological feasibility, this
work offers a simple yet robust tool for studying the dynamics of semantic memory search.

articles_hidden.title: Compassion and Awe as Eco-Emotions: Experimental Inductions and their Effect on Pro-Environmental Intentions
articles_hidden.authors: Ronan Bellemin; Aurélien GRATON; Anna Tcherkassof
articles_hidden.abstract: Eco-emotions are increasingly recognized as central psychological processes shaping how individuals perceive environmental crises and engage in collective responses. While negative eco-emotions have been widely studied, positive, self-transcendent emotions may offer more psychologically sustainable pathways to pro-environmental engagement. The present research examines two such emotions—compassion for the environment and awe at nature—and investigates their emotional profiles and social-environmental implications using experimental induction. Across two pre-registered studies, participants were exposed to situations designed to elicit compassion for the environment (Study 1; N = 165) or awe at nature (Study 2; N = 117). Participants then reported their emotional experiences, intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective actions, and provided open-ended definitions of the target emotions. Results showed that compassion and awe were successfully elicited and exhibited distinct emotional patterns. Compassion for the environment was significantly associated with higher intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective actions, whereas awe at nature was not, suggesting that eco-emotions may support different forms of social and environmental engagement. Qualitative analyses revealed conceptual overlap between French participants’ spontaneous descriptions and English-language theoretical definitions. However, contrary to recent empirical categorizations, compassion was generally considered to be a negative emotion. Together, these findings highlight the value of experimentally inducing discrete self-transcendent eco-emotions to clarify their specific emotional content and their distinct roles as socially embedded drivers of environmental engagement.

articles_hidden.title: Data-Matrix-Based Overall Goodness-of-Fit Testing for Confirmatory Factor Analysis: In-Sample Prediction Error for Observed Variables
articles_hidden.authors: Young Ze Kim; Gyeongcheol Cho; Hanjoe Kim
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conventional χ²-based tests in confirmatory factor analysis assess overall fit through covariance reproduction and remain the standard inferential tools for overall goodness-of-fit testing. However, they do not directly quantify the magnitude of model misfit and may become unavailable when estimation fails to converge or produces improper solutions.
We introduce and evaluate two data-matrix-based alternatives within structured factor analysis: the in-sample prediction error for observed variables (IPEo) test for a single model and the ΔIPEo test for nested models. IPEo quantifies the proportion of variability in the observed data matrix left unexplained by the hypothesized model, while its bootstrap p value provides an inferential decision. Monte Carlo simulations showed that the IPEo-based tests controlled Type I error, gained power with increasing sample size, and remained available when conventional χ²-based tests frequently failed. An empirical illustration further showed that the IPEo value and its p value provide complementary information about the magnitude and statistical significance of model misfit. These findings support IPEo-based testing as a complementary inferential framework for evaluating CFA model fit directly at the level of the observed data matrix.

articles_hidden.title: Visuospatial features influencing the evaluation of two-body interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Orlandi; Mohammad Soleyman Nejad; Matteo Candidi
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual evaluation of aesthetic, semantic, and emotional aspects of two-body interactions is fundamental for social cognition, yet the contribution of objective stimulus features to these evaluations remains largely unexplored. This study investigated how different visuospatial features of two-body implied interactions influence their evaluations in terms of aesthetic pleasure, symmetry, emotional valence, meaning, and interest. Across four studies involving 200 participants, we found that visually ‘entangled’ two-body interactions, defined by the extent of shared interpersonal space, were rated as more aesthetically pleasing, interesting, and meaningful than their disentangled versions. Using Representational Similarity Analysis and hierarchical multiple regressions, we identified the contribution of each stimulus feature to these evaluations. These findings suggest that two-body entanglement enhances the perceived dyads’ aesthetic and semantic value, possibly facilitating their configural processing. The study expands prior literature and highlights a dissociation between visuospatial features and mechanisms underlying pleasure and interest in dancing bodies.

articles_hidden.title: Eat your vegetables: Exploring food learning cues in 12-month-old infants
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Rioux; Karola Schlegelmilch; Annie E. Wertz
articles_hidden.abstract: Food learning in early life largely relies on social learning. Previous research has shown that infants learn something is edible when they directly observe someone else eating it. However, the role of other forms of food-related social information remains largely unknown. Food processing actions (e.g., chopping, mashing) are essential components of human food behaviors and a ubiquitous part of infants’ everyday lives. Here we examined whether infants (i) differentially attend to eating and food processing actions compared to control actions and (ii) learn that novel foods are edible after observing eating and food processing actions performed with them. We tested 12-month-olds’ responses to three different actions: eating, food processing, and a control action (touch). First, we showed infants side-by-side videos of an adult performing two different actions with novel foods across three between-subjects conditions and measured their gaze and pupil dilation with an eye-tracker. Then, we offered infants the novel foods shown in the videos and measured their choices and eating behaviors. Our eye-tracking results indicate that infants differentially attend to eating and food processing actions relative to the control action, and show increased pupil dilation for the control action relative to the two actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting). When asked to choose which novel food they could eat, infants chose the novel food they saw an actor eat, but only when that eating action was paired with the control action. These findings help identify important mechanisms that increase acceptance of healthy foods early in life.

articles_hidden.title: Same Effect, Different Magnitude: How the Choice of Pre- or Post-Treatment Standard Deviation Shapes Standardized Effect Sizes in Psychological Clinical Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Anika Buchholz; Anna Suling; Antonia Zapf; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles_hidden.abstract: Standardized mean differences (SMDs) are used to express treatment effects on a common metric, yet there is no consensus on whether mean differences should be standardized using the outcome standard deviation (SD) at baseline or follow-up. This study examined whether this choice systematically affects effect-size magnitude in a reproducible sample of 100 randomized psychological clinical trials. For each trial, SMDs were calculated using either the pooled baseline SD (SMDpre) or the pooled follow-up SD (SMDpost). The unweighted paired mean difference showed that |SMDpre| was, 0.11 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, 95% CI [0.07, 0.14]. In a multilevel meta-regression |SMDpre| was 0.082 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, equalling a 13% increase, 95% CI [0.042, 0.123]. Bland–Altman analysis indicated substantial between-study variation, 95% limits of agreement [−0.25, 0.46]. Secondary analyses including 2,228 effect sizes across all follow-ups mirrored this pattern, indicating a 7% increase of SMD magnitude associated to |SMDpre|, 95% CI [0.021, 0.044]. Moderator analyses suggested that discrepancies were larger in studies applying symptom-threshold eligibility criteria, and in secondary analyses, using the same measure both to determine eligibility and to assess the outcome and with longer follow-up. Importantly, 70% of included studies did not report how SMDs were operationalized. These findings demonstrate that the choice of standardizing SD systematically affects estimated treatment-effect magnitudes and that the discrepancy can become more pronounced under specific design conditions. Researchers should therefore carefully consider the choice of standardizer and explicitly report the time point and method used to derive the SD.

articles_hidden.title: Confirmatory Validation of the Singing Incongruence and Gender (SInG) Scale in an Independent Sample of Transgender and Gender-Diverse Singers
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Singing-related gender incongruence can be a significant source of distress for transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) individuals, yet general measures of gender dysphoria and speaking-voice instruments do not capture this domain. The Singing Incongruence and Gender (SInG) Scale was developed to address this gap, but its four-factor structure had not been confirmed in independent data.
Methods: Participants were an entirely new sample of 232 TGD individuals (141 nonbinary, 48 transgender men, 43 transgender women), with 883 cisgender respondents retained as a comparison group for known-groups validity and measurement invariance. Confirmatory factor analysis used robust weighted least squares on a polychoric correlation matrix. I also examined reliability, construct validity, a 12-item short form, and how the scale should be scored.
Results: The four-factor structure was confirmed, with all standardized loadings between .618 and .925 and better fit than a unidimensional alternative (comparative fit index .841 versus .618). Approximate fit fell below conventional thresholds, reflecting both a low ratio of cases to the 126 estimated parameters and some redundancy of item wording; a 12-item form fit better (.930), retained reliability and validity, and performed similarly in split-half cross-validation regardless of which near-equivalent items were retained. SInG scores predicted singing-voice discrepancy beyond age, identity subgroup, and general gender dysphoria (ΔR² = .192), and TGD respondents scored higher than cisgender respondents (d = 0.59; Misgendering d = 1.12).
Conclusions: The SInG Scale captures singing-related gender incongruence beyond what a general dysphoria measure explains, and is available in a brief 12-item form suited to clinical intake and choir screening. Because the subscales bear different relations to criterion outcomes, they should be reported alongside the total score.

articles_hidden.title: A Non-Parametric Approach to Modeling Accelerated Longitudinal Designs
articles_hidden.authors: Suryadyuti Baral; Jonathan Park; Emilio Ferrer
articles_hidden.abstract: Accelerated longitudinal designs (ALDs) offer an efficient means of studying large developmental periods by combining shorter longitudinal samples across overlapping cohorts. ALDs have been used to study processes that span large developmental epochs, such as cognitive development. However, traditional parametric approaches may impose structural assumptions that limit the accurate reconstruction of individual developmental trajectories. We investigate a nonparametric functional data analytic (FDA) approach for modeling latent trajectories in accelerated longitudinal data. This method allows for the recovery of smooth, continuous time trajectories that account for both shared and idiosyncratic patterns of change. We compare the FDA approach to the continuous time latent change score model with simulations that emulate nonlinear change processes often seen in developmental research. We apply both methods to two empirical datasets with individuals aged 5- to 22-years, where each person is assessed two or three times. Our results demonstrate that the FDA method captures the shape and timing of individual trajectories more accurately beyond the observed data. These findings suggest that FDA offers a robust and flexible alternative for modeling developmental change in ALDs.

articles_hidden.title: Voice Class but Not Fach: Acoustic Correlates of Operatic Voice Types in 8,681 Historical Recordings
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett
articles_hidden.abstract: The German Fach system divides operatic voices into roughly 25 categories within the familiar voice classes, distinguished by tessitura, vocal weight, timbre and agility. Whether these categories are acoustically recoverable has rarely been tested on singers a model has not seen. I analysed 8,681 public-domain 78-rpm recordings by 508 singers in 27 Fächer, labelling each singer with their documented career Fach. After a design audit, 153 singers were locked aside, 12 tests were specified in advance, and the frozen pipeline was evaluated once on the held-out singers. Seven-way voice class was recovered at a balanced accuracy of .54 (chance .15), and female-range versus male-range class at .97 without explicit pitch measures. Within a voice class, the Fach label did not generalise: tenor sub-Fach classification fell from .54 on discovery singers to .38 on held-out singers (chance .34), and no single-aspect model replicated. Treated as a continuous position on the taxonomy's tessitura ordering, however, soprano Fach was predicted on held-out singers (ρ = .44). Female-range voices in electrical-era recordings showed lower singer's-formant prominence and a higher Hammarberg index than male-range voices, differences that a synthetic audit showed are not measurement artefacts of high pitch. The Fach of the role being sung was more recoverable than the singer's label. Coarse voice class is acoustically robust; within a class, the evidence favours an ordering over the discrete categories the labels draw, and points to repertoire as part of what the labels encode.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Differences in Emotion Regulation May Not Be Unique to Expressive Suppression
articles_hidden.authors: Sooyeon Kim; Katharine Helen Greenaway; Peter Koval
articles_hidden.abstract: Controlling emotion expression is theorized to be more valued and thus more frequently used and beneficial among Easterners than Westerners. However, existing evidence relies on global self-reports capturing culturally informed beliefs about suppression rather than moment-to-moment suppression. Moreover, whether cultural differences are specific to suppression or reflect broader emotion-regulation patterns remains unclear. Using three experience-sampling datasets, we tested cultural differences in suppression across global and momentary self-reports and their specificity. Easterners reported greater suppression at both global and momentary self-reports. Cultural differences were specific to suppression at global levels but generalized to reappraisal and rumination at momentary levels. We found less support for cultural differences in the affective correlates of emotion regulation. However, there was moderate evidence that momentary suppression, reappraisal, and rumination were less strongly associated with negative affect among Easterners than Westerners. We provide the first comprehensive test of cultural differences in suppression and suggest they may reflect broader emotion-regulation patterns.

articles_hidden.title: Unsupervised transfer in relational category learning
articles_hidden.authors: Hilary Don; Micah Goldwater; Kit S Double; Evan James Livesey
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstraction of relational structures beyond surface features is essential for transfer of learning across contexts. However, learners often fail to apply relational knowledge outside the original learning setting. Our prior work shows that inference-learning can promote relational abstraction and supervised far transfer, but it remains unclear whether such learning supports spontaneous transfer without feedback. This study tested whether inference learning improves unsupervised far transfer across tasks with distinct surface characteristics. Participants learned to categorise stimuli based on monotonic versus non-monotonic relations among line lengths, under classification or inference-learning conditions. Transfer was assessed for luminance-based dot arrays and digit sequences, presented in counterbalanced order. Inference-learning led to stronger relational responding during training and significantly improved far transfer performance overall, even in the absence of feedback. Transfer accuracy was higher for digit sequences than dot arrays, particularly among participants who demonstrated strong relational learning. Moreover, an unexpected finding was that completing the digit task first selectively improved subsequent transfer to the dot task, suggesting that symbolic representations may scaffold relational alignment. These findings provide evidence that inference-learning fosters abstract relational representations that support far transfer, while also highlighting the role of representational format and task sequencing in enabling effective generalization.

articles_hidden.title: Empirically derived phenotypes can reduce diagnostic heterogeneity
articles_hidden.authors: Miriam K. Forbes; John F. Buss; Daniel P. Moriarity; Eiko I Fried; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson; Lorenzo Lorenzo-Luaces; Kasey Stanton; Ashley L. Watts; Gregory W. Forbes
articles_hidden.abstract: Diagnostic heterogeneity is a longstanding challenge for the classification of mental illness because people who receive the same diagnosis can differ markedly in their symptom presentations as well as in the mechanisms underlying those symptoms. High heterogeneity undermines both the clinical utility of diagnostic labels and what we can learn from research that treats disorders as coherent constructs. In this study, we examined heterogeneity across six internalizing disorders (specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, generalized anxiety disorder [GAD], major depressive disorder [MDD], and posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD]) using three complementary approaches to quantifying heterogeneity: 1) descriptive heterogeneity (how many symptom profiles can theoretically satisfy the diagnostic criteria, and how many are observed in practice), 2) person-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels capture people with similar symptom presentations), and 3) construct-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels group symptoms with similar patterns of association with external validators). Analyses drew on subsamples from a large convenience sample with elevated psychopathology, predominantly from Australia and the USA (n = 14,762, mean [SD] age = 38.0 [18.0]; 55% women). Results showed that specific phobia was consistently the least heterogeneous; social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, and GAD had mixed results; and MDD and PTSD were highly heterogeneous across all metrics. Notably, empirically derived phenotypes nested within each disorder substantively reduced heterogeneity relative to the DSM diagnoses. The study provides both a systematic multi-method approach to characterising different types of diagnostic heterogeneity, and a practical path toward more precise and informative constructs that can be implemented by rescoring existing data.

articles_hidden.title: Moral Goodness is Feminine
articles_hidden.authors: Jordan Wylie; Ana Gantman; Peter Mende-Siedlecki; Tianyi Xiong; Heleni Singer; Liane Young; Paul Bloom
articles_hidden.abstract: Care and communality are crucial features of morality. Given that women are consistently judged to be more caring and communal than men, we investigated whether the concept of moral goodness itself is seen as feminine. Indeed, at the representational level of faces, behaviors, impressions, and possibilities (N = 5,758), we find that moral goodness is feminized. Using reverse-correlation methods, we show that mental representations of the face of “a morally good person” is a woman’s face. Across 1,864 previously normed behaviors, we find that actions associated with moral goodness are stereotyped as feminine. In a novel impression updating task, we find that equivalent moral transgressions led to larger negative character updating for women than for men, suggesting that women face harsher penalties than men for deviating from everyday moral expectations. Finally, when asked to spontaneously generate possible responses to a moral dilemma, people produce fewer morally acceptable courses of action for men to engage in to solve the dilemma than they do for women, which is not moderated by benevolent sexism. In sum, moral goodness is gendered: people associate moral goodness with femininity.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing the Impact of Language on Visual Threat Detection:  cTBS over the anterior temporal lobe impairs semantic processing but not visual threat detection
articles_hidden.authors: Adam Fahmi; Nicola Thibault; Roxane Hoyer; Philippe ALBOUY; Isabelle Blanchette
articles_hidden.abstract: Constructionist models of emotion propose that conceptual knowledge is integral to emotion perception, but whether the rapid detection of threat depends on conceptual knowledge remains causally untested. The ventrolateral anterior temporal lobe (vATL), a core hub of the semantic system, offers a site for testing this dependence with neuromodulation. In a within-subject, sham-controlled design, 20 healthy adults received continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) over the left vATL and a sham stimulation in separate sessions. Before and after stimulation, participants completed three reaction-time tasks: a category membership task indexing semantic processing, a pattern matching task serving as a non-semantic control, and a visual search task measuring the threat superiority effect (faster detection of threatening than neutral targets). Relative to sham, cTBS slowed semantic categorization but not pattern matching, indicating that the stimulation disrupted semantic processing. In contrast, the threat superiority effect was present before and after both stimulations, and its magnitude did not differ significantly between conditions. Rapid visual threat detection therefore showed no detectable reliance on the conceptual knowledge supported by the left vATL. Constructionist accounts may need to distinguish the rapid prioritization of danger from the categorization and experience of threat, where conceptual knowledge may still play a role.

articles_hidden.title: Christian Nationalism as a Unique Predictor of Policy Attitudes and Voting Behavior: The Christian Nationalism Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Michael Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Christian Nationalism (CN) is a unique political ideology that has long been prominent in U.S. politics. Current measures of CN have poor psychometric properties (Davis, 2023). Study 1 (n=237) shows that CN predicts voting behavior and policy attitudes when controlling for established religious and political measures and provides an initial test of the Christian Nationalism Scale. Study 2 (n=603) replicates findings that CN is the best predictor of voting behavior and policy attitudes when accounting for established religious and political measures. A CFA shows excellent psychometric properties of the scale, and invariance testing shows similar factor structure across Christian denominations and racial groups. Study 3 (n=313) finds CN best predicts support for politicians who will restrict individual freedoms on topics related to traditional Christian values. These studies demonstrate that CN explains unique variance in voting (past and anticipated) and policy attitudes. This work provides a validated scale for future research.

articles_hidden.title: Work-focused cognitive behavioural therapy for common mental disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Finnes; Magnus Johansson; Robin Bernhardtz; Lars-Göran Öst
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Common mental disorders (CMDs) are a major cause of sickness absence and work disability. Although cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) effectively reduces symptoms, effects on return-to-work (RTW) outcomes are limited. Work-focused CBT (W-CBT) integrates RTW processes into treatment, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous with unresolved methodological challenges. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effectiveness of W-CBT on psychiatric and work-related outcomes, examined moderators of treatment effects, assessed methodological rigor, and identified common intervention components, with particular attention to how RTW outcomes are analyzed.
Methods
Systematic searches were conducted in Medline, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to December 2025. Randomized and non-randomized studies evaluating CBT with an integrated work focus among working-age adults on sickness absence due to CMDs were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using multilevel models with cluster-robust standard errors to address outcome dependency. Moderator analyses examined treatment content, number of sessions, and study characteristics. RTW outcomes were evaluated regarding their statistical properties, summary measures, and analytic methods used in primary studies. Risk-of-bias was assessed using Cochrane Risk of Bias toos version 2 and ROBINS-I. 
Results
Twenty-four studies comprising 26 W-CBT treatment conditions (n = 3,279 participants) were included. Large within-group improvements in psychiatric symptoms were observed and maintained at follow-up, while between-group effects were statistically significant but small. At post-treatment, 56% of participants had returned to work, increasing to 87% at follow-up, with a higher likelihood of full RTW in W-CBT compared with controls. Greater CBT content, stronger work focus, and higher treatment dose were associated with larger symptom improvements. However, RTW outcomes showed substantial heterogeneity. Many studies used analytic approaches assuming normally distributed data for outcomes that were bounded, skewed, or zero-inflated, or reported hazard ratios with limited comparability, constraining valid synthesis.
Conclusions
W-CBT is associated with meaningful symptom improvement and increased likelihood of RTW. However, misalignment between RTW outcome properties and analytic methods represents a major threat to validity. Future research requires improved outcome definitions, appropriate statistical modeling, and greater methodological consistency.

articles_hidden.title: Identifying attentional control mechanisms related to the performance of high- and low-skilled First-Person Shooter game players: With exploratory data on expert older-adult esports players
articles_hidden.authors: Inhyeok Jeong; Akinori Takeda; Daisuke Shimane; Masaki Takeda
articles_hidden.abstract: High-skilled First-Person Shooter (FPS) game players are known to have superior attentional control—the ability to select information relevant to a task (selective attention) and maintain an appropriate response (sustained attention). However, it is unclear whether the attentional control strategies between high- and low-skilled FPS players differ, and whether these differences are related to FPS performance. Therefore, we investigated differences in attentional control between low- and high-skilled FPS players using electroencephalography, as well as correlations between gaming performance and attentional control. In addition, as an exploratory aim, we examined the characteristics of older FPS players. We recruited 11 high- and 11 low-skilled FPS players (under 25 years) and five older FPS players (over 65 years). Participants completed a task responding to colors regardless of the semantic meaning (Stroop task), clicked on targets quickly and accurately (aiming task), and played an FPS (esports task), respectively. We measured event-related potentials (ERPs) during the Stroop task to evaluate attentional control. In addition, we examined the relationship between ERP components and performance on the aiming and esports tasks. As a result, high-skilled players showed significantly smaller ERP amplitude in the 150-250 ms time window and greater ERP amplitude in the 280-380 ms time window (parietal region) during the Stroop task. These results suggest that high-skilled FPS players allocated attentional resources to relatively later stages of stimulus evaluation and processing. Furthermore, ERP amplitude showed a significant correlation with performance on aiming and esports tasks. Notably, older adults performed comparably to highly skilled young players on the FPS task, despite exhibiting smaller ERP amplitudes than young adults. These results suggest that attentional control is related to FPS performance and may be different with age.

articles_hidden.title: The Ultimate Tutorial for AI-driven Scale Development in Generative Psychometrics: Releasing AIGENIE from its Bottle
articles_hidden.authors: Lara Lee Russell-Lasalandra; Hudson Golino; Luis Eduardo Garrido; Alexander P. Christensen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Psychological scale development has traditionally required extensive expert involvement, iterative re-
vision, andlarge-scalepilottestingbeforepsychometricevaluationcanbegin. TheAIGENIE Rpackageim-
plementstheAI-GENIEframework(AutomaticItemGenerationandValidationwithNetwork-Integrated
Evaluation), which integrates large language model (LLM) text generation with network psychometric
methods to automate the early stages of this process. The package generates candidate item pools using
LLMs, transforms them into high-dimensional embeddings, and applies a multi-step reduction pipeline
— Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA), Unique Variable Analysis (UVA), and bootstrap EGA — to
produce structurally validated item pools entirely in silico. This tutorial introduces the package across
eight parts: installation and setup, text generation, embeddings, item generation, the full AI-GENIE
pipeline, the GENIE pipeline for researcher-supplied items, advanced prompt engineering, and fully lo-
cal operation. Two running examples illustrate the package’s use: the Big Five personality model (a
well-established construct) and AI Anxiety (an emerging construct). The package supports multiple
LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, HuggingFace, and local models), offers a fully offline mode
with no external API calls, and provides the GENIE() function for researchers who wish to apply the
psychometric reduction pipeline to existing item pools regardless of their origin. The AIGENIE package
is freely available on CRAN at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=AIGENIE.

articles_hidden.title: Attention in model-based cognitive neuroscience: Mechanisms for optimization under constraint
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Ruth Weichart; Ryan Pierce Kirkpatrick; Jared Vance
articles_hidden.abstract: Two major criticisms of attention research are: 1) verbal theories lack the specificity to make falsifiable predictions about how the various mechanisms of attention operate; and 2) the term ``attention’’ is frequently ascribed to conceptually similar phenomena despite dissociable neural underpinnings. The field of model-based cognitive neuroscience is well-positioned to address (1) through mathematical formalization of hypothesized processes, but may perpetuate (2) insofar as similar algorithms and parameters may recur across modeling traditions without necessarily drawing upon a shared neuro-mechanistic basis. This review provides a function-first organization of the algorithms that have been hypothesized to implement or give rise to ``attention'' at various levels of processing: perception, decision-making, and learning. We ground mathematically-formalized processes in the performance-relevant objectives they serve and the processing constraints that limit them. In doing so, we provide a road map of the broader computational-level solutions that ``attention'' mechanisms have been invoked to provide.

articles_hidden.title: Yes, ChatGPT (and other models) need a psychiatrist: parallels between experimental neuropsychiatry and AI alignment science
articles_hidden.authors: Karthik V Sarma
articles_hidden.abstract: AI chatbots (such as ChatGPT or Claude) sometimes state false information with confidence, a behavior popularly termed “hallucination.” In their recent perspective, de Boer et al. [1] compared these errors to confabulation in patients with memory disorders, and asked whether ChatGPT needs a psychiatrist. I argue that it does, but for different reasons. False statements from chatbots may be better explained by how they are trained: first to produce contextually consistent text rather than true text, and later by being rewarded to produce answers. The more meaningful parallel lies elsewhere: because these systems learn to simulate human characters, they may also reproduce human personality traits and patterns resembling the symptoms of mental illness. Understanding them may require the methods of experimental psychiatry and psychology, and could advance our understanding of the human mind.

articles_hidden.title: mlstats: An R package for multilevel descriptive statistics and data preparation
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Dietrich
articles_hidden.abstract: Mobile research methods such as experience sampling, smartphone logging, and daily diary designs produce nested data, in which within-level fluctuations must be distinguished from between-level differences. Yet, there is no established convention for preparing and descriptively reporting such multilevel data. This paper introduces mlstats, an open-source R package that computes multilevel descriptive statistics — including intraclass correlation coefficients and within- and between-group correlations — in a single call, exports publication-ready tables, and decomposes variables for random effects within-between (REWB) modeling. Supporting both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, mlstats is freely available on CRAN with extensive online documentation at https://felixdidi.github.io/mlstats/.

articles_hidden.title: Why Testing Structural Theories Requires the Unconscious Condition
articles_hidden.authors: Zefan Zheng; João Pedro Parreira Rodrigues; Lukas Kob; Karla Matić
articles_hidden.abstract: Consciousness science has traditionally proceeded by contrasting neural activity when a stimulus is consciously perceived against activity when the same stimulus is not perceived. This contrastive approach is well suited to locating neural correlates of consciousness, but it says little about why an experience has the particular character it does. A recent structural turn addresses this gap by comparing the relational structure of qualia with the relational structure of a candidate physical substrate. We review the main structure-matching programmes and what they offer beyond the contrastive approach. We then argue that all of them rest on an assumption that has never been tested directly, which we call the structural exclusivity assumption: That a neural structure matching the qualia structure reflects the neural substrate of consciousness itself, rather than merely the processing of information that can occur without conscious experience. The assumption is empirical rather than philosophical, and the standard structure-matching design cannot test it, because qualia and physical structures are estimated while the content is consciously perceived. We set out the design that would test it, and review the psychophysical and neural evidence currently bearing on it. That evidence consistently suggests that relational structure survives absence of awareness, though no existing study settles the question. We argue that structure-matching and contrastive designs must be combined, and consider what follows for the selection of candidate structures and for the promise of the dissolution of the hard problem of consciousness.

articles_hidden.title: So much variety, so much to eat : The neuro-cognitive bases of visual food categorization in infancy
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Rioux; Pia Rämä; Elodie Farineaux; Lionel Granjon; Olivier Mascaro; Stefanie Peykarjou
articles_hidden.abstract: Food is fundamental to life. Yet, detecting members of the food category raises a substantial cognitive challenge as different foods do not have any apparent common visual features. Moreover, what is deemed edible and appropriate to eat also varies greatly across social groups. While the neuro-cognitive bases of visual food category representations are well documented in adults, their early ontogenetic origins remain unknown. The current study investigated the emergence of visual food categorization abilities in infants’ brains, using the fast periodic visual stimulation paradigm (FPVS) coupled with electroencephalography (EEG). In FPVS paradigms, images from a target category are periodically inserted into a rapid stream of base images from other categories. If the brain treats the target images as a distinct category relative to the base images, a distinct EEG response appears at the frequency of presentation of the target images. In our study, French-speaking adults, 12- and 6-month-old infants (n = 25 per age group) were presented with target food stimuli inserted into sequences of base stimuli from various non-food categories (e.g., man-made objects, plants). Results show that, similarly to adults, 12-month-old infants distinguished images of food from those of other categories. In contrast, 6-month-old infants showed no detectable categorization response for food images. The current study is the first to investigate the developmental course of visual food categorization in the human brain and showed that, by their first birthday, infants already group perceptually diverse foods into a single category.

articles_hidden.title: The cost of a violation: How children and adults determine the severity of social violations
articles_hidden.authors: Alyssa Doerksen; Alexis Sierra Smith-Flores; Madison Leigh Pesowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Social evaluations vary in severity, yet it remains unclear what determines these graded judgments. The same action can seem relatively minor in one context, but deeply objectionable in another. One possibility is that observers use a unifying utility framework to reason about costs imposed on the person affected. Across four preregistered experiments, we tested this possibility using ownership violations. Three- to 8-year-olds (N = 336) and adults (N = 336) evaluated scenarios that manipulated action severity, ownership status, resource scarcity, and subjective value while holding other aspects of the transgression constant. Across experiments, children showed adult-like patterns of evaluation, judging violations more negatively when they imposed greater objective or subjective costs on owners. These findings suggest that, even early in development, observers jointly consider whether an action violates a social norm and how it affects the person’s utility when determining the severity of social violations, in line with existing frameworks.

articles_hidden.title: When attention turns inward: Mind wandering reduces perceptual sensitivity across visual fields
articles_hidden.authors: Bianca de Haan
articles_hidden.abstract: We all mind wander from time to time, where instead of being focussed on our task, we start thinking about task-unrelated personal events or concerns. In daily life, however, mind wandering is often associated with reduced processing of external information. This is commonly explained by the decoupling hypothesis, which posits that processing of external sensory information is attenuated when attention turns inward. However, it remains unclear whether perceptual decoupling reflects a global, uniform attenuation of sensory processing, or a spatially-specific reduction linked to lateralised attentional mechanisms. In the current, pre-registered study, we used an online signal detection task to assess the impact of mind wandering on perceptual performance in the left and right visual fields. While performing the task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering or on task. Consistent with the decoupling hypothesis, perceptual sensitivity (d′) was significantly reduced on trials during which participants reported mind wandering compared to on-task trials. However, this reduction in sensitivity did not differ between stimuli presented in the left and right visual field. These findings suggest that perceptual decoupling during mind wandering reflects a global attenuation of sensory processing, and that attentional systems involved during mind wandering may be distinct from those associated with slower fluctuations of attentional resources such as reductions in alertness.

articles_hidden.title: Eye-Tracking Data Quality Across Human Infants, Adults, and Chimpanzees: Challenges and Solutions for Developmental and Comparative Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Daniela Schmidt; Ingmar Visser; Luke Maurits; Maleen Thiele
articles_hidden.abstract: Originally developed for adult humans, modern corneal-reflection eye-tracking has become applicable to diverse populations. This has driven its popularity in developmental studies with preverbal infants and comparative research with other animals, including nonhuman primates. However, these novel applications introduce unique methodological challenges, raising critical questions about data quality and the validity of cross-group comparisons. Here, we systematically investigated eye-tracking data quality (accuracy, precision, robustness) in 4-, 6-, 9-, and 18-month-old infants, adults, and zoo-housed chimpanzees. In Experiment 1, most strikingly, chimpanzees showed markedly lower accuracy compared to all human groups, including even 4-month-olds, who showed poorer accuracy than older infants and adults. Furthermore, some data quality metrics co-varied with key eye-tracking measures (e.g., number and duration of fixations, relative looking times), underscoring how data quality shapes inferences about psychological processes. Experiments 2 and 3 explored whether calibration adjustments can optimize data quality. In Experiment 2, modifying the conventional calibration procedure for chimpanzees yielded significant improvements. Compared to using an individual’s own 2-point calibration, another conspecific’s 5-point or a human 9-point calibration substantially enhanced accuracy. Conversely, in Experiment 3, a conceptually similar approach for human infants (using a peer’s or adult’s 9-point calibration) did not improve data quality compared to infants’ standard baseline (own 5-point calibration). Together, these findings offer profound implications and practical recommendations for navigating data quality challenges in comparative and developmental eye-tracking. Moving forward, we emphasize the necessity of species-specific method development and call for closer interdisciplinary collaboration to establish shared standards across application fields.

articles_hidden.title: Selective reductions amid global increases in neural information dynamics jointly track self-dissolution in meditation
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Andrew Atad; Pedro A. Mediano; Fynn-Mathis Trautwein; ‪Yair Dor-Ziderman‬‏; Henrik Röhr; Yoav Schweitzer; Ohad Nave; Stephen Fulder; Aviva Berkovich-Ohana
articles_hidden.abstract: The sense of self is fundamental to experience, yet its neural basis remains unresolved. Contemplative traditions and empirical evidence suggest it can be voluntarily dissolved while retaining awareness, offering a window onto this question. We combined magnetoencephalography with in-depth phenomenology in long-term meditators (N=45, mean 3,832 practice hours) who reliably modulated self-boundaries across rest, self-maintenance and self-dissolution. Meditation broadly increased entropy and information transfer, yet selective reductions characterized self-dissolution. Reduced posterior-medial high-beta entropy and within-cingulate information transfer differentiated dissolution from maintenance. Information transfer reductions from occipital, cingulate, limbic, and subcortical regions, alongside orbitofrontal entropy stabilization, correlated with dissolution phenomenology. Combined with posterior-medial high-beta power reductions, these correlates explained 52% of dissolution depth variance, yet only information transfer predicted held-out participants. We propose selfhood relies on distributed processes that can be reconfigured in meditation through relaxed priors, gated bottom-up evidence, and stabilized evaluative dynamics, distinct from global disruption during psychedelic ego-dissolution.

articles_hidden.title: Control Dilemmas Exist on Different Levels of Information Processing: Flexibility and Stability Trade off at the Task Level
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Janker; Sebastian Musslick; Gesine Dreisbach
articles_hidden.abstract: Our cognitive system must manage two opposing demands: staying focused on one task (stability) and switching between tasks when needed (flexibility). Traditionally, a trade-off has been assumed between these two control modes. Recent studies questioned this idea. However, they do not consider that experimental manipulations can influence stability and flexibility at different levels of information processing and that a trade-off may only exist within the same level. We introduce a novel paradigm designed to investigate flexibility and stability at different levels of information processing (task vs. stimulus level). Participants switched between two categorization tasks while ignoring distractors. Distractors either came from the same (within-task) or the alternative task (between-task) and were either response-congruent or incongruent. In Experiments 1 and 2, participants categorized words superimposed on distractor images representing the generic response categories (task level interference). In Experiment 3, they categorized letters or digits flanked by distractor letters or digits (stimulus level interference). Reduced interference from between-task distractors compared to within-task distractors in Experiments 1 and 2 show shielding at the task level. At the stimulus level (Experiment 3) both distractor-types interfered to the same extent, indicating that the shielding against between-task distractors got bypassed by the automatic retrieval of learnt stimulus-response associations. Across all three experiments, shielding against between-task distractors in the previous trial improved subsequent performance, when the task repeated (i.e. it improved stability), but impaired performance, when the task switched (i.e. it impaired flexibility). This finding supports a trade-off between flexibility and stability at the task level.

articles_hidden.title: Isolating domain-specific and domain-general contributions to global confidence
articles_hidden.authors: Sophie Bavard; Andrew McWilliams; Flora Chartier; Karim N'DIAYE; Stephen M Fleming; Marion Rouault
articles_hidden.abstract: While metacognition - our ability to evaluate our own cognitive processes - has been extensively studied by measuring trial-by-trial self-assessments of task performance (local confidence), real-world decisions often require a broader perspective, drawing on evaluations of performance over wider timespans (global confidence). Despite its pervasive influence on decision-making and mental health, it remains unknown whether global confidence is formed through similar or distinct processes across cognitive domains. Here we employ a novel gamified approach to compare how global confidence is formed in the domains of memory and perception. In memory, we found that both local accuracy and confidence contributed to global confidence, whereas in perception, global confidence was predicted by local confidence alone. By comparing the formation of global confidence across domains, our study provides new insights into the mechanisms underpinning self-evaluation, paving the way for the development of metacognitive interventions in education and psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a Sequencing Framework for Teaching and Using Self- Enactable Behavior Change Techniques: A Conceptual Review and Proposed Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandre Mazéas; Nikos Ntoumanis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Self-enactable behavior change techniques (BCTs) may help individuals initiate and sustain health behavior change. However, existing taxonomies provide limited guidance on how such techniques should be selected, taught, combined, and sequenced over time. This perspective aimed to review previous approaches and to develop a conceptual framework for organizing and sequencing self-enactable BCTs for intervention design and participant learning.
Methods: A critical conceptual review was conducted to identify published approaches to BCT grouping, temporal organization, prerequisites, and stage-specific sequencing. Literature identified through four databases was synthesized alongside the compendium of self-enactable BCTs to inform a five-step framework-development process. 
Results: The review showed that existing taxonomies and sequencing approaches provide useful classifications but limited guidance for progressive teaching and self-enactment. To address this gap, we proposed a framework comprising 108 self-enactable BCTs organized into nine clusters and 27 groups. We mapped prerequisite relations, classified techniques by their predominant prospective or reactive function, and sequenced their groups across the Model of Action Phases. 
Conclusion: Our framework provides a theory-informed structure for teaching and applying self-enactable BCTs. It is intended to guide intervention design and generate testable hypotheses about technique sequencing that need to be empirically explored in future studies.

articles_hidden.title: Validácia veľkých jazykových modelov pri kvantifikácii obsahového prekryvu psychodiagnostických škál
articles_hidden.authors: Viktória Gajdošová; Matus Adamkovic
articles_hidden.abstract: Krízu replikovateľnosti v psychológii prehlbuje aj netransparentný výber psychodiagnostických škál. Výskumníci často predpokladajú zameniteľnosť škál deklarujúcich meranie rovnakého konštruktu bez toho, aby overili ich skutočný obsahový prekryv, ktorého manuálna kvantifikácia expertmi je subjektívna, časovo náročná a neškálovateľná. Overovali sme, či veľké jazykové modely (GPT-5.1) a sémantické vektorovanie (text-embedding-3-large) dokážu posúdiť obsahovú podobnosť škál. Automatizovane sme replikovali tri expertné štúdie z domén depresie, mánie a traumy a porovnali štyri prístupy: sémantické vektorovanie, hybridnú metódu (extrakcia symptómov pomocou LLM a vektorovanie), zero-shot a chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. Výsledky naznačujú, že LLM sa dokážu priblížiť expertnému úsudku, no ich úspešnosť nerastie so zložitosťou prístupu. Sémantické vektorovanie fungovalo najlepšie pri položkách s jednotným formátom; pri komplexných položkách extrakcia symptómov zlepšila poradie dvojíc škál, no prekryv nadhodnocovala. Najvýkonnejší bol zero-shot prompting, ktorý bez ohľadu na zložitosť textu dosiahol strednú až dobrú konzistenciu s expertným hodnotením (ICC: trauma 0.86, depresia 0.64, mánia 0.54). CoT prompting paradoxne zhodu znížil, možno v dôsledku „over-reasoningu“. Voľbu metódy odporúčame prispôsobiť dátam a zdrojom: sémantické vektorovanie je rýchle a lacné pri jednoduchých položkách, kým zero-shot prompting je univerzálny. Využitie vidíme ako podporný nástroj pri výbere a porovnávaní dotazníkov z hľadiska obsahovej validity.

articles_hidden.title: The locus coeruleus – norepinephrine system as a regulator of social perception
articles_hidden.authors: Maryam Ziaei; Camilla Bay Panduro Jensen; Hazim Hussein; Claire O'Callaghan; Valerio Zerbi; Heidi I. L. Jacobs
articles_hidden.abstract: Social perception allows us to rapidly interpret others' emotions, intentions, and actions, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we propose a framework linking neuromodulatory function to large-scale networks involved in social perception. The framework centers on the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC–NE) system as an orchestrator of cortical networks. We argue that social perception is optimized when moderate tonic LC activity is paired with strong phasic responses to social-emotional cues, enabling selective attention, flexible updating of expectations, and accurate interpretation of social information. By contrast, both reduced and excessive LC activity are predicted to impair social perception. LC hypoactivity limits engagement with socially relevant cues, whereas hyperactivity produces diffuse arousal, distractibility, and hypervigilance, reducing discrimination of relevant from irrelevant social signals. We further propose that social perception emerges through modulation of local cortical gain, large-scale brain networks, and perceptual evidence accumulation, providing a mechanistic bridge between cellular processes and social behavior. Finally, we outline testable predictions and consider how disrupted LC function may contribute to social cognitive deficits in aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and neuropsychiatric disorders. By placing the LC–NE system as orchestrator of adaptive social perception, this framework offers a unifying account of how neuromodulation shapes social behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Does Singing Together Foster Learning, Well-being, and Prosociality in Children? Evaluation of the EVE Project in French Priority Education.
articles_hidden.authors: Romain di Stasi; Carla Aimé-Jubin; Camille Basile; Dalila Bovet; Rana Esseily
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has highlighted the effects of musical engagement on children’s social, academic, and personal development. However, most studies have focused on instrumental training, while the few studies on choral singing have reported effects on self-esteem in children and adolescents and social inclusion in adults. This study examines the impact of choral singing on academic achievement, social interaction, and well-being in children. This research was conducted within the “EVE project,” a three-year choral singing program organized by the Philharmonie de Paris in two socioeconomically disadvantaged schools in Paris and its suburbs. Using a longitudinal design, the study evaluated 133 children in the first year (94 EVE, 39 control), 123 in the second year (86 EVE, 37 control), and 112 in the third year (81 EVE, 31 control). At each yearly assessment, children completed three social interaction tasks (sharing, cooperation, and helping), measures of school learning abilities using the BMT-i test, and well-being questionnaires. Our results showed that regular participation in choir singing was associated with improvements in verbal memory, but no evidence of improvement was observed for working memory, dictation performance, or mathematics achievement. Choir participation was also associated with higher well-being and greater social interaction during cooperative tasks, as reflected by increased smiling and gaze toward peers. Overall, these findings suggest that choral practice may be associated with selective near-transfer benefits, particularly for verbal memory, and underscore the social nature of musical engagement and its potential to support children’s well-being and social bonding.

articles_hidden.title: Towards Natural Behaviour Processing for Representation and Prediction of Digital Human Behaviour
articles_hidden.authors: Clemens Stachl; Brittany I Davidson; Gabriella M. Harari
articles_hidden.abstract:
Studying how people behave and understanding why their actions unfold differently are
major goals of psychological science. However, most research relies on nomothetic
approaches that aggregate behavioural data into summary statistics, obscuring
person-specific patterns that afford person-specific understanding. The progressing
proliferation of digital technologies such as smartphones, wearables, and computermediated
systems now generates fine-grained, temporally ordered records of everyday
behaviour, creating unprecedented opportunities to study both systematic interindividual
differences and patterns of intra-individual variation. Here, we propose
Natural Behaviour Processing (NBP) as a framework for analysing digital behavioural
data using sequence modelling approaches adapted from natural language
processing. We argue that behaviour shares critical structural properties with
language: both involve a repository of possible actions (vocabulary), systematic
patterns governing how elements typically combine (grammar), and context-dependent
meaning (semantics). These structural parallels motivate applying sequence-based
models that have revolutionised language processing to the study of behaviour more
broadly. We review pioneering studies on diverse topics of research, including life
outcomes, decision-making, social media use, consumer behaviour, online education,
and health, demonstrating that sequential approaches capture person-specific patterns
that are typically lost in aggregation. We discuss the challenges facing NBP adoption,
including the tension between predictive modelling and theoretical understanding, the
need for large-scale curated behaviour datasets, and methodological training
requirements. The adoption of NBP could transform the way psychology
operationalises, conceptualises, and ultimately understands human behaviour by
simultaneously accounting for person-specificity in real-world complexity while
maintaining predictive performance at population levels.

articles_hidden.title: Moment-to-Moment Affect During Film-Induced Somatic Anxiety
articles_hidden.authors: Micah G. Allen
articles_hidden.abstract: Studying sustained anxiety requires tracing how unpleasant arousal develops, persists and subsides over an unfolding experience. We characterised a 13.5-min first-person film of people undertaking dangerous activities at height as an induction for this purpose. Using an open-source browser-based platform developed for this study, online participants continuously rated their own valence and arousal and completed the somatic subscale of the State-Trait Inventory for Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety before and after viewing. In the confirmatory sample (N = 124), arousal was elevated during the film's rising and sustained phases and declined towards the end, while valence was more unpleasant during the sustained phase than during the opening. Group-mean trajectories closely reproduced the temporal shape observed in an exploratory sample (n = 21; arousal r = .99; valence r = .94). Somatic anxiety increased after viewing (dz = 1.03). Participants reporting larger increases rated the film as more arousing (ρ = .24) and more unpleasant (ρ = −.38). The open-source platform and reference trajectories provide a reusable resource for studying the temporal course of affect during a sustained anxiety induction.

articles_hidden.title: Reimagining Psychotherapy: Toward an Integrative Afrocentric-Decolonial Framework for Relational Healing and Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Ohiro Oni-Eseleh
articles_hidden.abstract: Western models of psychotherapy practice are often inadequate to address issues related to African identity, which is rooted in communal existence, cultural histories and systems that shape perceptions of illness and healing. In African cultural contexts, psychotherapy plays out against the background of relational patterns grounded in African tradition and enduring histories of colonialism. Grounded in individualism and intrapsychic causation, this article draws from African philosophy and decolonial literature as it conceptualizes the adaptation and practice of psychotherapy in African settings. What is proposed is a relational model of psychotherapy practice that is informed by the importance of decoloniality, rooted in consciousness of culture and history, and an intellectual and practical embrace of epistemic and community-embedded care. Such an approach strengthens clinical practice while challenging global mental health to review its epistemological assumptions and determinations of what expertise means. Specifically, this article highlights the need to incorporate African cultural perspectives into psychotherapy to enhance the efficacy of treatment in that culture.

articles_hidden.title: Memory precision fluctuates with theta rhythmicity in humans
articles_hidden.authors: Troy Houser; Riley Acker; Dagmar Zeithamova
articles_hidden.abstract: Rodent research indicates that the hippocampus naturally oscillates between memory encoding and retrieval phases at theta rhythm, indicating that the timing of when information reaches the hippocampus can determine encoding success. However, non-invasively probing such oscillations is challenging in humans. Here, we employed a recently developed dense sampling approach to construct a time course of memory encoding success. Using an attention-grabbing cue expected to reset theta phase, we varied the delay between the cue and to-be-remembered stimulus. Experiment 1 replicated recent finding that human associative memory performance fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, with the best fitting frequency at 8 Hz. Experiment 2 tested and confirmed a new prediction that memory precision also fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, consistent with hippocampal models postulating oscillations in the relative engagement of alternative processing pathways. Together, these findings suggest that the rapid neural fluctuations underpinning memory processes are robust enough to be observed using the dense behavioral sampling approach. Moreover, this work substantiates models of episodic memory and provides new avenues to study models of hippocampal function in humas noninvasively, providing evidence from a purely behavioral approach that human mnemonic discrimination fluctuates with theta rhythm.

articles_hidden.title: iTemplate2: An Open-Source Python Toolbox for Automatic Eye-Movement Analysis of Dynamic Facial Stimuli
articles_hidden.authors: Naiqi G Xiao; Rafael Román-Caballero; Wei Fang; Sara Ripley; Danyang Han; Laurel Trainor
articles_hidden.abstract: Template-based gaze-to-face registration enables standardized analysis of eye movements by mapping gaze coordinates onto a canonical facial template, reducing variability introduced by manual area-of-interest (AOI) definition across heterogeneous stimuli. However, existing implementations are largely restricted to static images, rely on semi-manual landmark annotation, and depend on proprietary software, limiting scalability and reproducibility. These constraints become increasingly problematic as research shifts toward dynamic stimuli, wearable eye-tracking, and open-source workflows. We present iTemplate2, a fully open-source Python-based redesign of the original system. The framework introduces four key advances: (1) support for dynamic stimuli via frame-wise coordinate transformation, including a normalization module for wearable and scene-based eye-tracking data; (2) integration of MediaPipe’s Face Landmarker for automated detection of 478 facial landmarks per frame, with multi-face tracking and identity persistence mechanisms that reduce manual annotation requirements; (3) a complete Python reimplementation using NumPy, pandas, OpenCV, PyQt6, and Apache Parquet, providing a cross-platform graphical interface without commercial dependencies; and (4) expanded visualization and analysis tools, including interactive heatmaps, snap-to-landmark AOI definition, and extraction of facial blendshape parameters for concurrent expression analysis. The system is applicable across diverse domains, including infant face scanning, cross-cultural gaze research, clinical screening, and naturalistic social interaction paradigms using wearable eye-tracking. It robustly processes complex multi-face video datasets that are difficult to analyze using conventional template-based methods. iTemplate2 modernizes the template-based registration framework for contemporary behavioral research, converting idiosyncratic visual data into a unified, reproducible analytical space. The software is freely available as an open-source tool at https://osf.io/54v9e/overview?view_only=5ac289558a3d4897a02336124ae409a1.

articles_hidden.title: Learning to Enumerate Reorganizes Magnitude Representations
articles_hidden.authors: Lauren S Aulet
articles_hidden.abstract: Human adults show a number bias in magnitude perception, weighting numerical information more heavily than continuous magnitudes like area. However, developmental research suggests this bias is not innate: young children show an area bias that reverses to a number bias only later in development. What drives this shift? Here we use deep neural networks as a tool for testing computational sufficiency, asking whether learning to estimate number is by itself enough to reorganize how a visual system weights magnitude. We trained ResNeXt-50 networks on an enumeration task (labeling the number of dots in an image, an operationalization of a functional outcome of counting) and measured representational bias by linearly decoding number versus cumulative area from penultimate-layer features, with the two dimensions decorrelated by design. Untrained networks showed a robust area bias, with area more decodable than number. Critically, networks trained to estimate number showed a reversal, with number becoming substantially more decodable than area, and this shift emerged after a single epoch of training. The effect was not a trivial consequence of training on a dimension: a matched control trained to estimate area did not produce the mirror-image effect, because enumeration training actively suppressed area information rather than merely amplifying number. Principal component analysis confirmed a reorganization of representational geometry, with numerosity becoming the dominant axis of variation (r² = 0.95) and area variance strongly reduced. These findings provide a computational proof-of-concept that learning to enumerate can restructure magnitude representations, suggesting that the perceptual primacy of number in adults may be partly a consequence, rather than a precondition, of symbolic number acquisition.

articles_hidden.title: Latent visual mechanisms as computational phenotypes: Toward a precision science of vision
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Vision science has traditionally sought mechanisms shared across observers, treating individual differences as noise. Yet factor-analytic and latent-variable studies show that variation among observers is highly structured, recovering reproducible dimensions in contrast sensitivity, color, stereopsis, motion, and face recognition, among others. What are these latent dimensions? I propose they be treated as candidate computational phenotypes: a term borrowed from computational psychiatry and re-operationalized for vision as a stable, measurable pattern of visual information processing recovered from the covariance structure of individual differences. A computational phenotype is not a latent factor, mechanism, endophenotype, or biomarker; it occupies Marr's algorithmic level, between behavior and biology, and earns the name only by meeting stringent criteria of reliability, replication, convergent validity, and mechanistic relevance. I review candidate phenotypes drawn from many laboratories, recast development, aging, and disease as perturbations of phenotypic structure, and turn the strongest objection (that vision has no common factor) into support, since the relevant phenotypes are narrow and mechanism-specific. The payoff spans audiences: diagnostic profiles for clinicians, a non-invasive way to count and test visual mechanisms for basic scientists, and performance-predicting traits for human-factors work. The framework moves vision science from the average observer toward a precision science of visual computation.

articles_hidden.title: Canine-Assisted Interventions and Symptoms Associated with Borderline Personality Disorder: A Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Pestell; Richard Gorman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is associated with symptoms including self-harm, suicidality, impulsivity, anger, and mood disturbance. Although psychotherapeutic approaches are commonly used in treatment, there remains interest in alternative and complementary approaches for managing BPD-related symptoms. Canine-assisted interventions (CAI) have been investigated across a range of mental health settings, though their relevance to BPD-related symptoms has not previously been described.

Aims:
This scoping review aimed to map the available research on CAI addressing symptoms associated with BPD, describing study populations, intervention characteristics, outcome measures, and gaps in the evidence.

Methods:
A systematic search was conducted across 5 databases. Studies were considered eligible if they examined the effects of CAI on predefined BPD-related symptoms, involved CAI interventions, and reported primary empirical data. Study populations, intervention characteristics, outcome measures, and reported findings were tabulated and summarised descriptively.

Results:
Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria. Studies varied in their populations, intervention formats and outcome measures, and coverage of the selected symptoms was uneven. Most studies reported reductions in at least some BPD-related symptoms following CAI. However, several studies demonstrated important methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, non-randomised designs, and limited control for confounding. Most included studies did not recruit participants with a formal diagnosis of BPD specifically.

Conclusion:
Existing research on CAI does address several symptoms associated with BPD, but spans diverse populations, interventions and outcome measures. There are, however, gaps in symptom coverage and research involving populations specifically diagnosed with BPD, providing priorities for future investigation.

articles_hidden.title: Not “born that way”: Homophobic social preferences and non-essentialism of sexual orientation in childhood
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Peretz-Lange
articles_hidden.abstract: Although prejudice begins early in development, very few studies examine the developmental roots of homophobia. We explored the onset and developmental timecourse of homophobic social preferences as well as the cognitive and environmental factors predicting these preferences. We were particularly interested in whether children would essentialize orientation (e.g., consider it inborn and uncontrollable), since essentialism often positively correlates with prejudice but negatively correlates with adolescents’ and adults’ homophobia. As environmental predictors, we explored parents’ anti-prejudiced values and children’s LGBTQ contact. A diverse sample of participants from across the United States (n = 128 six- to nine-year-olds, 60 girls & 68 boys, 42% White & 58% of color) selected between heteroparental and homoparental peers in a Playmate Preference Task and then completed an essentialism assessment. Parents reported their anti-prejudiced values and children’s LGBTQ contact. Homophobic social preferences were present by age seven and increased across childhood. Moreover, despite children’s pervasive essentialist tendencies, participants overwhelmingly rejected the idea that being in a same-gender vs. other-gender marriage reflects any internal uncontrollable characteristic. Instead, children viewed this as a matter of choice. Essentialism was very low overall and did not predict social preferences. Instead, parents’ values and children’s LGBTQ contact predicted these preferences. In sum, children view orientation as reflecting a choice rather than an intrinsic nature, and then rely on the adults in their lives to determine how to feel toward that choice. Homophobic social preferences therefore emerge early and in the context of behavioral views of orientation. Social, cognitive, and developmental implications are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Forging ahead, pulling back, and acting strategically: Climate activists’ responses to criminalisation and repression in the UK
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Gardner; Sunniva Davies-Rommetveit; Jenny Douch; Anna Aretha Sach
articles_hidden.abstract: In response to the post-2018 rise in climate protest, many liberal democratic countries have witnessed the criminalisation and repression of environmental activists. Instead of assessing macro-level effects of repression on activism, this paper explores the micro-level responses to surveillance, arrest, fines, and imprisonment. Drawing on socio-legal scholarship that understands the law as socially constructed rather than objective and external, this paper delves into the black box of political repression, offering an examination of how climate activists respond to state sanctions. Analysing a survey of 1,375 Extinction Rebellion UK activists through thematic analysis and quantitative coding, we demonstrate that individual biography and narrativisations of the law lead activists to forge ahead, pull back, or act strategically in response to repression.

articles_hidden.title: Felt but Not Detected:  Salience Versus Detectability of Affective Change in Ambulatory Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: Aleksandra Kaurin; Mario Wenzel; Paula Philippi; Jonas Dora
articles_hidden.abstract: Ambulatory assessment (AA) captures within-person fluctuations in daily life, yet not all observed change exceeds measurement error, and not all reliable change is subjectively experienced. We propose a preregistered dual-threshold framework distinguishing statistical detectability (smallest detectable change, SDC) from experiential salience (minimal important change, MIC). Adults (N = 250) completed a 14-day AA protocol with twice-daily and event-contingent assessments (5,982 observations), rating momentary stress, positive affect, and negative affect (0–4) and perceived change since the previous assessment. SDC₉₅ estimates ranged from 1.56 to 1.92 scale points, so roughly three-quarters of consecutive changes fell below reliable detection. Anchor-based MICs, in contrast, were 1 point for all constructs. Correspondence between detectable and perceived change was asymmetric: sensitivity was high (.77–.87), but specificity (.46–.56) and positive predictive values (.24–.31) were low, as participants frequently reported change without reliable change; directional reversals were rare. Reliable change strongly predicted perceived change (ORs 4.6–12.5). Event-contingent assessments, higher prior states, and person-level characteristics (e.g., impulsivity, emotion regulation) increased the general propensity to report change but did not moderate this link. Felt change thus precedes measurable change: detectability and salience are distinct thresholds that intensive longitudinal research must evaluate separately.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Lagged Panel Analysis Using Structural Equation Modeling: Trends and Suggestions Based on a Literature Review of 111 Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Asuka Nishida; Satoshi Usami
articles_hidden.abstract:
Cross-lagged panel analysis based on structural equation modeling (SEM) has been widely used in the behavioral sciences. The present study provides a literature review based on 111 studies published in major psychology journals that conducted cross-lagged panel analysis. Through this review, we offer an overview of current trends in study design, analytical methods (e.g., estimation method, missing data handling), and model selection, and discuss practical challenges and implications for future applications. A major finding is that the use of the random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) has increased substantially (41% of the studies) over the past few years. At the same time, most studies rely on longitudinal data with a small number of measurement occasions (e.g., T = 3 − 4). Studies that employed the RI-CLPM on the grounds that it enables inference about within-person relations tended to conduct only limited comparisons with potential alternative models, and only 3% of the studies evaluated model fit from the perspective of local fit (i.e., residual correlations). Although many studies using psychological scales relied on sum scores, only 40% of the studies examined longitudinal measurement invariance, suggesting that there is
still room for improvement.

articles_hidden.title: Increased monetary incentives enhance goal-directed reinforcement learning but fail to suppress automatic learning processes
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi; Noham Wolpe; Nitzan Shahar
articles_hidden.abstract: Adaptive reinforcement learning requires assigning outcomes to the features of actions that causally determine them. Yet humans also learn reward associations with action features that are explicitly known to be outcome-irrelevant, and these associations can bias subsequent choices. Whether such maladaptive learning is regulated by motivational incentives remains unclear. Here, we tested whether increasing monetary stakes differentially modulates the influence of outcome-relevant and outcome-irrelevant learned values on choice. Participants (N = 287) completed a multi-armed bandit task in low- and high-stakes conditions while explicitly instructed that card identity predicted reward whereas card location did not. Computational modelling revealed that higher stakes increased the influence of outcome-relevant values on choice, but did not change the influence of outcome-irrelevant values. Critically, outcome-irrelevant value influences persisted even though they produced substantially greater monetary losses under high stakes. These findings show that monetary incentives selectively enhance the use of outcome-relevant learned values without improving the selectivity of credit assignment. More broadly, they suggest that only some components of reinforcement learning are sensitive to motivational control.

articles_hidden.title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL):  A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
