articles_hidden.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Jonathan Wolf-Phillips
articles_hidden.abstract: Leadership research has catalogued many styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but has offered few accounts of the regulatory mechanisms through which leader-follower relationships operate. We propose that attachment, understood through social neuroscience, supplies one such mechanism. Humans regulate environmental demands relationally, and attachment organises this social regulation of a finite bioenergetic budget under challenge. When followers face threat, dependence or uncertainty, this relationship can come to serve attachment functions, and the leader's reliability as a security provider bears on how much of followers' regulatory resources remains available for work. Building on the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we develop an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework spanning social allostasis, attachment and caregiving, predictive regulation and biobehavioural synchrony. We position AIL relative to evolutionary accounts of leadership and derive nine propositions that distinguish attachment processes from exchange, trust and identification, measurable from self-report to physiology and brain activity.

articles_hidden.title: Stability, Asymmetric Recovery, and Sociodemographic Heterogeneity in Social Health Trajectories Across Social Disruption: A Four-Wave Hidden Markov Model
articles_hidden.authors: Karoline Huth; Lisanne Catharina Johanna Steijvers; Senne Maria Catharina Elisabeth Wijnen; Olga Schiepers; Matty Crone; Rik Crutzen; Nicole Dukers-Muijrers
articles_hidden.abstract: Social health is a key pillar of overall health, yet knowledge of distinct social health states, how these change during long-term social disruption, who is at risk of social ill-health, and how social health states affect mental and physical illness remains limited. We used Hidden Markov models to analyse prospective data from 954 adults aged 40 and over who were assessed before, during, and after the onset of the 2019–2025 pandemic. This enabled us to identify latent social health states based on network size, density, loneliness, and emotional support, and to estimate transition probabilities between states over time.  We examined the impact of sex, education, and age on state membership and trajectories, as well as the association between states and depressive symptoms and physical health. Three states were identified: socially isolated (15.9%), moderately connected (55.5%), and socially thriving (28.6%). Most participants (72.5%) remained in one state throughout the observation period; 14.4% deteriorated, 6.5% recovered, and the rest fluctuated.  Being male and having completed a practical education were associated with the socially isolated state, while being female was associated with the thriving state, as well as state deterioration. Worse states showed a graded association with depressive symptoms. Social health is characterised by three relatively stable states, even in the face of persistent social disruption. Nevertheless, many individuals exhibited persistent deterioration even after social restrictions were lifted. The differing risk across sociodemographic groups highlights the need for targeted strategies to promote resilient social health.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing resurgence as persistence in the Valproic Acid rat model of Autism Spectrum Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Ana J O Cerveira; Eldereis de Paula; Andréia Schmidt; Fernando Eduardo Padovan-Neto
articles_hidden.abstract: Behavioral persistence poses a clinical challenge in patients with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), as targeted problematic behaviors resist elimination and reemerge upon treatment discontinuation (resurgence). Prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA) has been proposed as a rat model of ASD that would increase behavioral persistence, but findings in this model have been inconsistent. This study investigated whether prenatal VPA exposure increases persistence by assessing the persistence of target responding on a three-phase resurgence procedure: Training (target response reinforced), Elimination (target response placed on extinction while an alternative response is reinforced), and Testing (alternative response also placed on extinction, producing resurgence of target responding). Male and female Sprague-Dawley rats prenatally exposed to saline (SAL) or VPA were compared. Target and alternative response rates did not differ between SAL and VPA animals in either sex at any phase, nor did the proportional change from target to alternative responding during Elimination or the magnitude of resurgence at Testing. Males did, however, display higher resurgence magnitudes than females in both prenatal conditions. Together, these findings indicate that VPA-exposed rats do not behave more persistently, but contribute to the investigations of potentially ASD-related traits in this animal model in a behavioral analytic perspective.

articles_hidden.title: Regardless of Task Demands, Delayed Goal-Directed Processing Persists in Adult ADHD
articles_hidden.authors: Jahla Osborne; Jacob Sellers; Han Zhang; Su Wang; Sarah Liberatore; Chandra Sripada; Priti Shah; John Jonides
articles_hidden.abstract: Inhibitory control challenges have long been theorized to underlie deficits in ADHD, but the precise mechanism(s) have remained unclear. Recent research using “forced-response” conflict tasks and computational modeling, capable of distinguishing the time-dependent contributions of habitual and goal-directed response preparation, has provided evidence that supports the idea that delayed goal-directed processing underlies inhibitory control challenges in adult ADHD. Still, it remains unclear how habitual and goal-directed responding adjust with increased (or decreased) interference that requires more (or less) inhibitory control, which matters because daily life involves varying levels of interference. To address this gap, we recruited adults meeting criteria for ADHD to complete a forced-response version of the arrow flanker task. We created circumstances of increased and decreased interference by manipulating the size of target and non-target (distractor) stimuli relative to each other. We utilized a crossover design, in which participants completed the arrow-flanker once while medicated and once while unmedicated (counterbalanced). Results showed that goal-directed responses were prepared more slowly for participants when unmedicated, regardless of interference circumstance. We directly tested the interaction between medication and interference, and the presence of medication did not especially help in one interference circumstance over the other. These findings add to a growing body of literature working toward better understanding the nature of inhibitory control within adult-ADHD.

articles_hidden.title: The role of pragmatic context in children’s quantification of parts and wholes
articles_hidden.authors: David Barner; Hannah Bryer; Miguel Mejia; Mahesh Srinivasan
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do children sometimes include the pieces of broken things when asked to count (e.g., “Count the forks”)? In five experiments, we test two ideas: (1) that adults, but not children, exclude parts from counts by reasoning that speakers must only be interested in whole objects with functions that fulfill desired goals, and (2) that only adults exclude parts on the basis of a Gricean inference, on which it is assumed that if a speaker wanted parts to be counted, they would say so. In Experiments 1-3, we find that although children and adults are somewhat less likely to count pieces of objects when speaker goals are explicitly mentioned, large developmental differences remain unexplained. In Experiments 4-5, we provide evidence that children differ most from adults when pieces are presented in the presence of complementary parts (with which they together would form a whole), and that these pieces are significantly more likely to be conceptualized and labeled as “parts”, especially by adults. Together, these findings suggest that adults – but not children – are more likely to exclude broken parts from their counts in response to requests like “Count the forks!” when they are also able to understand that more informative requests could have been made (e.g., “Count the pieces of fork!”).

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking Spaced Practice Under Limited Instructional Time: The Benefits of Repetition Depend on Spacing
articles_hidden.authors: Meng Cao; Paulo F. Carvalho
articles_hidden.abstract: Spacing and repetition are two fundamental principles of learning, yet under limited instructional time, increasing repetitions necessarily shortens the intervals between encounters. Prior research found that more repetitions with shorter spacing produced better learning than fewer repetitions with longer spacing, but the respective contributions of spacing and repetition remained unclear. The present study sought to disentangle these contributions and replicate prior findings. Data were collected in 2026 from 120 English-speaking U.S. adults. Participants learned Indonesian-English word pairs three or six times under both massed and spaced schedules within a fixed instructional time. Retention was assessed immediately, one day, and three days later, and forgetting curves were used to estimate initial memory strength and forgetting rate. We replicated the advantage of more repetitions with shorter spacing. Spaced practice produced greater initial memory strength and slower forgetting than massed practice, whereas additional repetitions increased initial memory strength only when practice was spaced. These findings suggest that, under time constraints, additional repetitions benefit learning primarily when spaced, indicating that the advantage of repeated practice depends on the accumulation of learning across spaced encounters.

articles_hidden.title: Artificial observers and real individual differences: A roadmap for a computational psychometrics of vision
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly used as models of vision, yet they are evaluated against the average observer: average performance, average neural response, average representational geometry. This discards one of the richest constraints on theory: stable individual differences. Fitting the average is necessary but not sufficient. I argue that future models should be judged not only by their fit to mean human performance, but by whether populations of artificial observers reproduce the covariance structure and latent factors found across human observers. Two mature but disconnected literatures motivate this. Decades of factor-analytic psychophysics and electrophysiology show that interindividual variation is signal, not noise: the pattern of correlations among observers reveals the number and tuning of underlying mechanisms, and fractionates vision into many narrow factors rather than one general ability. Meanwhile, neural networks differing only in random initialization develop measurably different internal representations, so any single trained network is one sample from a distribution of possible observers. Joining these yields a computational psychometrics of vision: construct a designed population of artificial observers (varying in architecture, initialization, training diet, and front-end sampling), submit them to the same latent-variable analyses used on humans, and test whether the recovered factor structure matches. Recent work showing that seed-varied networks align with specific individuals is an existence proof. This article generalizes it into a framework, a staged roadmap, and a benchmark, together with the safeguards that keep such a benchmark from becoming an optimization target, for testing hypotheses about human visual variation with artificial observer populations.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Accuracy Evaluation of an LLM-Assisted Workflow for Screening and Data Extraction in Large-Scale Syntheses
articles_hidden.authors: Vsevolod Scherrer; Franzis Preckel; Moritz Breit
articles_hidden.abstract:
Large-scale research syntheses are labor-intensive and prone to human error, and large language models (LLMs) could support their screening and data extraction. Building on current recommendations, we developed an integrated workflow for title and abstract screening (Step 1), full-text screening (Step 2), and data extraction (Step 3), and evaluated it in a preregistered proof-of-concept study.
The study updated a meta-analysis on the rank-order stability of cognitive abilities, in which records may report several nested coefficients. Every step used ensembles of five LLM-instances, and we evaluated 2,960 workflow configurations against a human gold standard of 892 records, of which 692 records with 102 coded effect sizes formed the evaluation set. Without human review, Steps 1 and 2 retained 96.72% and 100.00% of eligible records. At Step 3, the LLMs missed 35.05% of gold effect sizes in rule-based extracted text but none in text from machine-learning-based parsing, which also lowered their coding error from 10.16% to 2.61%. In the recommended configuration, human review was confined to Step 3, where checking effect sizes of 5 of 40 records and 16.43% of the cells raised specificity to 100.00% and coding accuracy from 97.39% to 99.24%.
We derive five recommendations: (1) refine criterion-specific prompts on a calibration set, (2) use machine-learning-based PDF parsing for data extraction, (3) aggregate ensemble ratings leniently at screening and strictly at data extraction, (4) focus human review on data extraction, targeted via flags and ensemble disagreement, and (5) identify nested effect sizes in a separate stage with unique identifiers.

articles_hidden.title: Theories of Symbolic Number Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Hillary Mastarciyan; H Moriah Sokolowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding numerical symbols (e.g., the verbal number word ‘six’ or the Arabic digit ‘6’) is fundamental to the development of mathematical knowledge, yet how humans acquire meaningful representations of numerical symbols remains an ongoing theoretical question. In this review, we examine major theoretical accounts of symbolic number learning and consider how these perspectives explain the emergence and development of symbolic numerical knowledge. We focus particularly on the processes through which children establish meaningful connections between numerical symbols and their referents, addressing the longstanding symbol-grounding problem in numerical cognition. By synthesizing perspectives across developmental psychology and cognitive neuroscience, we identify areas of convergence and divergence among existing theoretical accounts and highlight key unresolved questions. Building on this synthesis, we propose the Grounded-to-Abstraction Theory, in which symbolic number knowledge emerges through a reciprocal process whereby small number words are initially grounded in exact quantity representations, and learning these symbols simultaneously scaffolds attention to numerical information. As this system develops, attentional control and approximate magnitude representations support the extension of numerical meaning beyond small quantities, while the emerging verbal number system scaffolds the acquisition of Arabic digits, yielding increasingly abstract and interconnected numerical representations. This framework integrates and extends existing theoretical perspectives and generates testable predictions regarding the behavioural and neural mechanisms underlying symbolic number learning in children. Overall, this review positions symbolic number learning as a dynamic developmental process involving multiple interacting representational systems and provides an integrative theoretical framework for understanding how children develop increasingly sophisticated representations of numerical symbols.

articles_hidden.title: Day-to-day fluctuations in craving and the value of drugs and food in daily life
articles_hidden.authors: Sergej Grunevski; Emmanuel E. Alvarez; Emma M. Schweitzer; Julia Kong; Sahar Hafezi; Anna B. Konova
articles_hidden.abstract: Craving is a powerful urge for a specific target (e.g., food, drugs) that prompts decisions directed at satisfying craving. While prior laboratory studies suggest craving biases behavior by amplifying target-specific value, the real-world generalizability of this mechanism remains unknown. We validate and extend these findings in a 28-day naturalistic smartphone-enabled study in patients with opioid use disorder (N=67) and community controls (N=49) who reported on their food (savory, sweet) and drug (opioid) urges and willingness-to-pay values. Despite person-level (mean) covariation, food and drug urges fluctuated largely independently within individuals while maintaining target-specific relationships with value. Using dynamics in drug urge and value and computational modeling, we isolated a distinct, ecologically relevant craving “state” tied to drug cue exposure and drug use in daily life. This research shows craving acts on normative valuation processes in real-world decision making and offers a novel approach to infer clinically vulnerable moments for behavior change.

articles_hidden.title: The Climate Stance Inventory: Development and validation in a large longitudinal sample of UK adults
articles_hidden.authors: Leo Johnson; Orestis Zavlis; Laurence Wainwright; Omid V. Ebrahimi
articles_hidden.abstract: The climate attitude–behaviour gap persists, with individual variables explaining limited behavioural variance. To address this problem, we develop and validate the Climate Stance Inventory (CSI), a continuous measure of 15 recurring orientations towards climate change and climate action derived from the Norm Activation Model. In a three-wave longitudinal study, 1,503 adults from the United Kingdom completed the CSI and measures of climate appraisals and environmental behaviour over approximately 10 weeks. Across waves, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses identified a 15-factor solution that exhibited good fit (CFI = .979, RMSEA = .034), high internal consistency (α/ω = .69–.88) and test-retest correlations (r = .58–.89) and full longitudinal measurement invariance. Climate stances showed theoretically coherent associations with threat certainty, responsibility-related appraisals, efficacy, institutional trust and pro-environmental behaviour. In hierarchical regressions, they explained substantial additional variance beyond demographic characteristics and climate change anxiety in pro-environmental voting (14.2%), workplace behaviour (19.5%) and behaviour outside work (22.4%). The Bystander stance also explained unique variance beyond a conceptually adjacent established barrier measure. These findings support the CSI as a reliable, temporally stable and substantively valid measure that can distinguish different psychological routes to climate (in)action and support the development and evaluation of more targeted climate-belief interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Left Out for Too Long? Chronicity of Social Exclusion as a Key Factor in Explaining the Exclusion-Radicalism Link
articles_hidden.authors: Linda Dörr; Andrew Hales; Kipling D. Williams; Christiane Marie Büttner; Michaela Pfundmair
articles_hidden.abstract:
Chronic social exclusion has been linked to radicalization processes in real-world terrorism
cases. However, experimental research regarding this link has focused on situational
experiences of exclusion, not accounting for chronicity of exclusion. Given the differences in
the psychological consequences of chronic and short-term exclusion, across three studies, we
investigated the association between chronic social exclusion and radicalism (i.e., readiness
to engage in violent and illegal political action) as well as activism (i.e., readiness to engage
in non-violent and legal political action). We hypothesized that chronicity might act as a key
condition for the effect of social exclusion on radicalism. In a survey study (N = 370), the
frequency of different types of exclusion experiences positively predicted radical intentions.
In a quasi-experimental survey study (N = 324), participants who reported chronic exclusion
(vs. no exclusion) in their everyday lives reported higher radical intentions. Participants who
reported only short-term exclusion did not differ in radical intentions from those reporting no
exclusion. In a five-month longitudinal study with weekly assessments (N = 343, k = 5,319
assessments), average exclusion experiences across the five-month period (i.e., a chronic
assessment of exclusion) positively predicted radical intentions and behaviors. Across
studies, chronic exclusion was associated with radicalism, but not activism. Thus, chronic
experiences of social exclusion might drive radical intentions and behaviors, highlighting
chronicity as a relevant yet understudied factor of the exclusion-radicalism link. In light of
these findings, reducing chronic experiences of exclusion might represent a particularly
promising avenue for the prevention of radicalism.

articles_hidden.title: A curriculum for neural networks to process two-digit arithmetic like humans
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel Lozano; Markus Spitzer; Korbinian Moeller; Miguel Ruiz-Garcia
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding and operating on multi-digit numbers is a critical step in the development of mathematical skills and concepts. Empirical and computational modeling evidence suggest that multi-digit number magnitude is processed in a componential manner, decomposed into units, tens, hundreds, etc. However, computational models evaluating whether such componential processing generalizes to multi-digit \textit{arithmetic} have so far relied on discrete symbolic inputs rather than on noisy magnitude representations. Accordingly, we developed a hierarchical neural network model of multi-digit addition based on componential processing of noisy single-digit magnitude representations. To evaluate model performance we implemented two training curricula: (i) an all-at-once curriculum and (ii) a step-by-step curriculum, where single-digit addition is trained before progressing to multi-digit problems (following school curricula). Under the training conditions tested, only the step-by-step curriculum allowed the model to learn multi-digit addition. Once trained this way, the model reproduced the carry-over and problem-size effects observed in reaction times of children and adults, both across problem categories and across individual items. These findings generalize the idea of decomposed processing of multi-digit number magnitude to arithmetic and highlight the importance of structured, incremental learning in both cognitive modeling and education.

articles_hidden.title: Employing ventilation and mobile air cleaning in classrooms and elderly care homes for infectious disease reduction: multi-stakeholder perspectives on acceptability, feasibility and perceived effects
articles_hidden.authors: Stefanie H Meeuwis; Amy Louise de Bruijn; Jennifer Mareen Becker; Marloes Duijzings; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen
articles_hidden.abstract: Poor indoor air quality (IAQ) leads to increased health risks, including infectious disease and respiratory illness, and can decrease wellbeing. Poor IAQ is also associated with adverse effects on performance indicators, for instance student education. Air cleaning technologies, such as (mobile) air cleaning and mechanical ventilation, could improve IAQ but their efficacy depends on their correct use and maintenance. User perspectives on the application of these technologies are generally underexplored. User and policy maker perspectives on the acceptability, feasibility and perceived effects of (mobile) air cleaning and ventilation systems in classrooms and elderly care homes were investigated in a two-part study. First, semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted with participants from various organizations including primary schools and elderly care. Second, focus groups were conducted to assess stakeholder perspectives on the knowledge gaps amongst primary education staff elicited from the interview study. Taken together, the findings showed that although indoor air climate is generally acknowledged to be important for health and overall performance, several factors were identified that could complicate the implementation and use of novel technologies. These importantly include knowledge gaps in end users about the technology’s relevance and usefulness. The findings indicate the significance of education for end users and the necessity of understanding behavioral factors implicated in the implementation of innovative technologies for optimal efficacy of such devices.

articles_hidden.title: “Puzzling, Yet So Refreshing”: Experiencing the Value of Neurodiversity Within an Inclusive Choir
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Petit; Géraldine Dessertenne; Fanny Aprile; Lucie Jurek
articles_hidden.abstract: The social challenges encountered by autistic people are increasingly understood as a double empathy problem: a mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic individuals, rather than an autistic deficit. This paradigm highlights a need for inclusive spaces that foster mutual understanding, yet this remains challenging. Choral singing offers a promising medium to facilitate cross-neurotype dynamics, as it is thought to have evolved as a biological mechanism to foster social bonding. Accordingly, this qualitative study explored how 12 general population choristers experienced a 6-month neurodiverse choir shared with 8 autistic adolescents and 3 autism specialists. We used a two-stage qualitative design, first capturing individual experience through an open-ended online questionnaire, and subsequently deepening our analysis through a discussion with a community stakeholder panel. The findings revealed an intrinsically demanding experience, especially emotionally and cognitively, counterbalanced by important benefits, as it was also described as joyful and powerful, encouraging personal growth among the choristers and a shift in their perceptions of autism. These findings support the neurodiversity paradigm and suggest that choral singing may be a powerful double empathy solution, facilitating intergroup contact to reduce prejudice and thereby enhance the participation of autistic voices.

articles_hidden.title: A transdiagnostic computational account linking mental fatigue and cognitive effort
articles_hidden.authors: Yang Yang; Akina Umemoto; Senne Braem; Clay B. Holroyd
articles_hidden.abstract: Motivational impairments are common to many psychiatric conditions, yet associations between psychiatric symptoms and willingness to exert cognitive effort have been inconsistent. Previous studies have mostly analyzed cognitive effort at the moment when people choose to engage in an effortful task, overlooking fatigue before the choice and how the task is executed after the choice. Here we examined this process during a 75-min online experiment involving 529 adults with psychiatric profiles spanning a broad range of symptoms. Participants repeatedly chose between resting and performing a demanding working-memory task, carried out the selected activity, and reported their fatigue. We derived continuous transdiagnostic symptom dimensions and modeled fatigue, effort selection, and task performance across time. Across participants, fatigue accumulated over time, and higher pre-choice fatigue predicted effort avoidance despite high overall task accuracy. Higher anxious-depression scores were associated with greater initial fatigue, faster fatigue accumulation, and a progressively steeper decline in high-effort choices. By contrast, higher compulsivity/intrusive thought scores were associated with more frequent high-effort choices but lower accuracy after effort was selected. Motivational dysfunction therefore did not reduce to a general reluctance to exert effort, but emerged through distinct alterations in fatigue accumulation, effort selection, and task execution. A dynamic, process-based account that separates these stages may help reconcile inconsistent findings in effort-based mental health research.

articles_hidden.title: Same Effect, Different Magnitude: How the Choice of Pre- or Post-Treatment Standard Deviation Shapes Standardized Effect Sizes in Psychological Clinical Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Anika Buchholz; Anna Suling; Antonia Zapf; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles_hidden.abstract: Standardized mean differences (SMDs) are used to express treatment effects on a common metric, yet there is no consensus on whether mean differences should be standardized using the outcome standard deviation (SD) at baseline or follow-up. This study examined whether this choice systematically affects effect-size magnitude in a reproducible sample of 100 randomized psychological clinical trials. For each trial, SMDs were calculated using either the pooled baseline SD (SMDpre) or the pooled follow-up SD (SMDpost). The unweighted paired mean difference showed that |SMDpre| was, 0.11 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, 95% CI [0.07, 0.14]. In a multilevel meta-regression |SMDpre| was 0.082 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, equalling a 13% increase, 95% CI [0.042, 0.123]. Bland–Altman analysis indicated substantial between-study variation, 95% limits of agreement [−0.25, 0.46]. Secondary analyses including 2,228 effect sizes across all follow-ups mirrored this pattern, indicating a 7% increase of SMD magnitude associated to |SMDpre|, 95% CI [0.021, 0.044]. Moderator analyses suggested that discrepancies were larger in studies applying symptom-threshold eligibility criteria, and in secondary analyses, using the same measure both to determine eligibility and to assess the outcome and with longer follow-up. Importantly, 70% of included studies did not report how SMDs were operationalized. These findings demonstrate that the choice of standardizing SD systematically affects estimated treatment-effect magnitudes and that the discrepancy can become more pronounced under specific design conditions. Researchers should therefore carefully consider the choice of standardizer and explicitly report the time point and method used to derive the SD.

articles_hidden.title: Bridging Psychophysics and Psychometrics to Address Dyslexia Screening Floor Effects: An Adaptive-Timing Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Wanjing Anya Ma; Benjamin Domingue; Guilherme Lichand; Karine Votikoske Roncete; Lucas Iantorno Klotz; Carrie Townley-Flores; Adam Richie-Halford; Jason D. Yeatman
articles_hidden.abstract: As children learn to read, two skills develop in parallel: the complexity of words they can decode and the speed of word recognition. Reading assessments capture these processes with timed and untimed tasks, yet it remains unclear whether word processing speed and word difficulty are separable dimensions of reading ability or two manifestations of the same skill. The distinction has practical stakes: beginning readers decode too few words to be measured precisely, producing floor effects that limit early dyslexia screening. Here, we independently manipulated word difficulty and presentation time in a lexical decision task to test whether they constitute distinct axes of reading development. Through a research--practice partnership, we collected large-scale developmental data from 3,147 students spanning Grades 1--12 in the United States (English) and Brazil (Portuguese). Items presented with infinite presentation time were systematically less difficult but required longer response times than items under fast conditions, for students across development in both language contexts. Importantly, word processing speed and word difficulty were characterized by a unidimensional framework, indicating that presentation time extends a single difficulty continuum rather than measuring a second construct. We leveraged this result to design and validate a multistage adaptive-timing screener for dyslexia (N = 14,393 calibration; N = 841 validation). A K--2 validation study showed that adaptive timing reduced floor effects and improved screening precision and efficiency for beginning readers. By integrating the experimental precision of psychophysics with scalable psychometric frameworks, this work shows how basic science can be translated into universal school-based dyslexia screening.

articles_hidden.title: A Longitudinal Pilot Evaluation of a Single Session Digital Mental Health Intervention to Improve Satisfaction With Life Among Autistic Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Ty B. Aller; Francesca M Knudsen; Benjamin Covington; Heather Kelley; Michael Levin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background: Autistic adults experience higher rates of mental health concerns and additional barriers to accessing mental health care than adults without autism. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) are easily codesigned and contextualized to various groups, and provide a scalable option for improving mental health care access for autistic adults. While previous research has found DMHIs to be acceptable and effective among autistic adults, low adherence and engagement rates present a consistent barrier to the successful implementation. 
Methods: Our team codesigned a single session DMHI based in acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) for autistic adults. We tested the program in an open trial of N = 79 autistic adults that assessed outcomes at baseline, 2-week, and 6-week follow-up. 
Results: We found that the single session DMHI was feasible to deliver and acceptable among autistic adults. Improvements in subjective well-being, quality of life, psychological distress, and psychological flexibility were observed from baseline to the 2-week follow-up and were maintained at 6-week follow-up. 
Conclusions: Results provide support that single-session DMHIs may be a useful mechanism for disseminating evidence-based mental health supports to autistic adults. Results lay the foundation for more robust research on the efficacy of this ACT-based single session DMHI using randomized controlled trials.

articles_hidden.title: Life Control: A Psychological Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Leonardo Bonneti
articles_hidden.abstract: Life Control is the capacity to remain an active and effective director of one’s life under changing and constrained conditions. Existing psychological theories explain important elements of agency, motivation, self-regulation, resilience, and flexibility, but do not integrate the broader patterns through which people direct different parts of their lives. This article proposes Life Control as a framework of ten dimensions organised across four domains: Self, Growth, Others, and Life Organisation. The dimensions describe distinct but interacting tendencies involving emotional regulation, self-understanding, effort, responses to adversity, practical responsibility, relationships, and the allocation of personal and material resources. The theory also proposes four connecting claims. Self-direction is recursive because present actions shape both later capacities and future conditions. Rationality keeps action responsive to evidence, while a spark of delusion permits action before success is assured. Psychologically formative activities develop or maintain capacities through participation, and the Non-Outsourcing Principle predicts that assistance supports Life Control when it preserves such participation but may weaken it when it repeatedly replaces it. The framework generates testable predictions concerning the dimensions, their combinations, development over time, and the consequences of different forms of assistance.

articles_hidden.title: Factor Structure and Symptom Profiles of the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS): A Meta-Analytic Mean and Covariance Structure Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Johanna Einsiedler; Timo Gnambs
articles_hidden.abstract: The Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) is one of the most widely used clinician-rated instruments for assessing depressive symptom severity, particularly in pharmacological intervention studies. Despite its widespread use, evidence on the dimensional structure of the MADRS remains inconsistent. In this Registered Report, we propose a meta-analytic mean and covariance structure analysis of the MADRS to examine (a) which latent structure best represents MADRS responses and how reliably its factors are measured, (b) whether items or symptom dimensions function differently across clinical (diagnostic group, pharmacological treatment, assessment time point within treatment) and measurement-related (language version) moderators, and (c) whether diagnostic groups, pharmacological treatment regimens, and treatment stages are associated with distinct latent symptom profiles.

articles_hidden.title: Eye-gaze dynamics reveal the adaptive nature of real-time noisy-channel inference in speech comprehension
articles_hidden.authors: Rachel Anna Ryskin
articles_hidden.abstract: To understand spoken language, listeners must extract meaning from acoustic input that is variable and noisy. The noisy-channel framework posits that listeners overcome this uncertainty by rationally inferring the speaker's intent, combining prior expectations with a model of how the message may have been corrupted during transmission. However, the exact nature of this noise model and its sensitivity to context (e.g., speaker or acoustic environment) remain unknown. Here, I use eye-tracking to measure human speech processing as it unfolds on the millisecond timescale, and I use the representational geometry of a self-supervised speech model (HuBERT) to estimate the noise model. I show that spoken word comprehension is well captured as real-time Bayesian belief updating. Further, listeners flexibly tune their expectation of noise to the specific acoustic environment. These results extend the noisy-channel framework to the moment-by-moment comprehension of speech. More broadly, these findings demonstrate that the human language system continuously adapts its internal model to the statistical structure of the communicative environment. By linking noisy-channel inference with real-time perceptual dynamics, this work highlights the remarkable flexibility of human cognition in navigating uncertainty and opens the door to investigating internal representations in human and artificial speech recognition systems through their fine-grained temporal dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: What makes up the moral domain? Theory must answer to data
articles_hidden.authors: Meltem Yucel; Amrisha Vaish
articles_hidden.abstract: Jambon et al. (in press) seek to evaluate Yucel et al.’s (2022) proposal that fairness may be psychologically distinct from other, prototypical moral norms, and, in line with Social Domain Theory (SDT), to reassert fairness’ place within the moral domain. Here, we show that Jambon et al.’s own data and arguments, alongside a reanalysis of Yucel et al.’s (2022) data, undermine rather than support Jambon et al.’s claims. Across studies, fairness reliably differs from harm on the very measures (criterion judgments, justifications) the authors treat as diagnostic for establishing moral status. This pattern goes unaddressed by Jambon et al. in part because of inconsistent evidentiary standards as well as circular reasoning that assumes the very conclusion it seeks to demonstrate. These findings raise a more fundamental question: As currently conceived under SDT, to what extent does the “moral domain” constitute a psychologically coherent category?

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual Cues Can Influence Curiosity, Metamemory, and Memory Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Ashley Chen; Matthew Rhodes; Alan Castel
articles_hidden.abstract: Important information is often presented in large fonts, a tactic used to direct individuals’ attention and emphasize relevance. In a series of experiments, we tested whether font size, a perceptual cue that may communicate relative importance, may influence one’s curiosity, judgments of learning (JOLs), and recall. Participants were presented with lists of word pairs consisting of rare English words and their more commonly known synonyms. After being shown the rare word in small (12-point) or large (48-point) font, they rated how curious they were to learn its synonym, studied the synonym, and judged how likely they were to remember it at a later time before completing an immediate cued-recall test. We found that individuals exhibited greater curiosity towards large versus small items (Experiments 1a and 1b), but JOLs were unaffected by font size (Experiments 1a and 1c), perhaps due to a reliance on other perceptual cues (e.g., word structure, mental imagery) during encoding (Experiment 1c) or opportunities for pretesting attenuating the font-size JOL effect (Experiment 1d). Moreover, although large items were rated as more important to learn (Experiment 2), the positive relationship between font size and recall (Experiments 1 and 2) was only mediated by curiosity and not perceived importance (Experiment 2). Overall, our findings provide insight into how perceptual cues may influence how individuals select, process, and remember information, contributing to our understanding of how curiosity and memory are shaped by perceptual processes.

articles_hidden.title: Towards a Cognitive Science of Practical Wisdom for Ill-Defined Decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Abhishek Dedhe; Samuel Gregory Blane Johnson; Igor Grossmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Many challenges we face as individuals and collectives are ill-defined: What are the probabilities for different courses of action? How to compare distinct outcomes? Under such radical uncertainty, conventional optimization solutions fail, prompting calls for wisdom. Yet, the science of wisdom remains fragmented across disciplines. To fill this void, we reconstruct practical wisdom through the lens of cognitive science, asking what wisdom is for, how it works, and how it develops and evolves. Guided by criteria that make a cognitive science concept empirically tractable, formally precise, and continuous with broader theories of mind, we develop a two-level functional cognitive architecture of practical wisdom, in which evoked, higher-order metacognitive processes regulate a culturally-transmitted repertoire of object-level decision strategies. We outline formal elements of this architecture and examine its implications across persons, groups, societies, and natural and artificial intelligences. Finally, we derive testable predictions and close by asking what such a science offers back to the disciplines it draws on.

articles_hidden.title: The 2024 U.S. Election, Sexual and Gender Minority Adults’ Moving Plans, and Mental Health Symptoms: A Mixed-Methods Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Briana Shiri Last; Nguyen Tran; Dane Rivas-Koehl; Devin Hursey; Juno Obedin-Maliver; Mitchell Lunn; Annesa Flentje
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Since the 2024 U.S. Presidential election, the rights of sexual and gender minority (SGM) people have been at risk. The purpose of this mixed-methods study was to describe SGM people’s thoughts, plans, and decisions to move following the election and to examine whether these thoughts, plans, and decisions differed by participants’ sociodemographic characteristics and mental health symptoms. 
Methods: Participants completed an online survey between November 5, 2024 and September 20, 2025 for The PRIDE Study, a national, prospective, community-engaged cohort study of SGM adults. Participants responded to closed-ended questions about their: thoughts, plans, and decisions to move; sociodemographic characteristics; and mental health (anxiety, depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder) symptoms. Participants responded to open-ended questions about their moving destinations and moving reasons. 
Results: The sample included 3,301 participants (48.1% identified as transgender or nonbinary [TNB]). Most participants (85%) thought about, planned to, or decided to move to another state or country. Moving considerations differed by participants’ sociodemographics (e.g., participants with moving thoughts, plans, and decisions were more likely to be TNB than cisgender, ps<.05) and mental health symptoms (e.g., participants with moving thoughts, plans, and decisions had more symptoms than those with no moving thoughts, ps<.05). Participants’ reasons for moving included the increasingly hostile and anti-SGM sociopolitical conditions in their states and the country. 
Conclusions and Policy Implications: Following the 2024 election, many SGM U.S. adults made plans to or decided to move due to the changing policy environment. Psychological distress from anti-SGM policies may be driving individuals to move.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the eight-week convention: A rapid review of assigned program architecture and temporal change in mindfulness-based programs
articles_hidden.authors: Barry Tse
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Mindfulness-based programs (MBPs) are commonly organized around eight weeks, yet direct experimental evidence on the consequences of varying this architecture is sparse. In a contextual inventory of 39 established programs, 11 of the 15 with an unqualified fixed-week structure used eight weeks.

Methods: This rapid review examined direct evidence on assigned program length, session intensity, pacing, outcome and mechanism trajectories, and postprogram maintenance. APA PsycINFO was searched through Ovid from inception to September 3, 2026. The review used one database and one reviewer, and no protocol was prospectively registered. All 301 records were screened and 81 full texts were assessed. Risk of bias was appraised with tools matched to study design, and certainty was assessed for eight synthesis claims using an adapted Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach.

Results: Fifty-two reports representing 47 studies were included. Five reports directly compared assigned architectures that varied different dimensions; the remainder mainly described trajectories under one assigned program. Randomized length comparisons did not demonstrate reliable between-length differences, but none was designed to establish equivalence. In the largest controlled trajectory, Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction first showed statistically detected separation from usual care at session 2 for sleep, 4 for physical function, 6 for pain intensity, 7 for pain interference, and 8 for depression; these were power-dependent statistical crossing points, not minimum effective durations. The session of first detected separation also differed across mechanisms, mechanism-outcome coupling changed across sessions, and postprogram maintenance varied by outcome. No included estimand was judged at low overall risk of bias, and of the eight synthesis claims, two were of low certainty and six of very low certainty.

Discussion: The literature supports neither universal abbreviation nor preservation of eight weeks as an empirically optimized standard. The main conceptual advance is to separate evidence about change during a program from evidence about the consequences of changing the program: calendar length, contact, spacing, outcome timing, mechanism timing, individual heterogeneity, and durability are distinct design questions. Well-powered randomized architecture comparisons with aligned repeated measurement and prespecified noninferiority or optimization criteria are needed.

articles_hidden.title: Through the PRISM: Reinterpreting Psychedelic Cognition as Motivational Reallocation
articles_hidden.authors: Orchid2022*
articles_hidden.abstract:
Classic psychedelics such as psilocybin and LSD are known to acutely disrupt executive function, producing impairments in response inhibition, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. Paradoxically, these compounds often lead to lasting improvements in cognitive flexibility, insight, and goal-directed behavior in the days and weeks following administration. This apparent contradiction has traditionally been interpreted as a biphasic modulation of control capacity—initial impairment followed by compensatory enhancement.
An alternative account is proposed in the PRISM model (Psychedelic Recalibration of Internal Salience and Mental Effort Costs), which reframes cognitive outcomes not as shifts in capacity, but as changes in motivation for cognitive control. According to this framework, psychedelics may reduce the perceived cost of cognitive effort during acute states by disrupting habitual internally directed processes, such as Default Mode Network activity. Post-acutely, increased salience of emotionally or personally meaningful goals may enhance the willingness to engage in effortful, goal-directed cognition.
Rather than a global increase in executive ability, observed changes in performance may reflect a dynamic reallocation of motivational resources, explaining both acute dissociations and post-acute improvements in specific cognitive domains. This model integrates recent behavioral, neuroimaging, and pharmacological findings to offer testable predictions for future research. New experimental paradigms are outlined for dissociating motivational engagement from cognitive capacity, providing a mechanistic bridge between subjective psychedelic experiences and enduring adaptive outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Distinct Patterns of Reward-Related Neural Activation and Dopamine Neurophysiology in Adolescent Depression with and without Mixed Manic Features
articles_hidden.authors: Stefanie Fraga Gonçalves; Amar Ojha; Morgan Lindenmuth; Helmet Talib Karim; Teague R Henry; Rasim Diler; Cecile D. Ladouceur
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents with depression are at elevated risk for maladaptive risk behaviors, underscoring the importance of understanding neurobiological alterations in reward function in this population. However, reward function alterations associated with depression, particularly in the presence of co-occurring manic symptoms (i.e., mixed manic features), remain poorly understood. In this study, 154 12–18-year-olds (ndepression without mixed manic features = 65; ndepression with mixed manic features = 56; nhealthy controls = 33) and their primary caregiver completed questionnaires, clinical interviews, and fMRI during the monetary incentive delay task. Neural response during monetary reward anticipation, as well as tissue iron concentrations, important for dopamine neurophysiology, were derived from the striatum and used to predict group membership and severity of mixed manic features. Exploratory whole brain functional activation analyses were also conducted. Lower caudate activation (in the outlier-excluded analysis) was associated with membership in the depression with mixed manic features group. Across both depression groups, higher caudate and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) activation was associated with greater mixed manic feature severity. In addition, lower tissue iron concentration in the putamen and higher tissue iron concentration in the caudate were each associated with membership in the depression without mixed features group. These findings suggest that reward-related neural activation differentiates mixed manic features, whereas alterations in tissue iron characterize adolescent depression more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: When to Use Mixed Models and When RM-ANOVA - An Argument for Statistical Parsimony
articles_hidden.authors: Henrik Singmann
articles_hidden.abstract: When should researchers use linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) versus repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA) for analysing repeated-measures data? I first outline the conceptual and statistical differences between the two approaches: RM-ANOVA operates on aggregated difference scores, whereas LMMs model trial-level data using fixed and random effects to account for dependencies among observations. I then describe the key limitations of RM-ANOVA: its inability to handle missing data, partially within-participants factors, continuous within-participants covariates, and complex dependency structures such as crossed random effects designs. I also discuss the conceptual and computational challenges associated with LMMs, such as model specification and convergence issues. Using two simulation studies, I then demonstrate that when both methods are appropriate, RM-ANOVA -- especially with Greenhouse-Geisser correction -- generally provides better control of Type I error rates and statistical power equal to or greater than that of LMMs. Consequently, I recommend using RM-ANOVA in designs where RM-ANOVA is appropriate. LMMs should be reserved for cases that require the additional flexibility, such as complex designs, missing data, or advanced modelling goals.

articles_hidden.title: Infants trade off reward for information: longitudinal evidence for curiosity-driven information-seeking in the second year of life
articles_hidden.authors: Cécile Gabrielle Gal; Dimitris Askitis; Katarina Begus
articles_hidden.abstract: Curiosity-driven information seeking is a crucial behaviour thought to drive our progress as a species. Valuing information as rewarding has been established as a driver of curiosity in human adults and non-human primates, characterised by a stringent set of three criteria formalized by work in primates, but direct evidence in human infants remains absent. We followed N=125 infants longitudinally over three visits (12, 18, 24 months) and used an infant-controlled eye-tracking paradigm to test whether valuing information as rewarding could also underlie curiosity in infancy. In each trial, infants could reveal two hidden characters by looking at their hiding locations, yielding either high or low information-gain. Revealing the first character was coupled with a rewarding animation, while revealing the second character required to disengage and thereby trade-off the ongoing animation for information. We found evidence in support of all three curiosity criteria: throughout their second year of life, infants were willing to forego extrinsic rewards to obtain information , even when the information was strategically useless, and – from 18 months – in a way that scaled with information gain. Infants did not meet the third criterion at the youngest age, which we attribute to age-related cognitive-load effects. Individual differences in infants' sensitivity to information gain showed modest stability across the visits. Overall, this study establishes reward-based information-seeking as a conserved mechanism present from early infancy, with early individual differences that may carry lasting consequences for learning and cognitive development.

articles_hidden.title: iTemplate2: An Open-Source Python Toolbox for Automatic Eye-Movement Analysis of Dynamic Facial Stimuli
articles_hidden.authors: Naiqi G Xiao; Rafael Román-Caballero; Wei Fang; Sara Ripley; Danyang Han; Laurel Trainor
articles_hidden.abstract: Template-based gaze-to-face registration enables standardized analysis of eye movements by mapping gaze coordinates onto a canonical facial template, reducing variability introduced by manual area-of-interest (AOI) definition across heterogeneous stimuli. However, existing implementations are largely restricted to static images, rely on semi-manual landmark annotation, and depend on proprietary software, limiting scalability and reproducibility. These constraints become increasingly problematic as research shifts toward dynamic stimuli, wearable eye-tracking, and open-source workflows. We present iTemplate2, a fully open-source Python-based redesign of the original system. The framework introduces four key advances: (1) support for dynamic stimuli via frame-wise coordinate transformation, including a normalization module for wearable and scene-based eye-tracking data; (2) integration of MediaPipe’s Face Landmarker for automated detection of 478 facial landmarks per frame, with multi-face tracking and identity persistence mechanisms that reduce manual annotation requirements; (3) a complete Python reimplementation using NumPy, pandas, OpenCV, PyQt6, and Apache Parquet, providing a cross-platform graphical interface without commercial dependencies; and (4) expanded visualization and analysis tools, including interactive heatmaps, snap-to-landmark AOI definition, and extraction of facial blendshape parameters for concurrent expression analysis. The system is applicable across diverse domains, including infant face scanning, cross-cultural gaze research, clinical screening, and naturalistic social interaction paradigms using wearable eye-tracking. It robustly processes complex multi-face video datasets that are difficult to analyze using conventional template-based methods. iTemplate2 modernizes the template-based registration framework for contemporary behavioral research, converting idiosyncratic visual data into a unified, reproducible analytical space. The software is freely available as an open-source tool at https://osf.io/54v9e/overview?view_only=5ac289558a3d4897a02336124ae409a1.

articles_hidden.title: Neural Racing Accumulator Model Estimation With Lightweight Monotonic Flows
articles_hidden.authors: Malte Lüken; Stefan T. Radev; Lourens Waldorp; Andrew Heathcote
articles_hidden.abstract: Race models describe speeded decision-making as a race between competing runners that accumulate evidence in favor of available choice options. Their parameters can be estimated through the model likelihood that combines the probability and cumulative density functions of each runner. However, estimating parameters of complex race models whose runners have intractable densities with (hierarchical) Bayesian inference has been challenging: Numerical density approximations tend to be slow and amortized neural posterior estimation methods require complex network architectures that can be expensive to train and, in classical settings, tie the trained estimator to a specific prior distribution and generative model. We propose a flexible neural estimation method that decouples training from the choice of prior distribution or model parameterization. We train a small neural network together with a monotonic neural spline flow to simultaneously learn the runners' conditional probability density and cumulative density functions. We then combine both functions to efficiently estimate race model likelihoods that can be used in combination with modern samplers. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both tractable and intractable versions of the popular racing diffusion model. Based on our results, we argue that, when flexibility in choosing prior distributions or model parameterizations is needed, learning the model likelihood with lightweight neural density estimators is advantageous.

articles_hidden.title: Co-STARS: A Participatory Action Research Approach to Co-Producing Culturally Responsive Mental Health Literacy Training with Young Black People
articles_hidden.authors: Milan Antonovic; Megan A. Pope; Gerald Jordan; Balachandran Kumarendran; Luke Brown; Nadia; Ayan Mahamud; Lowri Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Young Black people in the UK face disproportionate mental health inequalities driven by stigma, racism, and structural exclusion. Although mental health literacy can promote early recognition and help-seeking, most interventions do not reflect Black communities’ lived realities. This study used Participatory Action Research (PAR) to co-produce a peer-led community mental health literacy training package with young Black people, alongside an e-learning resource to support culturally responsive practice among mental health and allied professionals.

Method: Eight young Black participants (M age = 24.5; five female) with lived experience of mental ill health from diverse cultural, religious, and gender backgrounds took part in four peer-led workshops and three refinement sessions. Guided by an anti-oppressive framework, participants identified priorities, developed content, and shaped the training. Data were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

Results: Four interconnected themes emerged: (1) Navigating Cultural Silences and Systemic Exclusions (stigma, cultural taboos, intergenerational trauma, and racialised experiences in education and healthcare); (2) Fighting to Be Heard (dismissal, misrecognition, and delayed care); (3) Reimagining Care Through Cultural Proximity and Community Anchoring (relational, culturally grounded, community-based models); and (4) Embedding Accountability and Cultural Reflexivity in Training (youth-led recommendations for train-the-trainer programmes emphasising structural competency, experiential learning, and supervision).

Conclusions: Co-production elevated young Black people’s expertise and produced a culturally responsive training package grounded in lived experience and structural realities. The findings highlight the need for preventative, relational, and equity-focused mental health approaches and support community-led, culturally grounded interventions to reduce disparities among Black and racialised youth.

articles_hidden.title: Children and adults infer traits from observed immoral behavior, but children preferentially use emotional expressions to predict future moral violations
articles_hidden.authors: Sophia Thierry; Rebekah Gelpi; Denise Arefhaghi; Jessica A. Sommerville
articles_hidden.abstract: Learning which characteristics of another person are reliable and relevant for predicting how that person is likely to behave in the future is fundamental to social cognition. This is particularly true of moral behavior given the importance of anticipating potential harm. Across three experiments (data collected between December 2020 and May 2022), we investigated how six- to eight-year-old children (total N = 94; 50 girls; predominantly Canadian) and adults (N = 48; American) weighed a character’s prior behavior and emotional expressions to infer whether that character would commit a future moral violation. Both children and adults used a character’s prior behavior and their emotional expressions to inform their predictions; however, children relied on emotional expressions to a significantly greater degree than adults. Further, children and adults attributed a negative trait (meanness) and state (anger) to characters who committed a prior moral violation. However, whereas trait attributions mediated adults’ predictions of future violations, neither trait nor state attributions mediated children’s predictions. These findings reveal developmental differences in both the cues used to predict others’ moral behavior, and in the representations underlying these predictions.

articles_hidden.title: Weak Distributive Inference in Language Acquisition
articles_hidden.authors: David Barner; Dimitrios Skordos; Elena Pagliarini; Alan Clinton Bale
articles_hidden.abstract: We find that children compute distributive inferences, and thus that they are capable pragmatic reasoners when alternatives can be derived without lexical substitution. This provides further evidence that they are not limited by other factors like working memory or pragmatic tolerance. In addition, we find evidence that children consistently computed weak distributive inferences. In the spirit of Fox’s (2007) grammatical account, such inferences require double application of Exh, one scoping above the universal quantifier and another below. Thus, not only do children compute implicatures, but they appear to adopt the more complex parse—embedding one operator inside another—rather than relying on the simpler, global option that generates a strong distributive inference.

articles_hidden.title: The validation of cognitive ability constructs: A theoretically motivated user’s guide
articles_hidden.authors: Kristof Kovacs; John Protzko; Andrew R. A. Conway
articles_hidden.abstract: How do we validate tests of cognitive abilities? We argue that the validation process depends fundamentally on the nature of the construct under investigation. There are two the different traditions in the study of validity: one emphasizes a realist approach, asserting that variations in an underlying attribute must causally produce variation in measurement outcomes, while the other prioritizes the utility and predictive value of test scores. We distinguish between reflective constructs, which represent real entities with causal properties, and formative constructs, which serve as useful statistical summaries. We propose that seemingly conflicting conceptions of validity are not mutually exclusive but rather represent appropriate approaches for different types of constructs; reflective constructs warrant a causal-realist interpretation of validity, while a predictive-utilitarian approach is sufficient for the validation of formative constructs. Specifically, for reflective constructs, a reductionist approach is appropriate, and researchers should aim to ground their validation efforts in an understanding of the withinperson cognitive processes that underlie individual differences. Conversely, formative constructs are best validated through their predictive utility. By providing a typology of constructs and a guide for validation, this paper aims to help researchers apply the appropriate criteria for cognitive ability constructs.

articles_hidden.title: Mental health consequences of extremely vivid mental imagery: A qualitative investigation of managing anxiety with hyperphantasia
articles_hidden.authors: Nicole McGowan; Reshanne R Reeder
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental imagery is the ability to mentally simulate sensory experience in the absence of an external stimulus, with individual vividness ranging from extremely weak or absent (aphantasia) to superlative and hyper-realistic (hyperphantasia): these ends of the spectrum are called “imagery extremes”.  Though most imagery extremes research is focused on aphantasia, given that mental imagery is thought to play a critical role in the presentation of mental health disorders, as well as being central to many therapeutic interventions, this study aimed to explore the lived mental health experiences of hyperphantasics with anxiety. Eight hyperphantasics were recruited from a database for those interested in taking part in mental imagery research. All participants had a diagnosed anxiety disorder, and experience of accessing mental health services within the UK. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis was used to analyse their semi-structured interviews. Three Group Experiential Themes were identified for all participants: 1) Blurred Boundaries with Reality, 2) Limitless Imagination, and 3) Pathways to Managing Anxiety. The multisensory and emotional intensity of hyperphantasic imagery experiences related to anxiety created a realness of experience which was difficult for participants to describe and manage. Limitless imagination could be perceived as a threat when participants were not in control of their imagery; however, it was a source of great joy and calmness when participants were in control. Participants managed their anxiety by disconnecting from their mental imagery and engaging in the world around them, or by finding ways to use their abilities to support themselves. Research and clinical implications are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Take it personally: Promoting a personalised neuroscience informed approach to cognitive rehabilitation following psychopathology.
articles_hidden.authors: Marie-José van Tol; Ernst H. W. Koster; Matthias Pillny; Ivan Grahek; Lisette van Der Meer
articles_hidden.abstract:
People suffering from schizophrenia, depression and other severe mental illnesses often suffer from cognitive problems. In most people, these problems persists after the major symptomatic episode is over, and in some cases cognitive problems also preceded an episode. Unfortunately, even after symptomatic remission, full recovery of cognitive functions often does not occur, thereby severely and enduringly impeding daily life functioning. Although it’s recognized in the field of psychiatry and psychology that these cognitive problems persist, there is little mechanistic understanding of how these problems arose and persist. We believe that this lack of a mechanistic understanding severely hampers mitigation of these residual problems and limits the ability for stable remission and potential for rebuilding a fulfilling live. 
In this perspective paper, we introduce a model inspired by behavioural economics that focuses on the decision making process underpinning cognitive control allocation. With this model we conceptualize the situational inability to engage in enduring and/or demanding cognitive daily life tasks, as a consequence of aberrant/maladaptive decision-making. We integrate insights from cognitive psychology, cognitive neuroscience, clinical psychology with practices of cognitive remediation in the field of severe mental illness. With this multidisciplinary approach, we offer hypotheses on how widely available therapies could be used to boost cognitive functioning following mental illness.

articles_hidden.title: A Step-by-Step Tutorial on the Stochastic Cusp Model in R
articles_hidden.authors: Renaud Mabire-Yon; Raoul P P P Grasman; Han L. J. van der Maas
articles_hidden.abstract: People facing similar circumstances may function very differently. The stochastic cusp model offers one possible explanation: the same conditions may support two stable levels of functioning. This tutorial shows how to understand, fit, and interpret the model in R, assuming familiarity with regression and basic R. Simple illustrations explain how stable states emerge and how changing conditions can alter them. A synthetic example links personal resources and acute stress to adaptive functioning. Readers learn to specify the model, check the fit, interpret coefficients and uncertainty, and examine its predictions. At average resources, the fitted distribution changes from one peak at low stress to two separated peaks at higher stress. The tutorial also explains which further observations would help distinguish a cusp hypothesis from competing explanations. Publicly available data, code, and archived output allow readers to reproduce the example.

articles_hidden.title: Co-Production and Development of ‘Resilience Rucksacks’: A Whole-School Preventative Approach to Support Young People’s Resilience
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Tupitsa; Clea Desebrock; Agnes Tait; Megan Devereux; Nevena Harris; Oluwatoyosi Alake; Asnea Tariq; Stella Chan
articles_hidden.abstract: The rising prevalence of mental health difficulties in young people, along with increased demands on mental health services, highlights an urgent need for developing effective preventative interventions. Whole-school approaches offer timely and accessible support; however, existing interventions show mixed efficacy, with many excluding the involvement of key stakeholders, especially young people with lived experience. This paper reports the development of a co-produced, whole-school intervention, ‘Resilience Rucksacks’, which aimed to equip young people with knowledge and practical skills to promote general resilience during a pivotal transition period from primary to secondary school. Project development comprised three phases: (i) a literature review to identify key factors that support youth mental health and resilience, (ii) stakeholder consultation via 7 steering group meetings with young people, school staff, and parents (n = 6-20 representatives per session) and a follow-up online survey (n = 197), and (iii) 20 co-production workshops with young people (n = 2-9 attendees per workshop) to develop evidence-based well-being tools. This process identified four biopsychosocial factors (sleep, physical activity, self-compassion, and social relationships) to be focused on due to their strong research evidence base and resonance with everyday experiences. The subsequent co-production workshops produced 7 main well-being tools designed to increase young people’s knowledge, skills, and confidence around mental health. This study critically highlights the value of co-production with young people to identify intervention targets and to design effective and accessible tools that support resilience and well-being development in their own environment.

articles_hidden.title: The effect of alcohol-specific episodic memories and alcohol cue exposure on value-based decision-making and ad libitum alcohol consumption
articles_hidden.authors: Amber Copeland; Tom Stafford; Cameron Crook; Michelle Pun; Aaron Bornstein; Lee Hogarth; James Murphy; Hanna Pickard; Frank Ryan; Justin Charles Strickland
articles_hidden.abstract: Background and Aims: Alcohol choice is governed by its subjective value, which can be experimentally modified. However, less is known about the moment-to-moment dynamics through which experimental manipulations of value influence observable choice behaviour. We tested whether an experimental manipulation intended to elevate alcohol value would alter computational parameters of value-based decision-making (VBDM) and alcohol choice, and whether these outcomes would mediate ad libitum alcohol consumption. Design: Pre-registered, randomised between-subjects experiment comparing two personalised experimental conditions: alcohol value (exposure to alcohol memories and multisensory alcohol cues) vs. control (exposure to non-alcohol memories and multisensory soft-drink cues), conducted over two separate sessions with baseline measures included as covariates. Setting: University laboratory in the United Kingdom (UK). Participants: 129 adults (63% male; mean age = 44 years; mean Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test [AUDIT] score = 16) who regularly consume alcohol (mean Estimated Weekly Alcohol Consumption [EWAC] = 42 UK units/week), randomised to alcohol value (n = 65) or control (n = 64) conditions. Measurements: At baseline and post-exposure, participants completed self-reported measures of alcohol craving and a value-based decision-making (VBDM) task where they chose between pairs of previously rated alcohol-related and non-alcohol images. A drift-diffusion model was fitted to behavioural data to estimate evidence accumulation rates (value sensitivity) and response thresholds (response caution). Participants also completed a concurrent choice task (alcohol vs. non-alcohol) that measured percentage alcohol relative to non-alcohol reward (enlargement; index of relative alcohol value), and a taste test to measure alcohol consumption. Findings: Some indices of subjective craving were responsive to the experimental manipulation, but there were no significant between-group differences at post-manipulation (ps ≥ .17). Baseline-adjusted analyses showed that response thresholds for non-alcohol decisions were higher in the alcohol value condition compared to control (p = .03, d = 0.40); however, Bayesian analysis quantified only anecdotal evidence for this effect (BF10 = 1.84). Other VBDM parameters, percentage alcohol choice, and alcohol consumed were unaffected by the manipulation (ps ≥ .19, BF10s ≤ 0.40). Furthermore, no value indices (computational or percentage choice) mediated the effect of the experimental manipulation on alcohol consumed. Conclusions: A personalised experimental manipulation intended to elevate alcohol value had modest effects on self-reported craving, but did not alter computational parameters of VBDM, relative alcohol choice, or ad-libitum alcohol consumption.

articles_hidden.title: Psychonautic Benchmarking: Towards Standardized Expertise Criteria in Non-Ordinary States Research
articles_hidden.authors: Juliana Estevez; David Lameiras; Giancarlo Allocca; Cody Gibbons; Leonardo Christov-Moore
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper addresses a methodological disparity between meditation research and research involving psychoactive substances. Studies of meditation routinely apply established criteria to distinguish expert practitioners from novices, while research with psychoactive substances screens for safety rather than classifying expertise. We analyze current benchmarking practice in meditation research, examine the limitations of participant selection in psychoactive substance research, and propose a multidimensional framework for psychonaut benchmarking that integrates quantitative exposure metrics, functional capacity assessment, phenomenological sophistication, typological profiling, and standardized competency evaluation. Drawing on parallels between the two domains, and incorporating a new competency instrument, the General Psychonautic Competence Assessment (GPCA), together with a proposed typological profiling component, the Psychonaut Profile Identification Assessment (PPIA), we aim to improve participant classification in research on non-ordinary states of consciousness. Both instruments are presented as proposals for collaborative development. Neither has completed psychometric validation, and the paper specifies the validation program each requires.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting dropout from psychotherapy with routine measurement-based care data: Which patients benefit from more complex prediction models?
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Athan McAleavey; Hans Jacob Westbye; Christian Moltu
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Treatment discontinuation in mental health care represents a significant individual and systemic challenge, with considerable associated costs. Machine learning (ML) may be able to accurately predict risk of dropout, which could be useful in psychotherapy. Methods. Data on 26,877 individual patients were extracted from the electronic encounter records and self-report databases of mental healthcare settings in Norway. We predicted risk of early treatment termination after attending one psychotherapy session, using data that would be available at (or shortly after) the first treatment session. We compared eXtreme Gradient Boosted decision trees (XGBoost) to penalized regression and standard logistic regression models. Results. Dropout prevalence was estimated at 19.7% of the sample. Of the tested models, XGBoost achieved very slightly better accuracy than the other models in AUC ROC (0.620 vs. 0.611-0.613 for the regression-based models). Exploratory analyses indicated that the small average increase in predictive accuracy was primarily due to better performance at the high end of the prediction scale. Discussion. While complex models only modestly improved overall prediction accuracy, exploratory analysis indicated that this small benefit may mask a strength of complex models for individuals with uncommon presentations and high or low risk for dropout. A stepped approach to model complexity may be appropriate in practice: many patients may only benefit from simple data collection and simple modeling strategies, while more detailed analysis could be useful when simple models identify unusual responses.

articles_hidden.title: Temporal Binding between Stimulus and Response
articles_hidden.authors: Takumi Tanaka; Kazuma Takada
