articles_hidden.abstract: Temporal binding—the perceived compression of time between successive events—has been studied primarily between voluntary actions and their sensory outcomes and is often interpreted as an implicit marker of the sense of agency. A broader alternative is that temporal binding reflects the reconstruction of subjective time in accordance with inferred causal structure. Motivated by this account, we asked whether a similar distortion also arises between an imperative stimulus and the response it elicits. Across three preregistered experiments, we found converging evidence for temporal binding between stimulus and response (TBSR). In Experiment 1, a Libet clock task revealed the hallmark bidirectional attraction pattern: relative to baseline judgments of each event in isolation, imperative tones were perceived later and stimulus-triggered responses earlier. Experiments 2a and 2b then assessed interval perception directly using psychophysical two-alternative forced-choice judgments. In Experiment 2a, stimulus–response intervals were judged shorter than physically matched stimulus–stimulus intervals. In Experiment 2b, the same compression emerged relative to a physically matched passive button press baseline, indicating that the effect cannot be reduced to overt sensory sequence or temporal contingency alone. Together, these findings show that temporal binding is not confined to action–outcome episodes but also arises in stimulus–response episodes. More broadly, the findings are consistent with accounts in which subjective time is shaped by inferred causal structure and pose a challenge to the view that temporal binding serves as a selective marker of the sense of agency.

articles_hidden.title: Reading and writing anxiety in Finnish school children aged 9-15: Associations with gender, grade level, and reading competence
articles_hidden.authors: Rosa Salmela; Santeri Holopainen; Tomi Rautaoja; Emilia Nordenswan; Katarina Alanko; Pekka Räsänen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: This study examined the level of reading and writing anxiety in a cross-sectional sample of Finnish school children and the moderating roles of gender, grade level, and reading competence. 

Method: We used a reading and writing anxiety questionnaire (RWAQ) that consists of three factors: workload-related reading and writing anxiety, evaluation-related reading and writing anxiety, and social reading and writing anxiety. Linear regression modeling was used to analyze how gender, grade level, and reading competence moderate different dimensions of reading and writing anxiety. Participants were 9,723 Finnish-speaking children in grades 3–9, including 4,832 girls and 4,891 boys.

Results: Finnish school-age children showed relatively low reading and writing anxiety overall, but it increased with age (lowest in grades 3–5, highest in grades 7–9). This was especially evident in girls’ social and evaluation-related anxiety, while boys reported higher workload-related anxiety across grades. Lower reading competence was linked to higher reading and writing anxiety, but this effect varied by gender. Math anxiety and general anxiety were controlled in the models, and both anxiety types predicted reading and writing anxiety strongly.

Conclusion: Together the results suggest that workload-related reading and writing anxiety, evaluation-related reading and writing anxiety, and social reading and writing anxiety are distinct dimensions of reading and writing anxiety, and that future research could benefit from accounting that grade level, gender, and reading competence may influence these dimensions differently.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Virtue: Courage's Associations with Aversive Intentions and Behaviors and Dark Triad Traits
articles_hidden.authors: Grzegorz Pajestka; Katarzyna Skałacka
articles_hidden.abstract: Individual differences associated with aversive behavior have been linked primarily to antagonistic personality traits. Less is known about whether characteristics typically regarded as adaptive also contribute. Courage is traditionally viewed as a virtue, yet theoretical accounts suggest it may also facilitate socially aversive behaviors. This study tested whether two operationalizations—psychological courage (PC) and courage as a character strength (VIA-C)—predict aversive intentions and behaviors beyond Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy). A community sample of 711 Polish adults completed measures of PC, VIA-C, the Short Dark Triad, and aversive intentions and behaviors. Variable-centered analyses (hierarchical regressions, two-part models) controlling for age, gender, and Dark Triad traits revealed domain-specific effects: both courage measures predicted higher aggressive intentions and greater frequency of aggressive behaviors; VIA-C additionally predicted aggressive and sex-/drug-related behaviors. Neither courage measure related to theft, reckless driving, or self-destructive behaviors, and PC showed a small protective association with self-destructive intentions. Latent profile analysis identified four classes defined primarily by Dark Triad levels rather than courage; no high-courage/low-antagonism profile emerged. Overall, findings challenge unqualified valorization of courage and underscore the need to pair courage-building with ethical frameworks, empathy training, and prosocial goal setting to reduce iatrogenic risk.

articles_hidden.title: Burnout- and Depression-Like Functional Collapse States — A Within-Person Biomarker Framework for Precision Psychiatry: State-Dependent Multisystem Regulation in High Processing Cost Phenotypes (HPCPh)
articles_hidden.authors: Simone Hauck; Luciana Terra de Oliveira
articles_hidden.abstract:
Burnout- and depression-like functional collapse is usually interpreted through isolated biological systems, such as hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal signalling or inflammation. This may miss state-dependent coordination across systems, particularly within individuals whose cognitive and/or sensory processing carries a high physiological cost. High Processing Cost Phenotypes (HPCPh), previously described by us, span neurodivergent and high-ability profiles, including autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, learning disorders and giftedness.

We present a systems-physiology framework derived from longitudinal within-person observation of 12 individuals followed in routine private clinical practice, comprising 532 laboratory collections over 10–25 years per person. Each collection is read as a physiological state and successive collections as transitions. Across the series, multiple regulatory systems changed configuration within individuals, and physiologically related marker pairs repeatedly departed from their expected relations. In three examples, multisystem configurations shifted back after changes in context over days, months or one year.

We interpret this pattern as multisystem regulatory containment: a coordinated reduction and redistribution of physiological throughput when information-processing demand exceeds sustainable capacity, rather than failure of a single system. We also introduce simple visual tools for reading routine laboratory data longitudinally within the person.

This retrospective case series is descriptive and hypothesis-generating. It does not establish specificity to HPCPh or normative longitudinal trajectories. Its purpose is to make a recurrent, context-responsive and potentially reversible physiological pattern visible and testable. If confirmed prospectively, this framework may be particularly relevant to neurodivergent and high-ability children and adults whose functional decline is poorly captured by conventional cross-sectional interpretation, and may inform both clinical care and the design of environments better matched to individual processing capacity. This may matter most in children, in whom such changes can have more lasting consequences.

articles_hidden.title: A Network Approach to Analysing Heart-Rate Variability
articles_hidden.authors: Han Sheng Ho; Emily Ortega
articles_hidden.abstract: Heart rate variability (HRV) reflects autonomic nervous system functioning and is commonly examined using statistical methods that compare individual HRV indices across demographic groups. Such approaches, however, may overlook group differences in how HRV components relate to one another. This study applies a network approach to delineate gender differences in the conditional relationships among short-term HRV indices and demographic characteristics in a Singaporean adult sample ($N = 2147$). Conventional regression analyses identified gender differences in average heart rate and low-frequency/high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio, whereas differences in root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) and standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN) were minimal and largely confined to specific age groups. In contrast, mixed graphical models revealed more pronounced gender differences in the conditional organisation of HRV. Among males, age was negatively associated with SDNN, SDNN was strongly associated with RMSSD, and weaker inverse relationships emerged between age and average heart rate and LF/HF ratio. The female network was substantially sparser, with an association observed primarily between ethnicity and LF/HF ratio, and no association between SDNN and RMSSD. These findings demonstrate that network analysis can reveal structural differences across gender that may be overlooked in traditional analyses. More broadly, they highlight the utility of psychological network analysis as an exploratory, hypothesis-generating tool for characterising multivariate conditional structures, even when the network theory underlying the approach is not assumed to hold.

articles_hidden.title: Hybrid Consciousness and the Cultural Evolution of Leadership
articles_hidden.authors: Rebekah Sēnānāyaka
articles_hidden.abstract: Ninety percent of human societies practise institutionalised alterations of consciousness. Across independent traditions, communities that develop governed protocols for sustained engagement with non-human organisms produce practitioners whose hybrid consciousness becomes the basis of social authority. Drawing on 27 months of apprenticeship-based fieldwork in the Peruvian and Colombian Amazon and comparative analysis of the 2,300-year Buddhist Bodhi tree tradition in Sri Lanka, I argue that inter-species contact protocols function as culturally evolved adaptive technologies that solve a recurrent problem in human social complexity: producing leaders whose authority is corruption-resistant and community-verifiable. The prestige these protocols generate is metabolically costly to acquire, continuously verified through public diagnostic performance, and resistant to capture because it depends on ongoing relationship maintenance with non-human agents rather than a one-time credential. Framed within cultural group selection, the convergence of this protocol structure across independent traditions suggests selective pressures on human sociality rather than local cultural production. The argument carries implications for cultural evolution theory, the study of religion and ritual, and contemporary encounters with non-human intelligence.

articles_hidden.title: A Transposed Bock–Aitkin EM Algorithm for Item Response Models with Many Items and Few Subjects
articles_hidden.authors: PRESTON DAVID BOTTER; Christopher Stewart
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language model benchmarks often contain many more items than evaluated systems. We develop a transposed Bock–Aitkin EM algorithm for 1PL and 2PL random-item models, including correlated difficulty and log discrimination. Capabilities are structural parameters; item effects are integrated over a normal population. We derive posterior-averaged scoring equations and distinguish exact marginal-likelihood theory from the implemented Laplace–cubature moment iteration, which can stabilize without solving the likelihood score. A simulation comparison uses 100 replications in each of 16 conditions. Capability recovery improves with more items for the transposed procedures, but population-correlation bias persists in small model cohorts. All variational fits in this comparison reached their iteration cap, limiting cross-framework conclusions. In an application to 98,032 WILD items, numerically eligible correlated transposed 2PL and variational 2PL have similar predictive performance, with log loss and Brier score favoring different procedures. JML 2PL has the lowest test Brier score but does not meet its numerical eligibility rule. The simulation and application use different fitting implementations and baseline settings, so they do not jointly validate a single numerical procedure. These exploratory findings concern point estimation and random-cell prediction, not calibrated parameter uncertainty or generalization to new models.

articles_hidden.title: Holding up a mirror: The mental health and well-being of academic psychologists
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Devendorf; David Disabato; Maya Nauphal; Jonathan Rottenberg; Sarah E. Victor
articles_hidden.abstract: The profession of psychology aims to improve societal mental health and well-being. Ironically, psychologists have neglected the study of mental health within the profession. We conducted the first comprehensive assessment of mental health difficulties across psychology disciplines in a sample (N = 1,261) of faculty and graduate students affiliated with U.S. doctoral degree granting institutions. Over 84% of respondents reported a lifetime history of mental health difficulties; 54% reported a lifetime diagnosis; 15% had clinically elevated current depression symptoms; 16% reported clinically elevated current anxiety symptoms; and 51% met Keyes’ “flourishing” criteria. The most common mental health concerns were depression, generalized anxiety disorder, panic attacks, suicidal thoughts, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Across all outcomes, graduate students reported significantly greater frequency and severity of difficulties. Clinically elevated current depression and anxiety were 3-4 times higher in graduate students (21% and 22%, respectively) compared to professor-level faculty (6% and 7%, respectively). Rates of flourishing were lower in graduate students than faculty (OR = 2.65, p < .001). Clinical-area respondents (92%) were more likely to report a lifetime mental health difficulty than non-clinical area respondents (83%). Interestingly, while there were no field-level differences in rates of current elevated anxiety, clinical-area respondents had lower rates of clinically elevated depression. Academic psychology is not an exception to the mental health crisis in higher education. Particularly urgent action is needed to improve graduate students’ mental health. We discuss both systemic and practical recommendations for the profession of psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Everyday Encounters with Economic Inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Carla Moccia; Matthew John Easterbrook; Matthias S Gobel
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on economic inequality has traditionally relied on macro-level indices, though a growing body of work examines how economic inequality is perceived in everyday life. Whether different forms of everyday encounters carry different political and psychological consequences remains unclear. Across four studies with London-based samples (N = 1,554), we used a situation-sampling approach to identify forms of real-world inequality encounters and test how they relate to appraisal, redistribution support, and psychological distress. Study 1 identified two forms of inequality: Structural Inequality, describing disparities in essential goods and institutions, and Lifestyle Inequality, involving differences in consumption, leisure, and social participation. Study 2 showed that Structural situations were perceived as more unequal and unfair and elicited stronger redistribution support than Lifestyle Inequality situations. Study 3a, reported in Supplementary Materials, showed that greater redistribution support for Structural Inequality situations was largely carried through greater perceived unfairness. Study 3b modelled Structural and Lifestyle Inequality content continuously: Structural Inequality was linked to redistribution support and distress through unfairness, whereas Lifestyle Inequality was linked to distress through upward social comparison. The political and psychological consequences of inequality therefore depend on the form of encounter, not only on its perceived magnitude.

articles_hidden.title: Heavy-Loaders and Light-Lifters: Individual Differences in Spontaneous Working Memory Use Are Stable Across Tasks in 6- to 10-Year-Old Children
articles_hidden.authors: Trevor Bissert; Candice Koolhaas; Zsuzsa Kaldy; Erik Blaser
articles_hidden.abstract: Naturalistic visuomotor tasks, like building a Lego model, allow one to trade off the use of external resources (here, looking at the instructions) versus internal resources (remembering steps in working memory). Prior work has revealed substantial individual differences in this sampling-remembering trade-off, with some individuals opting to sample less and remember more (‘heavy-loaders’) and others to sample more and remember less (‘light-lifters’). We hypothesized that these strategies are driven by subjective, but stable, assessments of the costs of sampling versus remembering. In this preregistered, developmental study, we tested this using two superficially different, but isomorphic tablet-based tasks: the Shopping Game and the Zoo Game. Children (N = 121, 60% female, age: 6.0-10.0 years) were shown icons of food items (or animals) and asked to select them in a store (or field) interspersed with distractors. Critically, children could not view the list and store/field simultaneously, but could toggle between them. List Study Time and Memory Use (correctly selected items), per visit, characterized strategy. As expected, we found substantial variability in Memory Use and Study Time between children that remained constant across age (0.5-5 items and 1-12 s, respectively), alongside significant, strong stability within children (>67% variance explained), both across the two tasks and over time (test-retest); heavy-loaders remained heavy-loaders and light-lifters, light-lifters. We also found that cognitive reflection (CRT-D) and age significantly predicted Memory Use. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explicitly characterize the individual differences and cognitive motivation predictors of children's spontaneous memory use.

articles_hidden.title: Metacognitive Skill Learning as a Mechanism of Advanced Meditation
articles_hidden.authors: Brendan Conway-Smith; Ruby Potash; Matthew Sacchet
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite growing interest in advanced meditation, the cognitive mechanisms underlying these capacities remain poorly understood. This paper develops a cognitive account of advanced meditation as a specialized form of metacognitive skill learning. Drawing on classic accounts of skill acquisition, we propose the automatization of metacognitive control as a mechanism through which meditative skill develops. Through sustained practice, practitioners become less reliant on explicit instructions as metacognitive control becomes increasingly automatic. This shift may allow meditative practice to become more effective, fluent, and less effortful. The resulting metacognitive control is directed toward well-defined phenomenological targets, including advanced absorption states and insight stages. By connecting cognitive mechanisms with neural findings and experiential descriptions, the account offers a testable framework for explaining the development of advanced meditative capacities.

articles_hidden.title: Usage frequency predicts lexicalization across languages
articles_hidden.authors: Temuulen Khishigsuren; Francis Mollica; Ekaterina Vylomova; Charles Kemp
articles_hidden.abstract: Languages are more likely to have lexical items for some concepts (e.g. CHILD and SUN) than others (e.g. PARENT and WEATHER). We present a large-scale quantitative analysis of factors that predict lexicalization across languages, and test in particular the hypothesis that usage frequency predicts lexicalization. We consider 854 concepts and demonstrate that average usage frequency across 46 languages from the Language Documentation Reference Corpus is a relatively good predictor of the typological prevalence of lexicalization across the 41 languages in the World Loanword Database (β = 0.25, 95% CI = [0.16, 0.33]) and across 262 languages from the Intercontinental Dictionary Series (β = 0.30, 95% CI = [0.23, 0.38]). This finding implies that cross-linguistic regularities in lexicalization can be attributed in part to shared usage patterns across cultures.

articles_hidden.title: Statistical Inference Regularized with Neural Networks and its Application in Psychometrics
articles_hidden.authors: Dmitry I Belov; Oliver Lüdtke; Esther Ulitzsch
articles_hidden.abstract: Likelihood-based methods such as marginal maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) are widely used for estimating item response theory (IRT) models and perform well in large samples. In small samples, however, these approaches may yield unstable estimates due to insufficient information in the likelihood, unless strong prior distributions are imposed. We address this problem by turning to the fundamentals of estimation via decision theory, showing that small-sample estimation can be viewed as an ill-posed decision problem in the sense that the decision function is sensitive to small changes in the data and, therefore, may not be continuous. We discuss how such ill-posed decision problems—both in IRT estimation and more broadly—can be regularized using neural network (NN)-based approaches that build a continuous map from observations into parameters. We formalize this approach within a general framework termed regularized decision theory and apply it to IRT models. Focusing on the 3PL, we study its properties via simulations.

articles_hidden.title: Methylphenidate, parent training, and neuropsychological outcomes in preschool ADHD: secondary analysis of a randomized placebo-controlled trial
articles_hidden.authors: Monike Nascimento Teixeira; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo; Guilherme V. Polanczyk; Adriana Argeu; Eliane Correa Miotto
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Methylphenidate (MPH) and behavioral parent training (BPT) are the most recommended interventions for preschoolers with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), but their effects on cognition in this age group remain understudied. This pre-registered secondary analysis of the MAPPA randomized controlled trial aimed to examine the effects of MPH and BPT on neuropsychological outcomes, each relative to an active control, and to compare the two interventions directly.
Methods. Preschoolers with ADHD (N =153) were randomized to three groups: MPH plus sham parent training (n = 51), placebo MPH plus BPT (n = 51), and active control (placebo MPH plus sham parent training; n = 51). Executive functions, social cognition, and verbal abilities were assessed at baseline and after 8 weeks. Linear mixed models tested time x group interactions, adjusting for IQ, sex, age, ADHD severity, and comorbidities, with a random intercept per child, and false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied within each cognitive domain. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02807870.
Results. Relative to control, MPH increased Flanker reaction times in the congruent (d = −1.00, pFDR = .009) and incongruent (d = −1.11, pFDR = .004) conditions. After correction, BPT did not differ from control, nor MPH from BPT. Within groups, only MPH showed executive improvements, with higher speed-accuracy scores (Hearts & Flowers d = 0.73; Flanker d = 0.60) and accuracy alongside slower responding.
Conclusions. To our knowledge, this is the first randomized trial to compare MPH and BPT on a comprehensive neuropsychological battery in preschoolers with ADHD. Compared with an active control, 8 weeks of MPH led preschoolers with ADHD to respond more slowly on the Flanker task without loss of accuracy. Within the MPH group, combined speed-accuracy efficiency and accuracy also improved, suggesting more deliberate processing. BPT showed no detectable effect on objective cognition, and neither intervention affected social cognition or verbal abilities. 
Keywords: ADHD, preschoolers, methylphenidate, behavioral parent training, executive functions, social cognition, neuropsychology.

articles_hidden.title: Childhood Instability Predicts Educational Attainment
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Caplin; Nora Harhen; Catherine A. Hartley; Ida Maria Hartmann; Søren Leth-Petersen; Johan Sæverud
articles_hidden.abstract: Educational attainment is a major determinant of health, wealth, and relationship quality, making it key for human flourishing. A diverse set of major childhood disruptions are known to predict poorer academic performance. Here we propose that childhood unpredictability constitutes a latent dimension of early-life environments underpinning these effects, suggesting everyday instability, in addition to major disruptions, should determine educational success. To test this hypothesis, we link population-wide Danish administrative records with a validated survey measure to quantify individuals' life disruptions, both major and minor. Among 2,793 respondents, greater unpredictability is associated with lower grade point averages and reduced high school completion, even after accounting for parental socioeconomic status and observed major life disruptions. Our finding that childhood unpredictability alters educational success, suggests a pathway through which disadvantage may be transmitted across generations and highlights everyday unpredictability as a potential target for interventions aimed at improving social mobility.

articles_hidden.title: Using Large Language Models to Contextualize Smiling in Psychotherapy Research
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Lund Trinhammer; Stella Grasshof; Jana Volkert; Pia Rasche; Anna-Maria Weiland; Sami Sebastian Brandt; Uwe Altmann
articles_hidden.abstract:
The meaning of a smile during conversation depends on what is being
said, yet psychotherapy research has historically analyzed facial movements independently of
context. We introduce a methodology that links both partners’ smiling in a dyadic setting to
the sentiment of a speech turn (positive, neutral, negative). Using open-weight models on local
hardware only, we transcribed and diarized attachment interviews, annotated the sentiment of
the participant’s speech turns with a large language model (LLM), and analyzed individual smiling
 and smile synchrony as a function of that sentiment. We applied linear mixed models to
test for differences in smiling according to sentiment. Across 70 interviews and 1,294 speech
turns, only the interviewer’s smiling differed significantly according to the sentiment of what
the participant was saying (interviewer d = .51, q < .001; participant d = .05, q = .165); the
pair smiled simultaneously more often during positive than negative turns (d = .21, p < .001).
By conditioning smiling on what is being said — sentiment annotated from the conversation
as it unfolds rather than created by experimental instruction — our method enables the kind of
context-sensitive analysis contemporary theories call for. The pipeline is open and reproducible,
runs entirely on local hardware so that no data leave the site, and can be easily modified for any
annotation scheme or clinical setting.

articles_hidden.title: Abstract concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
articles_hidden.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstract concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI). In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

articles_hidden.title: Emotional and Well-being Consequences of Discrimination and Collective Action Engagement
articles_hidden.authors: Shahrzad Goudarzi; Riana M. Brown; Ashley L Berkebile-Weinberg; Maureen A. Craig
articles_hidden.abstract: Inequality and collective struggles against it are psychologically taxing. Yet to be successful, social movements must persist through sustained action despite their toll on the participants, and many do. While the negative affective determinants of collective action, particularly outrage, are extensively studied, less is known about the accompanying positive psychological states. Using cross-sectional and experience-sampling methodologies, we find that engaging (and intending to engage) in collective action is marked by heightened subjective well-being and a range of positive feelings. Nonetheless, the positive consequences of engagement (but not mere intention) may only emerge when action is coupled with experiences of discrimination targeting outgroups (but not the self, personally, or ingroups) or in the absence of discrimination. This suggests that some psychological distance from discrimination supports the psychological benefits of collective action in grappling with inequality. Overall, this work can provide insight into a psychological mechanism contributing to sustained mobilization.

articles_hidden.title: Questions about Generative Language Models for Human Resources Decision Making
articles_hidden.authors: Dev K. Dalal; Gaurav Malhotra; Gregory Edward Cox; Adam T. Weber
articles_hidden.abstract: In this chapter, we discuss the gaps in the current understanding of how generative large language models (LLMs) make person judgments. Person judgments refer to inferences about someone's standing on a psychological construct, particularly when the judgment is made under uncertainty. We extend this concern to the application of LLMs to inform human resources (HR) decision making. We consider the ethical and legal implications of using LLMs to make person judgments to inform HR decision making. Finally, we outline a set of general research questions centered on  unstudied and understudied questions as it pertains to the use of LLMs in HR decision making.

articles_hidden.title: Co-STARS: A Participatory Action Research Approach to Co-Producing Culturally Responsive Mental Health Literacy Training with Young Black People
articles_hidden.authors: Milan Antonovic; Megan A. Pope; Gerald Jordan; Balachandran Kumarendran; Luke Brown; Nadia; Ayan Mahamud; Lowri Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Young Black people in the UK face disproportionate mental health inequalities driven by stigma, racism, and structural exclusion. Although mental health literacy can promote early recognition and help-seeking, most interventions do not reflect Black communities’ lived realities. This study used Participatory Action Research (PAR) to co-produce a peer-led community mental health literacy training package with young Black people, alongside an e-learning resource to support culturally responsive practice among mental health and allied professionals.

Method: Eight young Black participants (M age = 24.5; five female) with lived experience of mental ill health from diverse cultural, religious, and gender backgrounds took part in four peer-led workshops and three refinement sessions. Guided by an anti-oppressive framework, participants identified priorities, developed content, and shaped the training. Data were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

Results: Four interconnected themes emerged: (1) Navigating Cultural Silences and Systemic Exclusions (stigma, cultural taboos, intergenerational trauma, and racialised experiences in education and healthcare); (2) Fighting to Be Heard (dismissal, misrecognition, and delayed care); (3) Reimagining Care Through Cultural Proximity and Community Anchoring (relational, culturally grounded, community-based models); and (4) Embedding Accountability and Cultural Reflexivity in Training (youth-led recommendations for train-the-trainer programmes emphasising structural competency, experiential learning, and supervision).

Conclusions: Co-production elevated young Black people’s expertise and produced a culturally responsive training package grounded in lived experience and structural realities. The findings highlight the need for preventative, relational, and equity-focused mental health approaches and support community-led, culturally grounded interventions to reduce disparities among Black and racialised youth.

articles_hidden.title: Remembering how events unfold: Emotion and memory consolidation for naturalistic events
articles_hidden.authors: Charline Colson; Arnaud D'Argembeau
articles_hidden.abstract: Although emotional content is known to strengthen memory consolidation, its influence on how the unfolding of events is retained over time has received little attention. Building on the finding that negative events are remembered with less temporal compression and richer detail than neutral events, this study examined whether this emotional advantage changes over time, as would be expected if consolidation contributes to it. Participants viewed a series of negative and neutral videos and, either immediately or after a 24-hour or 72-hour delay, mentally replayed each event and verbally described it. Temporal compression was indexed by the ratio of video duration to replay duration, memory richness by narrative length and linguistic measures of episodic detail, and the preservation of event content by embedding-based similarity to descriptions produced during viewing. At immediate recall, negative events were replayed with less compression and described with more words and episodic detail than neutral events, replicating prior findings. After a delay, the emotional advantage in narrative length and episodic detail increased, and similarity to the video descriptions declined for neutral but not for negative events, whereas evidence for a corresponding increase in the emotion effect on temporal compression was less conclusive. These findings show that the emotional advantage in memory content for naturalistic, dynamic events is not fixed at encoding but increases over time, pointing to a role for consolidation.

articles_hidden.title: Autobiographical Editing Questionnaire: Measuring personally motivated distortion of shared memories and its relationship with the Dark Triad and dissociation
articles_hidden.authors: Noboru Matsumoto; Satoru Kiire; Rie Kubota; Hinako Kojima
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory distortions motivated by interpersonal manipulation are frequently observed in clinical and forensic contexts among individuals with borderline and narcissistic personality disorders. However, experimental studies (e.g., DRM paradigm) have provided limited evidence of increased false-memory susceptibility in personality disorders, possibly because laboratory tasks fail to capture personally motivated memory distortions. We developed the Autobiographical Editing Questionnaire (AEQ), a self-report measure of the deliberate reporting of distorted memories driven by personal motivations, in Japanese and English, and examined its associations with personality traits and dissociation. Across four studies, we confirmed the factorial validity of a 20-item cross-classified nested model, in which each item was jointly defined by four distortion-type dimensions (Maximization, Minimization, Concealment, and Fabrication) and five functional dimensions (Understanding, Empathy, Positive Impression, Negative Impression, and Self-Interest). Except for grandiose narcissism in the English version, the Dark Triad, the Vulnerable Dark Triad, and dissociation correlated positively with the functional dimensions. Consistent patterns emerged across both language versions: vulnerable narcissism was selectively associated with Maximization, Machiavellianism with Minimization, psychopathy with Concealment and Fabrication, and dissociation with Fabrication. These findings suggest that memory distortions observed in personality pathology are not entirely unconscious and can be meaningfully assessed by self-report.

articles_hidden.title: Deciding with muscles
articles_hidden.authors: Edouard Dendauw; Nathan J. Evans; Emma Michel; Axel Garnier-Allain; thibault gajdos; Mathieu Servant
articles_hidden.abstract: Sequential sampling models have a rich tradition in psychology and play a central role in our understanding of human decision-making. According to these models, decisions arise from the gradual accumulation of noisy evidence over time until a decision threshold is reached. This framework accounts for both choice behavior and reaction times and is further supported by neurophysiological evidence: neural activity in various brain regions exhibits accumulation-to-bound dynamics consistent with model predictions. Recent empirical findings extend this view, revealing that similar accumulation-like signals can also be observed in the electrical activity of response muscles, suggesting that decision signals may propagate continuously from perceptual processing through motor execution. This raises a fundamental theoretical question: How are effortful actions initiated when sensory evidence is weak, particularly under time pressure? We hypothesized that evidence-independent urgency signals provide the additional drive needed for the translation of decision signals into muscle activation in such contexts. To formalize this hypothesis, we extended the gated cascade diffusion model, a computational framework that links decision formation, motor preparation, and motor execution. We tested this model extension against behavioral and neuromuscular data from two experiments manipulating sensory evidence quality and required response force, with speed pressure additionally manipulated in Experiment 2. Model fits and formal comparisons with alternative accounts provided strong support for our hypothesis. These findings enhance our understanding of the interface between decision-making and motor systems, particularly in contexts that require effortful actions, which are common in everyday behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Spirituality Matters in Deconstructive Meditation: Comparing Secular and Buddhist-Based Mechanisms of Change in Depressive Vulnerability
articles_hidden.authors: Céline Stinus; Sophie Berjot
articles_hidden.abstract: This exploratory study extends a previously implemented randomized protocol to examine whether incorporating Buddhist-based spiritual and philosophical components into deconstructive meditation is associated with different patterns of psychological change. We compared secular deconstructive meditation (S-SI; n = 49), Buddhist-based deconstructive meditation (B-SI; n = 53), and a waitlist control condition (WL; n = 50) on depression-related outcomes (dysfunctional attitudes, identity threat, and depressive symptoms) and selflessness-related processes (connectedness to humanity, connectedness to nature, and cognitive decentering). Participants completed pre- and post-intervention assessments, and changes across conditions were examined using repeated-measures MANOVA. Within-subject mediation analyses further explored whether changes in selflessness-related processes were associated with changes in depression-related outcomes. Both active conditions showed greater reductions in depressive symptoms than the waitlist condition. Compared with S-SI, B-SI showed greater reductions in dysfunctional attitudes and identity threat, as well as larger increases in connectedness to humanity, connectedness to nature, and cognitive decentering. Within B-SI, changes in cognitive decentering and connectedness to nature showed significant indirect effects on changes in dysfunctional attitudes, whereas changes in connectedness to humanity showed significant indirect effects on changes in identity threat in both active conditions. None of the examined processes showed significant indirect effects on changes in depressive symptoms in either active condition. These findings suggest that the Buddhist-based condition may engage a broader range of self-related processes associated with depressive vulnerability. Given the exploratory, nonconcurrent design, these findings require confirmation in prospectively randomized comparisons.

articles_hidden.title: Give one way or another? Choosing between public goods and private transfers under inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Natalie Struwe; Yixuan Shi; Anwesha Banerjee
articles_hidden.abstract: Individuals who care about the well-being of others can act through voluntary contributions to public goods (e.g. education, health, social protection), or through private monetary transfers as redistributive measures, as seen in informal community support networks, and formal unconditional cash transfer (UCT) programs. This paper studies the strategic relationship between these two simultaneous channels of giving in unequal groups. Building on a model of altruistic preferences, we conduct a pre-registered, between-subjects experiment (n=478) that varies income inequality and the availability of simultaneous private transfers in a repeated, two-person, and non-linear public good game. We identify a significant reduction of public good contributions in the presence of private transfers at all levels of inequality, with individuals substituting between the two strategies regardless of endowment type. Notably, poorer group members also send transfers, and transfers occur even when initial endowments are equal. Exploratory analysis reveals that this behavior can be explained by positive reciprocity motivations. Importantly, allowing for transfers in highly unequal groups need not reduce aggregate earnings. Despite the substitution in the considered setting, transfers improve the income of the poorer individuals without harming the wealthier group members. Our results speak to the behavioral micro-foundations of public goods and private transfers as complementary instruments for reducing within-group inequality.

articles_hidden.title: Moving beyond single-shot studies  toward cumulative research
articles_hidden.authors: Balazs Aczel; Eiko I Fried; Sabine Hoffmann
articles_hidden.abstract: In this perspective, we argue that single-design, single-analysis studies leave too much uncertainty unresolved to provide sufficiently informative answers to research questions. Such single-shot studies remain common across many disciplines, yet they reflect numerous explicit and implicit design and analytical decisions. Yet without systematically examining the consequences of these choices, researchers cannot determine the extent to which empirical findings depend on them. We contend that uncertainties arising from variability in research design and analysis are an unavoidable feature of empirical inquiry and a major source of the persistent replication problems, conflicting and seemingly irreconcilable findings, and limited cumulative knowledge observed across many fields. To address this challenge, we present a unifying framework for existing methodologies that allow researchers to systematically explore, reduce, and integrate these often-overlooked uncertainties underlying empirical claims. We argue that many of the necessary methods already exist across disciplines, but their broader impact has been limited by a lack of a shared conceptual framework and interdisciplinary integration. By balancing hypothesis testing with exploration and theory building, and by systematically incorporating Space Analysis tools into research practice, scientific fields can move beyond isolated single-shot studies toward systematic research programmes capable of producing more reliable, robust, and cumulative scientific knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: Chronic pain and relationship satisfaction, social support, and social network size in chronic pain couples
articles_hidden.authors: Karolin Teichmüller; Gudrun-Karin Kindl; Heike Rittner; Andrea M.F. Reiter
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Chronic pain has detrimental effects on patients’ social integration and also affects patients’ significant others. This study asks if chronic pain patients, their spouses and pain-free couples differ in their self-reported relationship satisfaction and the quality and quantity of their social relationships with others.
Methods: Self-report data on relationship satisfaction (Partnership Questionnaire, PFB-K), perceived social support (Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, MSPSS), and social network size (Social Network Index, SNI) were collected online from 136 individuals, representing 34 chronic pain and 34 pain-free couples, matched on age and relationship duration. Chronic pain patients were recruited from a tertiary pain centre and presented with various pain conditions, mainly non-specific back pain, musculoskeletal pain and neuropathy. Pain-free couples were recruited from the general population.
Results: Linear mixed model analyses showed lower relationship satisfaction in chronic pain patients, and couples with longer relationship duration. The presence of chronic pain and longer relationship duration were particularly associated with reduced satisfaction on the PFB-K Tenderness subscale, assessing physical closeness. Moreover, patients perceived lower social support from friends but did not have fewer social contacts. Descriptively, chronic pain patients’ partners ranged between patients and controls regarding relationship satisfaction and perceived social support.
Conclusions: Chronic pain seems to complicate partnership, especially intimacy, and the quality of friendships for chronic pain patients, but not necessarily for their spouses. Our results highlight the need for multidimensional pain management strategies, which include assessing and targeting aspects of social functioning in romantic relationships and beyond.

articles_hidden.title: Extreme Response Style Generalizes Across Likert-Type and Visual Analogue Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Dominik Vollbracht; Malin Müller; Tanja Lischetzke; Mirka Henninger
articles_hidden.abstract: Response styles, such as the tendency to prefer extreme or midpoint response options, are a systematic source of variance in self-report data. Individual differences in response styles are largely consistent across traits and over time, but it is unknown whether they generalize across Likert-type scales and visual analogue scales (VAS). In a preregistered within-subjects study, N = 501 participants completed the HEXACO-PI-R, with two content-balanced item subsets presented on a 7-point Likert-type scale and on a VAS. We modeled extreme and midpoint responding as opposite poles of a single dimension, referred to as extreme response style (ERS), using conceptually aligned models: a partial credit model for the Likert-type items and a beta item response model for the VAS items, each extended by a person-specific ERS parameter. Estimating both models jointly in a Bayesian framework, we found that ERS on Likert-type scales and on VAS was substantially correlated (ρERS = .76, 95% CrI [.68, .83]). Individual differences in ERS thus generalized to a considerable extent across response formats. Choosing VAS instead of Likert-type scales therefore does not avoid the influence of response styles, which should be modeled in VAS data as well.

articles_hidden.title: The Effects of Group-Based Community Interventions on Social Reintegration of Marginalized Adults with Mental Illness: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Nina Thorup Dalgaard; jakob Kaarup Jensen; Jasmin Sami Adada; Maya Christiane Flensborg Jensen; Elizabeth Bengtsen; Mikkel Helding Vembye; Elizabeth Tipton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background 
Adults with mental illness who also experience social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, yet scalable interventions addressing both dimensions of recovery remain limited.

Aims 
To evaluate the effects of group-based community interventions on social reintegration and mental health among socially marginalized adults with mental illness.

Methods 
We conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions delivered in OECD countries. Searches identified 28,980 records; 62 studies met the inclusion criteria and 49 studies, contributing 349 effect sizes, were included in the meta-analysis. Outcomes were classified as social reintegration or mental health. Meta-analytic models accounted for dependent effect sizes within studies.

Results 
Group-based community interventions improved social reintegration (g = 0.195, 95% CI [0.122, 0.268]) and mental health (g = 0.215, 95% CI [0.090, 0.340]) relative to control conditions, corresponding to effects approximately 2.3 and 1.4 times larger, respectively, than the typical improvements under treatment as usual. Effects varied substantially across studies and outcomes, while measured moderators explained little of this heterogeneity. Effects on social reintegration and mental health were positively associated. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses and showed little indication of publication bias. Nearly half of studies were preregistered and contributed approximately two-thirds of all effect sizes. Preregistered studies yielded smaller social reintegration effects than non-preregistered studies, although the average effect remained statistically significant and substantively meaningful.

Conclusions 
Group-based community interventions can improve both social reintegration and mental health among marginalized adults with mental illness, suggesting that they may support multidimensional recovery. Their potential value therefore extends beyond scalability and lower delivery costs to substantively meaningful improvements in outcomes. However, substantial unexplained heterogeneity indicates that benefits are unlikely to be uniform across populations, interventions, and settings.

What is already known on this topic
Adults experiencing both mental illness and social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, while existing systematic reviews on group-based interventions have largely focused on specific diagnoses, intervention types, or psychiatric symptoms.

What this study adds
Across 49 studies contributing 349 effect sizes, group-based community interventions produced positive average effects on both social reintegration and mental health. Effects in the two domains were positively associated, but substantial heterogeneity remained largely unexplained.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Regression Effect: Investigating Time-Order Effects on the Cross-Modal Correspondence of Brightness and Loudness Within the Global Psychophysical Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Katharina Naumann; Annemarie Oelert; Jürgen Heller
articles_hidden.abstract:
This exploratory experimental study investigates the contribution of stimulus
presentation order to the regression effect in cross-modal matching of brightness and
loudness. Previous research has largely relied on the magnitude production paradigm to
obtain individual cross-modal matches, which induces distinct stimulus roles (i. e., a
fixed standard vs. an adjustable comparison). The cross-modal matches typically
exhibit a role-dependent regression effect, that is, they gravitate toward the mean of the
adjusted stimulus’ range. This regression effect can be explained by the theory of global
psychophysics via role-dependent internal references. However, stimulus role and
presentation order were often confounded in previous experiments. To decouple these
variables, this study employed a two-alternative forced-choice paradigm. Participants
judged whether a noise sound or an achromatic disk appeared more intense. To hide
explicit stimulus roles and level selection across the luminance and sound pressure
spectra, several adaptive staircases were run interleaved, balancing presentation order
across a high number of trials. Results showed an order-dependent regression effect in
three of the seven subjects, suggesting these individuals used the first stimulus in a trial
as an implicit standard. The remaining four subjects did not seem to exhibit this
strategy. Irregularities in the adaptive staircases, deviations from the global
psychophysical model, and future directions are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking a “core moral concept” in infancy: A relationship account of infants’ responses to resource distributions
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Mackiel; Amanda Woodward
articles_hidden.abstract: Infants’ responses to resource distributions are commonly interpreted as evidence of early fairness expectations and evaluations. We systematically review and meta-analyze this literature and propose an alternative, the relationship account: infants may use allocations to infer how distributors are connected to recipients and whether they are available as potential social partners. Our meta-analyses of the reviewed literature identify an overall reliable tendency for infants to look longer at unequal outcomes and preferentially engage with equal distributors. However, we argue that the current body of evidence does not uniquely establish fairness reasoning. Instead, infants’ responses may stem from preferences, expectations, and predictions grounded in reasoning about relationships. We propose that infants treat a distributor’s allocation as evidence about their relationships with recipients and use this information to assess the potential for themselves seeking relationships with the distributors. We outline experiments that could distinguish between fairness and relationship interpretations of infants’ responses and conclude by highlighting the generative potential of a relationship-focused framework for understanding infant social cognition.

articles_hidden.title: A database of subjective evaluation ratings for decision-making research
articles_hidden.authors: Kianté Fernandez; Sumedha Goyal; Ian Krajbich
articles_hidden.abstract: Subjective value ratings guide everyday choices, and value-based decision-making research collects them in many experiments. Yet the field has no common method for eliciting them. Studies use different response scales, instructions, and stimulus sets, and their ratings are rarely shared in a form that allows them to be used together. We present the Liking Initiative, a curated database of 759,399 individual ratings from 38 studies (59 datasets) covering 2,217 items, rated by 5,377 participants summed across datasets. Each rating is provided along with dataset-level metadata documenting the response scale, the question asked, and the source publication. The database is available through a web application, versioned releases on Zenodo, and R and Python packages. Because many items were rated in more than one dataset, item-level ratings can be compared across samples, response scales, and laboratories.

articles_hidden.title: Generalizable experiment agents threaten online behavioral experiments
articles_hidden.authors: Talha Özüdoğru; Andrey Chetverikov; Richard Huskey; Leendert van Maanen; Christoph Strauch
articles_hidden.abstract:
Online behavioral experiments rely on the assumption that participants are human. Advances in large language models
(LLMs) challenge this assumption, but previous demonstrations have largely focused on surveys or agents built for individual
experimental tasks. Here, we introduce the Artificial General Experiment Agent (AGEA), a general-purpose agent developed
entirely through natural language prompting using a consumer-level LLM subscription. Without custom training for any
specific task, AGEA completed twenty-six online behavioral experiments across seven hosting platforms, independently
inferring each task’s structure. Benchmark comparisons across three cognitive domains, using the N-back, Tower of London,
and Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, showed performance within typical human ranges, including changes in accuracy and
response time with experimental conditions. It further completed, with human-like behavior, seven held-out studies prepared
in the spirit of adversarial collaboration between the co-authors. These findings show that agent participation can extend
across experimental paradigms and platforms. As general-purpose agents become cheaper and more capable, they pose a
growing risk to the integrity of online behavioral research, and safeguards must keep pace.

articles_hidden.title: What Makes a Child Go Bad? Genes, Choice, and Punishment in Original Sin
articles_hidden.authors: Madelief Isabel Kuijper; Kassandra Pomper; Josefina Benita Bernardo; Selim Sametoğlu; Elsje van Bergen
articles_hidden.abstract: This review reflects on Kathryn Paige Harden’s Original Sin through discussions in our Educational Genetics lab. We consider the book’s treatment of behavioural genetics, responsibility, punishment, religion, and parenting, highlighting both the power of Harden’s personal perspective and the limitations of its strongly American Evangelical framing. We conclude by reflecting on what science can, and cannot, tell us about why individuals behave badly.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond problem solving: Adaptive reframing in human and artificial intelligence
articles_hidden.authors: Valerio Capraro; Antonio Lieto; Francesco Rea; Giulio Sandini; Alessandra Sciutti; Vittorio Gallese; Walter Quattrociocchi
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on human and artificial intelligence has largely focused on problem solving: given a predefined problem, can an agent produce an effective solution? Yet many real-world challenges cannot be captured by a fixed problem representation. They require agents not only to solve problems, but also to recognize when the original problem representation has become inadequate and must be revised to reflect new evidence or changes in the problem itself. We argue that this capacity, termed adaptive reframing, constitutes a fundamental but under-researched dimension of intelligence. We propose a multidisciplinary framework for studying adaptive reframing across neuroscience, cognitive science, robotics, experimental economics and psychology, and complex systems. Adaptive reframing is defined as the capacity to revise the construction of a problem in response to changing evidence, causal structure, or social context. To support a systematic science of adaptive reframing, we introduce three complementary paradigms: the Dynamic Scenario Framing Task, the Perturbed Causal Model Task, and the Social-Affective Problem Setting Task. These paradigms provide a common framework for comparing humans and artificial agents in situations requiring problem reframing, and for building architecture-enhanced AI systems. We propose a shift from problem solving to adaptive problem framing as a central focus of intelligence research.

articles_hidden.title: What Fifty Years of Research on the Misinformation Effect Can Tell Us: A Meta-Analytic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Alfons Edmar; Nathalie Shekila Anna Enquist; Timothy John Luke
articles_hidden.abstract: This meta-analysis examines the impact of misleading or incorrect information on subsequent reports of witnessed events, with the aim of identifying key moderators of the misinformation effect – defined as reduced accuracy following exposure to misinformation. We synthesized experimental studies using the three-phase misinformation paradigm published between 1975 and 2025. A three-level mixed-effects meta-regression model was used to account for effect size non-independence and to examine moderators, including retention interval, warnings, overall test performance, and study characteristics. Across 480 studies and 1,998 effect sizes (N = 59,079), the average misinformation effect was substantial (g = 0.694, 95% CI [0.259, 1.128]) and highly heterogeneous (σ2 = 0.697, I2 = 92.21%). Control condition accuracy was positively associated with the magnitude of the effect, and post-misinformation warnings significantly reduced it. In contrast to prior findings, post-event testing did not significantly moderate the effect. These findings support the robustness of the misinformation effect and suggest that it reflects a combination of memory-related and strategic processes. Given the substantial heterogeneity observed, the misinformation effect may be better conceptualized as a constellation of related phenomena rather than a single unified effect, with important implications for theory and applied settings such as eyewitness testimony.

articles_hidden.title: Latent Profiles on the Intelligence and Development Scales – 2 and their Relationship with Classifications of Dyslexia and ADHD
articles_hidden.authors: Linda Visser; Selma Anne José Ruiter; Marieke Timmerman
articles_hidden.abstract: Objectives: The aim of the current study was to get insight in intelligence and executive functioning profiles and their relation with gender and dyslexia and ADHD classifications. Methods: We performed a latent profile analysis on IDS-2 data from 3,954 Dutch, German and Italian children (7 – 21 years). Results: The results showed six profiles differing in overall cognitive level. Three profiles were relatively balanced (below-average, low-average, and average), one showed high-average scores with a clear strength in visual short-term memory and two showed only slight strengths and weaknesses. There were large gender differences between the profile, amongst which a clear overrepresentation of boys in the profile with balanced below-average scores. This profile, along with the one with low-average scores, had relatively high rates of classifications for both ADHD and dyslexia and scholastic skills in the low-average range. For the other profiles, the scholastic skills scores were largely comparable to those on intelligence and executive functioning. Conclusion: Our results do not support the idea that ADHD or dyslexia classifications are related to specific weaknesses in a cognitive profile. This highlights the need for individualized assessment that takes into account both acquired academic competencies and innate cognitive capacities.

articles_hidden.title: How Does Child Maltreatment Affect Prosocial Behavior? Disentangling the Unique Contributions of Abuse, Neglect and Emotional Maltreatment
articles_hidden.authors: Philipp Berger; Marian S. Schulz; Tyler Colasante; Georg von Polier; Kai von Klitzing; Andrea Schlesier-Michel; Lars O. White; Tina Malti; Jan Keil
articles_hidden.abstract: Child maltreatment is a well-established risk factor for mental health problems and maladaptive developmental outcomes. However, beyond its well-documented links to psychopathology, child maltreatment can also disrupt social functioning and erode social support, further increasing vulnerability to adverse outcomes across development. Prosocial behavior—voluntary actions intended to benefit others—is a core component of social functioning and supports the formation and maintenance of positive relationships. Although child maltreatment has been consistently linked to lower levels of prosocial behavior in children and adolescents, findings regarding the unique contributions of specific maltreatment dimensions (i.e., abuse, neglect and emotional maltreatment) remain mixed. The present preregistered study therefore aimed to examine the unique contributions of abuse, neglect and emotional maltreatment to the development of prosocial behavior across childhood and adolescence. To this end, we applied structural equation modeling (SEM) to fine-grained and multisource dimensional assessments of maltreatment to examine their unique associations with self- and caregiver-reported prosocial behavior in a large sample (N = 812) of German children and adolescents aged 3 to 16 years. Results indicate that experiences of abuse - but not neglect or emotional maltreatment – were uniquely associated with lower levels of both self- and caregiver-reported prosocial behavior. For caregiver-reported prosocial behavior, these associations further varied by gender and age group: the negative association of abuse was more pronounced in boys, and neglect was additionally associated with lower prosocial behavior among adolescents. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between dimensions of child maltreatment, as abuse appears to play a particularly salient role in undermining prosocial development. Accounting for developmental stage and gender may further refine our understanding of risk pathways in social functioning to ultimately inform more tailored prevention and intervention strategies.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Assessment Tools Developed or Adapted for Indigenous Populations in North America, South America, and Oceania: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Jaden Seligman; Marianne Galliez; Anne-Marie Ergis; Benjamin Boller
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Cognitive assessment tools are important for understanding cognitive performance and identifying cognitive impairment. However, many commonly used cognitive assessment tools were developed and validated within Western cultural and linguistic contexts, which may limit their validity and cultural appropriateness for Indigenous populations. This review examines the existing literature on cognitive assessment tools used with Indigenous populations and evaluates the methodological quality of these studies and the cultural adaptations made to these tools. Method: A systematic search was conducted across six databases and was limited to studies examining cognitive performance in Indigenous populations. Citations were imported into Covidence, where titles and abstracts were screened for relevance. Data were extracted by two independent reviewers; study selection was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram. Studies were evaluated for risk of bias and methodological rigour using the NOS-xs, NOS, and CCAT critical appraisal tools. Results: Sixty studies were included, from North America (n=21), South America (n=10), and Oceania (n=29). Studies demonstrating greater methodological rigour frequently employed community-based participatory research (CBPR) approaches, involving community consultation to develop, adapt, and administer tests in culturally appropriate ways. Methodological rigour varied across studies, largely because of limited sample sizes in these populations. Conclusions: Establishing appropriate normative data can provide more valid reference points for interpreting cognitive performance in Indigenous populations. Cognitive assessments should be adapted to reflect cultural and linguistic differences, and further research on diverse Indigenous populations globally is needed. Risk of bias scores should be interpreted with caution, as existing critical appraisal approaches may not adequately capture culturally relevant methodological considerations. Future research should aim to develop more appropriate tools for critically appraising research involving Indigenous populations. This systematic review was registered in the OSF registry, with registration number 10.17605/OSF.IO/436Q8.

articles_hidden.title: The Cultural Evolution of Analytic and Holistic Thought: How Informational Ecologies shape Bayesian Reasoning
articles_hidden.authors: Tian Chen Zeng; Ivan Kroupin; Rahul Bhui; Joseph Henrich
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing body of evidence suggests that human cognition is shaped by culture, affecting processes from attention and memory to causal inference and concept representation. Such psychological differences are often described in terms of the analytic-holistic spectrum of cognitive styles. However, a unified mechanistic account of this variation remains elusive. In this paper, drawing on concepts from computational cognitive science and cultural evolution, we propose that the analytic-holistic spectrum reflects cognitive adaptations to different information ecologies. Cultural traits such as social organization, communication norms and prevalent learning modalities determine how observations are sampled, thereby affecting how much people should weigh parsimony when building mental models. We propose that information ecologies associated with holistic thought produce observations that more loosely reflect underlying structure (``weak sampling''), whereas those associated with analytic thought produce more diagnostic observations (``strong sampling''). These regimes license weaker and stronger applications of Bayesian Occam's Razor, respectively, which we show can provide a unified mechanism for cognitive differences along the analytic-holistic spectrum. By offering a computational lens on one of the most prominent empirical patterns in cultural psychology, we pave the way toward further informational-ecological accounts of how culture shapes cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Virtue: Courage's Associations with Aversive Intentions and Behaviors and Dark Triad Traits
articles_hidden.authors: Grzegorz Pajestka; Katarzyna Skałacka
articles_hidden.abstract: Individual differences associated with aversive behavior have been linked primarily to antagonistic personality traits. Less is known about whether characteristics typically regarded as adaptive also contribute. Courage is traditionally viewed as a virtue, yet theoretical accounts suggest it may also facilitate socially aversive behaviors. This study tested whether two operationalizations—psychological courage (PC) and courage as a character strength (VIA-C)—predict aversive intentions and behaviors beyond Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy). A community sample of 711 Polish adults completed measures of PC, VIA-C, the Short Dark Triad, and aversive intentions and behaviors. Variable-centered analyses (hierarchical regressions, two-part models) controlling for age, gender, and Dark Triad traits revealed domain-specific effects: both courage measures predicted higher aggressive intentions and greater frequency of aggressive behaviors; VIA-C additionally predicted aggressive and sex-/drug-related behaviors. Neither courage measure related to theft, reckless driving, or self-destructive behaviors, and PC showed a small protective association with self-destructive intentions. Latent profile analysis identified four classes defined primarily by Dark Triad levels rather than courage; no high-courage/low-antagonism profile emerged. Overall, findings challenge unqualified valorization of courage and underscore the need to pair courage-building with ethical frameworks, empathy training, and prosocial goal setting to reduce iatrogenic risk.

articles_hidden.title: Self-identity in anorexia nervosa
articles_hidden.authors: Stephen Gadsby
articles_hidden.abstract: Anorexia nervosa is widely characterised as a disorder of the self, in which sufferers come to identify with their illness. Yet what such identification amounts to remains poorly understood. I argue that there are two distinct forms of self-identity involved, individual identity and group identity. These emerge at different time points, stem from different factors, and bear different clinical consequences. By unpacking this distinction, I provide a pluralistic and psychologically plausible account of self-identity in anorexia—one that illuminates the disorder’s tenacity and points to new ways of understanding it.

articles_hidden.title: Day-to-day fluctuations in craving and the value of drugs and food in daily life
articles_hidden.authors: Sergej Grunevski; Emmanuel E. Alvarez; Emma M. Schweitzer; Julia Kong; Sahar Hafezi; Anna B. Konova
articles_hidden.abstract: Craving is a powerful urge for a specific target (e.g., food, drugs) that prompts decisions directed at satisfying craving. While prior laboratory studies suggest craving biases behavior by amplifying target-specific value, the real-world generalizability of this mechanism remains unknown. We validate and extend these findings in a 28-day naturalistic smartphone-enabled study in patients with opioid use disorder (N=67) and community controls (N=49) who reported on their food (savory, sweet) and drug (opioid) urges and willingness-to-pay values. Despite person-level (mean) covariation, food and drug urges fluctuated largely independently within individuals while maintaining target-specific relationships with value. Using dynamics in drug urge and value and computational modeling, we isolated a distinct, ecologically relevant craving “state” tied to drug cue exposure and drug use in daily life. This research shows craving acts on normative valuation processes in real-world decision making and offers a novel approach to infer clinically vulnerable moments for behavior change.

articles_hidden.title: Strategi Keluarga Tangguh Menjalani Pernikahan Jarak Jauh
articles_hidden.authors: Dwi Hardani Oktawirawan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Pernikahan jarak jauh terjalin karena berbagai macam latar belakang. Alasan yang mendasari bisa terkait dengan pekerjaan, pendidikan, hingga tugas keluarga. Hubungan yang dijalin dengan adanya jarak ruang tentu memunculkan berbagai tantangan. Permasalahan yang muncul seperti keterbatasan komunikasi, rasa kesepian, pembagian tugas dalam berkeluarga, hingga adanya kecurigaan terhadap pasangan dan potensi terjadinya perselingkuhan. Tantangan-tantangan tersebut harus dihadapi dengan berbagai macam strategi.

Berbagai macam upaya dapat dilakukan untuk menjaga kualitas dan ketahanan hubungan pernikahan jarak jauh. Upaya yang melibatkan pasangan bisa seperti menjaga komunikasi, terbuka, pengertian, menjaga komitmen, mengelola pembagian tugas, dan memaksimalkan waktu bertemu. Secara pribadi masing-masing pasangan dapat berpikir secara positif, melakukan aktivitas pengalihan, menjaga pergaulan, hingga cara lain dengan pendekatan religius. Adanya dukungan orang lain seperti teman dan keluarga juga dapat menjadi salah satu cara menjaga ketahanan hubungan pernikahan jarak jauh. Jarak yang secara fisik memisahkan pasangan tidak menjadi penghalang bagi keluarga pernikahan jarak jauh untuk membangun hubungan secara maksimal seperti keluarga lainnya.

articles_hidden.title: Old Test, New Tricks: Using Large Language Models to Generate New Divergent Thinking Test Items
articles_hidden.authors: Averie Elizabeth Linnell; Simone A Luchini; Austin Swanson; Roni Reiter-Palmon; Roger Beaty; Antonio Laverghetta
articles_hidden.abstract: Automated item generation (AIG) using large language models (LLMs) is emerging as a promising solution for scalable creativity assessments, yet the potential of AIG to create psychometrically rigorous creativity items has thus far received little attention. In the present study, we evaluated the psychometric properties of LLM-generated items for the classic Consequences task of divergent thinking, comparing them to human-written items. A sample of 192 undergraduates completed six Consequences tasks—two human-written, two standard LLM-generated, and two genre-inspired LLM-generated, drawing on sci-fi and fantasy themes—along with measures of personality, cognitive ability, and creative behavior. We found that LLM-generated items elicited significantly higher fluency and flexibility. Genre-inspired items (fantasy and sci-fi) additionally elicited higher originality, enjoyment, and positive valence ratings; LLM-generated items were similar to human-written items. Genre-inspired items did not unfairly advantage participants with more exposure to genre content, demonstrating measurement invariance. Together, these findings suggest that LLMs can generate consequences items with psychometric properties comparable to those of human-written items. We discuss the implications for creativity assessment, item bank development, and best practices for AIG in creativity research, and we provide the prompts we used for item generation to enable researchers to generate new Consequences items at scale.

articles_hidden.title: Shared and Divergent Multisensory Emotion Perception Deficits across Mild Cognitive Impairment, Alzheimer’s Disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia: A Systematic Review and Hierarchical Bayesian Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Yi Lin; Yangfan Lu; Enze Tang; Yang Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to decode others’ emotions from multisensory cues is central to social functioning. However, findings remain inconsistent regarding the extent to which this capacity is compromised in neurodegenerative diseases, leaving the underlying mechanisms unclear. This study aimed to delineate the shared and divergent patterns of multisensory emotion perception (MEP) deficits among clinically distinct populations of individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). We conducted a systematic review on 51 studies identified from Web of Science, MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO and PsycARTICLES to synthesize research trends in this field between 2001 and 2025. We applied a hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis (1,511 patients and 1,151 healthy controls) to quantify the deficits and their moderators. Meta-analytic results demonstrated a differential magnitude of MEP impairment across groups (FTD > AD > MCI), reflecting distinct socio-emotional vulnerabilities rather than a single disease continuum. Moderator analyses of 15 participant- and study-related factors showed that impairment magnitude was more strongly associated with age, sex, education, global cognitive functioning, publication year, and emotion category, and less strongly with region, paradigm, language, and modality. Sensitivity analyses indicated that these patterns remained robust to potential publication bias, though the results were less stable within the FTD cohort.
