We propose a Hierarchical Socio-Emotional Disintegration and Compensation Framework to explain the dynamic interplay between neurodegeneration-driven deficits and compensatory mechanisms. This framework advances mechanistic insight into the relationship between emotion and cognition, informing future clinical efforts to support the interpersonal well-being of aging populations.

articles_hidden.title: Validation of the Visual Perspective Questionnaire: Measuring Individual Differences in Own-Eyes and Observer-Like Perspectives in Autobiographical Memories
articles_hidden.authors: Peggy L. St. Jacques; Claudia Morales Valiente
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual perspective is a core feature of autobiographical remembering, yet relatively little is known about stable individual differences in the tendency to remember events from own-eyes (OE) and observer-like (OB) perspectives. The present study evaluated the psychometric properties of the Visual Perspective Questionnaire (VPQ), a brief four-item measure of OE and OB tendencies. Data were drawn from 15,043 undergraduate students, with convergent validity analyses conducted in a subsample of 1,712 participants. Reliability analyses supported scoring the VPQ as separate OE and OB dimensions. Simulation-based comparisons further revealed that the observed joint distribution of OE and OB more closely resembled a relatively independent framework than continuum or mutually exclusive alternatives. Extreme-profile analyses identified all four combinations of OE and OB, including high OE-high OB and low OE-low OB configurations that are difficult to accommodate within a strictly bipolar account. In the validation sample, OE and OB showed modest associations with object and spatial imagery, providing additional evidence of convergence with broader imagery tendencies. Together, the findings provide initial support for the VPQ as a brief measure of individual differences in visual perspective in autobiographical memory, and suggest that OE and OB are better represented as separate, coexisting dimensions than as opposite ends of a single continuum.

articles_hidden.title: How should fillers be selected for lineups? Comparing the match-to-description and match-to-suspect methods via a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Courtlyn Elkins; Myat Aung; Edwin James Burns; Ruth Horry
articles_hidden.abstract: Lineups should contain known-innocent individuals (fillers) who resemble the suspect. Two common filler selection methods are: the match-to-suspect method, where fillers are selected based on perceived similarity to the suspect; and the match-to-description method, where fillers are selected based on how closely they match the culprit description. This systematic review sought to examine how the match-to-description method has been implemented since it was first proposed and revealed the match-to-description method has been operationalised in various ways. Meta-analytic techniques were used to investigate how filler selection method impacts lineup outcomes. Results revealed the odds of making a suspect identification, both guilty and innocent suspect, are higher in lineups created using the match-to-description method than the match-to-suspect method. Results also revealed lineup construction method did not impact discriminability. However, the small number of studies directly comparing the methods limits our ability to draw conclusions. Thus, highlighting the need for high-powered, pre-registered research.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond speed and beyond prediction: The multi-faceted nature of speech processing in preschoolers and how it relates to language development
articles_hidden.authors: Meg Cychosz; Sonia Patrizi; Amy Martinez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Efficient language processing requires both prediction and flexible revision. Studies show young children can predict during online language processing, but less is known about their ability to quickly revise interpretations when initial predictions are infelicitous. We examined four- and
five-year-olds’ (N=60) phonological revision using an eye-tracking paradigm that captured children’s initial interpretation of a word and their subsequent revision and recovery. On average, word mispronunciations slowed children’s looks to the target object. But that average hid different responses: some children initially treated the mispronounced word as a new word before settling on the target one, while others treated it as the target word from the start. Standard analyses of children’s looking data often capture how quickly and completely looks converge on a target, not a trajectory that involves hypothesis and revision. We therefore characterized each child’s looking trajectory along numerous dimensions spanning mispronunciation sensitivity, rejection, recovery, and word-recognition efficiency. Children whose processing profiles showed the least rejection and revision had modestly lower vocabulary and phonological awareness scores, consistent with Bayesian inference and error-driven learning accounts in which the probabilistic prediction and resolution of mismatches may drive language development. Overall, preschoolers vary widely in how flexibly, not just how quickly, they interpret unexpected pronunciations, with implications for language development.

articles_hidden.title: Psychometric validation of the Spanish-language version of the Power of Food Scale in adults: convergent, discriminative, and trait–state associations with eating behavior and hunger
articles_hidden.authors: Sofia Abrevaya; Delfina Sarciat; Sofia Stancanelli
articles_hidden.abstract: The Power of Food Scale (PFS) is a widely used measure of hedonic hunger — the psychological impact of food environments on motivation to eat. No validated Spanish version exists for South American populations. This study adapted and validated an Argentine Spanish version of the PFS in 810 adults. Item analyses showed adequate variability and acceptable corrected item–total correlations. Internal consistency was high (α = .91). Parallel analysis and exploratory factor analysis supported the original three-factor structure. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated acceptable fit; a bifactor model showed improved fit with an Explained Common Variance of .73, supporting use of the total score. Measurement invariance across biological sex was established. Item response theory analyses confirmed adequate discrimination for most items. Convergent validity was supported by strong associations with hedonic eating, binge eating, and eating disorder symptoms, and negative associations with intuitive eating. PFS scores differentiated binge-eating severity groups (AUC = .86) and showed incremental validity over established measures. Regression-based normative data are provided. The Argentine Spanish PFS is a reliable and valid instrument for assessing hedonic hunger in adults.

articles_hidden.title: A Biosocial Approach to Molecular Research in Perinatal Mental Health: Insights from Allopregnanolone
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriella Mayne; Luwam Ghidei; K Joseph Hurt; Wei Perng; David P. Tracer
articles_hidden.abstract: Pregnancy requires dynamic physiological adaptation across multiple biological systems implicated in perinatal mental health. Researchers increasingly recognize the importance of social and structural determinants of maternal mental health, yet integrating these conditions with molecular research remains challenging. A biosocial approach builds on these efforts by asking what conditions – both biological and social – contribute to the molecular variation we observe. In this Perspective, we use allopregnanolone (ALLO), a progesterone-derived neuroactive steroid implicated in perinatal mental health, to illustrate this approach. Evidence reviewed here shows that ALLO is patterned across social and physiological contexts, while associations between ALLO and depression, anxiety, and psychosocial distress during pregnancy remain heterogeneous. These observations highlight two priorities for biosocial molecular research: better characterization of the contexts in which molecular variation occurs and direct testing of what those contexts contribute to our understanding of ALLO in perinatal mental health. A biosocial approach does not replace biological explanation with social explanation; it asks whether better characterization of both changes what we observe. This means measuring social experiences alongside physiological characteristics, then asking whether these conditions contribute to ALLO variation or shape its associations with psychosocial distress. Such approaches can investigate how adversity becomes biologically embodied and how supportive conditions may promote maternal adaptation and well-being. Recognizing biological plasticity is central to this work: molecular variation can reflect dynamic responses to ongoing conditions rather than fixed characteristics of individuals or populations. Molecular variation should not be treated as the endpoint of inquiry, but as a starting point.

articles_hidden.title: Thinking About What Others Think of Me: Engagement and Negativity of Self-Referential Mentalizing in Adolescent Internalizing Affect
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria Guazzelli Williamson; Gabriel León; Christopher James Machle; Ava Reck; Jennifer H Pfeifer
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescence is an important period for the development of mentalizing and self-referential processing, and a period of increased risk for internalizing disorders such as anxiety and depression. However, the relationships between these processes, particularly in adolescents’ daily lives, remain unclear. In this intensive longitudinal study, we investigate the relationship between two dimensions of self-referential mentalizing (SRM)—1) engagement in SRM, and 2) negativity of SRM—as well as their interaction, in relation to internalizing feelings and symptoms. 149 adolescent females (M = 16.26 years, Range = 13.83 to 20.38 years) completed one or more (M = 2.0 bursts completed per participant) 30-day diary bursts where they answered daily questions about 1) engagement in and 2) negativity of self-referential mentalizing (SRM) and daily feelings of anxiety and depression. They also completed questionnaires measuring severity of internalizing symptoms once at each burst. Using Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM), we find that, at the between-person level, while both SRM and negative SRM were associated with feelings of depression and anxiety, only negative SRM was significantly positively associated with feelings of depression and anxiety after controlling for SRM. Individual differences in SRM and negative SRM were also associated with psychiatric measures of generalized anxiety, overall anxiety, and depression. At the daily, within-person level, experiencing elevated SRM and negative SRM on a given day was associated with elevated feelings of anxiety and depression on that same day. Additionally, there was a significant interaction at the daily, within-person level such that daily SRM was more strongly associated with daily feelings of anxiety and depression when the content of that SRM was negative. Together, our findings suggest that negative SRM, in particular, may be key for understanding associations with overall feelings of depression/anxiety, as well as changes in daily affect at the within-person level. While SRM and feelings of depression and anxiety covary on a day-to-day basis, the strength of this daily coupling was largely unrelated to severity of internalizing symptoms, suggesting that these daily dynamics may represent normative, rather than clinical, processes—at least for female adolescents. Together, our findings highlight the importance of considering multiple dimensions of SRM jointly, with the negativity of SRM emerging as particularly important for understanding internalizing affect at both the between- and within-person level.

articles_hidden.title: Reporting of Race, Ethnicity, Sexual and Gender Minority Identity, and Youth Involvement in Evidence for Youth-Facing AI Mental Health Tools: Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Davis Austria; Farah Baklouti; Michael Arowolo; William T. Bryant; Charity Brown Griffin; Terri Collin Dilmore; Charlene Pope
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Youth-facing artificial intelligence (AI) mental health tools have moved from research prototypes to consumer products at scale, and nearly three in four (72%) US adolescents report having used an AI companion. Racial and ethnic minority and sexual and gender minority (SGM) youth carry a disproportionate mental health burden, yet how often the evidence for these tools reports who was studied has not, to our knowledge, been measured. The nearest prior review found race or ethnicity reported in 34 of 88 studies and examined gender-related indicators in none.
Objective: To measure what proportion of studies of youth-facing AI mental health tools report participants' race and ethnicity and SGM status; which groups are represented; whether outcomes are disaggregated by identity; the extent of minoritized youth involvement in design, development, or evaluation; and how reporting has changed from 2020 to 2026 and between rule-based and generative systems.
Methods: Scoping review under JBI methodology, reported against PRISMA-ScR, prospectively registered (OSF 10.17605/OSF.IO/XUZAE). Five databases were searched (2020 to 2026) with no identity term in any search string, because absence of identity reporting cannot be measured in a corpus selected on its presence. Search recall was validated against a seed set (88.6% as prespecified, 62/70; 91.1% under the operative eligibility interpretation, 82/90; 100% on the highest-priority tier under both). Identity reporting was charted for every study—absence is data.
Results: 100 studies were included. 42 of 100 (42.0%) reported neither race/ethnicity nor SGM status; 27 (27.0%) reported both. Decomposed into sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) data elements, race/ethnicity was reported in 42 (42.0%), gender identity in 41 (41.0%), and sexual orientation in 14 (14.0%). Outcomes were disaggregated by identity in 19 (19.0%). Involvement of minoritized youth in design, development, or evaluation was documented in 10 (10.0%), and in 0 of 36 studies of generative systems, against 6 of 40 (15.0%) rule-based conversational agent studies.
Conclusions: The evidence base for youth AI mental health tools under-reports the identities of the youth it studies; gender-identity reporting was more common in studies published from 2023 to 2026 than in studies published from 2020 to 2022, whereas sexual-orientation reporting remained uncommon in both periods; and participatory involvement of minoritized youth is unreported in the generative literature (0 of 36 studies). Reporting completeness is an actionable target for journals, funders, and developers.

articles_hidden.title: Digital Mental Health Tools to Support Evidence-Based Treatments in Youth Psychotherapy: A Mixed Methods Study
articles_hidden.authors: Josephine Halporn; John Parkhurst; Galen D. McNeil; Ruben G. Martinez; Ren Mondesir; Tierney McMahon; Ashley A. Knapp; Guo Sisi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mental health clinicians in private practice represent approximately half of the outpatient workforce. Clinicians in this environment have more global negative attitudes toward implementing evidence-based treatments (EBTs), despite the proven efficacy of EBTs in treating children and adolescents. Digital mental health (DMH) tools may help streamline EBT implementation, thus reducing demands on clinicians. However, little is known about how clinicians in this group perceive and use DMH tools with youth. 

Objective: This mixed methods study examined how clinicians in private practice currently use and perceive DMH tools. 

Method: Explanatory sequential design included survey data collection from 79 master’s- and doctoral-level licensed clinicians in two large, diverse urban regions within the U.S. Qualitative interviews were completed subsequently with 15 clinicians for purposes of thematic analysis. 

Results: More than half of survey participants endorsed currently using DMH tools (60.9%, n = 39) or being open to doing so (34.4%, n = 22). Those already open to and experienced in EBTs viewed DMH tools most favorably. Qualitative findings provided key insights into how clinicians are using DMH tools, as well as facilitators and barriers to their use.

Conclusions: DMH tools are being used to support elements of EBTs, and could reduce time spent out of session on tracking, preparation, and documentation for private practice clinicians. Future research should address barriers identified here in user-centered design processes with this group.

articles_hidden.title: Processing Speed, Not Multitasking, Drives Expert Decision-Making Under Pressure
articles_hidden.authors: Eleanor Ruth Alice Hyde; Robert Schmidt; Daniel J. Carroll; Claudia Christina von Bastian
articles_hidden.abstract: The cognitive mechanism underlying high performance during decision-making under pressure – such as in first-person shooter (FPS) games – is still unclear: advantages in multitasking or general processing speed? To resolve this, we classified N = 230 players (16-34 years) of the video game Counter-Strike into four expertise clusters (Novice, Skilled, Emerging, Expert), assessing their processing speed and task-switching performance. To better understand the source of expertise effects, we used drift-diffusion modelling (DDM) to estimate non-decision and decision components of performance. Experts exhibited significantly faster reaction times than Novices, but no specific multitasking advantage was observed. The DDM revealed that this speed advantage was driven by higher drift rates and shorter non-decision times. No expertise-related differences were found in boundary separation, the strategic component of decision-making. Findings suggest that expert performance in decision-making under pressure is characterised by advantages in general processing speed rather than being associated with greater multitasking capabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Impact of Soundscapes on Mental Well-Being and Physiological Stress: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Harley Glassman; Brandon T. Paul; Frank Russo
articles_hidden.abstract: Soundscapes represent the acoustic environment perceived by humans, a phenomenon that holds significant implications for psychological and physiological health. While urban noise is a known stressor, natural soundscapes are theorized to provide restorative benefits through mechanisms which replenish cognitive resources subserving mental well-being. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence from peer-reviewed literature to examine how diverse acoustic environments impact mental well-being and physiological markers. A comprehensive search across scholarly databases identified ten studies spanning urban, natural, and virtual reality settings. The evidence was evaluated for certainty and risk of bias to ensure the current literature was synthesized rigorously. Qualitative findings indicated that natural soundscapes (e.g., birdsong, water sound) consistently facilitate faster stress recovery, lower heart rate, and reduced skin conductance compared to anthropogenic noise. Neuroimaging data further suggested that exposure to natural sounds correlates with decreased activity in brain regions associated with stress regulation. Quantitative findings confirmed a positive effect of pleasant soundscapes on health outcomes, though significant heterogeneity was observed across studies, likely reflecting diverse methodologies and environmental contexts. Individual differences, including noise sensitivity and personality traits, were found to moderate these effects. These results support Restorative Environment Theory and suggest that integration of natural acoustic environments into urban planning and healthcare design may mitigate the negative impacts of noise pollution. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs to evaluate the chronic health effects of sustained soundscape exposure.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Large Language Model Diagnostic Classification in Neuropsychology
articles_hidden.authors: Anthony Hachem; Chloe Chui; Elliot T. Morgan; Ashika S. Bakre; Summer Rolin; Anthony Rios; Jeremy Davis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated promise in healthcare for clinical documentation and decision support. Much of the information in electronic medical records, however, is structured or clinician-synthesized documentation. There is less certainty about the capability of LLMs in devising clinically appropriate diagnostic hypotheses from unstructured data such as a patient interview.
Method: Deidentified clinical interview transcripts from 32 older adults referred for neuropsychological evaluation of memory complaints were submitted to 10 commercially available LLMs using an institutionally approved platform with a standardized prompt. Models classified each case using four categories: normal, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), dementia, or uncertain. Model classifications were compared with clinician reference diagnoses based on neuropsychological evaluation. 
Results: Model-inferred and reference diagnoses showed exact agreement rates from 18.8% to 56.2% with poor to slight chance-corrected agreement (Cohen’s κ = −.178 to .196). Classification errors across models were more often overclassification rather than underclassification. Using dichotomous cognitive status (i.e., normal versus impaired), seven of ten models showed sensitivity over 90% for identifying impairment, but specificity ranged from 0 to 60%. Workflow response time varied by model and was not associated with accuracy. 
Conclusions: Using unstructured and unannotated clinical interview data, general-purpose LLMs showed limited, model-dependent agreement with clinician diagnoses and a tendency to overclassify impairment. LLMs warrant further evaluation as tools that support clinical workflows, with revised prompting strategies and systematic efforts to improve classification.

articles_hidden.title: Oregon’s State-Regulated Psilocybin Services: Early Real-World Safety Signals
articles_hidden.authors: Jason B Luoma; Christina Chwyl; Dan Des Jarlais; Christopher Stauffer; Ximena Levander; Ryan Cook; Adie Wilson-Poe; Dennis McCarty; Philip Korthuis
articles_hidden.abstract: Interest in psilocybin has accelerated, with public access in the United States expanding through a rapidly evolving landscape of decriminalization, increased availability of psilocybin-containing products, and state-regulated facilitated service models (Hutchison et al., 2025). However, uptake may be advancing faster than the evidence base. Regulatory oversight is needed to inform population-level risk. Most supervised psilocybin safety data derive from clinical trials that enroll carefully screened participants and deliver interventions in tightly controlled settings. This limits the generalizability of safety data to the broader populations likely to seek services if psilocybin products are authorized for medical use in the United States (Tan et al., 2022).

articles_hidden.title: “The sun will still rise whether you’re an Olympian or not”: Exploring the changes in psychological state across four phases of injury rehabilitation among international figure skaters
articles_hidden.authors: Jamie Smokler; Isabelle Simm
articles_hidden.abstract: Injury is inherent within elite sport, often resulting in significant physical and psychological challenges. However, limited research has explored how elite figure skaters experience and interpret injury within the unique demands of their sport. This study aimed to examine the lived experiences of injury and rehabilitation among elite, international figure skaters. Eleven skaters (7 female, 4 male, M age = 24.09 years, SD = 4.36) with an average of 18.64 years of skating experience (SD = 4.15) participated in semi-structured interviews, derived from sport injury rehabilitation literature, conducted via Microsoft Teams. Interviews ranged from 31 to 102 minutes (M = 62.81, SD = 25.60). Data were analysed using a reflexive thematic analysis. Analysis revealed two overarching themes that progressed across injury recovery: psychological adaptation and reconstruction of athletic identity. Findings indicated that skaters initially experienced shock and catastrophic thinking, before progressing through sustained uncertainty, and active coping. Injury also challenged athletes’ sense of self, with skaters describing loss of purpose, and subsequent identity reconstruction though increased self-awareness and resilience. Evaluations, future research directions, and implications of findings are also discussed. Overall, findings highlight injury recovery as both psychological and physical, emphasising the importance of psychologically informed support throughout injury recovery.

articles_hidden.title: Neural Signatures of Impulsivity in Adolescence: A Multivariate Pattern Analysis of Reward and Loss Processing
articles_hidden.authors: Stefanie Fraga Gonçalves; Morgan Lindenmuth; Helmet Talib Karim; Rasim Diler; Cecile D. Ladouceur
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents experience mood disturbances and impulsivity that increase vulnerability to maladaptive risk-taking, yet the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of these phenotypes remain poorly understood. Thus, the current pre-registered study sought to optimize models predicting anhedonic, sad, and manic mood, as well as impulsivity, from multivariate frontostriatal neural responses during incentive (i.e., reward and loss) processing. Participants were adolescents (n=153, healthy 12–18-year-olds, 104 assigned female at birth) with moderate to severe depression, as well as some controls, to have a full range of symptoms. They underwent functional neuroimaging during a monetary incentive delay task and completed self-report questionnaires on mood and impulsivity. We optimized a pre-registered 3-fold nested cross-validation support vector regression model predicting impulsivity, which showed statistically significant but small predictive performance (R² = .02, MAE = .81). Feature importance analyses showed distributed signal across frontostriatal circuits, particularly cognitive and motor-related circuits. In addition, neural activity to loss anticipation followed by reward receipt and reward anticipation contributed most to model performance. As a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the model with depression-residualized impulsivity to account for shared variance with depressive symptoms. This model showed modestly improved predictive performance (R² = .04, MAE = .80) with a similar pattern of feature contributions. No models successfully predicted anhedonic, sad, or manic mood. These findings suggest that multivariate neural activity within cognitive- and motor-related frontostriatal circuits during incentive processing is associated with impulsivity, and not mood disturbances, in adolescents, including those with mild to moderate depression. Public health efforts aimed at reducing impulsivity (and potentially risk-taking) should consider the role of incentive processing.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Factor Structure: Item-Level Functioning and Measurement Invariance of the ERQ-CA in Brazilian Children and Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Dannielle Melo Nunes; Pedro de Leon Brito; Leandro da Silva Sauer; André Luiz de Carvalho Braule Pinto
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined the structural and item-level psychometric properties of the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire for Children and Adolescents (ERQ-CA) in 525 Brazilian youth aged 8–17 years (M = 13.84; SD = 3.18), of both sexes (50.87% girls), enrolled in public schools. Participants completed the ERQ-CA and mental health and well-being measures. We evaluated the proposed two-factor structure, measurement invariance across sex and age, item discrimination and threshold parameters using Item Response Theory (IRT), Differential Item Functioning (DIF), and associations with external indicators. The results provided partial support for two-factor model, with heterogeneous global fit indices and evidence of localized residual dependence. Measurement invariance analyses supported equality of factor loadings and thresholds across sex and age. Sensitivity analyses indicated that age-related loading invariance was somewhat dependent on how the age groups were defined. DIF was detected in two Suppression items, but its score-level impact was minimal for sex and small but detectable for age. Associations with external variables were predominantly small to moderate in magnitude and showed distinct patterns for Reappraisal and Suppression. Overall, the findings support the interpretability of the ERQ-CA while also identifying localized model limitations and group-related item functioning that should be considered when interpreting scores.

articles_hidden.title: Lifetime Prevalence and Co-occurrence of Offensive Gun Use, Defensive Gun Use, and Nonfatal Firearm Victimization in a National Sample of US Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Brian M. Hicks; Dorothy Stearns; Amanda Price; Mark A. Ilgen
articles_hidden.abstract: Firearm-related encounters have the potential for high risk of injury, but few studies have estimated the prevalence and co-occurrence among offensive gun use (OGU), defensive gun use (DGU), and nonfatal firearm victimization (NFV) in a national sample. We did so with data from the National Firearms, Alcohol, Cannabis, and Suicide survey (N = 7034) of US adults that assessed broad definitions of gun use and victimization (e.g., gun displays to shootings). Lifetime prevalence was 5.2% (95% CI 4.5% to 6.0%) for OGU, 12.6% (95% CI 11.5% to 13.7%) for DGU, and 31.5% (95% CI 30.0% to 33.0%) for NFV. Using survey weights to extrapolate to the US adult population, we estimate nearly 13.9 million adults have used a gun offensively, 33.3 million have used a gun defensively, and 83.3 million have experienced NFV in their lifetime. Most respondents (~80%) only reported gun use and victimization that did not involve firing a gun. There was a high rate of co-occurrence between OGU and DGU (OR = 33.8, 95% CI 23.7 to 48.0), and between NFV and OGU (OR = 5.3, 95% CI 3.9 to 7.2) and DGU (OR = 4.5, 95% CI 3.7 to 5.6). Rates of OGU, DGU, and/or NFV were higher among respondents who were males, lower income, lived in more dangerous neighborhoods, current gun owners, and had a job that required carrying a firearm. Occupational firearm carriage was associated with especially high rates of OGU (20.5%, 95% CI 15.8% to 26.1%), DGU (49.6%, 95% CI 43.9% to 55.2%), and NFV (50.9%, 95% CI 45.2% to 56.5%). A large minority of Americans have had a firearm-related victimization experience, and a smaller but substantial proportion have used a gun for defense. OGU, DGU, and NFV frequently co-occur but event-level information is needed to delineate the mechanisms of overlap.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Average Changes: How the Distribution of Youth Mental Health Shifted Before, During, and After the COVID-19 Pandemic
articles_hidden.authors: Lianne P. de Vries; Elske Marra; Imme Rahmon; Tinca JC Polderman; Meike Bartels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Stress can affect not only average levels of mental health, but also how positive and negative aspects of mental health relate to one another. The COVID-19 pandemic provides a unique context to examine those population-level differences. We investigated youth mental health before, during, and after the pandemic by examining mean levels, association between wellbeing and depressive symptoms, and latent mental health profiles.
	Using large population-based samples from the Netherlands of youth aged 12–25 years, we compared mental health before (N = 14,146, 58% female), during (N = 14,308, 55% female), and after the pandemic (N = 37,797, 62% female) in a repeated cross-sectional design.
	Wellbeing and depressive symptoms were stronger correlated during (r = −.70) and after the pandemic (r = −.69) compared to pre-pandemic (r = −.49, ps < .001). Latent profile analyses further showed differences in the population distribution of mental health. Pre-pandemic, two profiles were identified, whereas during and after the pandemic three-profile solutions provided the best fit, including a large group with intermediate levels of wellbeing and depressive symptoms (38-40%). Across periods, most youth were classified in a high mental health profile (51-86%), whereas a smaller proportion were classified in a low mental health profile (8-14%). Loneliness, self-rated health, optimism, and stress exposure consistently differed between profiles. 
	Youth mental health differed across periods in average levels, the strength of the association, and distribution of wellbeing and depressive symptoms. These findings show the value of moving beyond average effects when studying population responses to large-scale stress.

articles_hidden.title: Mere co-presence and evaluative observation differentially shape motor response execution and inhibition: Behavioral, signal-detection, and ERP evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Cuihong Liu; Guoliang Chen; Yi Wei; Yansong Li
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined how mere co-presence and evaluative observation shape motor response execution and inhibition in a Go/NoGo (GNG) task. In Experiment 1, 199 participants were randomly assigned to mere co-presence, evaluative observation, or control. Mere co-presence slowed Go responses and reduced self-reported concentration relative to both other groups without affecting Go accuracy or the NoGo commission error rate relative to control. Only in this group was slower responding associated with greater perceptual sensitivity (d′), suggesting compensatory slowing. By contrast, evaluative observation reduced the NoGo commission error rate and increased d′ relative to both other groups without affecting Go performance relative to control. Experiment 2 used a within-subject event-related potential (ERP) design (N = 44) and replicated the lower NoGo commission error rate and higher d′ under evaluative observation without affecting Go performance. Additionally, evaluative observation produced evaluation-related affective costs—increased evaluative pressure and anxiety—that predicted smaller d′ gains and attenuated its benefit in mediation analyses. Eletrophysiologically, evaluative observation attenuated NoGo-N2 and NoGo-P3 amplitudes without affecting Go components, suggesting that enhanced Go–NoGo discrimination facilitated inhibition by reducing early conflict-monitoring and later reactive-control demands. These findings suggest two dissociable pathways through which distinct forms of social presence shapes motor control.

articles_hidden.title: The Link between Warm Glow and Pro-Environmental Behaviors is Positive and Robust: A Scoping Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Linli Zhou; Cameron Brick; Disa Sauter
articles_hidden.abstract: When we engage in pro-environmental behaviors that align with our personal values, we can experience positive feelings, known as warm glow. Theories suggest a potential positive feedback loop such that people who anticipate feeling more warm glow are more likely to act pro-environmentally, and acting in line with their personal values may in turn elicit warm glow, thereby encouraging further pro-environmental behavior. There is considerable empirical work from psychology, marketing and economics investigating these relationships, but to date this work has not been systematically synthesized. A test of the strength and robustness of the theorized links is needed to answer the question of whether warm glow is in fact consistently related to pro-environmental behavior. We report a scoping review and meta-analysis probing the robustness of the associations between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Following the PRISMA guidance, we identified 94 papers with 251 effects based on 58,313 participants. A pre-registered three-level random-effects meta-analytic model was used to estimate overall effects and to examine moderation by behavioral domain and measurement approach. Sensitivity analyses were performed to test the robustness of the findings. Results indicate robust medium-to-large associations between both anticipated and experienced warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors (rs: .43 – .53). Substantial heterogeneity persisted after accounting for moderators, suggesting meaningful variation in effect sizes across studies. Overall, these findings provide strong evidence of a clear link between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Future research using experimental and longitudinal designs will help clarify causal pathways in the positive feedback loop.

articles_hidden.title: Towards Inclusive Developmental Science: Translating Community Perspectives into Research Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Maheen Siddiqui; Rianne Haartsen; Anita Song; Roksana Seif Amirhosseini; Ana Maria Portugal; Chiara Bulgarelli; Anna Gui
articles_hidden.abstract: Developmental science continues to face challenges in engaging diverse families and ensuring diversity within the research workforce, limiting whose experiences and perspectives are represented in research. This study provides an empirically grounded, parent-informed account of the barriers and conditions that shape inclusive research practice. We conducted three participatory focus groups with parents from ethnic minority backgrounds in the UK (n = 17; two online, one hybrid). Transcripts were analysed using thematic analysis and integrated with insights accumulated across a year of Diversity in Developmental Science Network activities, including an online seminar series and conference panel. Findings were organised into four themes: barriers and enablers to research participation; building trust with communities; inclusive research design and transparency; and representation and cultural safety. Parents highlighted accessible and flexible practices, meaningful representation, culturally responsive materials, transparent communication, and stronger researcher-community relationships. Network activities further highlighted structural barriers and diversity within research teams.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Average Effects: Childhood SES and the Shape of Adult Well-Being Distributions
articles_hidden.authors: Jinrui Liu; Shigehiro Oishi; Espen Røysamb
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on socioeconomic inequality and wellbeing focuses largely on mean-level analyses, leaving a distributional question underexamined: whether childhood financial circumstances (childSES) relate to not only where individuals land on average, but also who gains access to favorable outcomes and who remains at the lower end of the distribution. Using U.S. adult data from MIDUS 1 (N = 5570-5603), we applied generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS) to examine associations between childSES and life satisfaction (LS) and personal growth (PG) across mean, dispersion, and ceiling probability. Higher childSES was associated with higher mean LS and ~4% lower dispersion, reflecting a floor-buffering rather than ceiling-lifting effect. For PG, higher childSES was associated with greater odds of reaching the maximum score (OR = 1.15). These patterns largely replicated in MIDUS 2 (N = 3,541-3,556) and persisted after accounting for adultSES. Findings are limited to a U.S. sample from 1995-1996.

articles_hidden.title: Repurposing, redefining, and reimagining: A paradigm shift towards person-driven neuroscience in the digital age
articles_hidden.authors: Becky Inkster; Mark Sheppard
articles_hidden.abstract: The focus of neuroscience has traditionally hinged on collecting quantifiable physiological data that are often distanced from the lived experiences of people. In contrast, qualitative, subjective, and situational information provides rich context, but lacks the empirical precision needed to map to neural processes. To reconcile this gap, we established ‘The Lαβ’ as an interdisciplinary initiative that fuses person-driven experiences, personal reflection, and empirical neuroscience. People engage with their chosen experiences in their chosen settings while wearing a portable EEG headset. Timestamped information is then collected from a variety of sources. We introduce our novel neurotriangulation approach: A person‑driven synthesis of quantitative electrophysiological signals, qualitative observations, and subjective and situational information into a single analytic stream. Our aim is to provide people with opportunities for neuro-self-reflection. We use an ethics-first approach to preserve data sovereignty, privacy, autonomy, and agency for the individual. In this paper, we present real-world case studies to demonstrate our data collection, real-time field analysis, and co-interpretation methodologies. These case studies also underscore the neurotriangulation model as an approach to move beyond reductive, data-centric models toward a person‑driven paradigm. This shift allows neurodata to be more accessible, inclusive, and personally meaningful, while prioritising safety and subjectivity. This has the potential to reshape how we think about neuroscientific applications in fields such as education and training, anthropology, creative arts, wellbeing, and mental health. By repurposing and redefining the use of extant neurotechnology, we are reimagining a future in which our understanding of ourselves is person-driven, reality-based, and ethically sound.

articles_hidden.title: Bridging the Trust Gap: A Contractualist Framework for Trustworthy AI
articles_hidden.authors: Luis Marcos Vidal; Clara Pretus
articles_hidden.abstract: Trustworthy AI is defined by properties built into a system, but trust depends on how users perceive it, so a system can meet every requirement and still fail to be trusted. Human and artificial agents that justify decisions in contractualist terms, by appeal to what affected parties could reasonably accept, are trusted more than those that appeal to aggregate welfare or fixed rules, irrespective of the action selected, but why is unexplained. We propose that a contractualist justification discloses individualized regard, evidence that the affected party's standpoint entered the decision, which is what trust, as a judgment that an agent is willing to act well, is sensitive to. Perceived regard is the mediating inference and raises trust through two pathways: warmth, and the expectation that the agent's future decisions will take the perceiver's own stakes into account. The intentional stance is a gating condition rather than a mediator, deciding whether an agent can be the object of this inference at all, so the mechanism is shared by human and artificial agents and needs no genuine intentions. Such justification is the observable trace of virtual bargaining, a theory-of-mind process, and does not require agents with genuine mental states. We state five falsifiable hypotheses that discriminate the account from warmth, anthropomorphism, and mere-transparency alternatives, and identify moderators and a possible moral uncanny valley as further tests.

articles_hidden.title: Art Therapy for Recovery from Childhood Trauma in a Vietnamese Adolescent: A Case Study
articles_hidden.authors: THANH TU NGUYEN
articles_hidden.abstract: Childhood trauma is associated with self-injury and suicidal behaviour, yet traumatised young people often cannot put their experiences into words, particularly where family hierarchies limit emotional disclosure between children and parents, as in Vietnam. This case study describes a 17-year-old Vietnamese girl ("Lily") who presented with severe non-suicidal self-injury and previously undisclosed suicide attempts rooted in childhood adversity. She received a 12-session, three-phase intervention comprising House-Tree-Person (HTP) art therapy, prosocial community action and structured family sessions. Session records, journal entries, field notes and parent interviews were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, and pre- and post-intervention drawings using compositional and iconographic visual analysis. Three themes were generated: art as a bridge to concealed trauma; consolidation of gains through prosocial agency; and relational repair within the family. The final drawing was interpreted as reflecting psychological integration and post-traumatic growth. Art therapy, supported by family engagement, the young person's active cooperation and a compassionate therapeutic relationship, may offer a culturally responsive pathway to recovery. Findings from a single, clinician-interpreted case without long-term follow-up are illustrative and require further study.

articles_hidden.title: Antenatal infant sleep information in Western Australia: A mixed-methods study of what parents received and what they wanted
articles_hidden.authors: Heather Liebregts; Alex Metse; Andrea R. Steele; Kelli Kathleen MacMillan; Rhonda Marriott; Renita Almeida
articles_hidden.abstract:
Problem. Pregnancy is a finite window wherein parents' expectations of infant care develop, yet parents’ experiences of and preferences for antenatal infant sleep preparation are uncharacterised. 

Background. Parents in Western settings commonly report infant sleep problems, and interventions are predominantly behavioural. Antenatal provision addresses sleep safety rather than developmental-relational preparation. 

Aim. To describe what antenatal infant sleep information Western Australian parents received, their satisfaction, preferences for its timing and provider, and what they wished they had received.

Methods. A mixed-methods online survey of 185 Western Australian parents and expectant parents (180 with a child aged 0–3 years; five pregnant). Closed items addressed information received, satisfaction, and preferences; an open-ended item was analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

Findings. Just over half (53.5%; 99/185) received no antenatal information; where provided, midwives were the most frequent source (34.0%; 63/185) and satisfaction was modest. The antenatal period and first month were most endorsed (75.0%, 135/180; 66.1%, 119/180), with child health nurses (35.6%; 64/180) and midwives (30.6%; 55/180) preferred as providers. Four themes captured parents’ preferences: preparation for likely bedsharing; recalibrated expectations; validation of responsive caregiving; and non-prescriptive guidance.

Discussion. Provision was limited and only moderately satisfying. Parents sought guidance positioning them as decision-makers engaging with biologically typical infant behaviour. 

Conclusion. Relational, non-prescriptive preparation, including how to bedshare more safely, initiated antenatally by midwives and continued postnatally by child health nurses, would address an unmet need within existing perinatal care.

articles_hidden.title: Roles of conceptual development in the training and acquisition of compassion practices
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Condon; Lawrence Barsalou
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conceptual development is a fundamental feature of contemplative practice but has received little attention in contemplative science. In Buddhism, for example, the eightfold path begins with right view, which includes comprehension of interdependence, suffering, and so on. In Tibetan traditions, foundational practices introduce conceptual frames, including aphorisms and visualizations, that help access capacities for compassion and wisdom. In this article, we take a lifespan approach to examine how conceptual development supports compassion training. We focus on relational practices adapted from Tibetan Buddhism, which involve calling to mind sources of love, comfort, and safety to establish a secure base and an internal holding environment–an embodied stance of stillness, curiosity, and care for all physical and mental patterns. The theory of situated conceptualization (TSC) provides a nuanced cognitive neuroscience framework for understanding how situated and embodied experiences develop into conceptual knowledge across the lifespan, and it holds significant implications for how these practices can mature within a person over time.
	According to TSC, when meditations of compassion are engaged, the physical and affective qualities that occur within practice, such as warmth, care, and ease, can become part of the background conceptual knowledge for any mental pattern that arises within meditation. Over time, these qualities may increasingly emerge within the foreground of a given conceptualization. As patterns of mind are experienced and understood for what they are within an internal holding environment, the ruminative processes that fuel conceptualization can relax, and the constructed, empty nature of concepts and emotional states can more readily reveal itself–a process that supports advanced wisdom practices. Finally, because conceptualizations are situated in social and cultural contexts, the internal holding environment for patterns of mind can extend to all webs of connection that influence those patterns, becoming increasingly a capacity of compassion for the world at large.

articles_hidden.title: A Community-Based Implementation of The Family Check-up Is Associated with Lower Pediatric Emergency Room Utilization and Acute Care Services: A Health Service Utilization and Cost Analysis Study
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Schweer-Collins; Jonathan Woodward; Elizabeth Stormshak
articles_hidden.abstract: A large number of studies have shown that the brief three session Family Check-Up intervention is effective in promoting children’s social and behavioral development and in reducing problem behaviors. Research in this area has begun to examine the effectiveness of this program through real-world implementation studies. This brief report describes how a community-based implementation of the Family Check-Up is associated with reduced healthcare utilization, specifically acute care services including emergency department, inpatient, and urgent care utilization. Future implementation trials may benefit from including administrative data to examine the outcomes of the Family Check-Up in conjunction with cost and service utilization data.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond accuracy: extracting reaction-time biomarkers of sustained attention and cognitive flexibility from the UCancellation task
articles_hidden.authors: Boris Penaloza; Elnaz Vafaei; Anja Pahor; Susanne M. Jaeggi; Aaron R. Seitz
articles_hidden.abstract: Cancellation tasks are widely used measures of attention but are conventionally scored by metrics such as mean accuracy or concentration scores, disregarding the temporal structure of responding. Here, we derive two reaction-time (RT) biomarkers from our tablet-based UCancellation task in 388 young adults: intra-individual RT variability (RTV), a marker of sustained attention, and switch cost, an index of cognitive flexibility from transitions between two different task's target categories. Because consecutive targets are separated by a variable number of scanned distractors, both are confounded by search effort, which we remove with a scanning-load (p) correction framework. RTV behaved as a scored individual-difference measure: correction improved reliability and convergent validity against TOVA low-frequency RTV (n = 373), and a cross-target composite was the most reliable index. Switch cost behaved as a within-task phenomenon whose sign reversed with load—large and positive when targets were adjacent, reversing as scanning load increased—consistent with inhibition of return. Together, these metrics show that RT structure within a brief cancellation task carries attentional information that standard metrics alone does not capture.

articles.title: “AI” as gaslighting – Considering the affordances of stochastic generative systems in relation to anthropo-centered epistemic operations
articles.authors: Daniel Cardoso
articles.abstract:
This paper mobilizes the notion of ‘AI’ as a carcinogen, as developed by Berman, to then inquire and analyze what is the possible human impact that results from the democratization of the use of Large Language Models and Generative Pretrained Transformers, from the perspective of how epistemic frameworks are mobilized as a core component of sociability.
It then advances the proposal that we understand ‘AI’ as a case of the ‘Thomas Theorem’, and that, as such, LLMs and GPTs can effectively operate as systems of non-targeted, non-intentional, gaslighting.
From that approach, the paper follows up with a materially-grounded analysis of how the operations performed on data for the creation and usage of LLMs and GPTs mean that these technologies have the affordance of being episteme-fixative, and that such an affordance (as defined here) is specific to these technologies, in a way that allows for non-essentialist and non-deterministic analysis that considers both changes and continuities in both media systems and our everyday engagement with them.
It concludes by suggesting venues of inquiry that are made easier by the previous conclusions, and returns to capitalism’s uptake of technology, rather than to any immanent aspect of technology, as a central aspect to consider in evaluating the epistemic harms that might come out of these affordances.

articles.title: “Safe for now?” Boundary work and tensions of AI Adoption in Sign Language Interpreting and Speech-to-Text Reporting in Belgium and the Netherlands
articles.authors: Maartje De Meulder; Karolien Gebruers; Deborah Giustini
articles.abstract:
Abstract
This article examines how sign language interpreters (SLIs) and speech-to-text reporters (STTRs) in Belgium (Flanders) and the Netherlands understand and navigate artificial intelligence (AI)-driven language technologies in their professional lives. While speech-to-text reporting already faces displacement by automated transcription, sign language interpreting remains partly sheltered by the limited AI training data for Flemish and Dutch Sign Language. Drawing on an online survey (N = 134) conducted in 2025, and theorized through  boundary work, we identify three tensions structuring practitioners' accounts: a temporality tension, in which anticipated disruption coexists with present stability; an access tension, in which AI expands available options while enabling institutions to narrow the definition of "sufficient access"; and a professional identity tension, in which the technology threatening practitioners' livelihoods may simultaneously advance the profession's own emancipatory ideal. Respondents describe AI as a new third actor in interpreted interaction, shifting some practitioners toward editing and quality-control roles that lack institutional recognition. We argue that AI in language access is actively produced through practitioners’ ongoing boundary work and calls for recognizing them — alongside deaf consumers — as epistemic actors in governing just technological transitions.

articles.title: Associations between content and engagement vary across social media communities
articles.authors: Alberto Acerbi
articles.abstract: Research on social media engagement often seeks general content features that are associated with online success. However, social media platforms contain communities with different audiences, topics, and norms, and the same features may have different associations with engagement within different communities. This research considers 1,078,044 items from 587 communities in five corpora spanning Reddit, Stack Exchange, X, and YouTube. For each corpus, negativity, moralization, arousal, and in-group versus out-group language were measured. Their relationships with engagement were compared using multilevel models imposing one within-community slope per feature with models allowing slopes to vary across communities. Varying-slope models fit the data better in all five corpora. The estimated community slopes varied substantially in magnitude and, frequently, direction. Nevertheless, the average slopes from the varying-slope models remained small. The improved fit therefore reflects heterogeneity across communities rather than stronger average associations. These findings show that a weak average association can conceal stronger but opposing associations across communities. General claims about the content associated with social media engagement need to account for the specific communities in which that content appears.

articles.title: An Empirical Model of Mobile App Competition: The Role of the Revenue-Source Channel
articles.authors: Kohei Kawaguchi; Susumu Sato; Toshifumi Kuroda
articles.abstract: Mobile apps can earn revenue from download fees, in-app purchases, and in-app advertising, and mixed business models coexist within a market, unlike in many familiar markets where firms rely primarily on a single price per product. Because developers choose these revenue sources jointly, a shock to one source can induce adjustments in the others, including the activation or shutdown of a source, a mechanism we call the revenue-source channel. We develop an empirical model of app competition in download prices, usage prices, and advertising intensities, in which developers endogenously determine their business models. The model admits a competition-in-utility formulation that yields a tractable equilibrium characterization and a unified measure of disutility that applies to zero-priced apps. We estimate the model using data on roleplaying apps in the Japanese Google Play market during 2015–2017 and use it to assess how horizontal mergers, changes in platform transaction fees, and changes in advertisement prices affect app developers and consumers. In a merger of a paid app and a free app, a cost synergy at the free app is not passed through to consumers, whereas a quality synergy raises consumer surplus. A lower platform transaction fee can raise the average download price when previously free apps begin charging, while consumer surplus still rises. A higher advertisement price raises advertising intensity and slightly lowers usage prices, while modestly increasing consumer surplus, app profit, and platform revenue. These results demonstrate the importance of zero-priced apps and the revenue-source channel in markets where multiple revenue sources coexist.

articles.title: Scrutiny, sanctions, and attacks on scholars: Public acceptance and perceived deservingness in Switzerland
articles.authors: Niels G. Mede; Julia Metag; Mike S. Schäfer
articles.abstract: Different forms of critical and hostile public engagement with science have been documented worldwide. They range from valuable scrutiny to public protests, support for funding cuts, and attacks. Whether people accept such engagement, and whether they consider it deserved, has rarely been studied with representative data. Using a preregistered, nationally representative survey from Switzerland (n = 698), we examine acceptance of public scrutiny, support for sanctions, and attacks on scholars and their perceived deservingness when scholars speak out politically. We find that acceptance follows a graded hierarchy: Most respondents accept scrutiny, fewer accept sanctions, and hardly anyone accepts attacks. Two thirds consider criticism of politically outspoken scholars deserved, whereas attacks are largely rejected, although noteworthy minorities consider them deserved. Acceptance of attacks is associated with science-related populist attitudes, right-leaning views, younger age, lower income, and active online engagement. Moreover, perceived political distance from scholars is associated with acceptance of scrutiny.

articles.title: How Model Choice Obscures Forecast Uncertainty: The Rashomon Effect and the 2026 Senate
articles.authors: Jack T. Rametta; Christopher Hare
articles.abstract: Election forecasts report ostensibly precise predictions that depend on modeling choices. These include the size of the incumbency advantage, the weight on state partisan lean, and how strongly national conditions move individual races. We show that the record of Senate elections between 2010 and 2024 is insufficient to adjudicate such choices. While hundreds of Senate races provide information about race-level relationships, the role of shared national conditions must be learned primarily from comparisons across only eight election cycles. Indeed, of 120 plausible models varying these weights, 117 predict past elections similarly well. This “Rashomon set” illustrates how different assumptions can produce comparable predictive performance but distinct substantive findings. Our reference model predicts a 50.6% chance of Democratic control of the 120th Senate with 50.5 expected seats (90% interval 45–56). The 117-model Rashomon set, however, puts the chances of Democratic control anywhere between 43.2% and 57.6%. We recommend reporting this range alongside conventional predictive intervals from a single model.

articles.title: Electoral systems shape the entry and entrenchment of extremist parties
articles.authors: Chanuwas Aswamenakul; Tyler Marghetis; Brad L. LeVeck; Paul E. Smaldino
articles.abstract: Representative democracies aspire to represent voters’ viewpoints through their elected officials. At the same time, they may try to minimize extremist viewpoints that can destabilize democracy itself. Here we show that electoral systems navigate this tension by trading off between two vulnerabilities: extremist entry and extremist entrenchment. Using computational models, we investigate how electoral systems respond to the emergence of ideological extremism arising either through the introduction of a new party or through the gradual radicalization of an established party. Systems that more accurately represent public opinion are more permissive to new parties, including extremist ones. Conversely, systems that suppress extremist entry can also protect incumbent parties as they drift toward increasingly extreme and unrepresentative positions. Electoral systems therefore differ not only in how well they represent voters or how many parties they sustain, but in the vulnerabilities they create: institutional openness increases the risk of extremist entry, while institutional inertia increases the risk of extremist entrenchment. Democracies thus face a fundamental design challenge: The same institutional features that protect a democracy from one extremist risk also expose it to another.

articles.title: Stabilizing Without Integrating: Ethnopolitical Cartelization and Power-Sharing in Post-Ohrid Macedonia
articles.authors: Ognen Vangelov
articles.abstract: This article examines the long-term effects of Macedonia’s post-conflict power-sharing arrangement, introduced by the Ohrid Framework Agreement (2001), on interethnic integration and democratic accountability. While the consociational model is widely credited with stabilizing the state and ensuring minority inclusion, it has also contributed to the institutional entrenchment of ethnic segmentation, shaping the incentives of political competition and governance. The article introduces the concept of ethnopolitical cartelization to describe how consociational power-sharing facilitates the consolidation of dominant ethnic parties as gatekeepers to state institutions, limiting intra-ethnic pluralism while preserving interethnic parity. Drawing on institutional analysis and empirical evidence, the article argues that key features of the Macedonian model, such as ethnic veto mechanisms, proportionality rules, and decentralized governance, have incentivized the monopolization of political representation within ethnic blocs, most clearly exemplified in the long-standing dominance of DUI within the Albanian political segment. This dynamic has enabled the development of vertically integrated party structures that channel access to state resources through identity-based patronage and informal governance. The result is a form of segmented stability in which public administration, education, and language policy operate through parallel structures. The Macedonian case illustrates the broader limitations of consociational design in deeply divided societies: while formal inclusion is achieved, it may come at the expense of shared civic space, horizontal accountability, and democratic responsiveness. By segmenting political authority and embedding elite brokerage into the structure of governance, the system inadvertently entrenches the very boundaries it was designed to overcome.

articles.title: Tricky Trade-Offs on a Transparency Spectrum: How the Financial Times Approaches Transparency about AI Use in News
articles.authors: Liz Lohn; Felix M. Simon
articles.abstract: As news organisations adopt artificial intelligence (AI), they face growing pressure to be transparent about when and how it is used – yet practical approaches remain uneven. This paper examines AI transparency through an in-depth case study of the Financial Times (FT). Drawing on 13 semi-structured interviews with 12 senior managers across editorial, product, data science, and communications, together with internal documents, we show that the FT approaches transparency as a hybrid of policy, process, and practice, framed by a desire to safeguard both internal and external trust. Transparency is calibrated to context: internally, AI use is signposted in tools and reinforced through training and personal accountability; externally, the prominence of disclosure scales with system autonomy and editorial oversight, with stronger labelling for no-human-in-the-loop features than for AI-assisted, journalist-edited outputs. We identify nine factors that shape audience-facing disclosure – legal/provider requirements, industry benchmarking, nature of the task, human oversight, system novelty, audience expectations, perceived risk, commercial sensitivities, and design constraints – and five crosscutting challenges, including site-wide consistency (especially on mobile) and potential “transparency backfire.” Conceptually, our analysis links AI transparency to isomorphic pressures and to intersecting institutional logics. We argue that AI transparency in news is best understood as a spectrum, evolving with technological advancements, commercial, professional and ethical considerations and shifting audience attitudes.

articles.title: Doubly Preferential: The Treatment of Contested Experts in News Media
articles.authors: François Claveau; Jacob Hamel-Mottiez; Léon Gatien; Olivier Santerre
articles.abstract: This article contributes to the characterization of media bias by analyzing how Canadian news media select and contextualize messages originating from think tanks, an influential yet ideologically marked form of expertise. Drawing on a large media corpus (2017–2021), this article shows that Canadian journalists make relatively limited use of textual indicators of credibility, but that these indicators systematically reflect the ideological preferences already evident in their source selection. Think tanks that are more frequently solicited thus benefit from more favorable contextualization, corroborating the hypothesis of a doubly preferential treatment. The study concludes by discussing the normative implications of these practices for journalistic standards, such as impartiality, in the face of contested expertise.

articles.title: Commercial video games improve species-related knowledge, perceptions, and action
articles.authors: Katie Blake; Paul J Johnson; Diogo Veríssimo
articles.abstract: Digital media often mediates human-wildlife interactions. It is feared that overexposure to virtual animals will distort public awareness and valuation of real-world species. This is alarming given the current rate of extinction. Commercial video games have attracted much attention for their capacity to engage players with biodiversity and conservation. Yet their impact for this is unclear. We use an online experiment to explore whether this medium can improve species-related knowledge, perceptions, and actions, as well as test assumptions that digitised wildlife are favoured by players over real-world counterparts. Our findings are based on a sample of 272 players and 273 non-players of Planet Zoo, using species that feature in this title. We found that both gameplay hours and recency of playing Planet Zoo are positively linked to: more accurately identifying species’ names and conservation status; how much the species are liked; threat appraisals about the likelihood and impact of species loss; and increased donations. Players donated nearly twice as much to species protection as non-players on average (£7.16 versus £4.68), and they allocated the maximum possible donation value of £20 three times as often. Furthermore, we did not observe any detrimental outcomes for digitised wildlife on responses compared to real versions, and we found that any positive effects from experience with Planet Zoo tended to be greater for reptiles than mammals. Our findings do not support concerns that digital media necessarily has harmful implications for public engagement with biodiversity and conservation. Rather, we show that commercial video games might provide an avenue for players to better understand the natural world and take action to protect it, and they might even be particularly beneficial for less desirable taxa. We challenge more game studios to bridge the gap between virtual and real nature where appropriate, joining efforts to ensure that wildlife can also persist beyond digital spaces. We encourage more researchers to pursue this line of inquiry. Given the rapid loss of biodiversity, we cannot continue to overlook how these platforms with global reach might be leveraged to drive conservation action.

articles.title: The 128 Paths to Victory - Swing State Math in the U.S. Presidential Elections
articles.authors: N. Asger Mortensen; Joel D. Cox
articles.abstract: In U.S. presidential elections, outcomes are often predictable in most states, with variability primarily introduced by a small number of "swing states". While the specific swing states can fluctuate from one election cycle to the next, they collectively play a critical role in determining the overall result. In the 2024 election, seven key swing states contribute a total of 93 delegates to the electoral college. Without considering mutual correlations, each of the 128 potential electoral outcomes has an equal probability of approximately 0.8%. Due to an uneven distribution of "safe" delegates (219 Republican and 226 Democrat), the Democratic candidate holds a slight statistical advantage. Analysing all possible outcomes for the 2024 election suggests an estimated 55% probability for a Democratic win, compared to 42% for a Republican victory. The odds of a tie are approximately 2.3%, while the likelihood of either party achieving a clean sweep of all swing states is 0.8%. A detailed analysis of the 128 possible election outcomes reinforces the widely held view that securing Pennsylvania is crucial to electoral success. Notably, in 4\% of all possible scenarios, victory is achieved by the narrowest possible margin, and in every such case, it hinges on winning Pennsylvania.

articles.title: Patriarchal Norms of Reproductive Behavior as an Adaptation to the Demographic Challenges of the Neolithic Transition
articles.authors: Maksim Sapozhnikov
articles.abstract:
This article proposes an evolutionary-materialist hypothesis on the origin of three basic
patriarchal norms of reproductive behavior: restriction of divorce, control over female
sexuality, and parental control over the choice of a spouse, which convergently emerge in
societies transitioning to food production. These norms are viewed as an evolutionary
adaptation to the conditions of the Neolithic transition, having emerged at the social level.
Methodologically, the work is structured as a retrospective analysis of specific
demographic conditions that created pressure in favor of such an adaptation. The starting
mechanism is the reproductive strategy of "sex for resources"—the exchange of male-
provided resources for female reproductive access—which arose in the ancestors of
humans in the Paleolithic (or earlier) and was entrenched by sexual selection.
Retrospective analysis shows that the most likely demographic challenges of the Neolithic
transition, creating pressure in favor of the adaptation of reproductive behavioral strategies
at the social level, were: (1) a manifold increase in population density, facilitating the
switching of marital partners (primarily for men) and creating a threat of resource insecurity
for women with children; (2) the emergence or intensification of awareness of the direct
link between sexual intercourse and childbirth, which could reduce women's motivation for
sexual activity due to awareness of reproductive costs; and (3) the dissociation between
the timing of sexual and social maturation in males, as a result of which female hormonal
mechanisms of partner choice (romantic love) continue to target young men who are not
yet able to provide a family with sufficient resources under the new conditions. The
convergent emergence of patriarchal norms of reproductive behavior in isolated cultures
(Mesopotamia, China, the Aztecs, the Incas, and others) serves as evidence of their
reproductive effectiveness compared to possible alternative adaptations. The hypothesis
explains the specific role of older males (fathers) as the main agents maintaining these
norms. The article is theoretical in nature and provides a foundation for further cross-
cultural empirical research.

articles.title: "I don't give a shit anymore" – Future-Oriented Career Agency and Precarity at the Postdoc Stage
articles.authors: Julian Hamann; Kathia Serrano Velarde; Tim Fenkner; Jonas Gottschalk-Rayling; Sven Boniger; Michi Hügel
articles.abstract: This paper examines how postdoctoral researchers navigate precarious employment conditions and claim career agency during an uncertain career stage. Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative interview panel of 35 postdocs from particle physics and modern history, the study distinguishes between two forms of agency: empowered strategizing and restricted drifting. Strategizing postdocs actively align short- to mid-term career goals with opportunities arising from fixed-term contracts and grant funding cycles, while drifting postdocs prioritize present research activities over long-term planning. Through in-depth interviews conducted in three waves, the analysis reveals how temporal horizons are compressed by the cyclical nature of academic recruitment and funding. The findings highlight the dynamic interplay between structural constraints and different forms of individual agency. This work contributes a processual perspective on career agency and precarity and adds to career research and studies of precarious working conditions.

articles.title: Research dataset sharing and ethical researcher conduct: A commentary on Ghuge et al. (2026) and Kumar et al. (2026).
articles.authors: Margaret K. Merga; Saiyidi Mat Roni
articles.abstract:
This commentary is written for an audience within and beyond academia, as
it concerns a dataset from the international community of school library professionals
(SLPs). After briefly orienting the reader to commentary and data fabrication, we
respond to Ghuge et al. (2026) and Kumar et al. (2026), recent articles with the same
corresponding author. Kumar et al. (2026) strongly imply that amongst other
researchers, there was a fabrication of data in our 2026 article where some SLP
respondents disclosed experiencing significant risk related to their work roles, notably
though not exclusively in the US political context. Kumar et al.’s (2026) “reasonable
evidence” that we fabricated our data is based on our data availability statement and an
opinion poll sent to associates (N=100); this method does not test whether a dataset
exists. Ghuge et al. (2026) cites Kumar et al., (2026) to make a similar though far softer
claim. We consider Kumar et al. (2026) in relation to ethical conduct in research
methods and research respondent risk related to research ecosystem norms. Data
sharing cannot be simply conflated with ethical research conduct. If we cannot
guarantee anonymity where appropriate, at-risk populations will refuse to participate in
social science research.

articles.title: Evidence from China: A quantitative examination of China's new competition regime for the digital economy
articles.authors: Leonard Baum; Joanna J. Bryson
articles.abstract: Growing global concern about the problems associated with concentrated market power in the digital economy is leading to a renewed interest in competition policy. Since the late 2010s, China’s government has squarely confronted the problems of its own ‘Big Tech’ with a new competition regime for digital markets. The ensuing ‘tech crackdown’ of late 2020 provides a rare quasi-natural experiment to study the impact of antitrust regulation. Here we deploy a novel market capitalization approach that builds on the informativeness of China’s financial markets. Harnessing Bloomberg data of 1142 publicly listed firms for the period 2019 to 2022, we find that across China's digital economy, this unprecedented intervention is associated with both reduced market concentration and reduced market-capitalization growth, but no harms to revenue. Employing a difference-in-differences and event-study design, we identify a causal link between China’s new competition regime and a reduction in concentration in the primary markets of China's three most dominant digital platforms — Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent (BATs). Other empirical findings include a negative association between market concentration and the openness of digital markets and a non-relationship between market concentration and profits. Our results indicate that neither profit- nor revenue-based metrics are entirely appropriate for measuring digital market power effectively. We conclude by discussing the relative success of China’s digital competition policy as well as the relevance of these insights for global, including Western regulatory strategies.

articles.title: A Productivity Fixated World in the Age of AI: Investigating The Purpose of Human Art
articles.authors: Bruce Tan
articles.abstract: Modern society increasingly prioritizes final products over the creative process, a trend exacerbated by the rapid adoption of generative AI. This study aims to explore the impact of AI integration into the creative process on subjective well-being and fulfillment, and to determine whether these effects differ between individuals creating for leisure versus those creating for a profession. Within this research, a quantitative-focused survey was conducted with 200 adults, categorized using a 2x2 design: acting as either a hobbyist or a professional illustrator, and either utilizing or not utilizing AI. The data reveals a consistent drop in a person’s well-being across both hobbyist and professional groups when AI is utilized. The differences in fulfillment between hobbyist and professional groups were not statistically significant.
