While a positive correlation was found between a product-focused mindset and satisfaction among professionals using AI, the overall satisfaction for AI users across the board remained significantly lower than for those who didn’t use AI. These findings suggest that AI integration into creative tasks carries measurable psychological costs by separating the creator from the intrinsically beneficial creative process, along with social costs that taint the creator-audience relationship. These findings underscore the value of human creation, suggesting that the ongoing conversation surrounding AI adoption must extend beyond efficiency to account for value within the human process. An avenue for further research lies within AI use in other fields less traditionally considered a “creative” discipline, such as STEM, which show evidence of having similar psychological benefits arising from the process.

articles.title: Understanding First Nations Disconnection and Reimagining Connection: A yarn between Aboriginal women.
articles.authors: Cammi Murrup-Stewart; Tess Ryan
articles.abstract: Connection and belonging are significant processes concerning cultural identity, and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia, it has been at the forefront of discussions around the Social and Emotional Wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. One area that needs more investigation is that of those individuals on the margins of society who may find access to communities a complex practice. Furthermore, there has been an emergence of recent practices that move connection and belonging beyond more traditional ways of being towards modernity, which includes inclusiveness, accessibility and flexibility for those involved. Drawing on existing literature, collaborative yarning with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and reflective commentary, this article explores the many facets of connection and belonging and the ways in which many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples navigate between cultural traditions, socio-historical challenges and contemporary realities. We call for a reimagining of community spaces and practices to ensure they are inclusive and responsive to the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ lived experiences.

articles.title: Do Chatbots Sound Equally Sure in French and in Arabic? A Pilot Audit of Expressed Certainty in ChatGPT and Gemini
articles.authors: Houda Es-sqalli
articles.abstract: People increasingly ask chatbots about health and public services and pass the answers on to others. Whether they check first may depend on how sure an answer sounds. This pilot audit asks whether the certainty cues that chatbots give change with the language of the question. Ten questions on public health and public services in Morocco were asked once in French and once in Modern Standard Arabic to ChatGPT and Gemini (40 answers). Answers were scored with a bilingual lexicon of hedges and boosters. Both chatbots hedged less in Arabic than in French, and the pattern held under two alternative versions of the lexicon. A model-assisted second coding of 10 answers showed that the lexicon captured boosters well but missed about a third of hedges. With 10 questions and one run each, these results are a first look, not a finding. They motivate a larger audit with repeated runs and human validation.

articles.title: Do polls underestimate support for right-wing parties? Assessing variation in polling error by party family
articles.authors: Stuart Perrett; Will Jennings; Jonathan Mellon; Christopher Prosser; Christopher Wlezien
articles.abstract: Pollsters have underestimated support for notable right-wing electoral outcomes, including Donald Trump’s vote share in 2016, 2020, and 2024, the UK Conservative Party in 2015 and 2024, and Leave in the 2016 EU referendum. Do these outcomes reflect isolated polling failures, or a persistent partisan asymmetry in polling error across democracies? We provide the first comparative analysis of partisan polling error. Drawing on over 38,500 election-poll-party observations across 32 countries and 372 elections between 1945 and 2025, we use a Bayesian hierarchical modeling framework to estimate latent election-party polling error. We find that, on average, support for parties on the left is overestimated, while support for parties on the right is underestimated. This pattern is evident across countries, party classifications, and vote intention polling dating to the 1940s. In spotlighting persistent partisan asymmetries, our findings contribute to understanding institutional and contextual correlates of pre-election polling accuracy.

articles.title: Answering without disclosing: How officials under scrutiny compress what they say
articles.authors: Nasrul Ismail; William S. Harvey
articles.abstract: How do organisational actors withhold information while continuing to answer under scrutiny? Research on organisational silence has largely treated withholding as a question of whether actors speak. This article examines variation within speech through 1 781 question-and-answer exchanges from 102 recorded interview encounters with senior officials in prison health governance across three studies conducted between 2016 and 2023. Narrative absence was coded across six features and response timing was derived from audio and validated against blinded listener judgements. Higher narrative absence was associated with substantially shorter answers within encounters, and this association held across all robustness checks. Changes in response onset were much smaller, while pausing supported no independent association, and the automated measure of fillers and repairs failed validation. The findings identify controlled compression as a response form through which disclosure contracts while interactional responsiveness continues. Separating responsiveness from disclosure matters because organisational accountability is routinely assessed through visible responsiveness even though meaningful accountability depends on disclosure. An actor may therefore satisfy every observable requirement of cooperation while narrowing what is made available. The article shows that where speaking is expected, withholding does not cease but relocates into the answers themselves.

articles.title: Fairness Perception and Trust Erosion in Competitive Mobile Gaming: A Five-Year Longitudinal Study of a Persian-Language Backgammon Platform
articles.authors: Hanieh Hatefi Yousefi
articles.abstract:
Fairness perception is a critical yet understudied dimension of player experience in competitive mobile games. This paper presents findings from a five-year longitudinal qualitative study (2022–2026) examining how players construct, reinforce, and communicate beliefs about unfairness in a competitive mobile gaming environment. Using Inductive Thematic Analysis (ITA), we analysed a corpus of more than 52,000 player reviews collected across multiple mobile app marketplaces, supplemented by anonymised customer support interaction transcripts obtained through a research collaboration agreement.
Data were collected using a longitudinal sampling design that examined the same calendar month across five consecutive years, enabling the identification of long-term trends while reducing seasonal effects. Analysis identified seven operational themes describing players’ fairness-related beliefs and behaviours, which were subsequently consolidated into three higher-order meta-themes: Perceived Agency (the belief that game systems determine outcomes independently of player skill), Trust Erosion (the progressive reinforcement of manipulation beliefs through negative experiences and platform interactions), and Statistical Misinterpretation (the attribution of probabilistic outcomes to intentional system design). The proportion of 1-star reviews citing fairness-related concerns increased from 3% in 2022 to 18% in 2026, indicating a substantial decline in player trust over the study period.
The study further proposes a ten-stage Player Journey of Distrust, mapping the cognitive and emotional progression from initial doubt to entrenched beliefs about manipulation. Findings suggest that fairness complaints are often better understood as expressions of deteriorating trust rather than perceptions of technical malfunction. The paper discusses implications for transparency design, player communication strategies, support systems, and the broader study of trust in digital gaming environments.
Keywords: fairness perception; player experience; trust erosion; mobile gaming; thematic analysis; player psychology; app store reviews; cognitive bias; longitudinal qualitative research; trust in digital systems

articles.title: A STUDY OF THE EMERGENCE OF WELFARE CLEAVAGES IN SOUTH KOREA
articles.authors: Jihun Yeo
articles.abstract:
This study aims to trace the cause of an emerging welfare cleavage under circumstances where discourses on economic growth have been dominant in Korean politics. On the basis of the theories of interaction between changing social structure and social-norm dynamics, this paper explores the causes of an emerging welfare cleavage in the case of South Korea during the late 2000s. To analyze the change of economic structure and public awareness regarding public welfare, I used the data of macro-economic indicators and public opinion polls and utilized press releases to analyze discourses of political actors.
The linked-policies effects of an immature “developmental welfare regime” and neo-liberal economic policies caused social polarization and expansion of the poverty stratum in the course of a slowdown in economic growth in the 1990s and foreign exchange crisis in 1998. The existing norm (i.e., economic growth could solve problems concerning people's livelihood) that had been maintained in the era of rapid economic growth was weakened. A conflict between an education superintendent and the Gyeonggi-do Provincial Council triggered a debate on free meals and welfare in 2009. Civil society groups were organized on a national scale, and they started a discourse struggle to replace individual interests with public interests and to obtain social legitimacy. Political parties gradually accepted the welfare issue as the primary electoral pledge for their political interests after public preference regarding growth and distribution changed when confronted with political crises.
This study draws an implication that general factors affecting Western welfare states (e.g., power alliance and democratic institutions) influence East Asian welfare states by analyzing the case of South Korean welfare politics. It means that studies of East Asian welfare states can use explanatory building blocks partly from existing welfare theories rather than stressing the exceptionalism of East Asian welfare states. However, owing to the different economic and political structures of East Asian states from those of Western countries during the formative stage of welfare states, studies of East Asian welfare states need to consider path dependency in the historical context of East Asian political economy.

articles.title: Doubly Preferential: The Treatment of Contested Experts in News Media
articles.authors: François Claveau; Jacob Hamel-Mottiez; Léon Gatien; Olivier Santerre
articles.abstract: This article contributes to the characterization of media bias by analyzing how Canadian news media select and contextualize messages originating from think tanks, an influential yet ideologically marked form of expertise. Drawing on a large media corpus (2017–2021), this article shows that Canadian journalists make relatively limited use of textual indicators of credibility, but that these indicators systematically reflect the ideological preferences already evident in their source selection. Think tanks that are more frequently solicited thus benefit from more favorable contextualization, corroborating the hypothesis of a doubly preferential treatment. The study concludes by discussing the normative implications of these practices for journalistic standards, such as impartiality, in the face of contested expertise.

articles.title: Hate speech against scientists can backfire – but so can counterspeech: Evidence from a four-country experiment
articles.authors: Niels G. Mede; Lena Frischlich
articles.abstract: Hate speech against scientists can harm their well-being and undermine knowledge-based societies, and counterspeech by bystanders is often proposed as a remedy. But comparative evidence on how bystanders perceive hate speech targeting scientists and on whether counterspeech helps is lacking. In a preregistered experiment with quota samples weighted to national population margins from Denmark, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States (N = 2,769), participants saw a fictitious social media post by a scientist either alone, with a hateful comment, or with a hateful comment plus a counterspeech reply. Hate speech backfired: Participants rated the scientist’s post more positively in both comment conditions. Counterspeech had mixed effects: It increased participants’ intentions to speak up themselves, but in Germany and the United Kingdom it made the hateful comment appear more acceptable. Our findings advance research on attacks against epistemic authorities and demonstrate the value of comparative, multi-outcome designs.

articles.title: Empathy-Related Traits and Domain-Specific Self-Rated Creativity: Indirect Associations Through Five C-PETS Dimensions
articles.authors: Masahiro Yoshida
articles.abstract: This study examined statistical indirect associations between empathy-related traits and domain-specific self-rated creativity through five dimensions of the Creative Personality and Thinking Styles Scale (C-PETS). An online survey of 359 North American adults assessed Perspective Taking (PT), Fantasy (FS), and Empathic Concern (EC), the five C-PETS dimensions, and five domains of the Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS). Parallel multiple mediation models were estimated using 10,000 bootstrap samples and Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction. Significant total indirect effects were found for PT across all five K-DOCS domains, for FS across four domains, and for EC only for Self/Everyday creativity. After correction, significant specific indirect effects were limited to Challenge-Seeking (CS) pathways from PT and FS to all five K-DOCS domains. Because the data were cross-sectional and based on self-report, these results do not establish causal mediation. Instead, they indicate that challenge-seeking is a robust conditional statistical link between perspective-related empathy traits and domain-specific self-rated creativity.

articles.title: From Water Scarcity to Paceklik: Ecological Memory in Banyumas Literary and Expressive Traditions
articles.authors: Dwi Scativana Isnaeni
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Water is more than a physical necessity in communities whose everyday life has historically been closely connected with agriculture, seasonal rainfall, and the availability of water. It can become an object of desire, ritual expectation, narrative valuation, social celebration, and material anxiety. This article examines how such relationships are articulated across four Banyumasan literary and expressive traditions: Banyu Emas, Cowongan, Ricik-Ricik, and Ahmad Tohari’s Ronggeng Dukuh Paruk. The study employs qualitative comparative interpretation within an ecocritical framework and uses the concept of ecological memory in a deliberately bounded cultural sense. Rather than treating ecological memory as proof of a population’s psychological recollection of particular environmental events, the article defines it as the recurrent cultural articulation of human–environment relationships through forms in which environmental experience can be represented, performed, retained, and reinterpreted. The analysis finds that the four corpus units do not constitute a single environmental narrative or a continuous chain of cultural transmission. Their significance lies instead in the different ways cultural form transforms environmental experience. Banyu Emas renders water scarcity as a condition that gives water extraordinary value; Cowongan turns uncertainty over rainfall into ritual supplication and collective anticipation; Ricik-Ricik constructs the arrival of drizzle or rain as an occasion of happiness, humor, sociability, and play; while Ronggeng Dukuh Paruk connects drought with agricultural disruption, paceklik, food scarcity, and bodily vulnerability. The comparison extends ecological-memory discussion by demonstrating that environmental memory can encompass positive affect as well as crisis, including happiness, relief, humor, and anticipation. It also suggests that recurrence should not be confused with transmission and that continuity may occur through transformation rather than preservation. Ecological memory, in this formulation, persists because environmental relationships remain culturally productive even when the forms and meanings through which they are expressed change.

articles.title: AI Systems for Filmmaking: A Survey of HCI Research from a Labor-Centered Perspective
articles.authors: YUYING TANG; Lin Gao; Haotian Li; Baiqiao Zhang; Rebecca Fiebrink; Sebastian Deterding; Xiaojuan Ma; Huamin Qu
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into filmmaking and has attracted attention in human-computer interaction (HCI). Existing studies have primarily characterized AI systems for filmmaking by their capabilities and supported tasks, with limited attention to the organisation of filmmaking labor during system use. We review 31 HCI system papers and develop a three-layer taxonomy of labor sites, labor types, and human-AI allocation, examining where AI systems are positioned, what types of labor are involved during system use, and how those labor types are allocated between humans and AI. Our analysis reveals a concentration on individual below-the-line contexts, increasing attention to structural and meaning-making labor beyond execution, comparatively limited relational labor, and substantial variation in human-AI allocation across labor types. We further identify opportunities for the design and evaluation of AI systems that account for the broader organization of filmmaking labor. This review provides a labor-centered taxonomy for synthesizing AI systems for filmmaking and a basis for examining how AI may become involved in broader organizations of creative labor.

articles.title: Researcher well-being as a leading indicator in research-funding governance: A system dynamics exploration of top-down versus bottom-up allocation
articles.authors: Tomoko Sakai; Satoshi Sano
articles.abstract: Governments face a recurring dilemma in dividing public research funding between top-down, competitive, mission-oriented programmes and bottom-up, investigator-led institutional grants. This research note presents an exploratory system dynamics model that endogenizes researcher motivation, conceived following self-determination theory as a slow-moving stock of psychological capital, within the feedback structure linking funding allocation, research outputs, and societal returns. Simulation experiments across three policy scenarios reveal a consistent time-asymmetric pattern. First, accelerating the shift toward competitive funding produces an earlier but lower peak in societal returns, followed by sustained decline. Second, shifting toward bottom-up funding restores motivation but opens a transition valley in returns whose depth grows with transition speed. Third, delayed corrective reallocation exhibits hysteresis: once motivation is depleted, even aggressive reallocation requires roughly two decades before returns recover. One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis indicates that these qualitative patterns persist across the tested parameter ranges, while the level of long-run returns proves highly sensitive to the weight placed on discretionary research time, around which the baseline system undergoes a regime shift. The model implies that researcher well-being functions as a leading indicator of research-system health, preceding declines in publication-based lagging indicators. We derive three testable propositions and outline an agenda for empirical calibration, beginning with a national baseline survey of researchers being launched in Japan. For funding governance, the results imply that monitoring leading indicators and pacing allocation transitions matter as much as choosing the allocation ratio itself.

articles.title: Platform visibility and protest recirculation in the Cockroach Janta Party movement
articles.authors: Nitesh Kumar yadav
articles.abstract:
This paper examines how the Cockroach Janta Party connected digital communication and street
protest in India between May and July 2026. I draw on nineteen public documentary records and a
separate retrospective account of my participation. I follow calls to attend demonstrations, a
request to share protest photographs and videos, Sonam Wangchuk's involvement, and disputes
over platform access. In my early visits, I remember small gatherings, people who stayed only
briefly, and volunteers who hoped the protest would grow but were unsure how far it would spread.
These observations make it difficult to assume that online popularity leads to sustained
participation. I use a visibility-action-recirculation framework to examine how gatherings produce
material that returns to digital circulation. A limited comparison with Nepal's September 2025
protests considers how people maintain communication when services are restricted. The evidence
documents deliberate organizing and reported interruptions. It does not establish how
recommendation systems, emotional appeals or recirculated material affected attendance.

Keywords: Cockroach Janta Party; platform visibility; digital protest; recirculation; platform governance;
India; Nepal

articles.title: Exploring the Intersection of Language and Literacy in a Young Person with Autism, Learning Disability and Minimal Speech.
articles.authors: Barbara Rose Clogg
articles.abstract: It is argued that language and literacy are inseparable for users of alternative and augmentative communication, and that literacy can offer a route to the acquisition of fully functioning language for non-verbal individuals with autistic spectrum disorder. This applied linguistics project explores the intersection of language and literacy in a young person with autism, learning disability and minimal speech. By use of multimodal conversation analysis, it reveals the range of everyday literacy practices used by the young person and how these literacy practices are drawn upon to make meaning in interaction. It finds that literacy practices constitute a significant part of their multimodal communicative repertoire and offer affordances as a mode of communication that breaks the limitations posed by their disabilities and the forms of AAC available to them.

articles.title: MAGA Republicans as  “Particularistic Authoritarians” on the Welfare State:  Parallels with the European Populist Right
articles.authors: Jake Haselswerdt; Hang Qi; Suhyun Cho
articles.abstract: Has MAGA remade the Republican politics of the welfare state? While Republican voters have traditionally favored retrenchment, the so-called “populism” of the MAGA movement suggests that the social policy preferences of right-leaning Americans are due for reexamination. Drawing from the “particularistic authoritarian model” of European populist radical-right voters, we expect MAGA Republicans to favor benefits for deserving groups, stronger “workfare” policies, less social investment, and more restrictive deservingness criteria. We test these expectations using a 1,000-respondent module of the 2025 Cooperative Election Study. Factor analysis and regressions show that MAGA Republicans are substantially more supportive than non-MAGA Republicans of policies benefiting seniors and express levels of support comparable to those of Democrats and other respondents. MAGA Republicans also show somewhat stronger endorsement of restrictive deservingness criteria than other Republicans, while differences between the two Republican groups are less pronounced for social investment. Overall, the results indicate that MAGA Republicans do not simply favor either welfare state expansion or retrenchment. Instead, they distinguish among forms of social protection according to their beneficiaries and perceived deservingness.

articles.title: A golden era for open-ended questions? Using LLMs to scale the qualitative coding of open-ended survey responses
articles.authors: Ansgar Hudde; Shannon Taflinger
articles.abstract: Open-text questions in quantitative surveys can yield rich information from large samples, but analysing and coding these data using qualitative text analysis is resource-intensive. Large Language Models (LLMs) are a promising tool for scaling up such analyses, reducing time and costs. We first use thematic qualitative text analysis to create a typology of responses; we then let LLMs code texts based on our typology and instructions and compare their coding accuracy with that of student assistants, defining accuracy as agreement with a researcher-coded benchmark dataset. We assess performance on an interpretive coding task: applying a 15-category typology to approximately 1,400 open-ended responses from young US Americans about dating across party-political lines. We evaluate models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral, with and without training data. The most advanced models outperform student assistants, and performance further increases with training data. This study contributes by applying LLMs to a use case with great analytical potential, namely open-ended survey responses, and testing whether the resulting codes support the same substantive conclusions as hand-coded data. We offer applied social scientists practical recommendations for a division of labour in which researchers retain conceptualisation and codebook construction and delegate the standardised coding to an LLM.

articles.title: The Space Headright System: A Diachronic Analysis of First-Mover Elite Formation Mechanisms from Colonial Virginia to Twenty-First-Century Space Resource Law
articles.authors: Shungo Arai
articles.abstract:
This study examines how first-mover advantage was converted into durable elite dominance in seventeenth-century colonial Virginia, using this structural logic to critically evaluate twenty-first-century space resource law. Drawing on a Multilayered Frontier Capital Accumulation Model (MFCAM) that integrates frontier theory, world-systems theory, and institutional path dependence, the study addresses four research questions (RQ1–RQ4). Historical analysis shows how the First Families of Virginia (FFV), preempting land under the 1618 headright system, monopolized power through mutually reinforcing mechanisms of institutional pre-emption, marital closure, and symbolic capital accumulation, thereby converting land capital into political and cultural capital to maintain that dominance. At the same time, the study traces the formation of a lower-white stratum through indentured servitude, post-release landlessness, and racial divide-and-rule policies after Bacon's Rebellion (1676) and shows that elite and lower-class formation were two sides of the same institutional design. A comparison with the Massachusetts Bay Colony suggests these outcomes depended on early institutional choices.

Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes a "Space Headright System" (SHS) comprising priority access to institutional design, revolving-door relations between regulators and industry, and the accumulation of legal precedent. By examining Section 402 of the 2015 U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, the Artemis Accords, and national space resource laws, it assesses risks of lower-class formation such as space indentured servitude and space company towns. The study advances a conditional warning: if current legal trajectories continue, they suggest convergence toward a Virginia-type stratified order. To avert this, three policy recommendations (primary rules)—an international space cadastre, a Space Commons Fund, and treaty-based protections for later settlers—are proposed, alongside secondary design requirements to guard the implementing institutions against regulatory capture.

articles.title: “I wouldn’t trust her with my life but...” - Exploring trust in voice-based assistants through user-generated content
articles.authors: Katharina Frehmann; Jana Peters
articles.abstract: Investigating trust in conversational AI, such as voice-based assistants (VBAs), is increasingly important for understanding their rising popularity and the tasks users entrust to them. Howev-er, since VBAs are technical devices perceived as human-like and sometimes serving as infor-mation sources, it is unclear what forms trust in them takes. Technical, interpersonal, and media trust approaches may all be relevant, yet previous studies have not fully considered this poten-tial multidimensionality of trust in AI, especially regarding the inclusion of media trust. Fur-thermore, research on VBAs lacks qualitative studies that provide insights into users’ perspec-tives. This study therefore pursues two objectives: First, to develop a more comprehensive theo-retical perspective on trust in VBAs by integrating technical, interpersonal, and media trust ap-proaches. Second, to empirically explore signs of trust in VBAs in German user-generated online content. To this end, we conducted a qualitative content analysis of 169 postings about Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant found on marketplaces, under media coverage, and on dis-cussion platforms. The results show that users evaluate typical and new technical, interpersonal, and media trustworthiness indicators for VBAs and sometimes combine these dimensions when discussing AI capabilities. When explicitly speaking of trust, users mostly refer to the parent company in high-risk situations rather than to the VBA itself. Users also discuss aspects that may represent consequences, processes, and external factors of trust. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a preliminary model of hybrid trust in VBAs that can inform future research on trust in conversational AI.

articles.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
articles.authors: NIHR Policy Research Unit in Reproductive Health; Elena Proffitt; Nicola Merrett; Lois Harvey-Pescott; Jennifer Hall; Abigail McNiven; Abimbola Ayorinde; Kamilla Abdullayev; Rebecca French; Kelly Dickson
articles.abstract:
Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making.  Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making.  

Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings.  

This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

articles.title: From Governance to Government? The European Commission and the three faces of politicisation
articles.authors: Francesco Nicoli; Lorenzo Lombardi
articles.abstract: Research on the politicisation of the European Union has concentrated on reactive, bottom-up contestation of existing EU action. This article argues that such an understanding is incomplete because it conflates politicisation of issues with politicisation of institutions. We distinguish three faces of politicisation. Reactive politicisation refers to the public contestation of existing EU competences. Proactive politicisation occurs when supranational actors claim a political mandate in order to justify wider discretion. Induced politicisation emerges when intergovernmental conflict over already politicized state functions creates a vacuum that the Commission can try to fill, thereby inheriting the political character of the function itself. The empirical sections focus on induced politicisation. They reconstruct three episodes: Jean-Claude Juncker's attempt to use EMU deadlock to place the Commission at the centre of euro-area reform; the failed institutionalisation of an EU Finance Minister, a euro-area fiscal capacity, and a more political treasury function; and Ursula von der Leyen's attempts to centralise foreign-policy initiative during successive geopolitical crises. The argument is that politicisation does not only constrain supranational action. Under specific institutional conditions it can also widen supranational authority by transforming the Commission from guardian of the Treaties into a proto-governmental executive.

articles.title: Sectoral Credit Reallocation and Consumer Credit Expansion: A Difference-in-Differences and Decomposition Analysis
articles.authors: Gudzenko Vladislav
articles.abstract: This article examines sectoral bank-credit reallocation in Kyrgyzstan by combining a difference in differences (DiD) comparison around 2015 with a detailed accounting analysis for 2019–2025. The research question is how conclusions about reallocation depend on the comparison period, portfolio denominator and distinction between shares and real balances. Four focal lending categories are compared with a residual category in a historical series extended through 2025. The full-portfolio DiD contrast is +1.28 percentage points for 2010–2025, but −0.17 points when the window begins in 2012; the group gap already changes substantially before 2015. In the recent period, consumer loans rise from 11.8% to 33.6% of bank credit and account for 42.5% of the nominal increase in the outstanding portfolio. CPI-deflated non-consumer credit grows by 49.3%. Agriculture loses portfolio share while its real balance grows by 12.3%; industry and construction experience real declines of 34.7% and 17.5%. A symmetric decomposition separates the changing consumer-credit mix from redistribution within non-consumer lending. The integrated findings show why positive period-average sectoral contrasts can coexist with recent share losses and uneven real growth. DiD remains descriptive, and the decomposition is an accounting identity. Neither identifies the effect of accession or consumer-credit crowding out. Independent verification of the historical inputs remains incomplete.

articles.title: Workplace Mental Health and Psychological Safety: A Systematic Review of Interventions and Outcomes
articles.authors: Sarah Khairunnisa Budiyanto
articles.abstract:
Background. Workplace mental health and psychological safety are critical determinants of employee wellbeing, organizational performance, and public health. Despite growing recognition of their importance, evidence on effective interventions across occupational sectors remains fragmented, and the moderating role of psychosocial safety climate (PSC) is underexplored in existing syntheses.
Objective. This systematic review synthesizes global evidence on individual- and organizational-level workplace mental health interventions, with particular attention to psychological safety climate as a moderating construct and the differential effectiveness of universal versus targeted delivery models.
Methods. A comprehensive, PRISMA 2020-compliant search was conducted across  PubMed and Google Scholar databases, covering publications from 2011 to 2026. Ninety-seven records were identified; following removal of four duplicates, 93 deduplicated records were retained, encompassing systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, and qualitative syntheses. Quality appraisal employed ROBINS-I, QATQS, AXIS, Downs and Black, GRADE, and EPHPP tools.
Results. Individual-level digital interventions demonstrated the strongest measurable short-term effects: mindfulness-based eHealth programs (Hedge’s g = 0.60) outperformed cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT; g = 0.15) and stress management programs (g = 0.17). Web-based interventions improved psychological wellbeing (g = 0.37) and work effectiveness (g = 0.25), with effects sustained at follow-up (g = 0.23). Targeted delivery yielded markedly larger effects for stress management (g = 0.64–0.69) compared to universal delivery (g = 0.00). Universal CBT reduced depression across the general workforce (SMD = 0.16). Manager training significantly increased mental health knowledge (SMD = 0.73). Among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic, pooled disorder prevalence reached 36% for depression, 37% for PTSD, 27% for stress, 47% for anxiety, and 49% for insomnia. Organizational-level interventions showed mixed results with high heterogeneity.
Conclusions. Effective workplace mental health promotion requires multi-layered strategies that combine scalable digital tools with organizational structural changes and manager capability building. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs, under-represented worker populations, cost-effectiveness analyses, and the integration of PSC measurement into intervention frameworks.

articles.title: From “Robs to Riches”: Scandal Constructivation, Democratic Ambivalence, and Pagsasaayos in the Philippines
articles.authors: Karl Patrick Regala Mendoza
articles.abstract: This research note examines Philippine corruption scandals from the dual vantage of citizen and scholar. Building on my concept of scandal constructivation, I argue that scandals are not simply signs of democratic defect but communicative events that dramatize democracy’s ambivalence. The DPWH flood control scandal illustrates this: outrage turned comic in the “robs to riches” quip, while blame extended to contractors’ children, exposing relational accountability. Local publics—through gossip, assemblies, and social media—oscillated between vigilance and cynicism. In the Global South, scandals disrupt structures yet provoke repair, serving as resources for rethinking public engagement, legitimacy, and democracy.

articles.title: Regressive Restoration: A Process Model of Belief Rigidity Under Epistemic Destabilization
articles.authors: Mitchell Sanders
articles.abstract: Beliefs do more than represent the world; they can also regulate uncertainty, affect, identity, and significance. This article introduces regressive restoration as a temporal regulatory process in which epistemic destabilization increases reliance on coherence-restoring beliefs, the immediate stabilizing effects of those beliefs reinforce commitment, and that commitment subsequently reduces epistemic flexibility. Epistemic destabilization refers to conditions in which cues for determining what is credible, coherent, or socially shared become fragmented, overloaded, unreliable, or contested. The model proposes that available integrative resources– the momentary attentional, affective, and uncertainty-tolerance resources needed to remain engaged with conflicting information– moderate whether destabilization promotes adaptive accommodation or regressive restoration. The model distinguishes short-term stabilization from maladaptive rigidity. Coherence restoration is context-sensitive and may be functional, whereas rigidity is indicated when closure-oriented responses resist correction or persist across contexts in which reflective integration is possible. Regressive restoration is defined as a process rather than a trait or latent factor, and identity consolidation is treated as an important but nonessential amplifier. Five propositions specify the model’s distinctive predictions concerning regulatory function, temporal ordering, motivational amplification, correction resistance, and cross-context generalization. A focused empirical agenda is proposed to test whether immediate coherence, affective relief, or significance restoration predicts later belief rigidity beyond established informational and motivational mechanisms.

articles.title: A Middle Way proposal towards an equitable open access publishing model
articles.authors: Diogo Provete
articles.abstract: Open access promised to widen participation in science, but the article-processing charge (APC) that funds much of gold open access has shifted the cost of publishing onto authors, reproducing rather than removing exclusion for the Global South. Writing as a journal editor based in Brazil, I argue that the instruments now relied upon, namely fee waivers, purchasing-power-parity pricing and transformative agreements, are each useful but insufficient, because each treats a structural problem as a matter of discounting. Latin America's non-commercial diamond model, exemplified by SciELO, has shown that affordable open access is achievable at roughly a tenth of the cost of a commercial APC, yet it remains constrained by limited global visibility. I propose a “Middle Way”: a public–private model in which national governments fund and own the core publishing infrastructure as a public good, as Brazil is now doing through the nationalisation of SciELO, while commercial firms are contracted, on transparent and unbundled terms, for the services they perform better, chiefly discoverability and global distribution. Ownership stays public, and the commercial sector becomes a contracted supplier rather than the owner of the venue. The proposal's scope condition is ownership: it fits systems where the publishing venue is, or can become, publicly or institutionally owned.

articles.title: Are EU Kidding Me? Notes from a Poorly Drafted Social Media Ban
articles.authors: Michael Veale
articles.abstract: In September 2026, the European Commission published a proposed EU KIDS Act, responding to the demand for restrictions and further design obligations applying to digital services accessible to children, including social media. This Article argues that regardless of what one believes about the merits of this policy direction, the EU KIDS Act is not the legislative text we need. The scope and drafting are little short of chaotic, full of holes, enormous ambiguities, and unintended consequences. Recitals contradict articles. The use of scope borrowed from other pieces of legislation not designed for this purpose brings services into scope that should not be subject to the relevant provisions, like book-recommendation websites, music services, or exercise trackers. The infrastructural requirement for assurance of age and parental responsibility attestation simply omits enormous issues of complex families and childhoods. Complex design obligations are written in ways that can be plausibly interpreted as implicitly prohibiting entire swathes of products, such as voice assistants. This Article outlines these issues, and many more. The Commission should withdraw this proposal and reissue a workable and realistic text.

articles.title: El Encuadre de la Responsabilidad Ciudadana: Comunicación Digital del Servel en la Elección Presidencial y Parlamentaria 2025
articles.authors: Jaime Elorrieta
articles.abstract:
Los organismos electorales enfrentan un desafío comunicacional distinto al de los partidos o candidaturas: deben informar y movilizar al electorado sin abandonar su mandato de neutralidad. Este informe examina cómo el Servicio Electoral de Chile (Servel) resolvió ese desafío en su publicidad digital durante la elección presidencial y parlamentaria de 2025, a partir del análisis de 101 anuncios publicados en Google Ads y Meta Ads.
Los resultados muestran que la comunicación del Servel es abrumadoramente práctica: el 85,1% de los anuncios se centra en información procedimental —dónde votar, qué documentos llevar, cómo revisar el rol de vocal de mesa— por sobre la apelación emocional, cívica o sancionatoria. Contra lo esperable, el tono no escala hacia la urgencia a medida que se acerca la elección; en cambio, mensajes puntuales como el llamado al deber cívico o la alerta contra la desinformación aparecen concentrados en momentos específi cos de la campaña, no en un crescendo progresivo. La advertencia sobre multas por no votar, pese a ser un rasgo central del sistema electoral chileno, ocupa un lugar marginal (3% de la muestra) en la comunicación digital del organismo.

articles.title: Between resistance and negotiation. Intellectual property as a survival strategy for media facing AI and digital platforms
articles.authors: Javier Díaz-Noci; Javier Odriozola-Chéné; Rosa Pérez Arozamena; Koldobika Meso-Ayerdi; Simón Peña-Fernández
articles.abstract:
Introduction. Generative AI has intensified tensions between news organisations and technology platforms over intellectual property, audience traffic and journalism’s economic sustainability. The report examines how leading Spanish digital media have framed AI since ChatGPT’s emergence, while considering the subsequent disruption caused by Google AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Methods. The study combines quantitative content analysis with legal and industry analysis. It examines 242 AI-related articles published between January 2022 and December 2024 by leading Spanish digital-native and legacy outlets, selected according to GfK DAM audience data. Frequency distributions and contingency tables assess thematic frames and editorial positions.

Results. Intellectual property emerges as the central underlying conflict. Coverage concentrates on authorship (68%), ethics and legal liability (45%), business models and licensing (32%), and employment (21%). Legacy media generally frame AI as a threat to journalistic assets, whereas digital-native outlets emphasise efficiency and commercial opportunities. Civil society and journalists themselves remain marginal in the debate. Google’s AI-generated summaries further intensify concerns by retaining users within the platform and reducing referral traffic.

Discussion. Intellectual property is becoming both a defensive right and a bargaining asset. The sector is consequently shifting from litigation towards licensing, collective negotiation and technological adaptation, although confidential agreements may strengthen major publishers while marginalising smaller outlets.

articles.title: Citizens’ Support for EU AI Sovereignty Policy
articles.authors: Pascal König; B.J.A. Leidorf-Tidå
articles.abstract: This article examines EU citizens’ support for EU policy to attain digital sovereignty regarding Artificial intelligence (AI). Promoting domestic industries in AI is crucially important for attaining AI sovereignty. Yet, AI sovereignty policy ultimately hinges on support by the European public, and protective policy intervening in the EU AI market may be felt directly – and negatively – by citizens. Using survey data from Lithuania, the Netherlands, Romania, and Sweden, we examine how much citizens support AI sovereignty policy even if this comes with costs and study how political and AI attitudes are associated with this trade-off evaluation. The analysis shows that EU-centrism is positively associated with support for AI sovereignty policy whereas positive attitudes toward AI and higher trust in US and Chinese tech companies show negative associations. The results have important consequences for the EU’s possibilities to garner public support for an AI sovereignty policy agenda.

articles.title: Citizen Trust in AI Regulatory Regimes in Four EU Countries
articles.authors: B.J.A. Leidorf-Tidå; Pascal König
articles.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) applications is deemed crucial for uptake of the technology and the development of an AI market. In the present article, we argue that the institutional design of regulatory regimes matters for whether citizens trust AI systems. We study how trust in AI systems depends on who the responsible regulator is, the scope of the regulator’s scrutiny of AI systems, and the involvement of external stakeholders in regulatory oversight. Based on a conjoint design, we examine how respondents value these institutional design choices for the case of high-risk AI systems used in health care. Using samples from Lithuania, Romania, Sweden, and the Netherlands, with 4001 respondents overall, the pre-registered experiment shows that citizens have more trust in AI systems if vendors, civil society and especially independent researchers are involved in oversight, and if regulators actively scrutinize AI systems rather than relying solely on self-reporting. At least in two countries, citizens also seem to have more trust in AI systems if the sectoral health care regulator is the responsible regulator instead of a cross-sectoral regulator such as the national Data Protection Authority or a specific AI regulator.

articles.title: Digital Civic Activism and Configurations of Social-Identity Factors: Protest Campaigns in Gaming Communities on Reddit
articles.authors: Gudzenko Vladislav; Anastasia Poretskova
articles.abstract:
This study examines the conditions associated with successful digital protest campaigns in online video-game consumer communities. The theoretical framework combines the Social Identity Model of Collective Action (SIMCA) with research on digital political consumerism. The analysis covers 20 campaigns coordinated on Reddit between 2019 and 2024 and includes five conditions: discursive indicators of collective efficacy (EFFIC), group identification (IDENT), and group-based anger (ANGER), as well as the share of new/low-karma accounts (ANON) and the concentration of activity among the most active participants (LEAD). The empirical corpus contains 312,816 comments; an additional 8,055 comments were manually coded for validation and comparison with automated annotation. Fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) is used to identify configurations associated with outcomes.
None of the five conditions is necessary for a concession by the campaign target. The parsimonious solution contains three alternative configurations, but the most robust result is the combination of high group-based anger and low concentration of activity among the most active participants (ANGER × ~LEAD). This path survives most sensitivity checks and indicates that concessions in this sample are associated with mass, emotionally salient, and relatively decentralized mobilization. At the same time, cases of intense mobilization without concessions show that community-level characteristics are insufficient to explain outcomes without considering the cost of concession, the type of demand, and the position of the target organization.
Artificial-intelligence tools were used in the research process and in preparing this manuscript. A pretrained CardiffNLP model was used for emotion classification; Gemini was used for automated EFFIC and IDENT annotation; Claude models assisted with the development and checking of replication code; and ChatGPT was used to translate the manuscript. The research question, case selection, operationalization, calibration decisions, result validation, and substantive interpretation were performed by the researcher.

articles.title: “It’s Hard to See It Through Clinical Eyes When It’s Yourself”:    General Practice and Community Healthcare Professionals’ Experiences of Domestic Abuse, Disclosure, & Help-Seeking
articles.authors: Sandi Dheensa; Rebecca Cox; Judith Worthington; Paula Whittaker; Gene Feder; Alison Gregory
articles.abstract:
Background
Domestic abuse is highly prevalent and causes wide-ranging harms. Healthcare professionals are especially likely to receive disclosures and international policies call for a robust healthcare response to abuse.  But the needs of affected healthcare professionals (HCPs) have been sidelined. Globally, 42% of female HCPs report lifetime experience of domestic abuse. Our study aimed to explore how experiencing domestic abuse affects HCPs to understand the safety and support interventions needed. 
Methods
We used semi-structured interviews with 18 National Health Service primary and community HCPs and used Framework Analysis, drawing on four interrelated concepts: problem recognition, stigma, candidacy, and professional identity.  
Results
Perpetrators used HCP-survivors’ roles against them and domestic abuse had wide-ranging consequences for work. Remaining themes mapped onto HCP-survivors’ trajectory towards support, including problems with recognising and/or naming domestic abuse, the impact of recognising and naming it, reflections on different support options, consequences of workplace disclosure, support experiences, and reflections on what needs to change. Professional identity and profession-related factors affected each aspect of this trajectory, delaying recognition of domestic abuse and making help-seeking and positive support experiences less likely.  
Conclusion
Building an effective and compassionate healthcare response to domestic abuse will be impossible without attending to HCP-survivors’ needs and the inadequate responses of fellow HCPs. HCP-survivors are likely assets in improving responses to patients, colleagues, and students; but without support may experience trauma symptoms. We recommend improved first-line responses to HCP-survivors in workplaces and a move towards a recognition of HCPs as potential survivors in domestic abuse education, funding, and interventions.

articles.title: The distinctive nature of non-partisanship: How independents pursue and prioritize political information
articles.authors: Stuart Perrett; Delia Baldassarri
articles.abstract: The two major parties present American voters with increasingly stark electoral alternatives. How do independents make political decisions in this era of heightened partisanship? Prevailing accounts portray independents either as inattentive, low-information voters or as "undercover" partisans whose behavior mirrors that of Democrats and Republicans. We challenge both characterizations. Drawing on novel survey experiments, we compare the information-seeking behavior of independents and partisans by examining the importance they attach to different candidate attributes and the quantity of information they seek before choosing between candidates. We find that independents and partisans rank candidate attributes in similar ways, with both groups prioritizing issue positions over socio-demographic characteristics. Yet, independents rely less on candidate partisanship and acquire more information than partisans across a variety of hypothetical electoral conditions. These differences persist across levels of political knowledge, suggesting that independents and partisans use distinct decision rules when evaluating political candidates.

articles.title: Distributional Validity of a Korean Synthetic Persona Panel: Evidence From the Korea Media Panel Survey
articles.authors: Howard Kim; Keun Tae Cho
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM) personas are proposed as survey respondents, yet validation outside English-speaking contexts is scarce. We evaluate how well a Korean synthetic persona panel used to condition Gemini 3.5 Flash and EXAONE reproduces digital and artificial intelligence (AI) service-use distributions of the Korea Media Panel Survey. About 8,000 personas per model answered eight service-use items and eight attitudinal constructs; responses were compared with weighted survey estimates. The overall mean absolute error (MAE) was 14-19 percentage points (pp), with binary item-mean correlations of 0.70-0.91 across waves. Segment error across five axes was 14-18 pp, with between-group signed-error ranges of 49.6/34.7 pp (Gemini/EXAONE; 39.5/31.2 without the non-comparable teen cells). Errors were model-specific: an age stereotype (Gemini) versus an acquiescence-consistent level bias (EXAONE). Generative-AI overestimation was consistent with temporal misalignment; short-form underestimation was framing-sensitive and persisted under randomized order (both shown for Gemini). Post-hoc holdout calibration on 30% of the real data, with the correction form selected inside the calibration set, cut cell MAE from 18.3/15.1 to 4.9/4.4 pp, yet direct estimation from that subsample was more accurate than the calibrated panel (3.6 pp), a synthetic-informed shrinkage estimator beat its real-only counterpart by at most 0.7 pp, and the correction did not transfer competitively across waves. The calibrated panel kept an advantage only below roughly 250-860 real responses (at most 2.3 pp over a real-only shrinkage estimator) or, for one model, on unobserved segments. In this setting, synthetic panels are not survey substitutes; their value is diagnostic.

articles.title: Beyond compensation: Climate politics, mobilization, and transformative statecraft
articles.authors: Benjamin Braun; Leah Downey
articles.abstract: Governments have pursued decarbonization through a combination of subsidies for capital and compensation for people. Political scientists have identified the compensation of those who incur losses from climate policies as the the central challenge in building green coalitions and achieving a just transition. However, a decarbonization path aimed at limiting global warming to 2 degrees Celsius entails transformative change for virtually everyone. We argue that, under such conditions, a compensation-based approach reduces green backlash to pocketbook concerns; citizens to bundles of fixed preferences; and evaluation to policy-by-policy assessment. Proposing to move beyond compensating existing preferences, we contend that transformative statecraft reshapes preferences through political mobilization. From this perspective, a technocratic approach—focused on calculation and compensation—constitutes a binding constraint on green statecraft. We defend this mobilization-based approach against the objections of manipulation and deprivation of freedom and suggest that a democratic version of transformative statecraft is possible.

articles.title: Language Replacement and Individualism: Linguicide as a Measurable Cultural Variable
articles.authors: Isha Sarah Snow
articles.abstract: Cross-cultural research has linked grammatical features, especially the obligatory use of subject pronouns, to national individualism, but such links are hard to separate from language family, wealth and history. This study treats colonial language replacement as a measurable variable and asks whether colonized countries whose majority home language became a European colonizer's language are more individualist than colonized countries that kept their own. Using a 55-country dataset and a validated individualism index (Akaliyski et al., 2025), I compare 10 replaced-language and 9 retained-language countries, controlling for GDP and diagnostic infrastructure. Replacement was associated with 12.1 points higher individualism (95% CI [8.0, 16.2]). The association was larger where English, which requires overt subject pronouns, did the replacing (17.5 points) than where Spanish or Portuguese, which allow pronoun drop, did so (11.4 points), though the difference between the two was not statistically significant (p = .10). The replacement association persisted when census-based settler population share was controlled, and settler share showed no independent association. This test rests largely on a single case: Ireland, where the population remained and the language shifted, scored with the English-speaking settler states. Within Ireland (N = 3,057), residents of areas where more Irish was spoken in 1911 placed less weight on self-direction values today, while present-day daily use of Irish showed no association. Within Latin America, Indigenous language retention was inversely associated with individualism, but this could not be separated from national wealth. Replacement was not associated with autism prevalence once diagnostic capacity was controlled. I argue that language replacement offers a direct, measurable proxy for linguicide and a route for testing claims about language and selfhood.

articles_hidden.title: From Public Dominance to Private Expansion: Changes in Hospital Infrastructure in Spain (1986–2018)
articles_hidden.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez; Margarita Vega-Rapún
articles_hidden.abstract: In many countries, the growth of the private hospital sector coincides with a decline in beds per inhabitant. Spain is no exception, showing one of the lowest relative bed provisions in the EU. This study offers an exploratory analysis of the evolution of private hospital bed provision in Spain and its Autonomous Communities between 1986 and 2018. Using historical hospital catalogs from the Ministry of Health, we conducted graphical and cluster analyses to examine trends and classify regions by the share of private hospital beds. Results indicate a national trend toward fewer beds and a growing presence of the private, mainly for-profit, sector, with notable regional differences such as the Catalan model. This research provides comparative and long-term evidence on structural changes in Spain’s hospital system.

articles_hidden.title: Using large-scale supermarket transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases. Policy Insights from the FIO Food Project.
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Wilkins; Mark Alan Green; Mark S Gilthorpe; Alice Rose Kininmonth; Alexandra Johnstone; Michelle Morris
articles_hidden.abstract: A policy brief summarising recommendations for policy from FIO Food work package 2, which uses large-scale retail transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases.

articles_hidden.title: Occupational class inequality in non-monetary job quality in Europe, 1995-2024
articles_hidden.authors: Edvin Syk
articles_hidden.abstract:
Occupational class is central to research on inequality, but we have limited knowledge about how it structures non-monetary job quality across countries and over time. 
We examine four dimensions of job quality—autonomy, physical working conditions, work intensity, and work time quality—across eight occupational classes in 14 European countries from 1995 to 2024, using the European Working Conditions Survey. 
We compare class profiles over time, decompose variation into within- and between-class components, and benchmark occupational class against country, country-year, and income. 
Most variation in job quality is within occupational classes, but gradients remain pronounced for physical working conditions and autonomy, while work intensity is only weakly structured by class. Cross-national differences are modest on average but substantially larger among lower-skill than higher-skill classes. 
Occupational class thus remains an important source of inequality in some dimensions of job quality, but captures only part of the broader variation in working conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Attribute Relevance in Conjoint Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Stoetzer; Asya Magazinnik
articles_hidden.abstract: Researchers often rely on conjoint analysis to understand which attributes drive respondents' decisionmaking, yet standard estimands are not designed to measure attribute relevance. We introduce a novel approach to measuring attribute relevance in conjoint analysis by drawing on causal attribution methods. Our proposed estimand, the average probability of necessary and sufficient causation (APNS), captures the probability that swapping two profiles' levels on an attribute would change a respondent's choice. We establish nonparametric identification under assumptions related to preference heterogeneity, and provide simple difference-in-means estimators that can be applied to existing conjoint data structures. Two empirical applications illustrate the method. A candidate choice experiment in Germany reveals significant preference heterogeneity that leads standard estimands to mask relevance, while under the right assumptions the APNS recovers it. By contrast, in a replication of a prominent refugee experiment, we find that assuming preference homogeneity is unproblematic for many attributes of asylum-seekers.

articles_hidden.title: Using large-scale supermarket transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases. Policy Insights from the FIO Food Project.
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Wilkins; Mark Alan Green; Mark S Gilthorpe; Alice Rose Kininmonth; Alexandra Johnstone; Michelle Morris
articles_hidden.abstract: A policy brief summarising recommendations for policy from FIO Food work package 2, which uses large-scale retail transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases.

articles_hidden.title: An age-old advantage: Evidence for a consistent survival advantage for children of long-lived parents in Sweden 1880-2022
articles_hidden.authors: Ingrid K van Dijk; Niels van den Berg
articles_hidden.abstract: The average lifespan has increased strongly in the past decades, but not everyone has benefited equally. Establishing the degree of intergenerational persistence of survival generates insights into broad inequalities between individuals and families in their likelihood to live to high ages. Using established register-type data for two regions in Northern and Southern Sweden 1880-2022 linked to historical records, we show that even before the rise of the modern social gradient in health in the 1960ies, mortality is lower among descendants from long-lived parents (top survivors of their birth cohort). This shared survival advantage between parents and children persists over time even after considering SES. Mortality among the descendants of top survivors is lower in lifestyle-related causes of death, suggesting that behavioral factors could be a significant factor in explaining the survival advantage. Overall, we find that mortality concentrates in families in patterns that go beyond the influence of SES alone. Similarities between relatives in health and mortality therefore provide an important lens into inequalities in survival and health over time.

articles_hidden.title: BirthClim_IT: A Harmonized Municipality-Level Dataset on Fertility,  Environment, and Territorial Contexts in Italy, 2003–2022
articles_hidden.authors: Chiara Baldan; Anna Giraldo
articles_hidden.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Environmental conditions and climate change, alongside spatial heterogeneity in fertility, have received increasing attention in fertility research. However, research combining these perspectives remains limited, partly due to the lack of data linking fine spatial resolution with detailed demographic, environmental, and socioeconomic information. This is particularly relevant in Italy, where substantial spatial variation in fertility coexists with heterogeneous environmental conditions.
OBJECTIVE
This paper introduces BirthClim_IT, a harmonized longitudinal dataset designed to support research on fertility and its environmental and territorial contexts across Italian municipalities. The dataset description is accompanied by two empirical applications illustrating its use.
METHODS
The BirthClim_IT dataset combines monthly demographic information with environmental, climatic, geographic, and socioeconomic indicators for 7,896 Italian municipalities from January 2003 to December 2022. The dataset contains 126 variables, harmonized to the administrative boundaries in force on January 1, 2024. To address sparsity in monthly birth counts, we also provide a spatially aggregated version comprising 4,936 spatial units and a customizable aggregation procedure. 
RESULTS
The dataset provides both municipality-level and aggregated data, allowing fertility patterns to be examined jointly across space and time. The two descriptive applications illustrate its use in identifying distinct environmental profiles across Italian municipalities and in examining seasonal variation in fertility and environmental conditions.
CONTRIBUTION
Given the growing interest in environmental dimensions of fertility and increasing attention to the spatial dimension of demographic processes, BirthClim_IT provides a new and flexible resource combining fine spatial and temporal resolution with information spanning multiple dimensions of the demographic, environmental, and socioeconomic context.

articles_hidden.title: Survivors' Perspectives and Experiences of Intimate Partner Violence Perpetrator Intervention Programs and Associated Services: A Qualitative Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Alison Stafford; Chae Rose
articles_hidden.abstract:
This qualitative systematic review synthesises survivors’ perspectives of intimate partner 
violence perpetrator interventions and associated support services. Specifically, it examines 
how different relationship structures, such as intact, co-parenting, or separated 
arrangements, shape these experiences and determines which program features are 
perceived as supporting or compromising safety. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 
electronic databases were searched for peer-reviewed literature published after 1 July 2016. 
Although 13 studies met the initial inclusion criteria for descriptive mapping, the final 
thematic synthesis integrated 11 primary sources containing the specific contextual data 
required for qualitative analysis. The analysis generated three main analytical themes: the 
intervention environment, perpetrator behaviour patterns, and the survivors’ processing 
journey. Findings indicate that relationship structures influence how survivors experience 
these interventions. While individuals navigating ongoing contact or reconciliation attempts 
often report transactional partner compliance driven by child-access pressures or relationship 
motivations, those seeking complete separation report an environment of persistent 
hypervigilance. Survivors report that specialised advocacy and literacy provided by partner 
contact services support safety by deconstructing mutual-blame frameworks and shifting self
blame. Conversely, interventions are perceived as compromising safety when they rely on 
isolated compliance checks and operate separately from substance use and mental health 
services, creating a false impression of behavioural change. Ultimately, the qualitative 
evidence indicates that measuring progress through mere attendance alone provides a 
misleading indicator of risk, suggesting that future policy should prioritise coordinated 
communication across sectors and elevate survivor-defined safety as the key indicator of 
program success.

articles_hidden.title: Social media and the prevention or reduction of harmful gambling: a rapid evidence review with integrated lived experience
articles_hidden.authors: Jenny Sweetman; Liz Littlewood; Patricia Darcy; Greg Forshaw; Amanda Perry; su golder
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and aims: Research has established a clear link between social media use and harmful gambling. Existing systematic reviews highlight how social media platforms enable and normalise gambling. This rapid evidence review aimed to identify interventions using social media to prevent or reduce harmful gambling. 

Methods: Searches were conducted (January 2026) in MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO. Searches of grey literature searches, and backward and forward citations from included references, were also completed. Independent screening, data extraction and quality assessment was undertaken by two independent reviewers. Data were analysed using narrative synthesis methods. An expert by experience group directly informed each stage of the review process.

Results: From 1138 unique records, 10 studies met our inclusion criteria (2 randomised controlled trials, 2 cohort studies, 2 mixed methods studies and 4 qualitative studies). Included studies focused on brief messages, the impact of a social media platform outage, and the use of gambling support forums. Findings highlighted the benefits and potential risks of implementing gambling harm reduction strategies on social media, the role of interaction with others, and opportunities to use social media to better understand the process of recovery from problem gambling.

Discussion and Conclusions: There is some evidence that social media platforms could usefully support the reduction or prevention of harmful gambling. Further research is required, co-designed by those with lived experience to optimise engagement and impact, to better understand how online interventions can support different people and to assess the effectiveness through large high-quality randomised controlled trials.

articles_hidden.title: The Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies (DWRAP): de jure asylum policy for 205 countries, 1951-2022
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher W. Blair; Guy Grossman; Jeremy Weinstein
articles_hidden.abstract: More than two-thirds of the world's refugees and asylum-seekers are hosted in the developing world, yet the national laws governing their reception have never been measured comprehensively across countries or over time. We introduce the Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies (DWRAP), the most expansive coding of de jure asylum and refugee policy assembled to date. DWRAP records every national law pertinent to forcibly displaced populations in 205 countries from 1951 to 2022---951 legal instruments in all. From the text of each law, we hand-code 54 policy provisions, which we aggregate into 14 strands, five fields---access, services, livelihoods, movement, and participation---and a single index of policy liberality, released in three aggregation forms. The result is a country-year panel of 11,484 observations measuring displacement-policy liberality within and across countries over seven decades. Together, these data open the causes and consequences of refugee-policy change to global, historical analysis. They measure law rather than its enforcement---and so make the distance between the two visible and measurable.

articles_hidden.title: Resilience through Pathway Specificity for Managing Climate Shocks. A Review of Evidence from East Africa.
articles_hidden.authors: Mohamed Abdirahman Ibrahim
articles_hidden.abstract:
The study systematically reviews and synthesizes 74 empirical studies from East Africa, covering Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, and Somaliland. Using study-level, asset-based thresholds and other complementary indicators, the findings identify that household resilience is non-linear and requires targeted, specific programming. The Pathway-Specific Resilience Framework (PSRF), which the paper validates, divides the target populations into two groups: a resource-deficient group that needs asset assistance and external safety nets (socially supported livelihood resilience pathway) and an asset-based cohort that prioritizes asset protection and market-based interventions. The study found that households with constrained resources face limitations in asset accumulation, which leave them more vulnerable to persistent poverty traps. PSRF proposes poverty graduation that balances immediate protection with long-term resilience through a sequence of protocols. The first “Protocol “A” protects resource-poor (Socially supported pathway) households to prioritize consumption, direct transfers (e.g., assets), and human capital. Once households transition to “Protocol B”, the shift is from survival assistance to access to market, finance, and index-based insurance. Additionally, the PSRF integrates other cross-cutting measures to sustain immediate gains from the protocols and prevent relapses brought by climate shocks. These include basic infrastructure like access to water, healthcare, and education; Connectivity and information such as early warning systems, transport, telecommunications, and adaptation measures including climate-smart technologies. 
Key words: Pathway-Specific Resilience Framework (PSRF), Drought resilience, livelihood pathways, Social protection, East Africa

articles_hidden.title: Gene-Environment Interactions: Reconciling Scarr-Rowe and Compensatory Advantage Hypotheses
articles_hidden.authors: Sonia Petrini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Note: Version 3 adds a simulation benchmark accounting for SES differences in completion rates. Versions 1 ans 2 interpreted SES gaps in over- and underachievement as support for both the compensation and Scarr–Rowe hypotheses; this version shows that, with few exceptions, these gaps can be explained by baseline differences in completion rates alone.

Research on gene–environment interactions in education focuses on two main hypotheses: compensatory advantage, where genetic disadvantage is less consequential in resource-rich environments; and Scarr–Rowe hypothesis, where resource-rich environments reinforce ge- netic advantage. Although regression approaches frame these as mutually exclusive, the hypotheses concern differences at the extremes of the genetic distribution, as measured by a polygenic index (PGI). Compensation and reinforcing dynamics are here mapped to socioeconomic (SES) differences in the rate of overachievers (low-PGI individuals who at- tain a degree) and underachievers (high-PGI individuals who do not).
